It corrects corruption of a single Q-table copy, but inputs shared by the copies, such as the reward, and the voting code itself remain outside its protection. The analysis extends to Linear and Deep Q-Learning, where faults corrupt stored weights during learning and change actions during inference. Moving beyond benchmark environments, this work evaluates an online traffic light controller in a microscopic traffic simulator, where a single injected infinite value degrades accumulated vehicle waiting time by 148x while corrupting under 4% of the Q-table, and where triple modular redundancy corrected the faults injected in our tests, although glitching could still halt the device. Altogether, this work provides a basis for understanding and securing RL deployments against fault injection attacks.
papers.authors: Tom Slooff, Anthony Etim, Jiaqi Yu, Francesco Regazzoni, Jakub Szefer

papers.title: CoordX Types: A Trustless, Swappable Type System for Shared Records
papers.abstract: The CoordX Protocol carries signed and encrypted entries between parties. It proves who wrote each entry and who had permission to write it. It does not say what an entry means. That task belongs above the protocol layer. This paper describes the CoordX type system, the layer that gives entries a meaning. A type is a short document that says how to read one part of a shared record: which entries count, what each position means, what a party may do there, and what a party must do next. The type system has two key properties. It is trustless: a type is an ordinary signed object fixed by its digest, and every party evaluates it for itself over entries that the CoordX Protocol has already verified. No party has to trust a server, a registry or another party's software. It is swappable: a type names the interpreter it is written for, so many interpreters, of different capabilities and designs, can be used side by side in one record. We describe how to write type schemas, and we define the expressive power of the schema language. Payloads form a regular language. Entry structure forms a regular tree language. Every rule and every computed value is a total function in the primitive recursive class, so evaluation always halts. We compare this with KQML, FIPA-ACL and CBCL, and we relate it to language-theoretic security.
papers.authors: David Hyland-Wood, Rob Ewin

papers.title: Low Probability of Target Detection in Wireless Sensing by Harnessing Reconfigurable-antenna based Reflectors
papers.abstract: In this paper, we introduce low probability of target detection (LPTD) as a new security objective for wireless sensing systems, where the existence of a target is concealed from passive wardens. Unlike conventional communication security and covert communication, LPTD aims to protect the sensed target itself from malicious detection, rather than concealing transmitted signals or communication activities. Specifically, we propose a reconfigurable-antenna-based reflector-assisted target covertness scheme, where passive reflectors deployed around the target are harnessed as artificial scattering sources to confuse the warden. By adjusting their reflection coefficients, these reflectors reshape the local scattering environment and mask the target-induced echo. We then analyze the warden's optimal detection strategy and derive the false-alarm and missed-detection probabilities, followed by a closed-form expression for its minimum total detection error probability. Numerical results validate the analysis and show that sufficient cooperation among reflectors can increase the warden's minimum total detection error probability to approximately 0.94--0.96, making target detection close to random guessing.
papers.authors: Yifan Zhang, Zhentian Zhang, Jantti Riku, Yichuan Wang, Xingwang Li, Tuo Wu

papers.title: Tokenized Reward Systems for Federated Learning: The Privacy vs. Fairness Tradeoff
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) systems increasingly rely on blockchain based reward mechanisms to incentivize participation while preserving data privacy. We design and empirically evaluate two complementary Solidity smart contracts for FL reward distribution: the first one that allocates rewards proportionally to a publicly disclosed quality score, and a privacy preserving variant that hides individual quality scores behind a zero-knowledge (ZK) proof of a threshold condition. Both contracts mint a non transferable, use-and-burn token maintaining a trustless incentive structure. We evaluate the two designs through MNIST training with adversarial behavior, including Sybil attacks, zero gradient and random noise, across three independent random seeds. Our results reveal a fundamental tradeoff between cryptographic privacy and incentive fairness. The privacy preserving architecture strictly degrades system robustness, doubling the adversary's average reward capture while introducing severe outcome variance. This vulnerability is driven by a structural self-inclusion bias within cosine-similarity scoring: as the global model converges, legitimate gradient updates naturally diminish, rendering them statistically indistinguishable from bounded noise. Adversaries exploit this dynamic to systematically breach the ZK threshold, triggering a late stage failure cascade that culminates in absolute adversary monopoly over the reward pool and the total exclusion of honest contributors. Alongside a closed-form theorem formalizing this privacy--Sybil resistance tradeoff, we map strict mainnet deployment boundaries via linear gas scaling models, explicitly incorporating the post-Fusaka EIP-7825 per transaction gas cap. Ultimately, while cryptographically secure, static threshold ZK gates fail as incentive layer fairness mechanisms under realistic FL convergence dynamics on standard benchmarks.
papers.authors: Andreas Sendros, Nikolaos Pavlidis, Vasilios Perifanis, Pavlos S. Efraimidis

papers.title: Privacy Leakage from Recurrent State in LLM Inference
papers.abstract: Personalized LLM services place private facts and application instructions into a prompt, then retain representations of that context for later inference. Latent-state LLMs compress part of this history into fixed-size recurrent state. The information preserved by its learned updates is implicit, and later computation can expose it even when an observer receives neither the private text nor the responses. We investigate privacy leakage from recurrent state through partial-state probing and physical observation of its use. Our methodology separates recoverable information, persistence through public dialogue, causal influence on later decisions, and leakage through power. Experiments with released hybrid implementations show that a small state observation supports multiple predictions about private facts and response rules, and that personal attributes generalize to unseen authors. The information remains inferable after public dialogue and changes later decision margins. Complete-read power recovers private facts under a fixed execution schedule. On a partitioned GPU, an unprivileged account infers age from whole-device power during public requests; a separate state-isolation experiment establishes the recurrent contribution to this channel. These findings extend context confidentiality to the lifetime and execution of retained state. They identify access-control responsibilities for serving systems, telemetry restrictions for GPU operators, and data-dependent power leakage for accelerator designers.
papers.authors: Weimin Fu, Shikun Liu, Qiying Li, Yuntao Liu, Pan Li, Xiaolong Guo

papers.title: The Price of Geometry for Private Distance-Sensitive Filters: $\ell_\infty$ versus $\ell_2$
papers.abstract: A distance-sensitive set representation stores a set $S$ in a metric space and must accept points within distance $r$ of $S$ and reject points farther than $cr$, each with error probability at most $\alpha$. Under differential privacy, even exact membership costs a privacy loss of $\ln(1/\alpha)$; we ask how much \emph{more} the geometry of the space forces. Earlier lower bounds cover only restricted mechanisms, such as partition-based ones or those whose outputs contain no scattered false positives (``dust''). We prove lower bounds for every mechanism. In $\ell_\infty^d$ with $c<3$ the extra cost is $\Theta_c(d)$, which proves a recent conjecture in this range; when $\lfloor cr\rfloor-r+1$ divides $2r$, a randomly shifted grid is optimal up to $\tilde O(\alpha)$ per dimension. In $\ell_2^d$ the extra cost is instead $\Theta_c(\min(d,\ln(1/\alpha)))$: a new mechanism that outputs a single very large ball shows that dimensions beyond about $\ln(1/\alpha)$ are free, so partition-based constructions are optimal in $\ell_\infty$ but not in $\ell_2$. The same arguments bound the space of every correct representation of $k$-sets, private or not: $\Omega(k(\log(1/\alpha)+d))$ bits in $\ell_\infty^d$ with $c<3$, and $\Omega_c(k(\log(1/\alpha)+\min(d,\log(1/\alpha))))$ bits in every $\ell_p^d$.
papers.authors: Paul Cesaretti

papers.title: SoK: Design Choices in Tendermint BFT Consensus
papers.abstract: Tendermint is a consensus protocol that tolerates Byzantine faults, implemented first by the Tendermint Core engine and now by CometBFT. Realizing the protocol's separation of agreement from execution, the Application Blockchain Interface (ABCI) of these engines keeps consensus apart from the replicated application, so one engine can serve many independent proof-of-stake chains. A sustained body of research proposes changes that span the protocol's mechanisms, from vote dissemination to block proposal and reward distribution, yet to our knowledge no survey studies the protocol and these works as one family, and broader surveys do not take Tendermint as their subject. We describe the baseline, the protocol as consolidated from its original descriptions, by its design choices. Each is a decision, such as how votes spread or how proposers rotate, through which the baseline provides safety and liveness or another property under its fault and timing model. We classify each work by the design choice it renegotiates, that is, modifies or replaces, by the properties it strengthens or weakens, and by whether its result needs a stronger model. Taking a broader perspective on that classification, we group the surveyed works' solutions into a few threads of concern in the baseline, namely its performance, the accountability of its validators, and the protection of exploitable information. For each thread, we identify the recurring strategies that their approaches follow. Together, these threads and strategies describe the current state of research on the Tendermint family. Where the strategies leave gaps, we pose future directions, each as an open question under an explicit fault and timing model.
papers.authors: Sanaz Taheri-Boshrooyeh, Yahya Hassanzadeh-Nazarabadi

papers.title: Bulletproofs are Optimal: Lower Bounds for Vector Commitments from Fiat-Shamir in Pairing-Free Groups
papers.abstract: Vector Commitments allow parties to commit to an (ordered) vector and to later succinctly open it at any desired position. In plain (i.e., known order and pairing-free) prime-order groups, all state-of-the-art constructions rely on the combination of a generalized Pedersen commitment and an inner product argument. This includes the celebrated constructions of Bootle et al. (EUROCRYPT 2016) and Bünz et al. (S&P 2018), and subsequent improvements. All of these achieve proofs consisting of $\Theta(\log n)$ group elements, and further provide useful properties including malleability, subvector opening and transparent setup. However, breaking the $O(\log n)$ barrier in the plain discrete logarithm setting has proven to be a hard problem. This is in stark contrast with other settings, e.g. from pairing-friendly groups or groups of unknown order, where constructions with constant-size commitment and openings have been known for over a decade. In this work we investigate whether this limitation is inherent to constructions based on prime-order groups. Specifically we prove new lower bounds for any accumulator (a weaker object than vector commitments, thus making our result more general), with interactive public-coin membership proof in Maurer's Generic Group Model. An implication of our result is that in such setting at least one of the following must occur: (i) the commitment has super-constant size; (ii) the opening proof contains $\Omega(\log n)$ group elements; (iii) the opening proof has length $n^{1-o(1)}$. Our bound further extends to primitives that directly imply accumulators/VCs including polynomial/functional commitments and inner product arguments.
papers.authors: Marian Dietz, Emanuele Giunta

papers.title: Collision Attacks on SHA-2: 39-Step SHA-256 below the Birthday Bound
papers.abstract: SHA-2 is the most widely deployed family of hash functions, and its security margin is measured by the number of steps collision attacks reach. Li et al. gave the first classical collision attack on 38-step SHA-256, with an estimated complexity of $2^{104.3}$. The challenge is to extend the attack to more steps while retaining its advantage over generic collision search. In this paper, we show that collisions for 39-step SHA-256 can be found at an estimated cost below the $2^{128}$ birthday bound. We keep the published 39-step characteristic and change how its conditions are satisfied. We introduce joint message-word pinning, a technique that fixes two expanded message words, $W_{16}$ and $W_{17}$, to the values prescribed by the characteristic. For each chaining value, we solve for assignments to two state words that carry no direct condition, and every assignment returned gives both message words their prescribed values. To find these assignments, we first fix the value of a function with a small image and then solve the coupled equations for $W_{16}$ and $W_{17}$ in sequence. On 39-step SHA-256, pinning $W_{16}$ alone gives an estimated cost of $2^{123.4}$ scalar compressions per expected collision, and pinning both words reduces it by 14.6 bits to $2^{108.8}$. Under the uniform-chaining-value model, the measured probabilities and the cost of processing one first block give an upper bound of approximately $2^{124.6}$ on the expected cost of finding the first collision, even under worst-case clustering. For 38-step SHA-256, we reduce the estimated cost per expected collision from $2^{104.3}$ to $2^{90.9}$ by using a new differential characteristic and pinning $W_{16}$ alone. On SHA-512, pinning $W_{16}$ alone reduces this cost from $2^{125.4}$ to $2^{100.7}$ for 38 steps and from $2^{178}$ to $2^{131.3}$ for 39 steps.
papers.authors: Jiaying Gong, Yongzhuang Wei, Fengrong Zhang, Bohua Wei

papers.title: One Fabrication Is Enough: A Fake News Article Changes the Forecasts of LLM Forecasting Systems
papers.abstract: LLMs are increasingly used for forecasting, and the best forecasting systems retrieve news as evidence to strengthen their predictions. This also opens them to attack. We study the weakest attacker of this kind, who knows only the forecasting question and publishes fabricated news articles, with no access to the model, the retriever or its queries. We evaluate how far this attack reaches on stock questions and real prediction-market questions. Once the article is in the model's context, it reverses 74% to 82% of the forecasts that opposed it, on every frontier model we tested. The model cannot verify the fabrication and follows it anyway. Retrieval is the attack's entry point, and the systems built to retrieve well are the most exposed: the architectures of two leading deployed forecasting systems, whose agents search for every related article, retrieve the fabricated one in about 90% of runs. Accuracy cannot reveal this harm: the attacked forecaster is right when the attacker's direction turns out right and wrong otherwise, so its average accuracy barely changes while its forecasts follow the attacker's guess. We also propose a second attacker, who publishes two articles that argue opposite directions to make the forecaster unsure. The model does not hedge; it returns a confident forecast in a direction the attacker no longer controls. We then evaluate the two strongest published retrieval-time defenses, passage filtering and partitioned retrieval. Each stops the one-article attack but is bypassed by a one-prompt change to the attack. Together they stop both bypasses at four articles, but sixteen distorted copies beat them, and they change 29% of clean decisions and discard 39% of the genuine news. Partitioned retrieval also requires control of the retrieval index. Systems that search the open web have no such control and are left with the filter alone. For them, the attack still works.
papers.authors: Zeyu Zhang, Bradly C. Stadie

papers.title: obfsgen: Generative Tunnel Obfuscation
papers.abstract: Encrypted tunnels are widely used to circumvent censorship, which has drawn censors' efforts to detect and block them. As the circumvention tunnels in widest use have largely converged on TLS, detection has shifted from the content of their traffic to its shape, where recent research and real-world blocking events have revealed exploitable fingerprints of tunneling. Existing traffic-shaping obfuscators such as obfs4, however, are fundamentally limited in hiding these fingerprints, as their application-driven design can only add to the shape that the application creates. A schedule-driven obfuscator, which decides when and how much to send independently of the application, can give tunnels any shape but raises new challenges, first and foremost what a good shape is. This paper presents obfsgen, a schedule-driven obfuscator for tunneling traffic. obfsgen samples its schedule from a generative sequence model of normal traffic, which predicts the future shape of a flow from its whole history, to capture the long-range dependencies that make a flow's shape normal. Built around this model, obfsgen addresses system problems that such an obfuscator faces in practice, such as synchronization across a noisy network. We evaluate the (in)distinguishability that obfsgen offers, the performance overhead that it adds and the computational resources that it requires. We see the schedule-driven architecture as the next generation of tunnel obfuscators, and we hope that obfsgen and the rationale behind its design help make such obfuscators practical and deployable.
papers.authors: Kaidong Wu, Wentao Du, Shinan Liu, Diwen Xue

papers.title: Protecting Sensitive Knowledge Under LLM Unlearning: The Proxy Threat and a Superposition-Aware Defense
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning lets the owner of large language models (LLMs) remove specific entities from a trained model without retraining from scratch. Existing machine unlearning methods focus on removing the requested entities while maintaining utility. However, we observe that the representations of distinct entities in an LLM may overlap in shared parameter subspaces, a phenomenon known as knowledge superposition. Removing one entity may then affect other entities. This exposes a new security threat: legitimate unlearning requests can be exploited to remove sensitive entities that were never requested. This threat is unlike data poisoning or backdoor attacks. We define the attack as the Proxy Unlearning Attack (PUA), which selects removable proxy entities superposed with a sensitive target. The attack can even occur unintentionally, when benign users accidentally remove entities superposed with a sensitive one. In response, we propose Superposition-Aware Unlearning Protection (SAUP), a general defense framework that can be applied to unlearning requests to ensure a correct removal. SAUP performs in two stages. Before unlearning, it uses superposition detection to estimate which sensitive entities the request puts at risk. After unlearning, it decouples the shared representations and restores the affected entities, while keeping the requested entities suppressed. Our findings reveal that legitimate unlearning requests can be maliciously exploited through knowledge superposition. When dealing with unlearning requests, LLM providers need representation-level detection and recovery mechanisms to mitigate this threat and protect sensitive knowledge.
papers.authors: Jiayang Li, Tianqing Zhu, Longxiang Gao, Huajie Chen, Dayong Ye, Shang Wang, Huan Huo, Wanlei Zhou

papers.title: Poison-then-Hide: Finetuning-Activated Backdoor Attack on Pretrained Vision Encoders
papers.abstract: Backdoor attacks threaten the integrity of machine learning models by allowing attackers to control model behavior through triggers. Models can be compromised during finetuning by backdoor attacks through either poisoned data or adversarial training objectives. Because existing finetuning-activated attacks assume limited domain shift or frozen encoder layers, they often fail under full-model finetuning. We target a stealthy finetuning-activated attack where a dormant backdoor is implanted in a pretrained encoder, and later activated by finetuning on clean downstream data. We propose Poison-then-Hide, a novel attack that remains effective when the entire model is finetuned in a domain transfer. Our approach consists of three components: trigger optimization, base encoder poisoning, and targeted unlearning to conceal the backdoor. We evaluate our method on six datasets and three model architectures, and achieve state-of-the-art (up to 97%) attack success rates. We find that jointly learning the benign target task alongside the poisoning is critical to the attack's success. We demonstrate standard detection and mitigation defenses cannot fully remove the backdoor, which can reappear after benign finetuning.
papers.authors: Qixuan Jin, Abinitha Gourabathina, Vinith Menon Suriyakumar, Walter Gerych, Marzyeh Ghassemi

papers.title: When Safety Becomes an Attack Surface: Manipulating Abstention in Tool-Using AI Agents
papers.abstract: An AI agent's decision not to act can itself become an attack surface. We study warning-induced over-abstention, an availability attack in which adversaries place fabricated risk warnings in low-trust content to prevent legitimate task completion. Our central premise is that safe abstention requires evaluating both the claimed risk and the authority of the evidence supporting it. We develop controlled counterfactual task variants that vary risk content, source provenance, and warning wording, and evaluate a Verify-Before-Abstain protocol that corroborates warnings against authoritative records or the underlying content. Across three model families and 51 injectable AgentAbstain task pairs, caution-first prompting amplifies the attack. For Gemini, induced over-abstention rises from $9.8\%$ to $86.3\%$, despite unchanged clean-task completion. Matched wording comparisons further reveal sensitivity to warning language, with substantial variation across models and environments. Provenance-aware verification improves legitimate completion, while forgery and sensitive-content controls expose its dependence on authoritative evidence and its limitations in preserving confidentiality. These results motivate evaluating agent safety through the justification for restraint, alongside the safety of actions taken.
papers.authors: Charles Xiao

papers.title: What Does an RF Fingerprint Identify? A Cross-Corpus Evaluation of Hardware-Family-Associated and Unit-Level Signal
papers.abstract: RF fingerprinting benchmarks report how well a classifier separates transmitters, not whether that separability reflects the individual unit or its hardware family. We compare a benchmark's real hardware grouping with size-matched random groupings of the same devices, using calibrated, unclipped variational lower bounds under label-blind, device-level cross-fitting on devices never seen in training. On WiSig (OFDM Wi-Fi), the generation grouping exceeded all 999 matched random groupings (permutation p = 0.001, the resolution floor), although no grouping attained a positive certified bound, and the direction survives removing channel equalization. A preregistered replication on a LoRa corpus (chirp spread spectrum, three hardware models), with a front-end frozen on synthetic data, again exceeded all 999 (p = 0.001), and two sensitivity analyses judged by a reversal rule fixed in advance did not reverse the direction. This is a directional replication only: the excess magnitude reflects a miscalibrated null, the chain-rule decomposition leaves a residual of +0.296 bits, and capture order is undocumented. In a same-model corpus of 122 ESP32 radios, a temperature-calibrated held-out bound of +3.338 bits (label entropy 6.931 bits) indicates substantial device-specific identity, not separable from per-device capture-session effects; relying on the calibrated bound was decided after the uncalibrated bound changed sign. On synthetic transmitters a high-capacity convolutional decoder reaches 98.5% of a known 6-bit ceiling, and the audit protocol leaves chain-rule residuals of +0.072 bits (synthetic, fixed physical features) and +0.060 bits (WiSig, audit features). Two further corpora were excluded by preregistered ingest gates. Across WiSig and LoRa, hardware-family groupings consistently produced stronger identity-associated signal than size-matched random groupings.
papers.authors: Hyojung Han

papers.title: OverServe: Resource Amplification Attacks on SaaS Agents via Tool--Prompt Co-Design
papers.abstract: Advances in large language models (LLMs) are enabling software-as-a-service (SaaS) providers to automate longer business workflows with agents. In subscription-based SaaS deployments, model and tool calls consume provider resources without additional customer payments. Because the agent autonomously decides when to stop, a malicious tenant can send a prompt to the agent, exploiting its completion decisions to extend execution and waste provider resources. In this paper, we present OverServe, a multi-agent framework for constructing such attacks against SaaS agents. OverServe co-designs Model Context Protocol (MCP) status tools and completion-confirmation prompts for the attacker. Each tool call returns accurate status and terminates normally, yet the agent may repeatedly check an unfinished condition to satisfy the prompt. This consumes the SaaS provider's resources even after the original business task is completed. OverServe constructs service-specific tool--prompt pairs and uses separate tool and prompt reviews to guide candidate pair selection. Tested tool specifications trigger no alerts in the evaluated MCP scanners. We evaluate Qwen, Nemotron, DeepSeek, and Sonnet on selected tasks from nine benchmarks. All OverServe runs pass the original task checks. OverServe can reach a maximal amplification of API requests by $93.88\times$ while preserving the original task goal and collateral checks.
papers.authors: Ruiheng Yu, Oteo Mamo, Siyu Gan, Weikuan Yu, Mulong Luo

papers.title: An improvement to the KLPT2 algorithm
papers.abstract: In this short note, we present a tweak to the KLPT2 algorithm that reduces the size of the output from $O(p^{15.5})$ to $\tilde O(p^{14.5})$.Then, we show that the recent improvement by Nakagawa, Yoshizumi and Onuki to the KLPT algorithm is compatible with the Hermitian module splitting approach, further lowering the reduced degree bound to $\tilde O(p^{14})$.
papers.authors: Abel Laval

papers.title: Delegatable Keyed-Verification Anonymous Credentials
papers.abstract: Keyed-verification anonymous credentials (KVACs) are a variant of anonymous credentials (ACs) in which the issuer and the verifier are either the same entity or mutually trusted entities. Due to this design, KVACs can avoid some of the practical burdens of publicly verifiable ACs, such as requiring bilinear pairings, making them more practical in certain settings. Delegation of credentials is a powerful feature that enables applications where users, holding a credential, can delegate a restricted version of their credential to another user. This paper proposes the first delegatable keyed-verification anonymous credentials (DKVAC). We provide formal definitions of DKVAC, we design two pairing-free DKVAC constructions with delegation capability, we prove them secure, and we demonstrate their practicality with implementation benchmarks. Our two constructions present trade-offs between expressiveness and performance.
papers.authors: Omid Mirzamohammadi, Varesh Mishra, Jan Bobolz, Emad Heydari Beni, Aysajan Abidin, Dave Singelée, Bart Preneel

papers.title: When Evaluators of AI Agents Disagree: An Empirical Study of Native Scoring, LLM Judges, and Commit-Boundary Checks on tau2-bench
papers.abstract: Agentic workflows, in which a large language model (LLM) calls tools to read and write data, are evaluated in two ways. Benchmarks compare the final state against a gold answer. Deployed services have none; an LLM judge reads the transcript and decides. Practice treats the two as interchangeable. This paper measures whether they are. We ran 2,160 episodes in tau2-bench's airline and retail domains and recorded every database write. We scored each episode four ways: native scoring against gold state, an LLM judge, that judge given the policy document, and the boundary evaluator, a minimal rule-based check of whether a write was expected against whether one occurred in the trace. Two annotators independently labeled 120 episodes for task correctness, policy compliance, and commitment correctness. The judge repeated its verdict 98.2% of the time but agreed with native scoring on 56.2%. In 11 episodes the agent executed a forbidden write. The judge passed 10 to 11, with or without the policy or transcript. A stronger judge still passed 6. The boundary evaluator, with no model call, caught all 11; no judge significantly exceeded it on human labels. Forbidden writes occurred in 11.1% of episodes without gates. Verification, correction, and safe-termination gates did not reduce them significantly. The traces show a candidate cause: the gates' evidence digest dropped the order status and customer authentication, so valid requests were rejected. The choice of evaluator decides the conclusion; the minimal check exposes failures the judges miss. Traces, code, prompts, and labels are released.
papers.authors: Sungbin Im

papers.title: CapLite: Prompt-Injection Defense for Small Language Model Agents without Model-Written Security Artifacts
papers.abstract: Enforcement defenses against prompt injection, such as CaMeL, Progent, IPIGuard and DRIFT, ask the agent's own model to write a security artifact (a program, a privilege policy, a dependency graph or a constraint list) that code then enforces. We ask whether small language model (SLM) agents can be trusted to write these artifacts. Across 15 open-weight models, 13 of them between 1.7B and 12B parameters, they cannot: the policies, graphs and constraints that the agent's model writes admit attacks on 14 (Progent), 13 (IPIGuard) and 11 (DRIFT) of the models, and CaMeL's programs fail to run in up to 68% of episodes. We present CapLite, which derives its policy from the tool schemas, commits the write calls before any tool result is read, and admits a write only if every argument that decides whom or what it affects is stated in the user's request. This guarantees write integrity: injected text cannot add a write, and no write reaches a recipient, amount, object or destination that the user did not state. No attack succeeds in 13,935 attacked AgentDojo episodes. CapLite reaches utility under attack comparable to CaMeL's (29.0% vs. 27.2%) with fewer tokens than every other enforcement defense and than the undefended agent: 17.1k per episode, 18% of CaMeL's, and the highest utility per token of all enforcement defenses.
papers.authors: Zimo Xu, Wenzhuo Liu, Hideki Nakayama

papers.title: Verifiable Settlement and Pricing for Local Energy Markets: Architecture and Deployment on Hyperledger Besu
papers.abstract: We implement privacy-preserving local electricity exchanges using an automated market maker on the Hyperledger Besu network under QBFT consensus. The proposed protocol operator collects individual electricity positions off-chain and publishes aggregate supply and demand on the blockchain, where smart contracts compute market prices every fifteen minutes. Individual positions remain off-chain; Poseidon2 commitments and UltraHonk zeroknowledge proofs, generated from Noir circuits, verify aggregation, payments, and daily balance updates. The architecture retains community coordination while making financial execution independently auditable. Signed receipts and member-triggered recourse prevent unverified or partial settlement. In a ten-household experiment using simulated US residential profiles, daily settlement uses approximately 19 million gas and produces eight-member proofs in 2.4 seconds. Over four simulated days, local trading covers 34.4% of demand and reduces grid-only costs by 30.5% under assumed tariffs. Numerically computed __-Nash Equilibrium electricity profiles capture 83-88% of the social planner surplus.
papers.authors: Michele Fabi, Baptiste Leloup

papers.title: Bait: Mitigating Harmful Agentic Reinforcement Learning via Probing Reward Function
papers.abstract: We expose a safety vulnerability on nascent agentic reinforcement-learning-as-a-service. Specifically, with a cost as low as \$20, we show that safety alignment of a large language model (e.g., Inkling) can be completely subverted through rounds of harmful agentic reinforcement learning (agentic RL) with a toxic environment from its users. We also demonstrate that upon a successful harmful agentic RL attack via the service API, the attackers can potentially use the safety-degraded model to assist with real-world harmful activities, e.g., exploit software vulnerabilities and launch code re-use attacks. To mitigate harmful agentic RL, we propose Bait, a defense that mitigates the attack via proactively probing the reward function. Experimental results show that such a simple defense can sufficiently mitigate learning from a harmful reward function and can still learn from a benign reward function that promotes benign agentic tasks. Further analysis on both empirical and theoretical aspects shows that an adaptive attacker who assumes the knowledge of Bait defense cannot perfectly subvert it due to a systematic challenge. Source code is available at https://github.com/git-disl/Bait.
papers.authors: Tiansheng Huang, Ananth Balashankar, Virat Shejwalkar, Santosh Pande, Ling Liu

papers.title: Optimal Additive Integer Masks for One-Guess Vulnerability under an Absolute-Moment Budget
papers.abstract: We study the average one-guess success probability of an adversary who observes the ordinary integer sum of a finite-support secret and an independent integer-valued mask, subject to an absolute-moment budget on the mask. For a uniform secret on an interval the exact optimum and an explicit optimiser are obtained. For a biased bit the masks that achieve no increase over the prior baseline are characterised and their minimal cost is determined. The entire cost-vulnerability frontier is then determined for every bias. It is the piecewise-linear interpolation of an explicit sequence of points generated by cost-optimally shifted truncated geometric masks. It has infinitely many affine pieces, which accumulate at the critical cost, where the frontier meets the prior baseline with zero slope. The proof rests on a layer-cake decomposition of an arbitrary mask into truncated geometrics, along which both the vulnerability and the cost are exactly additive. The results give exact design guidance for additive integer noise under the average one-guess metric; they do not constitute a cryptographic masking scheme.
papers.authors: Joonas Pääkkönen

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving Spectrum Data Obfuscation in Next-Generation Spectrum Coexistence Systems
papers.abstract: In spectrum coexistence systems, the primary user (PU) activity must be partially disclosed for interference avoidance and coordination, while the exact spectrum occupancy information is often restricted due to security and regulatory constraints. To this end, subset-based disclosures can be employed in which the true frequency is included while ambiguity is introduced. This paper shows that naive randomized subset disclosures remain highly vulnerable to information leakage through inference, as temporal structure can be exploited to recover spectrum usage information. Under Markovian dynamics of the PU's spectrum usage, hidden Markov model (HMM) filtering with online learning is applied, while under periodic dynamics, period and phase estimations with phase-aligned statistics are used for inference. To address this vulnerability, structure-aware obfuscation strategies are introduced. For Markovian dynamics, history-based and belief-based schemes are designed to induce model mismatch and limit posterior concentration, while for periodic dynamics, cycle-dominance and decoy-based schemes are designed to manipulate phase-wise statistics and bias the inference process. These obfuscation schemes significantly hinder inference of spectrum information and offer principled disclosure solutions for spectrum coexistence systems.
papers.authors: Yalin E. Sagduyu, Tugba Erpek, Sastry Kompella, Joseph A. Molnar

papers.title: Chinese Whispers About Vulnerabilities
papers.abstract: The dissemination of information about known software vulnerabilities occurs online in various ways. Everything from email and development systems to social media are used. Given this variety and a dataset of about 382 thousand online references for about 55 thousand vulnerabilities, the paper demonstrates that the referenced online information sources tend to be mostly dissimilar statistically. The mean cosine similarity between them is only 0.22. Interestingly, the amounts of online references neither increase nor decrease similarity between the online information sources. In contrast, vulnerabilities primarily associated with GitHub and programming language ecosystems tend to have more dissimilar online references than other vulnerabilities. Also vulnerability reports, whether in bug tracking systems or bug bounty platforms, tend to increase dissimilarity. With these empirical results, the paper contributes to the efforts to narrow an enduring knowledge gap related to the online tracking and associated traceability of software vulnerabilities.
papers.authors: Jukka Ruohonen

papers.title: Preserve the Vulnerability, Break the Alert: Testing the Robustness of CodeQL Taint Tracking with Natural Rewrites
papers.abstract: Static application security testing (SAST) tools such as CodeQL serve as security gates in continuous integration and code review, and a gate is also read in reverse. When a previously reported alert disappears after a change, developers and the tools around them often take the vulnerability to be gone. That inference holds only if the analyzer is robust to changes that keep the vulnerability. We test this robustness for CodeQL's JavaScript taint tracking with natural, vulnerability-preserving rewrites. A large language model, given only the alert CodeQL exposes and no knowledge of its implementation, rewrites one function along a reported flow as a plausible maintenance change, and we verify by manual audit and controlled experiments that the flaw survives and the alert does not. On 172 flows that CodeQL detects in real npm vulnerabilities, three rewrites per flow silence 26.2% of them, at about USD 0.51 per silenced flow. The same generator, asked only to refactor the same functions with no knowledge of the alert, silences none of them. Every silencing rewrite traces to one of seven gaps at the library-modeling boundary, and 64 of the 70 rewrites cross a gap inside an API CodeQL already models. The largest is the WHATWG URL constructor, which propagates taint to a URL's query components but not to its pathname. The boundary is not specific to CodeQL. 74% of the silencing rewrites also silence an independently built taint analyzer, and 53% escape three analyzers combined. A disappearing alert after an ordinary-looking change is therefore weak evidence that a vulnerability has been fixed, the gaps point SAST developers to narrow and concrete repair targets, and robustness to natural rewrites belongs alongside detection rate in how taint analyzers are evaluated.
papers.authors: Zhezhen Cao, Weiyuan Ding, Bowen Xu

papers.title: CrossPloit: A Benchmark for Cross-Version PoC Migration in Python Web Applications
papers.abstract: Affected-version ranges in vulnerability databases decide which deployments scanners, patching pipelines, and incident responders treat as vulnerable, yet these ranges are often incomplete, so vulnerable releases are silently treated as safe. Auditing them requires executable evidence: given a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit for a listed version, show that the same vulnerability can be triggered on an earlier, unlisted version. This cross-version PoC migration combines source-code analysis, environment repair, and execution-based verification. We introduce CrossPloit, a benchmark of 127 migration instances across 45 CVEs in the Python web ecosystem. Each instance includes a version-pinned container, a reference PoC, and a vulnerability-specific oracle; two validators check that the observed effect arises from the disclosed vulnerability. Benchmark construction confirms 149 vulnerable prior versions absent from the affected-version lists of four databases, 127 of which require migration. Across 18 agent configurations (nine models and two harnesses), the best configuration resolves 58.3% of instances, compared with 8.7% for an adapted trace-guided baseline. Attack-vector shifts are particularly difficult: no configuration resolves more than 37.9% of these instances. Higher resolve rates are associated with a smaller share of missed-API failures and a larger share of incomplete executions among the remaining failures. In one configuration, withholding the reference PoC and its environment specification reduces resolve rate from 50.4% to 15.0%, highlighting the value of the supplied reference package. CrossPloit provides an execution-based measurement of under-reported exposure and of how far its enumeration can be automated.
papers.authors: Hung Nguyen-Huu, Nguyen Anh Tuan, Ting Zhang, Yue Liu, Chengran Yang, Lwin Khin Shar, Eng Lieh Ouh, David Lo

papers.title: Look Here, Then Decide: Small Decision Models in a Harness Find Memory-Safety Vulnerabilities at Scale on Commodity GPUs
papers.abstract: We ask whether small, open-weight decision models can support vulnerability discovery in open-source software at scale and what the surrounding system must provide. These models answer a typed question in one forward pass, returning scores for the permitted answers rather than text. Our harness selects widely packaged C and C++ projects and uses deterministic incomplete-fix miners and shape localizers to decide where to look. Intern-Decision-4B, a 4B-parameter open-weight decision model, then scores every candidate function. The scores rank the queues rather than accept or reject candidates, apart from a low reach-score floor that some queues kept. The search uses no frontier model. Alone, the model is weak: it separates vulnerable from benign functions with AUC 0.73, but a vulnerable function from its own patch with only 0.56. It is more useful for ordering candidates. On 75 public CVEs from projects without any of our findings, the fixed function reached its repository's top 25 in 21% of cases, 1.4 times as often as under random order of the same queues. Recall is bounded mainly by where the localizers look. On the campaign's own queues the model's order placed 7.5 times more confirmed findings in the top 10 than random order, an observed, selection-biased upper bound. On three GB10 systems, the harness searched more than 4,000 projects at 900-1,100 repositories per hour. The campaign confirmed 187 memory-safety findings; by worst-case CVSS v3.1, 12 are critical, 148 high, 23 medium and 4 low. The decision step runs at 4.4 decisions per second on one GB10 and 9.8 on a consumer RTX 4090 gaming PC, with matching scores. A small decision model supports vulnerability discovery through prioritization, while deterministic analysis and verification remain essential. All confirmed findings are being disclosed to maintainers under coordinated disclosure before publication.
papers.authors: Tim De Wachter, Kyryl Volkov, Myrto Eleftheria Gkogkou, Mathieu Huysman

papers.title: Intent-Aware Protection for AI Agents
papers.abstract: AI agents increasingly access enterprise data, invoke powerful tools, and act with limited human oversight. Existing security defenses primarily detect prompt injection, harmful outputs, or suspicious behavior, but do not determine whether an agent remains faithful to the purpose for which it was deployed. An action may contain no attack pattern and stay within granted permissions while still violating the agent's role, organizational constraints, or purpose. We introduce Intent- Aware Security, a framework that treats trusted agent intent as a first-class security object. We define Intent Preservation and Intent Drift, and operationalize them through an Intent Profile: an agent-specific representation extracted from organizational, role, and developer intent. We further introduce an Intent-Aware benchmark of 887 validated samples across 35 agents, built by a generation procedure that fixes ground-truth labels before LLM realization, and four Intent Profile-based protections: pre-execution detection, post-execution detection, input alignment, and system-prompt hardening. Across all evaluations, Intent Profile-based protection outperforms all profile-free baselines on the primary metric. On our benchmark, it raises four-class acro-F1 from 45% to 79% (Out-of-Scope F1 from 8% to 76%). On more than 10,000 executed AgentDojo trajectories, where ground truth comes from environment state, profile-based post-execution detection reaches 0.949 AUROC versus AlignmentCheck 0.909, 0.897 with raw agent configuration and 0.843 without context. Profile-based input alignment improves protection success by 7 points over DataFilter with a comparable benign utility. These results suggest that an agent's intended purpose can serve as a useful security reference for detecting and mitigating deviations from its deployed role and operational boundaries.
papers.authors: Fady Copty, Neta Haiby, Max Braitmaiere, Julia Korsunsky

papers.title: Harnessing Environmental Scatterers for Endogenous Target Covertness in 6G ISAC: A New Paradigm for Sensing Security
papers.abstract: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) is a cornerstone of 6G networks, enabling simultaneous data transmission and environmental perception. However, the ubiquitous radiation of sensing waveforms introduces a critical security vulnerability where the physical existence and characteristics of targets are continuously exposed to unauthorized wardens. Meanwhile, existing sensing-secure methods primarily focus on degrading a target warden's parameter-estimation accuracy, yet they fail to prevent wardens from detecting the target's physical presence. In this article, we first analyze sensing security threats in ISAC systems and survey existing sensing-secure methods. To address the critical gap, we propose a novel security paradigm termed endogenous target covertness. By intentionally harnessing environmental scatterers, such as known objects, ambient backscatter devices, and reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS), as ghost targets, the proposed scheme ensures a low probability that the warden detects the true target for the true target at the warden. This deliberately renders the true target's existence indistinguishable to the warden, while the legitimate base station can extract the true target's response using prior knowledge of the scatterers. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed scheme through a case study, proving that absolute target covertness can be achieved without consuming dedicated jamming power. Finally, we outline key open challenges and promising research directions to realize truly secure, ubiquitous sensing in future ISAC ecosystems.
papers.authors: Yifan Zhang, Boxuan Xie, Mingyang Yang, Ying Liu, Riku Jäntti, Zan Li

papers.title: Protocol-Aware Auditing of Domain-Blind Feature Attribution in Network Intrusion Detection
papers.abstract: Feature-attribution methods can query rule-violating network states through perturbations, coalitions, references, paths, and ablations, making explanations and their evaluation sensitive to model behavior outside the operational domain. We formalize this failure mode as domain blindness and prove valid-query invariance: when models agree on the required oracle information within a declared rule-valid set, a procedure confined to that set returns the same attribution. We instantiate one protocol-aware query-control principle in LIME, SHAP, Integrated Gradients, and DeepLIFT and audit paired configurations across four NIDS datasets and three classifier families. In six settings where standard LIME reports perfect top-feature repeatability, PA-LIME reveals substantial variability, with a mean of 0.575. Under FGSM followed by protocol repair, PA-DeepLIFT and PA-IG achieve the largest attribution-similarity curve areas, 0.452 and 0.413, while mean within-PA rank agreement rises to 0.366 from 0.217. PA-XAI therefore turns structured domain assumptions into explicit, testable controls for explanation auditing; support modeling, raw-flow reconstruction, and adaptive explanation attacks provide complementary validation layers.
papers.authors: Emmanuelli El-Mahmoud, Abanisenioluwa Kolawole Orojo, Pablo Rivas, Erika Leal

papers.title: Beyond the Diff - VulSpot: A Vulnerability Dataset Where No Vulnerability Goes Unlocalized
papers.abstract: A vulnerability detector is only as trustworthy as the benchmark that scores it, and today's real-world datasets tend to flatter detectors. They are often built once and never refreshed, so they quickly miss new vulnerabilities, their labels are either noisy or heavily filtered, and their random splits let models train on near-copies of test code and on future vulnerabilities. Above all, when a fix only adds code, such as a missing NULL check, they do not point at where the vulnerability was, preventing detectors from learning to localize some of the most common C/C++ weaknesses. We present VulSpot, a living benchmark for detecting, classifying, and localizing vulnerabilities, with over 500k functions in 21 languages from 24k registered CVEs, including over 15k vulnerable C/C++ functions. By linking the code added by a patch to the existing statement it protects, VulSpot locates the vulnerability in 99.3\% of the functions that previous diff-based datasets used to leave without a location. Rather than discarding uncertain labels, it tells users how reliable each one is, and it comes with leak-free splits, complementary code context, and hierarchical CWE labels. An automated pipeline refreshes VulSpot every month, so that each release brings vulnerabilities no model has seen yet.
papers.authors: Dyna Soumhane Ouchebara, Stéphane Dupont

papers.title: Speech Tokenizers are Vulnerable: Transferable Semantic Attack and Robust Tokenizer
papers.abstract: Speech tokenizers serve as speech front ends, encoding input speech signals into representations for downstream models, such as automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems and large audio-language models (LALMs). In this paper, we find that speech tokenizers are fragile at the semantic level: small perturbations can disrupt their semantic encoding process and consequently cause severe degradation in downstream ASR and LALM performance. To study this vulnerability, we propose T-SemAttack, a transferable semantic attack based on a semantic encoder ensemble. By jointly drifting the representation spaces of multiple semantic encoders, T-SemAttack effectively disrupts the semantic content of speech while preserving perceptual quality, thereby inducing error features. We further analyze layer-wise representation drift and cross-model gradient alignment. Our findings show that perturbations can induce substantial shifts in deep semantic representations and that the input gradients of different surrogate encoders exhibit directional alignment. These observations suggest that shared adversarially sensitive directions in the input space may be a key factor underlying cross-model attack transferability. Building on these, we introduce ROSETok, a robust speech tokenizer that combines noisy training with robust semantic distillation to improve reconstruction fidelity and downstream SpeechLLM robustness. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets, 9 open-source and black-box ASR systems, and 4 LALMs demonstrate that T-SemAttack achieves strong transferable attack performance, while the proposed Robust Speech Tokenizer exhibits robustness under high-fidelity reconstruction and downstream tasks. Our code and demo are available at https://wxzyd123.github.io/t-semattack.
papers.authors: Zhisheng Zhang, Yifan Mi, Yixuan Zhou, Haiyun Li, Shengbo Cai, Dongfu Song, Ziang Xu, Jie Hao, Zhiyong Wu

papers.title: Social Engineering Attack Detection in Corporate Communications
papers.abstract: Social Engineering attacks continue to pose a significant risk to the corporate world with a growing level of sophistication. It is difficult to distinguish between authentic and phishing communication via email, chat, and phone. They pose a risk of exposing trade secrets and confidential communications and can create a chain of attack from lower-level employees up to executives. Therefore, we study this growing threat using real-world datasets to build baseline machine-learning models. Our TF-IDF models classify emails as phishing or safe, achieving accuracy above 90%. We build on this by exploring whether psychological manipulation and persuasion indicators can be measured to play a significant role in detecting phishing. Instead of relying solely on surface-level lexical features, we derive interpretable lexicon-based indicators of urgency, trust, greed, and other persuasion cues from the combined email dataset. By evaluating these manipulation-oriented features on their own, we measure how much signal they carry (ROC-AUC of 0.74 on a held-out test split) and test whether they transfer to held-out email sources.
papers.authors: Hanzla Hamid, Pappu Jha, Nick Rahimi

papers.title: Adversarial Risk in the Generative AI Era Necessitates Dropping the Small Epsilon Ball
papers.abstract: Adversarial Machine Learning research is currently centered on the search for the epsilon-ball: minimal perturbations designed to fool models while remaining imperceptible to humans. We argue that this fixation on $\ell_p$ norms is a metrological trap that communicates a distorted perception of risk to defenders, one that is unaligned with real-world system vulnerabilities. This paradigm misleads defenders into optimizing for narrow, mathematical robustness at the expense of systemic security, while simultaneously incentivizing attackers to exploit non-overlapping alternative adversarial pathways. Ultimately, we argue that the dominance of the $\ell_p$ ball does not just fail to reduce harm---it may actively facilitate it by communicating a false sense of security against the wrong threats.
papers.authors: Andrew C. Cullen, Neil G. Marchant, Paul Montague, Jiani Xie, Benjamin I. P. Rubinstein

papers.title: CuEVM: Scaling Smart Contract Execution on GPUs
papers.abstract: Smart contracts on Ethereum blockchain process transactions worth billions of US dollars daily. They run on top of Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) which executes transactions sequentially. This execution model creates a performance bottleneck, especially for new blockchain workloads with large numbers of transactions, such as security testing. We present CuEVM, a GPU-native and semantically complete EVM execution engine that treats transaction execution as a massively parallel data processing problem. It employs novel data structures and GPU-aware scheduling to accelerate execution. Unlike prior works that transpile the contract and rely on a host CPU for many operations, CuEVM supports complete EVM semantics natively on the GPU. It passes 100% of the Ethereum VMTests and 96.2% of the full execution-test suite. On a single commodity GPU, CuEVM executes over 8 million ERC-20 transfers per second, outperforming existing baselines by up to two orders of magnitude. We build a smart contract fuzzer, called CuEVM-fuzz, on top of CuEVM. The fuzzer achieves over a million end-to-end executions per second, up to 23x and 4.8x higher than the state-of-the-art CPU-based and GPU-based baselines, respectively.
papers.authors: Nhut-Minh Ho, Tien Tuan Anh Dinh, Quang Trung Ta, Fredrik Svantes, Xiaokui Xiao, Beng Chin Ooi

papers.title: A Tutorial on Oblivious Random Access Memory
papers.abstract: Abstract—Oblivious RAM (ORAM) is a key technique for pro- tecting memory access patterns in systems with untrusted mem- ory, including secure processors, trusted execution environments, and multi-party computation. This article presents a tutorial overview of ORAM concepts and designs from an algorithmic and cryptographic perspective. We review the security goals and threat models underlying ORAM, describe the most popular ORAM constructions and their core mechanisms, and discuss practical considerations for implementing ORAM. The tutorial aims to provide readers with a clear foundation for understanding ORAM-based memory protection and its applications.
papers.authors: Elaine Shi, Srinivas Devadas

papers.title: Homomorphism in Expectation: Leveled Homomorphic Encryption with Range-Relative Correctness
papers.abstract: Lattices have dominated the development of homomorphic encryption for deep computation. We introduce $\textit{Homomorphism in Expectation (HIE)}$, a new construction showing that encrypted addition suffices for both addition and multiplication in deep real-valued computation. Given any additively homomorphic encryption scheme over $\mathbb{Z}_2$, we construct range-relatively correct leveled homomorphic encryption for arithmetic circuits $C$ of $\textit{arbitrary}$ polynomial depth. For depth bound $d$ and any chosen public input bound $r>0$, our scheme supports inputs in $[-r,r]$. Outputs lie in $[-\eta_C,\eta_C]$, where $\eta_C=C(r,\ldots,r)$ is the circuit's maximum output range magnitude over this input range. Decryption returns an answer with error at most $\varepsilon\cdot\eta_C$ except with probability $\delta$. Each input requires $\ell_{\mathsf{in}}=O(d+\log(1/\varepsilon))$ base ciphertexts, and each output requires $\ell_{\mathsf{out}}=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/\delta))$ base ciphertexts. For $n$ inputs, online evaluation uses only ${\sim}\ell_{\mathsf{out}}\cdot n\cdot\ell_{\mathsf{in}}$ ciphertext additions and ${\sim}\ell_{\mathsf{out}}\cdot |C|\cdot\ell_{\mathsf{in}}$ memory accesses. Our construction begins by encoding real-valued inputs as encrypted bitstreams, allowing multiplication through encrypted bit addition. The direct approach incurs costs exponential in circuit depth, limiting efficient evaluation to logarithmic depth and requiring non-compact input ciphertexts. We overcome these limitations with new encoding and circuit evaluation techniques, which eliminate the exponential overhead, enabling compact homomorphic arithmetic at arbitrary polynomial depth from additive encryption alone.
papers.authors: Zeyu Liu, Xianhui Lu, Ruida Wang, Xinxuan Zhang

papers.title: ASCENT: Algebraic Structured Compilation of Exact Norms for Succinct Lattice Proofs
papers.abstract: Norm bounds are semantic constraints in lattice cryptography: satisfying the modular equations is not enough unless the witness also satisfies the prescribed shortness bound. Existing norm reductions either introduce slack, or rely on general sumcheck style machinery whose transcript cost grows with the witness length. We introduce a reduction-of-knowledge compiler for exact $\ell_2$-norm constraints. It compiles the original norm language for a committed lattice witness into a narrow structured relation consisting only of commitment-opening constraints, tensor-structured witness-public inner-product claims, and relaxed admissible shortness bounds. Exact norm soundness is enforced inside the reduction, so the remaining proof obligation is structured and algebraic. The compiler adds only $O(1)$ prover-to-verifier communication, measured in ring and field elements, independent of the witness length $N$, and requires only $O(\log N)$ verifier work. The same techniques can also extend to a folding mechanism for broader quadratic relations, including R1CS-type circuits. At $128$-bit security, our concrete estimates give transcripts of about $27.69\mathrm{KB}$ for exact norm reduction and $27.75\mathrm{KB}$ for the R1CS folding application. This is about $3$--$4\times$ smaller than LatticeFold+, about $2$--$3\times$ smaller than SALSAA, and remains close to the compact estimates reported for Cyclo.
papers.authors: Lizhen Zhang, Shang Gao, Bin Xiao

papers.title: A New Class of PRFs and Efficient VRFs from Isogeny-based Group Actions
papers.abstract: Polynomial-in-exponent pseudorandom functions (Poly-style PRFs) based on group actions have recently emerged as a promising framework for post-quantum cryptography, offering compact keys and efficient verifiability. However, the security of these constructions over composite-order class groups remains poorly understood. Prior work suggested that security is governed by the largest prime factor of the group order. In this work, we show that this intuition is flawed. We present two generic attacks demonstrating that the effective security of Poly-style PRFs is determined instead by the smallest prime factor of the group order. As a consequence, existing parameter choices, including CSIDH-512 and SCALLOP-based settings used in recent VRF constructions, are insecure. Our enhanced attack achieves advantage close to one with complexity $O(\sqrt{p})$, where $p$ is the smallest prime factor of the group order. To address this inherent vulnerability, we introduce a new design paradigm, {\em restrict-then-expand}, and formalize a general class of multivariate polynomial PRFs (\textsf{MP}-PRFs) from group actions. The key idea is to eliminate exploitable structure via carefully restricted input domains, and then recover expressiveness through a provably secure expansion technique. We show that \textsf{MP}-PRFs unify and generalize existing constructions, including Naor-Reingold-style and Poly-style PRFs (with restricted input domains), while achieving security in the generic group action model with twists ($\mathrm{GGAM}^{\mathsf{T}}$) for arbitrary composite-order groups. In addition to this, our construction supports flexible polynomial-size input spaces with fixed output length and admits efficient and compact proofs of correct evaluation. Building on this framework, we obtain new group-action-based VRFs that are both practical and provably secure. At a proof-soundness level close to 128 bits, our VRF instantiation requires 320 group-action evaluations for either proof generation or verification, compared with approximately 69,000--109,500 group-action evaluations in prior work, while retaining short keys and proofs. Overall, our results establish a robust and efficient approach to constructing post-quantum PRFs and VRFs from group actions, resolving fundamental limitations of existing Poly-style designs.
papers.authors: Junbo Yang, Willy Susilo, Dung Hoang Duong, Partha Sarathi Roy, Yannan Li, Kazuhide Fukushima, Shinsaku Kiyomoto

papers.title: DetTreeChain: Parallel Block Production on an N-ary Block Tree with Bounded Lane Divergence
papers.abstract: Nakamoto-style blockchains append one block at a time to a single chain, and raising the block rate increases forking and weakens security. We present DetTreeChain, a ledger in which up to $N$ blocks are produced in parallel and placed without later merging or reordering. Blocks form an $N$-ary tree in which each block's slot follows from its parent and its lane. A locally derived Parent Queue Pool lets only two consecutive parents receive children, so lanes never drift more than one parent apart, and links between consecutive blocks of a lane make each lane a hash chain. As in several earlier designs, transactions are routed by what they spend, here a hash of the spent locking scripts, so blocks of different lanes cannot conflict and payments to other lanes need no cross-lane protocol. The rules are consensus-agnostic. Under proof of work, miners choose their lane, and an adversary with more than $1/(N+1)$ of the total hash power can outpace one lane. In a 25-minute run of our Rust prototype, six nodes converged on identical trees and difficulty targets, and 65% of slots were filled against 63% predicted. In simulation with delays of 5% of the lane interval, a single chain at the same block rate wasted 1.7 to 3.3 times as much work as 2 to 8 lanes, although nodes more often held later-discarded blocks. Among Bitcoin transactions whose spent scripts could be rebuilt, about 95% kept their inputs in one lane, mostly because they spend a single output.
papers.authors: Mahesh Karri, Nikhileswara Rao Sulake

papers.title: Neural Cipher Bench: Cost and Portability of Corner-ReLU Cipher Implementation
papers.abstract: Edge and Internet of Things (IoT) devices run neural networks on GPUs, neural processing units (NPUs), and microcontrollers (MCUs) through machine learning (ML) runtimes. Deep Neural Cryptography (DNC, EUROCRYPT 2026) expressed AES as a bit-exact ReLU network with fixed weights, using a corner-ReLU construction that keeps the cipher inside the affine+ReLU operators such runtimes execute. What this construction costs on edge and IoT hardware, and whether real ML backends execute it correctly, had not been measured. We implement SM4, ARIA, Camellia, and ChaCha20 (spanning substitution–permutation, Feistel, and add–rotate–XOR structures) alongside AES on a shared corner-ReLU core under one construction policy, derive a cost model for width, depth, and neuron count, and measure five execution paths on four platforms. All ciphers admit bit-exact networks whose width and depth diverge with cipher structure, and the model's width predicted where GPU throughput drops. Every configuration passing the correctness check fell below its classical baseline (best 0.80×, SM4 on the GPU), by hundreds to thousands of times for the S-box ciphers on the MCU, and keeping the activations on chip through fusion raised throughput 1.4–3.5× and moved the peak past the predicted cache limit without closing the gap. Some AES configurations on the Apple Neural Engine returned valid-looking but incorrect outputs with no error or warning, a failure reproduced in a minimal graph without project code. Mathematical bit-exactness therefore does not guarantee backend-level bit-exactness, and exact workloads offloaded to edge NPUs require output validation.
papers.authors: Siwoo Eum, Minwoo Lee, Gyeongju Song, Seungwon Lee, Uijae Kim, Doyun Park, Minseo Kim, Wai Kong Lee, Zhe Liu, Anupam Chattopadhyay, Hwajeong Seo

papers.title: When One Bit Is (Almost) Enough: A Low Leakage Chosen Plaintext Side Channel Attack on AES
papers.abstract: In order to thwart Side Channel Attacks (SCA) and keep secret safe, countermeasures such as masking can be implemented to hide information. However, when a defect occurs in software or in hardware, a portion of the information may still leak. If the leak is sufficient, the state-of-the-art techniques can still be performed up to a potential brute force search to cover a missing part. However, if only a short portion of the information leaks, the completion of the attack can be hard, and considered as failed. In this paper, we describe a new chosen plaintext strategy on AES algorithm to recover the secret key even in very low leakage condition. As an example, but not limited to, we describe the methodology adapted to one of the worst case scenario: only one bit position leaks over the 128-bit output of SubBytes AES sub-operation along rounds. As a drawback, a heavier cost in terms of number of traces is required due to the chosen plaintext approach.
papers.authors: Antoine Wurcker

papers.title: Bounding the security of the Bromberg-Shpilrain-Vdovina hash function
papers.abstract: The Bromberg-Shpilrain-Vdovina hash functions are a family of Cayley hash functions indexed by an integer parameter $k\ge 2$. Hashes are matrices in $SL_2(p)$ where $p$ is a large prime. We present an attack which finds collisions of length $O(\log p)$ whose average-case time complexity is $O(p^{0.28})$ when $k=2$ and $O(p^{0.36})$ when $k=3$ under an assumption in the spirit of Zaremba's Conjecture on continued fractions. This is an improvement on the more general attacks of Mullan-Tsaban and Slaughter which have average-case time complexity $O(\sqrt{p})$. For any $k$, the average-case time complexity of our attack is $O(p^{1-\delta_k+o(1)})$ where $\delta_k$ is the Hausdorff dimension of a certain Cantor set. This tends to $O(\sqrt{p})$ as $k\to\infty$, so our attack has time complexity comparable to Mullan-Tsaban and Slaughter's attacks as $k$ grows. We give examples of collisions for large primes found by our attack when $k=2, 3$.
papers.authors: Eilidh McKemmie

papers.title: An Agile Homomorphic Encryption and ML-KEM Scheme for Privacy-Preserving Health Data Processing
papers.abstract: The storage and processing of health data raise serious privacy con- cerns; therefore, the data must be encrypted. Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) allows computations on encrypted data, which makes it a very promising technology in this context. However, although the efficiency of FHE algorithms has improved in recent years, they remain very complex. The security of several prominent FHE schemes is based on variants of the Learning With Errors (LWE) problem, which is also the basis of Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM), the new post-quantum standard for asymmetric encryption. In this paper, we propose an agile cryptographic scheme – combining ML-KEM and BGV – that allows efficient implementations in an embedded use case. We describe the parameter selection for the proposed scheme and show its feasibility with a proof-of-concept implementation.
papers.authors: Daniel RESENDE, Nadia El Mrabet, Ulrich Kühne

papers.title: Threshold Batched Attribute-Based Encryption from Succinct LWE
papers.abstract: Batched identity-based encryption (BIBE) enables a single compact key to decrypt ciphertexts associated with a designated batch of identities. Batched attribute-based encryption (B-ABE) extends this functionality to attribute-based access control, while threshold batched attribute-based encryption (TB-ABE) further distributes the decryption capability among multiple parties. Existing constructions of TB-ABE rely on bilinear pairings, motivating post-quantum alternatives. In this work, we give, to the best of our knowledge, the first lattice-based candidate construction of TB-ABE. Our construction combines the succinct polynomial-digest mechanism underlying lattice-based BIBE with key-homomorphic evaluation for arithmetic-circuit policies and linear secret sharing. We prove security under the ℓ-succinct LWE assumption, assuming the required share-uniformity property of the underlying ramp threshold sharing scheme.
papers.authors: Shayeef Murshid, Ramprasad Sarkar, Mriganka Mandal

papers.title: Practical Confidential Clustering for Federated Learning using Efficient Secret-Sharing
papers.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) often suffers from statistical heterogeneity, where diverging data distributions prevent a single global model from achieving high utility for all participants. Clustered Federated Learning (CFL) addresses this problem by grouping similar clients to train personalized sub-models, yet performing such clustering while ensuring strict confidentially with minimal communication overhead remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces CCFL, a framework for Confidential Clustering that executes clustering logic, including distance computations and centroid updates, entirely within the encrypted domain using Replicated Secret Sharing (RSS). CCFL orchestrates a unified pipeline that integrates client-side feature extraction, an anonymization server for oblivious shuffling, and Multi-Party Computation (MPC)-based clustering to ensure both input privacy and participant unlinkability. By employing a ring-based Euclidean distance optimization, CCFL significantly reduces interactive rounds, achieving up to $46.7\times$ computational speedup under realistic LAN and WAN constraints. Our one-shot clustering approach decouples heavy cryptographic computation from the training loop, allowing the system to scale seamlessly to thousands of clients with negligible edge overhead. Finally, downstream evaluations confirm that CCFL achieves a superior privacy-utility trade-off, matching or outperforming state-of-the-art personalized FL paradigms without exposing sensitive feature geometries.
papers.authors: Cédric Prigent, Sonia Ben Mokhtar

papers.title: How to Revoke Users in Encryption Schemes?
papers.abstract: Revocation is essential for keeping encryption secure as keys leak, devices are compromised or users leave the system. We revisit the problem of revocation for encryption schemes and give, to our knowledge, the first approach combining anonymous, collusion-resistant revocation with unchanged keys and access rules, succinct ciphertext overhead and a trustless revocation authority, i.e. that cannot decrypt. Revoking a user publishes one random-looking pseudonym, without telling encryptors whose key was revoked. A party can decrypt future ciphertexts only if it is unrevoked and satisfies the original access decryption rule. Our core observation is that revocation is, at heart, witness encryption for the statement that one satisfies the access rule and that the pseudonym bound to one's key has not been revoked. Although general-purpose witness encryption remains far from practical, we observe that the statements arising from revocation are simple and algebraic, and we show that they fall within the special-purpose framework of Garg et al. (CRYPTO 2025), which compiles short arguments of knowledge (called ``gadgets'') into efficient witness encryption using bilinear groups. Our technical contribution is a pair of succinct non-membership gadgets for this framework, one for a single hidden pseudonym and one that certifies non-revocation jointly for all users selected by an access rule. Both gadgets are generic and modular, as they compose with the gadgets expressing a wide range of access rules, and thus provide a single revocation mechanism that is designed once and reused across different encryption schemes, without redesigning either the scheme or the revocation. These gadgets yield the following applications. First, we give a black-box transformation adding revocation to arbitrary independently instantiated public-key encryption, with constant-size cryptographic ciphertext overhead. For unrevoked users, confidentiality continues to rely only on the security of the underlying scheme. Then, we demonstrate applications to advanced encryption scheme, constructing revocable schemes for distributed broadcast, registered attribute-based, and registered threshold encryption, with succinct cryptographic ciphertext components and threshold decryption shares. We prove adaptive security of our schemes in the generic bilinear-group and random-oracle models.
papers.authors: Sanjam Garg, Dimitris Kolonelos, Benjamin Ostrovsky, Guru-Vamsi Policharla

papers.title: From Degree Three to Degree Two: Statistical Randomized Encodings for All Functions
papers.abstract: A randomized encoding represents a function by a simpler randomized map whose output allows recovery of the function value while revealing essentially no further information about the input. Perfectly correct and perfectly private encodings of degree three over $\F_2$ are known for every Boolean function, but degree two cannot provide these guarantees for all functions (Ishai and Kushilevitz, FOCS 2000 and ICALP 2002). Whether degree two suffices when small statistical errors are allowed in both correctness and privacy has remained open. We construct quadratic randomized encodings of every Boolean function with exponentially small correctness and statistical privacy errors. The degree bound holds jointly in the input bits and independent uniform random bits, and the construction, encoder, decoder and simulator have complexity polynomial in the total size of mod-2 branching programs computing the function's output bits and in the security parameter. Our encodings also achieve decomposability and output locality three, meaning that each encoded bit depends on at most three input and random bits. These results resolve the degree-two and locality-three questions for statistical randomized encodings (Ishai, 2013). As an application, we obtain one-way functions of optimal output locality three from one-way functions in polynomial-time uniform $\mathrm{NC}^1$, improving the previous locality-four result under the same assumption (Applebaum, Ishai and Kushilevitz, FOCS 2004). We also obtain quadratic multiparty randomized encodings with negligible correctness and statistical privacy errors against semi-honest corruption of any coalition of parties. Previous general constructions for $k\ge4$ parties provided perfect correctness and privacy against at most $\lfloor 2k/3\rfloor$ corruptions (Applebaum, Ishai, Karni and Patra, CRYPTO 2022). Through known reductions, our encodings yield non-interactive reductions of every functionality to a fixed three-party functionality and three-round protocols in the two-round OT-hybrid model, with negligible correctness and statistical privacy errors against every coalition. They also yield non-interactive client--server protocols for every function whenever a majority of the servers is honest, even when corrupted servers collude with any set of clients. This server threshold is optimal in this model when privacy is required against arbitrary client coalitions.
papers.authors: Emmanuela Orsini, Arpita Patra

papers.title: Adaptively Secure (Threshold) Batched IBE from Static Assumptions
papers.abstract: Batched identity-based encryption (batched IBE) lets a key authority release one short decryption key for a set of identities and a batch label/epoch. It has been used to mitigate maximal extractable value (MEV) attacks on public blockchains. Existing constructions either use the generic-group and/or random-oracle models, or rely on $q$-type assumptions whose size grows with the batch-size bound. In this paper, we present the first adaptively secure batched IBE scheme from static assumptions. Our scheme supports an exponential identity space and an exponential epoch space, and its ciphertexts, digests, and batch keys consist of a constant number of group elements independent of the batch size.
