Our scheme relies on composite-order bilinear groups, and we prove its adaptive security assuming hardness of static subgroup decision assumptions and a static pairing assumption, with a security loss polynomial in the security parameter $\lambda$ and the number of key queries. Our proof does not rely on $q$-type assumptions, random oracles, generic-group arguments, or complexity leveraging. We also present a threshold version with adaptive challenge security under static corruption, and translate our scheme to prime-order bilinear groups under the static MDDH assumption.
papers.authors: Sourav Das, Pratish Datta, Aditi Partap, Swagata Sasmal

papers.title: SEC: One-Share Everywhere-Short Secret Sharing from Lossless Expanders
papers.abstract: We introduce \(\mathsf{SEC}\), an expander-code-based ramp secret sharing scheme over \(\mathbb{Z}\)-modules, particularly suitable for lattice-based distributed cryptography. It is everywhere-short: bounded secret coefficients yield bounded share coefficients, and the integer reconstruction vectors have bounded entries. Moreover, each participant receives exactly one share, regardless of the number of parties and the privacy and reconstruction thresholds. This improves on prior schemes with bounded share coefficients and bounded entries in the integer reconstruction vectors, in which the number of sub-shares or shares per participant grows either with the number of parties and the threshold or with the security parameter. The construction rests on a coding-theoretic observation: in the bi-adjacency matrix of a lossless bipartite expander, unique-neighbor peeling completes every sufficiently small set of columns to a square unimodular submatrix. We prove correctness, everywhere-shortness, and linearity, and give a publicly computable entrywise bound on the reconstruction vector our algorithm returns for each authorized set. For privacy, we introduce hard-core local leakage resilience, which strengthens the leakage-resilience notion of Nielsen and Simkin (EUROCRYPT 2020) to protect a hard-core function of the secret, and we prove that \(\mathsf{SEC}\) satisfies it against correlated multi-query local leakage under the \(\mathsf{MatrixHint\text{-}MLWE}\) problem, which admits a reduction from the standard \(\mathsf{MLWE}\) problem. For \(n=60\) participants and security parameter \(\kappa = 128\), \(\mathsf{SEC}\) achieves privacy threshold \(6\) against \(2^{64}\) leakage queries and empirical reconstruction threshold \(46\). The ideal entropy-coded secret and share sizes are about \(3.5\) KiB and \(6.4\) KiB, respectively.
papers.authors: Muhammad Arzaki, Muhammed F. Esgin, Amin Sakzad, Ron Steinfeld

papers.title: Multi-Hop Functional Encryption
papers.abstract: In this paper, we initiate the study of multi-hop functional encryption ($\mathsf{MHFE}$), a new primitive for computing over encrypted data in recursive and multi-stage workflows while enabling controlled release of intermediate outputs. $\mathsf{MHFE}$ supports dynamic directed-acyclic computation graphs in which each node is labeled by a function and is equipped with a restricted secret key that reveals only that node's output, yet the computation can continue downstream on a forwardable encrypted state. In doing so, $\mathsf{MHFE}$ simultaneously overcomes (i) multi-hop fully homomorphic encryption's need for a globally trusted, always-online decryption key to reveal intermediate values, (ii) standard FE's lack of a native mechanism for forwarding reusable encrypted state across stages and handling evolving datasets without a fresh recomputation, and (iii) Multi Party Computation's deployment friction stemming from interaction and liveness/coordination requirements (at the cost of a central key-issuing authority). We formalize $\mathsf{MHFE}$ security via the simulation paradigm extending standard FE collusion resistance to the multi-hop setting; this simulation-based notion captures the intended information flow in recursive computations most accurately by characterizing an adversary's entire view as simulatable given only the authorized intermediate outputs. Our security games impose a natural topological-order on queries: a hop key for a node may be requested only after the ciphertexts/keys on all incoming edges to that node have been fixed. We then give the first generic simulation-secure construction of public-key $\mathsf{MHFE}$ for all polynomial-size circuits from any IND-secure standard FE for circuits.
papers.authors: Pratish Datta, Jiaxin Guan, Alexis Korb, Amit Sahai

papers.title: SoK: Understanding Virtual Machines over Fully Homomorphic Encryption
papers.abstract: We survey the current literature on fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) from a virtual machine (VM) perspective. We observe that programs behave in an intrinsically different way over FHE than on plaintext, forming a new paradigm of computation that is fundamentally constrained by the obliviousness of data. To better understand the computational properties, we compile more than 125 works to formulate a cross-layer systematic view of FHE VMs, with a special focus on understanding the concrete programming models over encrypted data. In particular, we identify three distinct forms of VMs over FHE, namely, the SISD VM, the SIMD VM, and the hybrid VM. To aid the cross-layer systematization, we also discuss how current FHE compilers and hardware accelerators can be applied to enhance the usability and performance of the respective VMs. In the experiment, we test eight VM instructions with varying precision as well as two end-to-end application programs to quantitatively assess the concrete design trade-offs for each of the VM paradigms. We conclude that FHE VMs of different types exhibit distinct utility and performance characteristics, necessitating new design methodologies to be developed in a cross-layer manner.
papers.authors: Song Bian, Ziwei Ma, Yunhao Fu, Haowen Pan, Ruiyu Shen, Zhou Zhang, Ran Mao, Zaidong Li, Yintai Sun, Ruoyi Li, Zhenyu Guan

papers.title: Incrementally Verifiable Oracle Aided Computation
papers.abstract: Incrementally verifiable computation ($\IVC$) allows a prover to maintain a short proof that can be efficiently updated after each computation step, without retaining or recomputing the preceding execution. In the context of AI safety, the need for incremental verification is particularly important, as AI systems interact with users over time and perform further computation after each interaction. However, standard $\IVC$ schemes do not directly address a crucial feature of AI tasks: their dependence on external information and expertise. Indeed, the UK AISI Alignment Team~\cite{IrvingM25} emphasizes that verification methods for AI safety should accommodate access to external information and human judgment. This is the topic of this paper. We construct $\IVC$ schemes for {\em oracle-aided} computations under the Learning with Errors ($\LWE$) assumption by first constructing succinct non-interactive arguments ($\SNARG$s), and then extending them to the incremental setting. We consider the following two settings, where below, $\lambda$ is the security parameter, $n$ is the input length, and $T$, $S$, and $Q$ are the time, space, and oracle-query bounds. \begin{itemize} \item \textbf{Robust computations.} For bounded-space computations, including non-deterministic computations, in which every accepting purported execution on a false input contains at least an $\varepsilon$-fraction of incorrect oracle answers, we construct {\em privately verifiable} $\SNARG$s and $\IVC$. For $\IVC$, the corresponding robustness condition is imposed on the claimed configuration. Public parameters, private verification keys, and proofs have length $\poly(\lambda,S,\log T,1/\varepsilon)$, and verification uses $O(\lambda/\varepsilon)$ oracle calls. We complement this result with a lower bound ruling out (deterministic) publicly verifiable $\SNARG$s and $\IVC$s with public parameters of length $o(n)$, and $o(Q)$ verifier oracle queries. \item \textbf{Signed oracles.} For oracles that digitally sign their query-answer pairs, we construct publicly verifiable $\SNARG$s and $\IVC$ without a robustness assumption, and with oracle-free setup and verification. Public parameters and proofs have length $\poly(\lambda,S,\log T)$. For deterministic computations with oracle query and answer lengths $\poly(\lambda,\log T)$, we remove the dependence on $S$, obtaining public parameter and proof lengths $\poly(\lambda,\log T)$. \end{itemize} All our constructions have adaptive completeness and soundness. Sub-exponential hardness of $\LWE$ suffices for all constructions; polynomial hardness suffices in the deterministic signed-oracle setting when $T$ is polynomially bounded in $\lambda$. All cryptographic assumptions are required to hold even given access to the underlying oracle.
papers.authors: Shafi Goldwasser, Yael Tauman Kalai

papers.title: The isodual constant of the LLL potential: exact values and structure
papers.abstract: The LLL potential $\Psi^2(B)=\prod_k\det\mathrm{Gram}(b_1,\dots,b_k)$, minimized over the bases of a lattice $L$ and normalized by its determinant, defines an isodual lattice invariant $\eta(L)$. Its supremum $\eta_n$ over $n$-dimensional lattices, introduced in ePrint 2007/105, is the staircase case of the generalized Hermite constants of Watanabe and Meyer, for which explicit values were known only for $n\le4$. We prove that $\eta_5=6$, attained only by $D_5$ and its dual: the flag analogue of Korkine and Zolotarev's value of $\gamma_5$. The natural reduction to four-dimensional lattices, through a function $\Phi_5$, does not suffice: the global maximum of $\Phi_5$ is $2^{16}/(3^4\cdot5^3)\approx6.4727$, attained not at $D_4$ but at an even $135$-modular lattice $M_*$, which we have not found in the literature. A second stage, over the lifts of the remaining region, completes the proof; both stages are computer-assisted, with about $9\times10^9$ leaves, each re-proved in interval arithmetic by a separately written checker; code and data are public. We also prove $\eta_8=2304$, attained by $E_8$, and show that $E_6$, $E_7$, $E_8$ and their duals are strict local maxima of $\eta$ (for $n=6,7$ these are the conjectured extremal lattices). Asymptotically, $\log\eta_n=(\frac14+o(1))\,n^2\log n$. For lattice reduction we introduce the $\Psi$-Hermite constant $\mu_m$, the largest first Gram–Schmidt norm in a potential-minimal basis of an $m$-dimensional lattice, and bound it through $\eta_m$. This gives $\mu_m=\gamma_m$, Hermite's constant, for $m\le5$, and $\mu_m\le\exp(O(\log^2 m))$ in general.
papers.authors: Nick Howgrave-Graham

papers.title: MPCTM: MPC-Based Trajectory Matching on Unmanned Autonomous Systems
papers.abstract: Emerging technologies such as Unmanned Autonomous Systems (UASs) are increasingly being deployed across several application domains. Their deployment, however, introduces safety risks, especially when unmanned vehicles operate in shared operational spaces (e.g., air, land, or maritime) and may follow collision-prone paths. This creates the need for solutions that can detect possible collisions among pre-planned trajectories, thereby improving operational safety and reducing risk. At the same time, revealing trajectories in plaintext leaks sensitive information, such as traversal patterns, deployment and infrastructure locations, and potentially private user data. In this paper, we present a privacy-preserving trajectory matching protocol based on Multi-Party Computation (MPC). We introduce an end-to-end secure scheme for collision detection that reveals no information beyond the prescribed output. Our solution models the behaviour of UASs along their paths, accurately capturing collisions that may occur between discretely sampled points. We further propose a lightweight, MPC-friendly model and discuss the trade-off between accuracy and efficiency for the two approaches. We provide a proof-of-concept implementation of our scheme and compare it to the closest state-of-the-art solution. Our evaluation shows that our work MPCTM, in the dealer mode, improves the online latency upon previous work by over 2x in our modelled protocol and by 8x in our lightweight protocol. In autonomous mode, our protocol results in a slow-down of 2.5-3x, while providing a more expressive model with no false negatives and fully preserving privacy of the trajectory data.
papers.authors: Dominik Roy George, Martin Zbudila, Barry Van Leeuwen

papers.title: Jazzline: Composable CryptoLine Functional Correctness Proofs for Jasmin Programs
papers.abstract: Jasmin is a programming language for high-speed and high-assurance cryptography. Correctness proofs of Jasmin programs are typically carried out deductively in EasyCrypt. This allows generality, modularity and composable reasoning, but does not scale well for low-level architecture-specific routines. CryptoLine offers a semi-automatic approach to formally verify algebraically-rich low-level cryptographic routines. CryptoLine proofs are self-contained: they are not integrated into higher-level formal verification developments. This paper shows how to soundly use CryptoLine to discharge subgoals in functional correctness proofs for complex Jasmin programs. We extend Jasmin with annotations and provide an automatic translation into a CryptoLine model, where most complex transformations are certified. We also formalize and implement the automatic extraction of the semantics of a CryptoLine proof
papers.authors: José Bacelar Almeida, Manuel Barbosa, Gilles Barthe, Lionel Blatter, Gustavo Delerue, João Diogo Duarte, Benjamin Gregoire, Tiago Oliveira, Miguel Quaresma, Pierre-Yves Strub, Ming-Hsien Tsai, Bow-Yaw Wang, Bo-Yin Yang

papers.title: Secure Information Flow in Quantum Programs
papers.abstract: Information-flow security aims to prevent the leakage of confidential information through program execution. This problem becomes fundamentally subtler for quantum programs, because their states may involve superposition and entanglement, and their executions may involve intricate interactions between classical and quantum variables. This paper develops semantic foundations and verification methods for secure information flow in quantum programs. We formulate two notions of information-flow security. The first is a noninterference-based definition that naturally generalizes its classical counterpart. The second is a simulation-based definition that explicitly models an attacker, providing a clear operational interpretation of security. We prove that these two notions are equivalent. To verify the information-flow security of quantum programs, we develop a proof framework based on quantum Hoare logic. A key challenge is that the standard self-composition technique, which expresses information-flow security in Hoare logic by composing a program with a renamed copy of itself, fails in the quantum setting due to an obstruction analogous to the no-cloning theorem. To overcome this challenge, we introduce self-conjugation, a novel technique that leverages the deferred measurement principle and properties of unitary operations. We demonstrate our framework on examples drawn from the quantum one-time pad, quantum error correction, and anonymous entanglement generation.
papers.authors: Zhicheng Zhang, Mingsheng Ying, Lirong Xia

papers.title: Sable: A Small-Field Sumcheck Argument for Bit-Exact Inference of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: We present Sable, an argument system and single-GPU prover for the statement that a committed, integer-quantized transformer produced a given token sequence from a given prompt, bit for bit. Sable fixes an integer function F_O with no floating-point step, in which every rounding, normalization, softmax and sampling decision is determined by its inputs, and proves it with a constraint system whose relations provably never wrap modulo the 31-bit KoalaBear prime. The proof batches zerochecks and LogUp-GKR lookups into one sumcheck per domain, and commits to every witness tensor and weight in one multilinear commitment built from Reed-Solomon codes, BLAKE3 Merkle trees and a mixed-length BaseFold opening. The prover streams the model layer by layer on one GPU. On one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU, Sable proves all 64 layers of Qwen2.5-32B in 92.5 s for 4,096 tokens and 398 s for 16,384 tokens, and covers Qwen3-32B and the mixture-of-experts Qwen3-30B-A3B (4,096 tokens in 121.8 and 84.7 s). A proof costs 41 to 50 times the serving time, or 6.4 cents per 4,096-token request at public GPU prices, and 40 to 64 times less time per parameter and token than zkLLM. On WikiText-2, F_O's greedy token matches the BF16 model's at 86.3% of positions; on Qwen3, F_O is within 1.6 points of BF16 on MMLU and 1.7 points on GSM8K. A verifier with a compiled core checks a proof on one CPU core in 19 to 56 s. In the random-oracle model, the interactive proof has round-by-round soundness error 2^-103. The proof is not zero-knowledge, so the system targets open-weight models. Code: https://github.com/moonmath-ai/Sable
papers.authors: Tomer Solberg

papers.title: Access Cost Tradeoffs in Mixed-Mode Oblivious RAM
papers.abstract: A mixed-mode oblivious RAM (ORAM) lets each memory request be marked public or private: public requests disclose their addresses, private requests hide them. We ask how much work such a scheme must do, and which requests must do it, in the cell-probe model—with a passive server that only reads and overwrites addressed words. We examine the expected amortized per-request cost on randomized workloads with independent modes and uniformly random addresses. For array size $n$ and client memory $m\le n^{1-\varepsilon}$ words, let $H=\log_2(2+n/(m+1))$. Our main result is a tight tradeoff between the cost of public reads and private writes. We show that if a request is private with probability $0<p\le1/2$ and private requests cost at most $Q$ probes on average, then every scheme with $m\le n^{1-\varepsilon}$ has expected public-read cost\[ \Omega\!\left(\max\left\{1, \frac{H}{\log_2(2+1/p+Q/H)}\right\}\right), \]even when the server learns the kind (read/write) of each private request. For polynomial $m$, we provide constructions that match this bound whenever $Q$ exceeds a threshold that we identify for both $Q$ treated as an expectation over the workload and as the average cost for the worst-case workload. In particular, at constant private frequency $p$ a logarithmic private budget forces logarithmic public-read cost, and constant public-read cost requires private cost $(n/(m+1))^{\Omega(1)}$. This answers, for passive servers, the question posed by Zhang, Wang, and Weng, whose PIR-based scheme achieves constant public and logarithmic private bandwidth with server computation. Our lower bound proof fixes the public query and changes its private history; crucially, we charge them separately. Our constructions combine a public cache with linear merges of hash tables. Two further groups of results concern public writes and total work. Firstly, we give a cost tradeoff between public writes and private reads. Secondly, for workloads mixing private operations, public reads, and public writes with probabilities $p,r,a$, we show that every scheme with $m\le n^{1-\varepsilon}$ has total cost per request $\Omega(\max\{1,H/\log_2(2+1/p)\})$ when private request kinds are hidden, and a construction with polynomial client memory matches this bound with a constant independent of $p,r,a$. We also separately bound the costs of reads and writes in this workload. Lastly, public requests can in some cases be made cheaper by offloading their cost to preparation in earlier requests or cleanup in later ones. For both public reads and writes, we show localized tradeoffs constrained to a subset of requests, which demonstrate some of the limitations of such offloading.
papers.authors: Wojciech Ciszewski, Emanuele Ragnoli

papers.title: Adaptive Leaky LWE and Its Security
papers.abstract: The Leaky LWE problem, proposed by Lai, Swarnakar, and Woo (CiC '25), studies whether LWE samples remain pseudorandom in the presence of noisy linear information about their secrets and errors. In Leaky LWE, the leakage matrix may depend on the public matrix, but must be chosen before the LWE challenge is revealed. We study $t$-round adaptive Leaky LWE, where each leakage matrix may depend on the challenge and all preceding leakage answers. Under explicit norm, smoothing, and sampling conditions, we reduce Gaussian-secret LWE to this problem at the corresponding source parameters for polynomially many rounds. The reduction preserves the public-matrix distribution and access to its correlated oracle, and supports rectangular leakage matrices and non-spherical discrete Gaussians over arbitrary orders in number fields.
papers.authors: Chuanqi Zhang, Muhammed F. Esgin, Ron Steinfeld

papers.title: Overcoming Padding in Cryptography via Hardness of Certifying Random Strings
papers.abstract: Modern cryptography relies on a provable security paradigm where the security of a primitive is established from the intractability of one or more computational problems. Hybrid arguments are central to this approach. Somewhat unexpectedly, many security proofs in the literature that use this methodology require hybrids with description-size larger than the real scheme. To argue security, the real scheme is artificially padded to match this size. This so-called “superfluous padding” phenomenon is surprisingly commonplace and poses a barrier to achieving succinct cryptographic primitives where the size of the scheme parameters does not grow with the input length. We present a framework to eliminate padding in cryptography. We demonstrate several applications, including rate-1 iO, succinct (and extractable) witness encryption and succinct non-interactive arguments with short CRS for subclasses of NP, and multi-input functional encryption for functions with unbounded arity. To obtain our results, we establish a new connection between cryptography and proof complexity. Central to our approach is the notion of proof-complexity generators (PCGs) [Krajíček'01, Alekhnovich, Ben-Sasson, Razborov, Wigderson'04], which, informally speaking, formalizes the hardness of certifying random (incompressible) strings with propositional proof systems. Our applications are derived from a master theorem that lifts cryptographic security on “compressible instances” to security on any instance under the existence of PCGs. Due to its broad scope, this theorem might find future application
papers.authors: Yao-Ching Hsieh, Abhishek Jain, Jiatu Li, Surya Mathialagan

papers.title: From Attack Surface to Defense Architecture: Compositional Security for Agentic Coding Harnesses
papers.abstract: AI coding harnesses couple language models to shells, filesystems, and network sockets, turning the harness into an automated Living-off-the-Land (LotL) platform: once an adversary injects instructions into retrieved content, dual-use binaries such as bash, curl, and find become the payload. We argue that security in agentic systems is a structural property of the cognitive architecture and permission composition rather than an emergent property of individual models. Static regex blacklists miss structural evasions, whereas LLM-as-a-Judge guardrails incur high latency while over-blocking benign work. We present ActiveSecHarness, a neurosymbolic reference-monitor architecture built around Separation of Intelligence and Authority. It combines (1) Macaroon-inspired HMAC capability tokens across four Trust and Authority Rings, (2) a 2D product taint lattice $\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{trust}} \times \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sens}}$ and a workspace provenance ledger that prevents secret laundering across disk, (3) deterministic Ring-0 OS/tool guards, and (4) bytecode certificates, split-horizon audit logs, self-healing security test synthesis, and an adaptive UserWikiManager. Across $N=252$ fixtures ($120$ attack, $120$ benign, $12$ kill chains), a live local LLM judge (qwen3:4b) refuses $98.3\%$ of benign work at $142.3\,\mathrm{ms}$ latency, whereas Ring 0 achieves $\mathrm{ABR}=1.000$ and $\mathrm{FPR}=0.000$ in $12.7\,μ\mathrm{s}$ ($11{,}200\times$ faster). In a multi-step trajectory ablation, an oracle Conseca-style stateless policy misses $4/12$ kill chains ($\mathrm{ABR}=0.667$) and coarse Boolean taint blocks $83.3\%$ of benign workflows, while our 2D product lattice achieves $\mathrm{ABR}=1.000$ and $\mathrm{FPR}=0.000$ at $\approx 20\,μ\mathrm{s}$ per step.
papers.authors: Simon Hegelich, Bardh Prenkaj, Habiba Sarhan, Morteza Shahrezaye, Kolja Hegelich, Christian Montag, Ralf Schneider, Erik Cambria

papers.title: MOAI: Module-Optimizing Architecture for non-interactive secure transformer Inference
papers.abstract: Privacy concerns have been raised in Large Language Models (LLM) inference when models are deployed in Cloud Service Providers (CSP). Homomorphic encryption (HE) offers a promising solution by enabling secure inference directly over encrypted inputs. However, the high computational overhead of HE remains a major bottleneck. To address this challenge, we propose MOAI, an efficient HE-based, non-interactive framework for secure transformer inference. MOAI gains significant efficiency improvement from: (1) a novel evaluation flow that combines column and diagonal packing with consistent strategies across all layers, eliminating expensive format conversions. (2) rotation-free algorithms for Softmax and LayerNorm that significantly reduce the number of costly HE rotations, removing 2,448 HE rotations in BERT-base inference. (3) Column packing removes rotations in plaintext-ciphertext matrix multiplications and interleaved batching further reduces the rotations in ciphertext-ciphertext matrix multiplications. MOAI uses at least 1.7x fewer HE rotations compared to the state-of-the-art works across all matrix multiplications of BERT-base. As a result, we achieve a $52.8 \%$ reduction in evaluation time compared to the state-of-the-art HE-based non-interactive secure transformer inference, THOR (Moon et al., CCS 25). We then apply MOAI on the Powerformer's framework and achieve a $55.7 \%$ reduction in evaluation time compared to Powerformer (Park et al., ACL 25), which approximates Softmax and LayerNorm with simpler functions in transformer and proposes HE-based non-interactive transformer inference. We report an amortized time of 2.36 minutes per input on a single GPU environment. We show the extendibility by applying MOAI in LLaMA-3-8B. Our implementation is publicly available as open source.
papers.authors: Linru Zhang, Xiangning Wang, Jun Jie Sim, Zhicong Huang, Jiahao Zhong, Huaxiong Wang, Pu Duan, Kwok-Yan Lam

papers.title: How wide must an eavesdropper be? Leakage of a toric-code logical bit to a strip and the Nishimori point
papers.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computers hand pieces of each logical qubit to separate decoder modules and shared readout lines. How much does a piece reveal? We prove that for any region and any Pauli noise, including correlated noise, an observer's optimal advantage in learning a logical bit is exactly 1 - 2 P_fail, where P_fail is the failure probability of maximum-likelihood decoding confined to that region. Two lessons follow. Geometry, not noise, provides the protection: a region that misses a single column of the code learns exactly nothing at any noise level, while a region that spans the code is protected by noise only at impractical distances (d > 350 for one row at a 10^-3 flip rate). And width is a poor guide to risk: under i.i.d. noise a two-row strip learns exactly as little as one row, yet below threshold an eavesdropper needs a width growing only as ln d. Through the identity, the strip's operational threshold is the Nishimori point of the random-bond Ising model, and a Walsh-Hadamard transfer matrix up to width 16 locates it to within a few thousandths. On two IBM Heron processors (d = 3, 5), an emulated strip adversary shows the predicted jump at width three, and non-uniform qubit errors let a trained attacker profit from the second row that uniform noise makes useless. We turn these results into design rules for partitioned decoding and multiplexed readout. Code and data are included.
papers.authors: Konstantinos Karagiannis

papers.title: The Closest Vector Problem on Gadget Lattices: Efficient Algorithms and Voronoi Geometry
papers.abstract: Gadget lattices are a prominent family of lattices widely used in lattice-based cryptography, error-correcting codes, and computational complexity. We present efficient algorithms for the Closest Vector Problem (CVP) on power and CRT gadget lattices and their duals, handling arbitrary real-valued target vectors. For the parity-check power gadget lattice, we give a practical, deterministic O(n) linear-time exact CVP solver based on a new, specialized "deferred greedy" graph-cut technique. Through an explicit characterization of the Voronoi cell, we provide a comprehensive analysis of existing decoders: we prove that the standard BDD algorithm of Micciancio and Peikert (2012) unexpectedly solves CVP exactly for odd base b and integer targets, but degrades to a worst-case approximation factor of n^0.5 for binary base b=2 and continuous targets. Furthermore, we prove that standard pruned sphere decoding requires exponential time exp(Omega(n)) even when using a geometrically optimal basis. For the dual (generator) power gadget lattice, we construct an obtuse superbasis---proving for the first time that it is a lattice of "Voronoi's first kind"---which yields a polynomial-time O(n^3) exact CVP algorithm via graph min-cut reductions. Geometrically, we determine all successive minima and enumerate the facets of their Voronoi cells. In particular, we show that while the parity-check lattice has a sparse Voronoi cell with n^2+n facets, the generator lattice reaches the theoretical upper bound of 2(2^n-1) facets. Finally, we observe that CRT gadget lattices and their duals admit an orthogonal basis, yielding trivial linear-time CVP algorithms.
papers.authors: Daniele Micciancio

papers.title: A Focus on Hermite Constant 11
papers.abstract: This paper assembles the dimension-eleven argument in a series on the Hermite constants in dimensions ten, eleven and twelve. The root paper reduces a hypothetical lattice of minimum 4 and determinant below 972 to a chain of sections of ranks eleven, ten and nine. Its rank-nine section is marked by a perfect form below an explicit determinant cutoff. The global finite computation leaves 4 487 813 candidate forms and excludes all but ten by certificates. We state the mathematical content of these certificates, describe their data and checking rules, and prove why every valid certificate excludes the corresponding form. The four formats are trace, domain, glue and tree certificates; each tree must cover its entire stated domain. One of the ten remaining cases, 0052:005247066, is treated here by a complete gluing cover. Five companion papers settle the other nine. We also prove the common inequalities used by those local arguments. The resulting bound is $\gamma_{11}=4/\sqrt[11]{972}$, conditional on the attributed rank-nine classification, the rank-ten census and the stated global and local finite checks.
papers.authors: Rémi Géraud-Stewart, David Naccache

papers.title: The Hermite Constants in Dimensions 10, 11 and 12
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a series of seven papers establishing $\gamma_{10}^{10}=4^{10}/768$, $\gamma_{11}^{11}=4^{11}/972$ and $\gamma_{12}=4/\sqrt{3}$, under the attributed classification of perfect forms of rank nine and the explicitly stated computational inputs. The argument treats the dimensions in order. In dimension ten, a section orthogonal to a shortest dual vector is compared with a perfect form. A completed exact census leaves three possible reference forms, and matrix inequalities exclude a determinant below 768 in each case. In dimension eleven, two successive sections give a chain of ranks eleven, ten and nine. The dimension-ten bound controls the determinant of the last section. The verified global census and preliminary certificates reduce the problem to ten local cases: nine are treated in five companion papers, and one in “A Focus on Hermite Constant 11”. The local arguments combine contact geometry, section bounds and finite rational covers. Mordell’s inequality then gives the dimension-twelve upper bound, matched by the Coxeter–Todd lattice. We prove the common reduction, explain the dependency between the papers, and state exactly which finite assertions must be checked. The accompanying Lean development verifies the complete analytic deduction from those inputs; external exact checkers verify the large certificate data.
papers.authors: Rémi Géraud-Stewart, David Naccache

papers.title: Revisiting the Security of OleF, t-OleF, and OlÆF
papers.abstract: We revisit the security of OleF, t-OleF, and \olaef\ and identify two independent security flaws. First, we establish a mask-compensation relation between continuation and termination processing in OleF and t-OleF. Exploiting this relation, we construct a two-encryption-query distinguisher against OleF with advantage $1-2^{-2n}$. We further give two concrete AXU hash families for which the same attack applies to t-OleF, revealing flaws in the original DOSPRP and SPRTOP security proofs. We extend these attacks to \olaef\ through valid encodings, breaking its privacy and integrity. In particular, the integrity forgery succeeds with probability $1$ under full-domain verification when the target expansion length is $1$ and extends to larger expansion lengths under suffix-only verification. Second, we refute the claimed ideal RUP integrity bound for variable-expansion online authenticated encryption. Even with an ideal tweakable online permutation, prior unverified decryption queries at smaller expansion lengths can reveal part of the target authentication suffix. We construct counterexamples showing that two such decryption queries and one forgery attempt achieve a success probability of $3/8$, exceeding the claimed bound of $1/4$. We also derive a general expression for the forgery success probability. Finally, we discuss the corresponding repairing
papers.authors: Tingting Guo, Peng Wang, Shuping Mao, Yan Jia, Jiadong Han

papers.title: Designing Quantum-Safe Network Architectures via Certified Randomness Distribution
papers.abstract: We propose an alternative design for quantum-safe network architectures, based on distributing certified randomness generated by different trust-level QRNGs. Our modular methodology aggregates high-trust entropy from upper network layers with local contributions, enhancing the security guarantees of locally available random sequences. Leveraging the physical guarantees of QRNGs and symmetric-key cryptographic algorithms for node authentication, our approach enables immediately deployable, quantum-safe infrastructures. Such a paradigm bypasses the practical security limitations of current QKD-based solutions, while avoiding massive key sizes and latency inherent to asymmetric PQC implementations.
papers.authors: Filip-Ioan Ceară, Diana Maimuţ

papers.title: On Composing Oracle Separations
papers.abstract: Black-box separations constitute very powerful technical barriers against constructing primitives from specific building blocks. However, they give surprisingly little indication on the usefulness of \emph{combining} several such building blocks in a single construction. We propose a set of technical conditions, under which (fully) black-box separations compose with each other. That is, if two black-box separations $P_1 \stackrel{BB}{\nRightarrow} Q$ and $P_2 \stackrel{BB}{\nRightarrow} Q$ satisfy our conditions, then $Q$ is also separated from black-box combinations of $P_1$ and $P_2$. When applicable, these conditions can be established without unpacking the full technical details of the base separations. As our main application, we show that combining indistinguishability obfuscation (iO) with collision resistant hash functions is unlikely to yield hard problems in the complexity class $SZK$, and thus unlikely to suffice for primitives such as lossy functions or fully homomorphic encryption. Previous lower bounds on iO only applied to combinations of iO with one-way permutations (Asharov-Segev, FOCS '15 and Bitansky-Degwekar-Vaikuntanathan, SIAM Journal on Computing '21).
papers.authors: Willy Quach, Felix Rohrbach

papers.title: γ₁₁: Unequal Triangles and Adapted References — the macadamia 0050
papers.abstract: This paper settles the ninth of the ten macadamias of the series on the Hermite constant in dimension 11: the perfect form $P$ = 0050:024468269 of rank 9, of determinant 8192/9 at minimum 4. The root paper reduces $\gamma_{11}$ to chains $L\supset M\supset N$ of lattices of ranks 11, 10, 9, each with minimum at least 4; we prove that every admissible chain whose rank-9 member is admissibly marked by $P$ has $\det L\ge 972$. No argument at rank 10 can do this, because an actual lattice of rank 10 with determinant $3328/3<4\cdot 972^{9/11}$ lies over $P$. The proof is computer-assisted, with explicit finite checks. Its decisive step is elementary: the three additive dual vectors of a section covector and the first normal usually have different lengths, and keeping the three lengths in the circle obstruction, instead of their maximum, gives a determinant cap that sharpens every subsequent contact and spectral bound. Adapted reference forms turn the contact conditions into exact rational tests, a common slack is retained throughout, and four computational results reduce the problem to a five-parameter root, exhausted by a finite cover of 6 993 terminal regions replayed in exact arithmetic.
papers.authors: Rémi Géraud-Stewart, David Naccache

papers.title: γ₁₁: One Selected Contact, Two Linked Blocks — the macadamia 0030
papers.abstract: This paper is one of five companion papers completing the proof of $\gamma_{11}=4/\sqrt[11]{972}$ announced in the root paper and assembled in “A Focus on Hermite Constant 11”. The root paper reduces a lattice of rank 11 with minimum 4 and determinant below 972 to a chain of sections of ranks 11, 10 and 9 whose rank-9 member is admissibly marked by one of 4 487 813 perfect forms; ten of them, the macadamias, lie under an actual lattice of rank 10 and need proofs of their own. We settle the first, the form 0030:030301719 of $\Lambda_9$ under $\Lambda_{10}$, where the bound has little margin. The argument selects one contact of the reference lattice from the actual metric, keeps the off-diagonal column shared by two eight-dimensional blocks of the section metric, applies one determinant–trace theorem to both blocks, and closes with a rational cover of three scalar parameters. The proof is computer-assisted: its finite inputs are three outer-range covers, two middle-range covers with 10 498 and 1 140 leaves, an annulus tree with 3 567 leaves and four smaller trees, every leaf checked in exact rational arithmetic.
papers.authors: Rémi Géraud-Stewart, David Naccache

papers.title: γ₁₁: Reduction by Sections — the macadamias 0019 and 0017
papers.abstract: The root paper of this series reduces the value $\gamma_{11}=4/\sqrt[11]{972}$ of the Hermite constant in dimension 11 to a statement about chains $L\supset M\supset N$ of lattices of ranks 11, 10 and 9 whose rank-9 member lies over one of 4 487 813 perfect forms of rank 9; the $\gamma_{11}$ paper settles all of them but ten, the macadamias. This paper settles two of the ten: 0019:030884313 (the form $P_S$ of the root paper, an extension of $E_8$ by a simplex vector) and 0017:001746552 (the form $P_K$, KAPPA9.2). We prove that every admissible chain whose rank-9 member is admissibly marked by the form has $\det L\ge 972$. The method is a reduction by sections: for 0019 the nine simplex contacts turn the problem into one about an eight-dimensional covariance matrix, and a tree of 17 347 nodes with 7 743 scalar determinant witnesses covers the remaining box; for 0017 a two-vector flag bound and the decomposition of the section metric along a short-dual plane and its rank-seven kernel reduce the problem to five parameters, covered by a tree of 3 010 595 nodes. The proof is computer-assisted: every finite check is stated as a Computational result, and the verification records in the certificate archive are named.
papers.authors: Rémi Géraud-Stewart, David Naccache

papers.title: γ₁₁: A Finite Spectral Relaxation — the macadamia 0008
papers.abstract: The root paper of this series reduces $\gamma_{11}=4/\sqrt[11]{972}$ to a statement about chains of lattices $L\supset M\supset N$ of ranks 11, 10 and 9, cut along shortest dual vectors, whose rank-9 member lies over one of 4 487 813 perfect forms. Ten of these forms, the macadamias, lie under an actual lattice of rank 10 of small determinant and need a proof at rank 11, where the bound 972 is attained. This paper settles the form 0008:022143116, which lies under a section of $K_{11}$ with 276 minimal vectors: every admissible chain whose rank-9 member is admissibly marked by this form has $\det L\ge 972$. In coordinates aligned with the form, the section metric is $S=I+E$ with three blocks of size three. Two sufficient flag tests come from short dual covectors and integral triangles; local reductions, proved from rational comparisons and Bernstein or Sturm certificates, remove explicit regions of the parameters; every remaining real spectrum is mapped, with explicit allowances, into a finite relaxation on 81 grid nodes, which a tree of 400 nodes with 1 091 rational certificates, replayed in two exact arithmetic implementations, excludes. The proof is computer-assisted, with explicit finite checks stated as one Computational result.
papers.authors: Rémi Géraud-Stewart, David Naccache

papers.title: γ₁₁: Contact Geometry — the macadamias 0001, 0014, 0059 and 0015
papers.abstract: The root paper of this series reduces the value $\gamma_{11}=4/\sqrt[11]{972}$ of the Hermite constant to a statement about chains of lattices $L\supset M\supset N$ of ranks 11, 10 and 9 whose rank-9 member lies, in the sense of Voronoi, over one of 4 487 813 perfect forms; the $\gamma_{11}$ paper excludes all of them but ten, the macadamias. This paper settles four macadamias, the forms 0001:010488327, 0014:001749549, 0059:016902802 and 0015:030291998, by one method: the geometry of the contacts of the form. A section frame of short dual vectors forces the first gluing of $M$ over $N$ to lie near one of finitely many coherent centres; at such a centre the rank-10 metric is compared with an explicit reference lattice, whose Delaunay cells and contact identities give a uniform bound on its covering radius; and a primitive-extension inequality turns that bound into $\det L\ge 972$. The proof is computer-assisted: every finite check it uses is stated as a Computational result with the records of the certificate archive that certify it, and all comparisons are between explicit rational numbers.
papers.authors: Rémi Géraud-Stewart, David Naccache

papers.title: More Keys, Less Commitment: Key-Committing Attacks on BBB Accordions via Encode-then-Encipher and a Key-Committing Transform
papers.abstract: Cryptographic accordions with beyond-birthday-bound (BBB) security are being actively studied in connection with NIST’s ongoing standardization effort. We show that BBB security of an accordion does not necessarily strengthen key commitment of AE built from it: in many BBB accordions, additional keys introduced for BBB security give an adversary extra degrees of freedom. Exploiting this observation, we present $O(1)$ key-committing attacks on a broad range of AE schemes built from BBB accordions, mostly via the Encode-then-Encipher (EtE) paradigm, including CHCTR2, eCTR-based accordions, THCTR, HCTR+, TCT2, and bbb-ddd-AES under a natural polynomial-hash instantiation. To address this issue, we propose CACH, a black-box transform from BBB-secure accordions to robust AE (RAE) with key-committing security. CACH achieves BBB multi-user RAE security and achieves $t/2$-bit key-committing security with a $t$-bit tag for $n \le t \le 2n$ in the ideal-cipher model. CACH uses only AES-based components and supports all AES key sizes, making it compatible with NIST’s design goals. We instantiate CACH with CHCTR2. CACH-CHCTR2 with AES-256 outperforms EtE-HCTR2 with Rijndael-256 and EtE-CHCTR2 for short messages.
papers.authors: Donghoon Chang, Yukihito Hiraga, Yusuke Naito, Yu Sasaki, Takeshi Sugawara

papers.title: 5G CATS: 5G-Based Cryptographic Authorization Against Trafficking of Semiconductor Devices
papers.abstract: Enforcing export controls on AI accelerators requires verifying where a chip operates after deployment. Round-trip time measurements can bound a chip's distance from a trusted landmark, but any jitter in honest replies forces the verifier to loosen its timeout, giving an attacker slack to relay traffic over fiber from a restricted region. Prior approaches either cross the untrusted host stack or rely on noisy power-line channels that inflate this slack. We present 5G CATS, a location certification system that pairs a co-packaged 5G radio, cryptographic engine, and hardware interlock on the GPU package with 5G Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication (URLLC) base stations. Terminating the radio link inside the package removes the host software, PCIe fabric, and baseboard management controller from the verification path. We map an authenticated challenge-response protocol onto 5G's slot structure, replace permanent key erasure with short-lived execution leases, and specify a cross-check of the chip's reported serving cell against the carrier's own attachment records. In ns-3 and 5G-LENA simulations of an unloaded cell, our URLLC-based radio profile narrows the 99.9th percentile round-trip spread to 2.60 ms, more than ten times narrower than default 5G. A tracer rejects every round of a fiber relay from 300 km, against 2,000 km for default 5G. Against a 3,000 km attacker, a tracer stays safe at up to 1,410 km from the chip, against at most 619 km for PowerCATS's published model, while default 5G is never safe.
papers.authors: Sreevikram Rajaraman, Derek Ladd, Nicholas Heinrich-Barna, Srinivas Shakkottai, Jeyavijayan Rajendran

papers.title: No finite rulebook can certify every safe program: an impossibility theorem for gatekeeping AI agents
papers.abstract: An AI assistant writes small programs, and a gatekeeper must decide, from the code alone, whether each one may run. Suppose the rules are fixed: never perform a forbidden action, never let the output depend on a secret, always answer eventually. Can two rulebooks, one listing what is allowed and one listing what is not, both be complete, if every rule must be backed by evidence that a machine can check in finite time? We prove that they cannot. Checkable evidence can only establish what a finite record settles, and ``never'' and ``eventually'' are never settled by a finite record. For prohibitions the failure is one-sided: every violation can be caught by watching, but no safe program can be cleared for good. For confidentiality and responsiveness, neither side can be. We characterise exactly which rules about visible behaviour evidence can confirm, and we show that any sound rulebook of $n$ bits omits a compliant program of about $n$ bits. A time limit makes everything checkable, but only by running the program for essentially the whole limit, so a finite machine is not a feasible one. Finally, we show what a gatekeeper can still guarantee: not a verdict on every program, but a checkable list that contains everything it must allow and nothing it must refuse. Simulations on 2.2 million random programs and on self-referential adversaries show that the obstruction is adversarial rather than typical, and that the one error a longer test never removes is the liveness part of confidentiality.
papers.authors: Tomas Perez-Acle

papers.title: Latent Barrier Steering: Hierarchical Safety for Generative Planning
papers.abstract: We introduce Latent Barrier Steering (LBS), a hierarchical semantic-to-path framework for safe flow-matching-based generative planning. Existing control-barrier-function (CBF) safety filters for diffusion and flow-matching planners act locally on generated samples, either during sampling or after prediction. Such repair is effective for small violations, but can struggle when a new constraint blocks the whole selected behavior mode rather than merely perturbing it locally. LBS decouples behavior selection from path certification through two coordinated interventions: it first steers the generator's behavior latent toward rollouts with larger safety margin, then decodes the steered latent and applies a path-space CBF quadratic program (QP) only for residual violations. We show that latent steering increases the margin available to the path-space corrector, yielding finite-time recovery guarantees and reduced correction burden. Experiments across navigation and robot end-effector planning tasks show that LBS preserves safety while improving goal reaching and reducing correction burden compared with path-level safety filters.
papers.authors: Renhao Zhang, Mingzhe Li, Bruno Castro da Silva

papers.title: MammothDP: Private Boosted Decision Trees Ready for Trusted Hardware and Leakage-free Hyperparameters
papers.abstract: Data spaces like the European Health Data Space (EHDS) require the protection of sensitive data in studies during the data's processing and the study's release alike. In this work, we investigate how to implement this mandate using established trusted execution environments (TEEs) and timing side-channel hardening to protect the processing even under a compromised server, and the state-of-the-art differential privacy (DP) notion to protect the release of studies on tabular data. This combined setup could seem to complete the picture, but in fact raises unexpected security challenges that we mitigate by introducing MammothDP: a significant milestone towards a holistic machine learning system based on the recent gradient boosted decision tree learner S-BDT that is provably DP if used within a privacy filter, timing side-channel hardened, and deployed on a TEE. To achieve a strong privacy-utility tradeoff, we introduce two novel components: an early stopping criterion that adaptively selects the number of trees without any privacy overhead, and an improved rollback protection that is no longer vulnerable under timing side-channel attacks.
papers.authors: Moritz Kirschte, Thorsten Peinemann, Kari Kostiainen, Jan Wichelmann, Thomas Eisenbarth, Esfandiar Mohammadi

papers.title: GARD: Gradient-Guided Adversarial Representation Defense against Backdoors in Multimodal Contrastive Learning Models
papers.abstract: Multimodal contrastive learning models such as CLIP are vulnerable to backdoor attacks with diverse trigger structures, ranging from localized patches to globally distributed perturbations, with recent attacks increasingly optimizing these triggers in the representation space. Existing post-hoc defenses based on clean fine-tuning may leave backdoors active, while trigger-inversion methods depend on accurately estimating the attack target and trigger. We observe that backdoored encoders exhibit structure-dependent representation sensitivity: global perturbations preferentially expose distributed backdoors, whereas local patch perturbations are more effective for localized backdoors. Based on this observation, we propose Gradient-Guided Adversarial Representation Defense (GARD), a target- and trigger-agnostic post-hoc defense. GARD optimizes complementary global and local adversarial probes to maximally displace clean-image representations, and then realigns the perturbed representations with detached clean anchors while preserving image-text alignment. The resulting model requires no additional computation at inference time. Across six visual backdoor attacks and two CLIP visual backbones, GARD reduces the attack success rate below 1% in all 12 evaluated attack-backbone combinations while maintaining competitive clean accuracy. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of adversarial representation probing for repairing backdoored multimodal contrastive encoders.
papers.authors: Yuhong Wang, Yujun Cai, Lei Feng, Songze Li

papers.title: What a CAGE 4 Score Measures: An Audit of a Learned Cyber-Defense Benchmark, Its Reference Defenders, and the Tables Built on Them
papers.abstract: CAGE Challenge 4 is the benchmark on which learned multi-agent cyber defenders are compared. We reproduce its two reference defenders, KEEP and H-MARL Expert, in a pinned container and show that three things read from it measure less than they are taken to measure. First, the simulator silently discards any action asserted for an agent whose previous action is still running, and charges one point for a discarded Restore as for one that runs. The documented observation does not expose the busy flag. Both reference defenders read it in their own wrappers, and switching that check off at evaluation costs KEEP's released policy 99.58 points per episode and H-MARL's 145.98, in both cases the charge for Restores sent to busy agents, with H-MARL's executed actions unchanged step for step. On a supervisory harness, holding interventions until the agent is idle is worth 25.3 and 27.6 points per episode at the published setting. In training, the check decides how a busy step enters the trajectory. Trained without it, KEEP leads at a hundred updates in all four paired seeds and trails from two hundred on in all four. Continued to two thousand updates on three seeds, the repaired recipe ends inside the released interval on one seed and short on two, by 27 and 125 points, a spread across training seeds far wider than the released reproduction interval. Second, the evaluation seeds the environment but not the policy, so a reported mean is one draw, and 88.9% of per-episode outcome variance is the policy's own sampling draw. Third, recovery precision depends on the truth it is scored against. Across five published comparison tables, none states the artifact, sampling, criterion and adversary that would make its numbers comparable. We release the instrument, our patches to both defenders, the traces and checkpoints behind every number, and a five-item disclosure checklist.
papers.authors: James Rice, Ji Hwan Park, Andres Kwasinski

papers.title: Isolation Is Not Confidentiality: Security Boundaries of Geometric Access Control in RAG
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems increasingly rely on vector databases containing documents governed by different access-control policies. Recent search-preserving geometric approaches enforce such access control by structuring the embedding space so that transformed embeddings, which we call protected representations, remain retrievable without exposing information across policy boundaries. We provide a unified security analysis of this paradigm, covering policy isolation, representation confidentiality, query forgery resistance, and policy-membership hiding. We consider both a curious cloud service provider observing the protected representations stored in the vector database and a curious user holding aligned pairs of original embeddings and protected representations. Evaluating the available implementations of the works proposing these geometric transformation mechanisms across three encoders, we find that geometric transformations preserve retrieval utility and provide strong policy isolation, but do not provide the other security properties. A curious user can recover the original embeddings from a few hundred pairs and forge policy-compatible queries at a higher cost that grows with encoder dimension for secret per-policy transformations. Moreover, policy-dependent geometry can leak policy membership even when unauthorized retrieval is prevented. These results show that policy isolation, confidentiality, forgery resistance, and membership hiding are distinct security objectives.
papers.authors: Steve Nouyep, Maxime Puys, Sébastien Salva

papers.title: Domain-Invariant and Language-Model-Assisted Acoustic Side-Channel Attacks on Keyboards
papers.abstract: Acoustic side-channel attacks (ASCA) recover typed text from the sound of keystrokes, using only a commodity microphone and no access to the victim's device. Prior work establishes that such attacks succeed under idealized laboratory conditions - a single keyboard, a fixed microphone, a quiet room, and training and testing on the same device but leaves open the question that matters for security: whether keystroke inference survives the open world of unseen keyboards, diverse users, noisy environments, and compressed transmission channels. The answer developed here is that it does, provided the acoustic model is made explicitly domain-invariant and its noisy predictions are corrected by a language model.
papers.authors: Bikrant Bikram Pratap Maurya

papers.title: Splitting for Stability: a Modified Reward Scheme for Transaction-Fee-Only Regimes
papers.abstract: As Bitcoin's block subsidy declines over time, miner revenue will come to depend increasingly on transaction fees. In fee-dominated regimes, winner-take-all reward structures can create incentives for undercutting and fork-based mining strategies, leading to instability and reduced transaction throughput. To prevent this instability, we propose a reward-splitting mechanism in which the winning block producer receives an $α$-portion of the block reward, while the rest is distributed among other miners; this incentivizes mining on previous blocks with higher rewards, while preserving the incentive to produce blocks with high rewards. We evaluate the proposed reward structure through analysis and simulation. Our analysis derives a local profitability condition for one-step Function-Fork deviations, showing how the winner-side reward, loser-side subsidy, and honest hash power jointly determine whether undercutting is profitable. Simulations show parameter regions in which honest behavior dominates fork-based deviations. In the cases where forking becomes dominant, the learned strategy is the least aggressive variant studied. The analysis and simulations suggest that suitable reward-splitting parameters can reduce the honest participation needed to suppress aggressive forking strategies relative to the winner-take-all structure studied in prior work. Finally, we show that the modified reward scheme does not appear to worsen selfish mining incentives. Together, these results suggest that reward redistribution can mitigate fee-driven fork incentives without introducing stronger selfish mining incentives, providing a possible direction for incentive design in fee-era proof-of-work systems.
papers.authors: Eric Brigham, Baigang Chen, Nicholas Hopper

papers.title: Useful Work Can Increase Energy Use: Demand Elasticity and Proof of Useful Work
papers.abstract: A serious criticism of Bitcoin's Proof-of-Work is its enormous electricity consumption. Proof-of-Useful-Work (PoUW), introduced by Ball, Rosen, Sabin, and Vasudevan (2017), in which mining performs useful computations, was suggested as an alternative to reduce electricity expenditure, with matrix multiplication (MatMul) as a recent concrete instantiation by Komargodski and Weinstein (2026). Perhaps surprisingly, we show that switching to PoUW may increase the total electricity consumption, echoing Jevons' paradox. Intuitively, the PoUW mechanism acts as a subsidy that lowers the effective price of the useful work. Recall that demand is elastic if a discount of x percent in the price leads to an increase of more than x percent in the quantity demanded. If demand is elastic, the resulting increase in quantity demanded leads to a net increase in total electricity consumption; if inelastic, total electricity consumption decreases. Even then, the electricity consumption due to PoUW never vanishes, since the mining subsidy is spent on useful work that would not have been produced without the subsidy. This result is proved in a simple model with electricity-only costs, no PoUW overhead, and an unchanged mining subsidy. The analysis extends to less restrictive settings with adjusted thresholds.
papers.authors: Isaiah Hull, Or Sattath

papers.title: Enabling Memory Encryption Using Ascon Derivatives
papers.abstract: Keeping data stored in memory confidential is a tough challenge when assuming an adversary with physical access to it. First, we have fine-grained access to typically 256 to 512 bits at once, so nonces or tags of the typical sizes used for authenticated encryption would lead to a sizeable overhead. Second, we have stringent performance requirements, including low latency that directly impacts CPU performance and, more generally, strict area and energy constraints, especially for the high bandwidth of memory interfaces. Currently, memory encryption solutions typically rely on the AES block cipher. In this paper, we explore ways of using Ascon as a building block for memory encryption. Our analysis shows that Ascon-based constructions achieve better performance than AES-based HCTR2 and can also compete with XTS-AES while providing larger block sizes.
papers.authors: Sergej Deutsch, Christoph Dobraunig, David Durham, Simon Johnson, Krystian Matusiewicz, Carlos Rozas, Alexander Tereschenko

papers.title: DKG: A Dual-Layer Knowledge Graph and LLM Co-Driven Framework for Fully Automated Side-Channel Analysis of Cryptosystems
papers.abstract: Cryptographic algorithms underpin billions of devices, from payment smartcards to smartphone secure enclaves and industrial controllers. Yet their physical implementations risk leaking secret keys. Non-profiled side-channel analysis (SCA) evaluates whether such leakage enables key recovery, but executing it end-to-end remains expert-intensive. Large language model (LLM) agents now automate complex workflows across many domains, yet reliable key recovery requires specialized SCA knowledge that must be extracted and organized from scattered technical literature. In this paper, we propose DKG, a dual-layer knowledge graph and LLM co-driven key-recovery agent framework. We introduce the first graph schema designed specifically for SCA: an upper layer of configuration components and a lower layer of diagnostic strategies, joined by cross-layer relationships. An LLM-driven three-step extraction pipeline (Locate & Rewrite, Triple Extraction, and Knowledge Fusion) builds the graph from raw technical documents without manual annotation, and at runtime the retrieved knowledge drives a closed-loop autonomous attack workflow. Built from a corpus of 166 technical documents, the graph contains 1,334 entities and 1,813 relationships. On eight datasets covering AES, DES, and SM4 across smartcards, FPGAs, and MCUs, DKG with DeepSeek-V3.2 achieves a 97.5% end-to-end key-recovery success rate. By comparison, ReAct-RAG, a text-retrieval-augmented agent, achieves only 68.8%. Across the open-weights backbones DeepSeek-V3.2, GLM-5, and Qwen3.5, DKG achieves an average success rate of 93.3%. To the best of our knowledge, DKG is the first framework to achieve consistent end-to-end automated key recovery across diverse implementations. Its automated pipeline lets the graph grow with new literature, and its dual-layer organization provides a basis for extending DKG to additional SCA techniques.
papers.authors: Wenquan Zhou, An Wang, Yaoling Ding, Jiakun Li, Jingqi Zhang, Liehuang Zhu

papers.title: Undine: Distributed Extendable Merkle Tree Storage with Private Retrieval and Efficient Reconfiguration
papers.abstract: Clients of transparency logs, public-key directories, and shielded blockchain pools require authenticated access to an ever-changing Merkle tree, without storing it in full or revealing which entry they open. We seek to distribute storage and query work across independent servers as the data grows and participants join, leave, change their shares, or misbehave. We present Undine, which combines a distributed Merkle tree encoding with private retrieval from independently-maintained fragments. Maintainers can choose and efficiently adjust the size of their stored fragments, to offer a flexible tradeoff against the number of maintainer replies needed for authenticated data reconstruction by clients. Maintainers can also perform authenticated updates and appends, at a write cost of just twice the number of modified Merkle nodes. Undine uses a linear encoding of the Merkle tree nodes to divide evenly the storage and retrieval load across maintainers. This is combined with a private information retrieval (PIR) protocol that operates directly over the linearly-encoded fragments. Undine avoids repeated storage and computation for nodes shared by Merkle paths across records, producing the same PIR replies with work over tree values linear in the filled prefix. Record sizes adapt as the prefix grows to balance query and reply sizes. Clients verify against the Merkle root, without commitments to individual PIR databases. Computational query privacy holds against any coalition. Undine is also secure against selective-failure leakage (i.e., deductions from acceptance), up to the PIR backend's correctness error, given enough timely honest replies, fixed public timing, and no reply-dependent follow-up. We evaluate UndineLog, our append-only implementation of Undine combined with YPIR. On a height-50 sparse Merkle tree with a 4GiB prefix of nonempty 32-byte leaves and a reconstruction threshold of 64, a maintainer replies in 100ms (single-core); a client can process 192 replies from maintainers and reconstruct a verified opening in 380ms, even with 64 corrupted replies. Scaled up to 1TiB and 256 threshold , a maintainer answers in 1.13s. Existing shielded pools can use this service without consensus changes.
papers.authors: Nicolas Alhaddad, Harry Eldridge, Julia Guskind, Eran Tromer, Mayank Varia

papers.title: Twisted Towers: A Faster and Fully Costed SexTNFS Attack
papers.abstract: We study the Special exTNFS attack on discrete logarithms in the target group $\mathbb{G}_T$ of BLS12-381. We give a (6,2) design in which every step is priced in one instruction-level model: relation collection, cofactorisation, filtering, linear algebra, the Block Wiedemann generator and both individual logarithms, at success probability at least 0.39. The design rests on an explicit twisted tower. The sextic base field has an involution $\sigma$ and a unit $c$ with $c\,\sigma(c)=-1$, so $\tau:(y,x)\mapsto(\sigma y,cx)$ has order 4 and acts on $\mathbb{F}_{p^{12}}$ as $\mathrm{Frob}^3$. Relations and ideals then come in orbits of four. The quotient linear system has Gaussian-integer entries read modulo $r$, and ten Schirokauer maps suffice. A norm-2 element of the base field enables a coset sieve. We also observe that yield estimates over TNFS coefficient cubes count unit multiples $(\varepsilon a,\varepsilon b)$ as distinct relations. For the valid polynomial pair closest to the published BLS12-381 design, only $2^{-2.81}$ of the smoothness-weighted cube points give distinct relations. Under stated heuristics the ledger is $2^{115.72}$ dense $\mathbb{F}_{p^{12}}$-multiplication equivalents, about $2^{130}$ AArch64 instructions. Under our instruction model and transferred pricing assumptions, the design is estimated to cost 0.74 to 1.08 bit less (about 0.8) than a fundamental-domain version of the published design. Under the published cost models the difference ranges from 0.57 bit in our favour to 0.19 bit against. Nothing was run at full size, and the practical security of BLS12-381 is unchanged.
papers.authors: Gautam Botrel

papers.title: The Minimum Bucket Capacity for Reliable Path ORAM
papers.abstract: Path ORAM hides memory access patterns by storing $N$ data blocks in a binary tree whose buckets have capacity $Z$, using a client-side stash for blocks that cannot be placed in the tree. Smaller buckets reduce storage and communication costs but increase the risk of stash overflow. The revised Path ORAM analysis in 2014 established an exponentially decreasing stash overflow probability for $Z \geq 5$. Experiments suggest small stashes at $Z=4$ and substantially larger ones at $Z=3$. However, it remained unknown whether $Z=4$ admits a uniform exponential stash bound or whether such a bound is impossible at $Z=3$. We establish a sharp threshold at $Z=4$ for binary Path ORAM with tree depth $L=\lceil \log_2 N \rceil$. For $Z=4$, we prove that, uniformly over all database sizes and fixed access sequences, the stash size $S$ after the final refill satisfies \[ \Pr[S>R] \leq \frac{23}{28}\left(\frac{5}{7}\right)^R \] for every integer $R \geq 0$. For $Z=3$, we exhibit a family of instances on which a single sequential scan of all $N$ blocks produces a stash of size $\Omega(N)$ with probability bounded away from zero. Thus, four is the minimum bucket capacity admitting a uniform exponential stash bound: a logarithmic stash suffices for polynomial-length executions with inverse-polynomial failure probability at $Z=4$, whereas at $Z=3$ no sublinear stash can make the overflow probability vanish uniformly. Our proofs connect the actual Path ORAM process with dependent node loads to an auxiliary model with independent geometric node loads. This independence enables a recursive analysis of overflow that avoids the union bound over rooted subtrees used in the previous $Z=5$ proof. The main challenge is to transfer bounds from the auxiliary model to the actual process, which requires different techniques for the upper and lower bounds. For $Z=4$, we develop a two-stage randomization argument that bounds the actual process's exponential overflow moment by that of the auxiliary model. For $Z=3$, we develop a local continuous-time approximation with controlled errors that transfers an overflow surplus from the auxiliary model to the actual process, yielding the linear stash lower bound. Together, these arguments establish the sharp threshold at bucket capacity four.
papers.authors: Yijia Chang, Man Ho Au

papers.title: Round-Optimal Statistical Verifiable Secret Sharing with Polynomial Complexity
papers.abstract: Verifiable secret sharing (Chor, Goldwasser, Micali, and Awerbuch; FOCS'85) is a central primitive in secure computation, and its round complexity has been studied extensively. Rabin and Ben-Or [STOC'89] established the feasibility of statistical security up to $t<n/2$ corruptions, and Patra, Choudhary, Rabin, and Rangan [Crypto'09] showed that three sharing rounds are necessary. The work of Applebaum, Kachlon and Patra [STOC'23] introduced the first round-optimal VSS with three rounds of sharing and one round for reconstruction, albeit with exponential communication in the number of parties. We give the first round-optimal statistical VSS that has polynomial communication and computation for $t<n/2$. This resolves the efficiency question left open by Applebaum, Kachlon and Patra. The protocol is obtained from a new notion of weak secret sharing, in which the reconstruction-time freedom of a corrupt dealer is limited to choosing verification keys, which is of independent interest.
papers.authors: Chen-Da Liu-Zhang, Elisaweta Masserova

papers.title: Registration-based Encryption with Logarithmic Registration
papers.abstract: Registration-based encryption (RBE) preserves IBE's identity-only encryption interface while eliminating key escrow: users generate their own keys, and a Key Curator manages only registered public keys. However, this design introduces a new challenge: user registration, since every joining user rrequires KC to update the registry. Although theoretical RBE constructions achieve polylogarithmic registration, they rely on costly cryptographic techniques and remain impractical. In existing deployable black-box RBE, registration takes $O(\sqrt{N})$ time ($N$ denotes the maximum user capacity). This gap between theoretical registration efficiency and deployability makes registration a key performance bottleneck for large-scale deployments of pairing-based RBE. This work presents a black-box pairing-based RBE construction under the decisional $(R,S,T,f)$-Diffie-Hellman assumption. Build on the multilinear tree, when registering a user's public key, KC updates only the corresponding root-to-leaf path associated with the user. Therefore, registration in our construction takes $O(\log \sqrt{N})$ time for the maximum user capacity $N$. Moreover, we provides membership and non-membership verification, and their batch verification supports to check registration status of multiple users. Experiments show registration and key generation complete in milliseconds when $N=10^7$. Compared with Glaeser et al. (CCS'23), our scheme accelerates registration by up to \(158\times\) and key generation by up to \(230\times\) with practical overheads.
papers.authors: Xingfu Yan, Guiqiu Liao, Fan Yang, Haining Yang, Zheng Gong, Fucai Luo, Bowen Zhao

papers.title: Constructions of Boolean Correctors with Optimal Nonlinearity and Vectorial Correctors Beyond Optimal Linear Correction Order
papers.abstract: Correctors are postprocessing functions that reduce or eliminate statistical bias in raw bitstreams produced by physical noise sources in true random number generators. In this paper, we develop a framework based on binary Krawtchouk polynomials for analyzing and constructing Boolean and vectorial correctors. This framework reformulates the Walsh-layer criterion into finite moment constraints on support-layer counts and preimage-layer counts. We also establish universal upper bounds on the nonlinearity of correctors, and necessary conditions on the achievable correction order. For Boolean functions, we prove that $(n-1)$-correctors are either the parity function or its complement. Then we characterize the support-layer profiles of $(n-2)$- and $(n-3)$-correctors and establish upper bounds on nonlinearity. For $n=2^k\ge 8$, a self-addressing construction yields $(n-2)$-correctors achieving the optimal nonlinearity $2^{n-1}-2^{n-1}/n$ with resiliency $n/2-2$ and algebraic degree $k+1$. Notably, this provides the first known infinite family of nonlinear correctors achieving both optimal correction order and optimal nonlinearity for that order, while having a resiliency strictly lower than the correction order. Furthermore, using constant-weight addressing, we construct $(n-d-1)$-correctors that asymptotically meet the nonlinearity upper bounds for every fixed $d\ge 1$. Our profile characterization also reveals inherent limitations of injective Maiorana--McFarland constructions at correction order $n-3$. For vectorial functions, we construct nonlinear $(s(2^m-1),m,s2^{m-1}+\ell-1)$-correctors for every $m\ge 2$ under certain conditions on $s$ and $\ell$, with resiliency at most $s2^{m-1}-2$. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first infinite family of nonlinear correctors whose correction order simultaneously exceeds that of optimal linear corrector and its own resiliency. Finally, we introduce a secondary construction that lifts these vectorial correctors to larger input dimensions while preserving their correction-order advantage. This approach yields a nonlinearity of $2^{n-1}-2^{n-n_0-1}$, where $n_0$ is the input dimension of the base corrector, along with explicit resiliency and a flexible algebraic degree.
papers.authors: Zhaole Li, Deng Tang

papers.title: How Well Do SAST Tools Work Across Languages? An Empirical Study Using OCPP Implementations
papers.abstract: As electric vehicle (EV) adoption accelerates globally, securing electric vehicle charging station (EVCS) software becomes increasingly critical. The Open Charge Point Protocol (OCPP), widely adopted for EVCS management, places significant responsibility on developers to securely implement specifications that are subject to multiple interpretations. The variety of OCPP implementations across different programming languages provides a unique opportunity to evaluate security tooling in a real-world, multi-language context where implementation variability may introduce vulnerabilities. This study provides the first empirical evaluation of Static Application Security Testing (SAST) tool performance across multiple programming languages using OCPP implementations as a real-world test corpus. We applied both comprehensive multi-language tools (SonarQube and Semgrep) and language-specific analyzers to twelve OCPP 1.6 implementations--each written in a distinct programming language--to examine how detection patterns vary across language ecosystems. Total issues ranged from just two in Rust to 1,689 in Java. Mature programming languages like Java yielded substantially more findings than newer languages like Rust, likely because established languages have more developed SAST tool ecosystems rather than inherently worse code quality. These results suggest that developers should consider available SAST tooling when selecting implementation languages for security critical systems.
papers.authors: Zachary Wadhams, Emma Sheppard, Dalton Arford, Clemente Izurieta, Ann Marie Reinhold

papers.title: Location Matters: Sparse Latent-Variance Attacks for Face Privacy against Diffusion Personalization
papers.abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models can learn and reproduce an individual's identity from only a few reference photos, creating risks of unauthorized and misleading content generation. Proactive defenses address this risk by adding adversarial perturbations to facial images before release, thereby disrupting identity acquisition during downstream personalization. However, existing methods typically rely on dense $L_\infty$-bounded perturbations, whose accumulated distortions can become visible around facial structures. Recent methods improve protected-image quality, but often at the cost of reduced protection effectiveness. In this paper, we propose Sparse Encoder Attack on Latent Variance (SEAL), a sparse adversarial protection framework that modifies only 5% of the spatial locations in a facial image. SEAL combines a differentiable top-k masking scheme that jointly optimizes perturbation locations and values with a variance-oriented objective over the frozen VAE encoder's latent distribution to disrupt identity-consistent representations. A saliency-guided dispersion penalty further discourages perturbation concentration in perceptually salient facial regions. Experiments on CelebA-HQ and VGGFace2 show that SEAL achieves the best protected-image quality among the compared methods, exceeding 41 dB PSNR with 0.97 SSIM and at most 0.07 LPIPS, while reducing identity similarity to at most 0.15 after diffusion personalization. These results demonstrate that sparse location optimization enables strong identity protection while preserving high visual quality. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Lvxan/SEAL
papers.authors: Shuting Yang, Shuxin Li, Linyan Dai, Xinwei Zhang, Dong Huang, Renyang Liu, See-Kiong Ng

papers.title: Pulse or Provenance? What rPPG-Based Deepfake Detectors Learn
papers.abstract: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) has been proposed as a physiological cue for deepfake detection, based on the premise that synthesized faces lack a genuine cardiac signal.
