We first evaluate coding agents on 96 tasks that require implementing a new backend application in a repository where other applications already exist. Second, we investigate repository-level code generation on 20 pairs of tasks in real C/C++ projects. In each task, the agent is asked to complete code critical to memory safety. We find that in both settings, insecure existing code leads to agents writing vulnerable code more often. In backend generation, insecure neighbors reduce the share of correct and secure implementations by 3.4% on average, and in C/C++ repository-level coding, the average gap between secure and insecure contexts reaches 35.4%. Prompting to follow existing code-style or to be careful about security increases, respectively decreases, how strongly agents propagate vulnerabilities, but neither stops them. When asked to explain their implementation choices, coding agents attribute them to following another code site in 76.5% of cases, even though they recognize the introduced vulnerability in 69.9% of cases. These findings show that agents use existing vulnerabilities as templates for new ones indiscriminatorily, turning each contribution into an opportunity to introduce more vulnerabilities. As such, as agents write a growing share of production code under decreasing human review, code bases can increasingly degrade in security if security vulnerabilities are not thoroughly fixed continuously.
papers.authors: Chenhao Sun, Niels Mündler-Sasahara, Mark Vero, Martin Vechev

papers.title: When Coding Agents Get Arms: Safety Risks Across the Digital-Physical Boundary
papers.abstract: Advances in spatial understanding have enabled frontier models to power coding agents that control a real robot arm zero-shot and end-to-end, without task-specific demonstrations or retraining. This brings two new safety challenges. First, the extensive knowledge of frontier models lets these agents perform tasks that earlier VLA and WAM paradigms could not, opening the door to new forms of capability misuse. Second, coding agents can access digital resources such as web pages and emails. Threats in these resources, such as indirect prompt injection, can carry over into the physical world when the agent controls a robot. We therefore introduce ArmedAgent, the first systematic benchmark to evaluate both risks for coding agents performing zero-shot robot control. It covers robustness, malicious use, and indirect injection across 36 tasks in 5 scenarios, evaluated in simulation and validated on a physical robot arm. A distinctive portion of the tasks target harmful behaviors that earlier VLA paradigms could not perform. Testing several frontier models, including GPT-6-Astra, under widely used agent frameworks, we find substantial safety risks in current systems.
papers.authors: Yiming Sun, Mi Zhang

papers.title: Tracing MCP Security Vulnerabilities: Constructing and Analyzing an MCP Security Vulnerability Dataset
papers.abstract: As a core protocol for integrating large language models (LLMs) with external data sources and tools, the Model Context Protocol (MCP) has quickly become a key interface in emerging AI agent systems. As the MCP ecosystem expands, reported vulnerabilities have also increased, creating a growing software-security attack surface. However, MCP vulnerability information remains scattered, noisy, and difficult to study systematically. This paper addresses that gap by constructing a curated MCP vulnerability dataset from CVE disclosures. Starting from 119 MCP-related records retrieved through February 2026, we filter unrelated cases out and obtain a validated snapshot of 24 MCP vulnerabilities. Our filtering methodology explicitly addresses acronym ambiguity and achieves 96.7% inter-rater agreement on a sampled exclusion audit while retaining all known high-severity MCP cases identified in public advisories. Using this initial dataset snapshot, we find that 87.5% of validated vulnerabilities are Critical or High severity, and that injection and path traversal vulnerabilities account for 66.7% of cases. We further identify recurring issues involving insufficient input validation, inadequate access control, and protocol-level security gaps. Through six representative case studies, we illustrate common exploitation patterns and map them to practical defenses. We release the dataset, reproducibility tooling, and a sustainable maintenance workflow as a foundation for future MCP security measurement, benchmarking, and defense research.
papers.authors: Xu He, Sagar Patel, Shu Wang

papers.title: Beyond AUROC: Deployment-Aware Evaluation of Model-Internal Jailbreak Detectors
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in user-facing systems, where jailbreak attacks can bypass safety controls and induce harmful and policy-violating outputs. Recent model-internal detectors use hidden representations, gradients, or internal signals to identify such prompts, but their practical security value depends critically on behavior at low false-positive operating points rather than on area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) alone. We study two data dependencies that shape this behavior: calibration data, which determine the detection threshold, and reference data, which can influence detector scores. Across four model-internal detectors, four LLMs, and twelve jailbreak families, thresholds calibrated on curated benign prompts frequently fail to preserve their false-positive rate (FPR) budgets on real-user traffic. Recalibration improves false-positive control but reveals substantial family-level coverage gaps, including cases with high AUROC but low true-positive rate (TPR). Causal reference-set interventions show that changing reference composition can substantially alter family-level detection and that improving coverage of one attack family can reduce coverage of others. These findings show that calibration and reference data are part of a detector's security behavior. We therefore recommend evaluating model-internal jailbreak defenses using realized FPR on deployment-like traffic and per-family TPR at explicit low-FPR operating points, with AUROC used as a complementary ranking metric rather than the primary security measure.
papers.authors: Mohammad Tehabsim, Basil Al-Housani, Nour Alhussien, Phung Lai

papers.title: CyberBinGym: Can AI Agents Turn Binary Patches into Real Exploits?
papers.abstract: Security fixes usually reach users as compiled updates, but deployment delays leave unpatched systems exposed. During this window, comparing patched and unpatched binaries can reveal how to exploit a vulnerability, turning a defensive update into actionable information for attackers. Existing benchmarks do not measure this capability: they expose source code, rely on human-crafted challenges, or evaluate binary comprehension without requiring exploitation. We introduce CyberBinGym, a benchmark containing 100 tasks derived from real vulnerabilities in 53 widely used projects, spanning six vulnerability families and three levels of analysis complexity. Agents receive stripped vulnerable and patched binaries without source code or vulnerability information, and must combine static and dynamic analysis to recover and exploit the vulnerability. Evaluation separately measures vulnerability recovery through differential crash testing and end-to-end exploitation through flag retrieval, with trajectory audits to reject reward hacking. The strongest evaluated agent recovers the target vulnerability in 88% of tasks and exploits it in 20%. Providing the patched binary raises its exploit rate from 10% to 25% on a matched 20-task subset; with standard binary hardening enabled, it still exploits two of its 20 previously successful tasks. These results demonstrate that current agents can turn released binary patches into working exploits in a controlled setting, although exploitation remains unreliable. These capabilities lower the barriers to targeting unpatched software and compress defenders' effective response window, increasing the urgency of timely patch deployment.
papers.authors: Lambang Akbar Wijayadi, Zhaoqi Xiao, Zhun Wang, Hongwei Li, Wenbo Guo, Heng Yin, Zhenkai Liang, Dawn Song

papers.title: Towards Lightweight IoT Intrusion Detection: Feature Optimization and Explainable Machine Learning for Resource-Constrained Environment
papers.abstract: Machine learning-based intrusion detection systems (IDSs) can improve IoT security but often rely on large feature sets that increase computational overhead and limit deployment on resource-constrained devices. This paper presents a resource-efficient and explainable feature optimization framework for lightweight IoT intrusion detection using the CICIoT2023 dataset. A Random Forest model was used to rank feature importance and identify compact feature subsets. Experimental results show that a three-feature model achieved an MCC of 0.9622 while reducing the feature space by 92.1%, whereas a six feature model achieved an MCC of 0.9675 with an 84.2% reduction. Furthermore, a fifteen-feature model achieved an MCC of 0.9744, preserving 99.97% of the performance of the full 38-feature baseline model while reducing the feature space by 60.5%. SHAP-based explainability analysis validated the selected features and provided interpretable insights into model decisions. The results demonstrate that lightweight, explainable, and high-performance IoT intrusion detection can be achieved using only a small subset of carefully selected features, significantly reducing resource requirements with minimal loss of detection effectiveness.
papers.authors: Shaker Nawasra, Munther Abualkibash

papers.title: A Case Study of a Phishing Cluster Targeting German Universities
papers.abstract: In light of recent ransomware attacks, this study analyzes and measures the impact of cyberattacks against academic institutions in German-speaking areas. First, we provide an overview of 25 confirmed cyberattacks against universities in German-speaking areas between February 2022 and February 2023. In this time frame, we find that 5% of all German universities have experienced a confirmed cyberattack with a measurable impact. Second, we document victimology and Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTP) of a phishing activity cluster spanning more than three years and showing a particular focus on universities in German-speaking areas. Of the 93 targeted universities, 58 (62%) are German, representing a significant fraction with approximately 14% of the total number of universities (423) in Germany. A notable technique is that the phishing emails are sent via university infrastructure, using valid, compromised credentials of university-associated personnel and involving university Virtual Private Network (VPN) tunnels.
papers.authors: Raphael Springer, Alexander Schmitz, Joel Taddey, Gerhard Senkowski, Artur Leinweber, Christian Dietrich

papers.title: BACGUARD: Fact-Grounded Runtime Mitigation of Broken Access Control
papers.abstract: Broken Access Control (BAC) has been the foremost category in the OWASP Top Ten since 2021, primarily due to the challenges in enforcing authorization at the application layer. Traditional mechanisms depend on logic embedded in the application, referencing relational database information such as permissions, roles, or ownership. However, missing or incorrect checks can go undetected by external systems, leaving applications vulnerable. This paper presents BACGUARD, a reverse proxy designed to enforce authorization for unmodified applications. BACGUARD reconstructs authorization relations by leveraging authenticated user data from session stores and object ownership from relational schemas. It evaluates whether users are permitted to access resources and blocks unauthorized requests in real time. Unlike existing approaches, BACGUARD bases its authorization on database joins, making the system resilient to forgery. For most requests, decisions are made deterministically. In cases where access control violations are only apparent in response data, such as cross-user data leakage, a language model is used as a fallback. Evaluations on six applications, including those with known vulnerabilities, demonstrate that BACGUARD's hybrid deterministic and language model-based approach blocks all tested attacks with a false-positive rate below 0.7%. Competing solutions like Web Application Firewalls are less effective and more disruptive. The results highlight BACGUARD's primary contribution: the external reconstruction of authorization facts, enabling robust enforcement even when the application itself is flawed.
papers.authors: Moses Ndebugre

papers.title: Say Shibboleth: Fingerprinting the LLMs and Harnesses Behind Agentic Attacks
papers.abstract: We study the fingerprinting of agentic cyberattacks. Our objective is to reliably infer information about the attacker's configuration, such as LLM version and harness, from telemetry. To achieve this, we introduce a technique we call shibboleth traps: modular honeypot services designed to elicit discriminative behaviors from agentic attackers. The traps make informative interactions a condition for obtaining resources the agent seeks, eliciting model declarations and characteristic writing without requiring a successful prompt injection. To achieve harness fingerprinting, we introduce general mechanisms to indirectly probe peculiar execution behaviors of harnesses. These probes reveal how a harness masks secrets in tool output, enforces command time limits, and schedules tool calls, using only the effects visible in subsequent requests. We show that combined declarative and behavioral inference distinguishes among 15 candidate models with an average 90% top-1 accuracy, with behavioral classifiers evaluated on held-out harnesses or task families. In a separate experiment across four harnesses, fixed probe rules identify the correct harness with 92% accuracy. When instructed to conceal their identity, agents still leave useful behavioral evidence even as their declarations become uninformative.
papers.authors: Dario Pasquini, Reworr, Giuseppe Ateniese, Manish Bhatt, Sergej Epp

papers.title: Harness Matters: Measuring and Dissecting Security Resilience in Web Agents
papers.abstract: Web agents extend LLMs from text generation to real-world web interaction by relying on execution harnesses that interpret user goals, perceive webpages, plan actions, and ground model decisions into browser operations. While prior work has recognized that agent security depends on more than the backend model alone, how harness design quantitatively shapes web-agent security remains insufficiently measured. To systematically study web-agent harness security, we first characterize web-agent harnesses as a four-stage execution workflow covering goal interpretation, webpage perception, reasoning and planning, and action execution. Based on this abstraction, we build WebTrap Farm, a systematic and extensible evaluation framework covering three representative attack categories: malicious user prompts, malicious prompt injection, and deceptive web design. To avoid conflating security with task capability, we use paired usability calibration tasks to separate genuine defensive behavior from capability limitations. Our evaluation shows that existing web-agent harnesses remain vulnerable to typical attacks, with some unsafe behaviors occurring even without explicit attack content, revealing harness-intrinsic security failures (RQ1). Statistical analysis further shows that both harness and backend model significantly affect security outcomes, indicating that deployed-agent security is jointly shaped by the harness and backend model (RQ2). Finally, we localize where defensive behavior emerges across workflow stages and identify more secure design mechanisms, providing actionable guidance for building more robust web agents (RQ3). These findings highlight the web-agent harness as an important security boundary and motivate moving beyond model-centric defenses toward harness-level security design.
papers.authors: Xinyi Wu, Jiagui Chen, JiaYi Dong, Geng Hong, Xudong Pan, Jiarun Dai, Mingxuan Liu, Min Yang

papers.title: On the Relative Security of Prompt Injection: Mechanised Definitions, Defences and Verdicts for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: An LLM agent that reads untrusted content, such as an email or a web page, may follow instructions hidden in it. Noninterference is too strong for such agents, since a useful agent lets untrusted content influence what it does and may disclose the user's data by design, and declassification needs a release policy written for each task. We instead state security relative to a reference agent, which runs the same plan under the same runtime monitor with a model that never obeys untrusted content. An agent is relatively secure if every leak it has is a leak the reference already has. Our framework, PlanTERS, instantiates relative security, a notion from speculative execution, with a small agent language in which the attacker chooses how the model follows instructions, a composition with runtime monitors, and attacker models that differ in what they observe. A fence theorem shows that revoking injectable tools at the first untrusted read, and never granting them back, makes every plan relatively secure at the event level on finite runs, for every model behaviour in which each injection is a single call and the model obeys on a schedule fixed in advance; with a fairness condition, this extends to possibly infinite runs. We prove or refute relative security for agents with fences, budgets, approvals, loops and dual LLMs, in Isabelle/HOL.
papers.authors: Brijesh Dongol

papers.title: Least-Privilege Auditing of Agent Tool Calls with Intent Graphs and Reasoning-Guided Escalation
papers.abstract: LLM agents that call tools are exposed to indirect prompt injection: instructions hidden in tool outputs can steer an agent into calls the user never asked for. We present a runtime audit that derives an executable intent graph from the user's objective and the deployment's tool catalog with one LLM call per task, and checks every tool call against it with a deterministic loop that makes no LLM call (median 5.7 microseconds per call). Two further mechanisms recover utility. Lookups of the user's own state bypass the audit, because the harm of an attack lies in its write or outward step. The calls that remain flagged are escalated to a reasoning guardian, in the spirit of tool-integrated reasoning models such as START: a reasoning model that sees only the objective, the plan, the call history without tool outputs, and the flagged call, and can verify facts with a restricted Python-expression tool. A current agent showed no baseline attack success, so end-to-end validation remains open.
papers.authors: Doron Shavit

papers.title: ErosionBench: Probing Alignment Decay in Enterprise Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: As enterprises delegate consequential work to multi-agent LLM systems, benign-looking requests can escalate into unsafe actions as they propagate across sessions through poisoned shared state, long-context documents, and trusted peer messages: no single message is malicious, yet the assembled tool action is. Prior benchmarks isolate a single agent under prompt injection or score multi-agent attacks by their final output, leaving cross-session erosion of shared state out of scope. We introduce ErosionBench, an environment-grounded benchmark that executes such attacks and verifies alignment decay at the process level, scoring the realized tool call against authorized intent and provenance with deterministic contracts, not output text. Each scenario is authored as a deterministic state graph before any prose is rendered, so every state change traces to a known cause. It spans four enterprise domains and four decay mechanisms across 1,728 scenarios with matched benign controls, labeled against the OWASP Top-10 for LLM Applications, plus 198 image-based attacks, each paired with a text equivalent, so a defense must survive the same attack in either channel. Perimeter defenses suppress attacks only by over-refusing 54-92% of legitimate work, so a low attack-success rate can conceal severe over-refusal. As a reference defense, we propose a calibrated Meta-Auditor pairing synchronous state checks with asynchronous trajectory monitoring; on a family-disjoint 906-scenario held-out split it reaches 98.5% recall at a 2.9% false-positive rate. Since it monitors trajectory, not surface content, its detection is channel-invariant: the strongest auditor flags image-delivered attacks about as reliably as their text equivalents (recall gap $\leq$2 points per model). Across GPT, Gemini, and Claude auditors, calibration keeps false positives low while recall tracks model capability, strongest for Claude.
papers.authors: Riya Bharathwaj, Akshara Prabhakar, Roshan Ram, Avni Kothari, Sarah Tan, Huan Wang, Silvio Savarese

papers.title: Enmo Safety: External, Non-invasive, Model-agnostic Oversight for Off-the-Shelf Language Models
papers.abstract: We study a safety harness that improves itself without touching model weights. Enmo Safety wraps a chat model with a deterministic input assessment, trigger-matched safety guidance, spotlighting of untrusted content, and an output guard. A reflector model turns failures into one bounded update per round, and an update is kept only if it lowers harm without raising refusal of benign prompts on a held-out dev split. Every version is snapshotted and every decision ledgered. We evaluate a bare model, the seed harness and the evolved harness on six open benchmarks (HarmBench, AdvBench, JailbreakBench, XSTest, AgentHarm, deepset prompt-injections). On 150 items and on a 290-item holdout, none of the before/after differences on two models was statistically significant. A fourth iteration ran six policy models on a fresh 300-item split: the harness cut the unsafe rate significantly on two models (12.9% to 7.1%, p = 0.035; 10.2% to 3.6%, p = 0.036), not on the other four, and raised agentic-harm labels on two. Whether the rules fired was unrelated to outcome (Fisher p from 0.30 to 1.0), and the helpfulness clauses made agentic harm worse than no harness on obfuscated attacks. A reworded clause and an input-normalisation step form harness v22, at a measured cost in benign tool-task refusal. Each cell is one run, so these estimates do not establish a general safety improvement. Code, harness versions and ledger: https://github.com/rioryugen/enmo_safety
papers.authors: Mohammed Nayeem Khan, Sarun Kumar K. S., Allan Kevin T., Chirag Vaidya, Vrishank Tiwari

papers.title: Treating the Model as an Untrusted Component: Deterministic Policy Enforcement, Human Approval and Taint Tracking Against Prompt Injection in Tool-Using Agents, with Validation on Open-Weights Models
papers.abstract: Tool-using LLM agents act on instructions embedded in the data they read, so prompt injection is a structural rather than a prompt-wording problem. We compare in-prompt defences (hardened prompts, spotlighting, LLM detectors) with deterministic enforcement outside the model (four reference monitors of increasing strength), human approval and taint tracking, judged by one effect-based oracle independent of every defence in an executable environment of 13 tasks and 12 tools, with argument-fuzzing attackers and severity-weighted harm. In an evaluation with real open-weights models (Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B; 156 attack episodes per defence and model), the models proposed the attacker's call in 64% and 84% of attack episodes behind the task-bound monitor, which admitted 1.3% and 7.7%; guardrail effects depended on the model (a prompt guardrail moved obedience from 67% to 65% and from 86% to 55%, spotlighting plus a detector to 12% and 0%) against static attacks. Simulation with an assumed model covers what no real run did: under the assumed erosion law a persistent adaptive attacker or a compromised model drives every guardrail stack to 100.0% attack success, whereas the task-bound monitor holds severe actions at 0.0%; its residual (harm 0.69/10) falls by 62% under taint-triggered human review, and a human layer without a deterministic monitor fails against approval spamming unless each episode has a deterministic approval budget. Implementation quality matters: a naive monitor admits 18 of 33 effective attack variants, a hardened one 6 and a capability-bound one 1. The real-model evidence is limited to two open-weights models and static attacks, the human-approval and taint results are simulation-only, and the larger model's detector stack contradicts the assumed erosion law. Code, data, a two-rater oracle audit and a notebook for repeating the real-model evaluation are provided.
papers.authors: Mustafa S. Aljumaily, Nawar S. Alseelawi, Raghad Alshabandar

papers.title: BeaverDam: A Post-Quantum Threshold Key Recovery Protocol from a One-Time Threshold Oblivious Random Function
papers.abstract: Secure backups are a practical necessity of E2EE messaging apps, typically relying on password-protected key-recovery (PPKR) protocols. These allow users to turn a human-memorable password into a cryptographic key with the help of a server. Recently, Signal and Juicebox proposed threshold PPKR (tPPKR) protocols, removing the trust on a centralized server. Unfortunately, known solutions are only classically secure, lagging behind the shift toward post-quantum (PQ), or to be more precise, hybrid secure E2EE. We present BeaverDam, a novel tPPKR protocol that is PQ secure with efficiency close to existing classical protocols. It also easily extends to hybrid security, standing as the first concretely efficient hybrid-secure tPPKR protocol. BeaverDam relies on a new primitive we introduce --- one-time threshold oblivious random functions (tORF). Unlike full-fledged OPRFs, which are notoriously difficult to construct in a PQ-secure manner, one-time tORF offers weaker but sufficient security guarantees tailored to the tPPKR setting. We then construct an efficient one-time tORF called Beaver, inspired by multi-party computation (MPC) techniques. Owing to the one-time feature, we only need to securely compute a 2-wise independent hash function, making our protocol very efficient. We conclude by presenting a practical instantiation of BeaverDam and comparing its performance to state-of-the-art classical tPPKR protocols, namely Signal's SVR3 and Juicebox.
papers.authors: Benedikt Auerbach, Shuichi Katsumata, Kaoru Takemure, Ida Tucker

papers.title: New Results in Adaptively-Secure Broadcast Encryption and Succinct Computational Secret Sharing from Standard Lattices
papers.abstract: Projective pseudorandom generators (PPRGs), introduced by [Applebaum et al.; STOC'23], expand a short seed into a long pseudorandom string, with a special feature that one can generate a short $\textit{projected}$ key, for any set $S$, such that it reveals the output bits in $S$ while preserving pseudorandomness of the remaining bits. They demonstrated that PPRGs can bypass the 'representation size barrier' in computational secret sharing schemes, and designed PPRGs assuming hardness of a variety of standard cryptographic assumptions. Later, [Hsieh, Waters, and Wu; EUROCRYPT'25] showed that PPRGs can also be used to design adaptively-secure broadcast encryption in the standard model, without relying on unprovable heuristics. In this work, we design succinct computational secret sharing schemes for graph access structures and adaptively-secure flexible broadcast encryption in the standard model, both with optimal parameters. The main driver for both our results is a new construction of a compact programmable pseudorandom set sampler (PPS), introduced by [Goyal and Yadugiri; CRYPTO'26], from standard Learning with Errors (LWE) assumption [Regev; STOC'05]. We show that PPS generically imply PPRGs with many useful properties and, moreover, by replacing PPRGs with PPS we can achieve full succinctness in the underlying applications to secret sharing and adaptive security compilers for broadcast encryption. This yields the $\textit{first}$ flexible broadcast encryption scheme in the standard model from $\textit{any}$ falsifiable assumption with fully compact ciphertext size, and a succinct computational secret sharing for evolving graph access structures with optimal share size from standard LWE.
papers.authors: Rishab Goyal, Saikumar Yadugiri

papers.title: SNARKs from LWE via Non-black-box Reductions
papers.abstract: We construct the first succinct non-interactive arguments of knowledge (SNARKs) from the polynomial-hardness of Learning with Errors (LWE) for a subclass of UP languages whose witness unambiguity has a polynomial-size Extended Frege ($\mathcal{EF}$) proof. Our construction achieves the following soundness guarantee: For any fixed sequence of false instances $\{x_\lambda\}_{\lambda\in\mathbb{N}}$, there exists a (non-constructive) constant $c>0$ such that, whenever the uniform random CRS length exceeds $\lambda^c$, the construction achieves infinitely-often soundness for this sequence $\{x_\lambda\}_{\lambda\in\mathbb{N}}$: for any polynomial-time cheating prover $\{\mathcal{A}_\lambda\}_{\lambda\in\mathbb{N}}$, the probability that $\mathcal{A}_\lambda$ outputs an accepting proof for $x_\lambda$ is negligible for infinitely many $\lambda$. As intermediate results, we also obtain: - SNARGs for any NP language that has polynomial-size $\mathcal{EF}$ proofs of witness unambiguity for all instances outside of the language, based on polynomial-hard LWE, achieving the same style of soundness guarantee. - SNARKs for all true instances in any language $L \in \mathsf{UP}$ where every instance has a polynomial-size $\mathcal{EF}$ proof of witness unambiguity, under polynomial hardness of LWE, without soundness guarantees for false instances. To achieve our main result, we employ a non-black-box soundness reduction. Along the way, we introduce a new logical proof system, the \emph{Cryptographic Extended Frege} ($\mathcal{CEF}$) system, which extends $\mathcal{EF}$ with rules for formalizing the indistinguishability in cryptographic security proofs. Building on the Encrypt-hash-and-BARG framework of [Jin–Kalai–Lombardi–Vaikuntanathan, STOC’24], we further obtain SNARGs for NP languages that have $\mathcal{CEF}$ proofs of non-membership, which may be of independent interest.
papers.authors: Zhengzhong Jin, Mingqi Lu, Bo Peng

papers.title: More Salt, Please: A Simple Compiler for Post-Quantum Strong aPAKE
papers.abstract: Resistance to precomputation attacks is a central security goal in password-based cryptography, as it drastically increases the runtime of brute-force attacks on breached password hashes. Strong asymmetric password-authenticated key exchange (saPAKE), which enforces such precomputation resistance, is standardized by the IRTF and deployed today at large scale. Unfortunately, no practical and easy-to-deploy saPAKE exists yet that withstands quantum attackers. Current constructions use rate-limiting tools such as oblivious pseudo-random functions (OPRFs), of which post-quantum versions are significantly more costly and complex than their discrete-log based counterparts. In this paper, we take a new approach to precomputation resistance. Starting from the compilers from PAKE to aPAKE by Gentry-MacKenzie-Ramzan (Crypto 2006) and Liu-Lyu-Han (Asiacrypt 2024), we propose a password file ratchet that adds precomputation resistance to these compilers through continuously updating the password file. The update is a simple salted hash. With a variety of practical post-quantum PAKEs at hand, this yields a ready-to-deploy post-quantum saPAKE at the trade-off of a changing server state.
papers.authors: William Riccardo Duro, Sebastian Faller, Julia Hesse, Máté Horváth

papers.title: SETH: Subcode Equivalence in the Head
papers.abstract: The Multi-Party Computation in the Head (MPCitH) paradigm has proven to be a versatile tool to design post-quantum digital signature schemes. Recently, MPCitH was improved with Threshold Computation in the Head (TCitH) and Vector Oblivious Linear Evaluation in the Head (VOLEitH). In this paper, we propose two polynomial models for the Subcode Equivalence Problem (SEP) and derive TCitH and VOLEitH signatures from them. The resulting scheme has better performance when compared to other SEP-based signature schemes and also features shorter signatures when compared to other schemes based on similar assumptions.
papers.authors: Marco Baldi, Michele Battagliola, Rahmi El Mechri, Laura Mattiuz, Marco Rinaudo, Paolo Santini, Riccardo Schiavoni, Edoardo Signorini

papers.title: Actively Secure PIR from Verifiable Linear Relations over Rings
papers.abstract: Privately retrieving data from a database without revealing which element is being retrieved is a fundamental problem in cryptography with many diverse applications. State-of-the-art solutions to this problem are generally based on homomorphic encryption, which offers security only against passive adversaries. In this work, we contribute to the recently introduced notion of Verifiable Private Information Retrieval (vPIR), which leverages verifiable computation to achieve security against active adversaries. We present a new sum-check based interactive oracle proof for linear relations over power-of-two cyclotomic rings, and show how to instantiate it into a vPIR protocol using Ring-LWE. Our solution is concretely efficient, offers the best possible security guarantees and is plausibly post-quantum secure. We additionally provide an open-source Rust implementation. Our server time improves on prior work's IOP by more than an order of magnitude, leading to a factor two end-to-end performance improvement. Compared to vPIR prior work, on a 4 GiB database, our offline communication and client storage are of 128 MiB, against 3.29 GiB. Preprocessing is run once per database and amortized over an unbounded number of queries.
papers.authors: Louis Tremblay Thibault

papers.title: Independent Leakage Does Not Save Evasive LWE: Refuting Folklore Fixes in the Private-Coin Setting
papers.abstract: The evasive learning with errors (evasive LWE) assumption has enabled a wide range of advanced cryptographic constructions from lattices in the past few years. The simple intuition that LWE remains secure even when additional ``non-zeroizing'' short preimages are given has proved highly versatile in applications. Unfortunately, recent counterexamples have refuted its general private-coin formulations, showing that having the short preimages along with arbitrary auxiliary leakage about the secret and target matrices can invalidate this intuition. To preserve important applications, particularly witness encryption, the community has sought to repair the assumption by restricting the allowed leakage. One folklore proposal requires the secret and target matrices, together with their respective leakage, to be generated independently. This restriction appears to preserve the application to witness encryption while ruling out all previously known counterexamples. In this work, we refute this proposal. Assuming LWE and indistinguishability obfuscation, we show that both the binding and hiding variants of private-coin evasive LWE are false even with the independent sampler restriction. Our counterexamples exploit only auxiliary leakage about the target matrix. We sample the secret honestly from a standard uniform or Gaussian distribution, independently of the target and its leakage, and we use no auxiliary information about the secret.
papers.authors: Yao-Ching Hsieh

papers.title: Structured Quantum Hardness from Unstructured Assumptions
papers.abstract: Whether useful structured hardness can arise from unstructured assumptions is a fundamental question in complexity and cryptography. The longstanding Bennett–Gill question asks whether $\mathsf{NP}\cap\mathsf{coNP}$ remains hard relative to a random oracle; [GIKKLS, STOC 2023] recently gave a conditional affirmative answer in the classical setting. We establish the quantum analogue: if $\mathsf{UP}\not\subseteq\mathsf{BQP}$, then $\mathsf{NP}^{O}\cap\mathsf{coNP}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathsf{BQP}^{O}$ with probability $1$ over a random oracle $O$. Beyond extending the classical result, this separation has a distinctly quantum significance: Shor’s algorithms defeat canonical number-theoretic hardness candidates, while lattice assumptions and other leading post-quantum cryptographic assumptions do not directly supply hard languages with two-sided classical certification on every input. Our conditional oracle separation provides evidence that such structured quantum hardness can nevertheless arise from unstructured sources. Complementing this result, we rule out fully black-box quantum reductions of worst-case quantum hardness in $\mathsf{NP}\cap\mathsf{coNP}$ to post-quantum injective one-way functions and indistinguishability obfuscation. This barrier excludes a broad class of black-box approaches to deriving structured quantum hardness from generic cryptographic primitives, providing partial evidence that the non-black-box techniques in our first result are essential.
papers.authors: Xiao Liang, Takashi Yamakawa, Chak Fai Yung

papers.title: Weights Come Almost for Free in Ramp Threshold Cryptography
papers.abstract: A weighted threshold access structure assigns a weight to each party and authorizes a subset of parties whenever their total weight exceeds a prescribed threshold. Most existing approaches to designing multiparty cryptographic protocols in the weighted threshold setting, however, either incur complexity that grows with the total weight assigned to the parties or remain far from concretely efficient. Toward \emph{concretely efficient} weighted threshold primitives, we take a different route and relax to the \emph{ramp} setting, in which two thresholds are prescribed: a subset whose total weight falls below an $\alpha$ fraction of the total is unauthorized, while a subset whose total weight exceeds a $\beta$ fraction is authorized. Exploiting the gap between these two thresholds, we obtain the following results. 1. Given any weighted ramp threshold access structure with privacy threshold $\alpha$ and reconstruction threshold $\beta$, where $0\!<\!\alpha\!<\!\beta\!<\!1$, we present a weight compression technique that reduces the total weight to $\approx n/(2(\beta-\alpha))$ while preserving the authorized and unauthorized sets. Combined with the standard player-virtualization paradigm, this yields concretely efficient weighted threshold cryptographic protocols with only a multiplicative overhead of $\approx 1/(2(\beta-\alpha))$ over their unweighted counterparts. Previously, the best known compression technique in this setting, due to Benhamouda et al.~[ITC'23], achieved total weight $\approx 5n/(\beta-\alpha)$. 2. Player virtualization has an inherent drawback: a party's share size and workload grow in proportion to its (compressed) weight, so the parties in which the most trust is placed also bear the largest computational and communication costs. Thus, although the \emph{overall} overhead is $O(1)$, the cost borne by a single party can still be $O(n)$ times that in the unweighted setting. Our second result removes this imbalance. Building on our compression technique, we construct a linear secret-sharing scheme in which every party receives a share of size $\widetilde{O}(1)$, independent of its weight, for a total share size of $\widetilde{O}(n)$, nearly matching the $O(n)$ complexity of standard unweighted threshold secret sharing.
papers.authors: Aarushi Goel, Mingyuan Wang

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving Multi-Institutional Clinical Prediction via Multiparty Encrypted Newton-CG Logistic Regression
papers.abstract: Multi-institutional clinical prediction can benefit from larger and more diverse patient populations, but privacy and data-governance constraints often prevent pooling patient-level records. This study aims to enable collaborative logistic-regression training while keeping such records local. We developed a framework combining multiparty Cheon–Kim–Kim–Song (CKKS) homomorphic encryption with Newton–conjugate gradient optimization. Each institution computes local gradient and damped Hessian contributions, while only encrypted fixed-dimensional statistics are aggregated. The global Newton system is solved by encrypted preconditioned conjugate gradient with diagonal preconditioning and delayed division, making the dominant homomorphic cost depend mainly on model dimension. We evaluated the framework on nine clinical-prediction tasks from NHANES 2017–2018 and on the PIMA Diabetes and Breast Cancer Wisconsin datasets. Across the nine NHANES tasks, mean absolute deviations from pooled-data plaintext Newton training were below 0.002 for area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, area under the precision–recall curve, and average precision. Five-fold cross-validation accuracy was (77.21 ± 1.28)% on PIMA Diabetes and (96.42 ± 1.44)% on Breast Cancer Wisconsin. Under a common 20-iteration budget, the proposed method achieved approximately 3.85× faster training and nearly 90% lower peak memory use than a reproduced multiparty encrypted first-order baseline, while attaining a lower final relative gradient and closer agreement with plaintext Newton. These results show that exploiting locally computed Newton statistics can preserve predictive utility while substantially reducing encrypted training cost, supporting privacy-preserving multi-institutional clinical prediction without pooling patient-level data.
papers.authors: Xiaokang Dai, Weijie Miao, Wenyuan Wu, Yong Feng

papers.title: Vector Commit-and-Reduce Schemes
papers.abstract: Hash-based argument systems are seeing increasing adoption in practice, owing to their ease of deployment, fast provers, and plausible post-quantum security. However, they still lag behind elliptic-curve counterparts due to their large proof sizes and (comparatively more) expensive verifiers. Attempts to optimize these metrics have focused on one of the two ingredients underlying these arguments, namely Interactive Oracle Reductions, leaving the other ingredient, Vector Commitments (VC) schemes largely ignored. This is in part because Merkle trees are the best known hash-based VC scheme to date. To make progress on this front, we introduce Vector Commit-and-Reduce (VCR) schemes. These generalize VC schemes by allowing both the commitment and opening algorithms to be interactive protocols, and moreover by allowing the opening algorithm to be a reduction instead of an argument. By requiring VCR schemes to satisfy strong round-by-round knowledge soundness notions, we show how they can be used to construct hash-based reductions from IORs. Our transformation extends prior work which used (non-interactive) VC schemes. We also provide a construction of a VCR scheme, Canopy, that greatly reduces proof size and verifier time by reducing the vector opening claims to proximity claims about certain (committed) codewords. This latter feature enables us to use a wide variety of techniques for proving, batching, and accumulating these claims, and indeed we use these to obtain both concrete and asymptotic improvements for hash-based arguments and reductions. For SNARKs based on the Bolt code [CRYPTO 2026], we reduce proof sizes by 50\% and verifier hashes by $3\times$ with only a 5-15$\%$ prover overhead. For SNARKs based on the Reed-Solomon code, we reduce proof sizes by 20$\%$, and verifier hashes by $1.5\times$ with only a 20$\%$ prover overhead. We also construct hash-based Proof-Carrying Data where the recursion overhead is $O(\lambda \sqrt{\log N})$ hashes; in comparison, the state-of-the-art requires $\Omega(\lambda {\log N})$ hashes.
papers.authors: Anubhav Baweja, Pratyush Mishra, Tushar Mopuri, Bharath Namboothiry

papers.title: Symbolic forward secrecy analysis of ML-KEM
papers.abstract: Post-quantum Key Encapsulation Mechanisms (KEMs) rely on generic transformations to achieve active security. Specifically, ML-KEM (FIPS 203) applies the Fujisaki--Okamoto (FO) transform to a lattice-based public-key encryption scheme, Kyber.CPAPKE, to construct an IND-CCA2 secure key exchange protocol, ML-KEM. While NIST standards and associated special publications discuss guidelines for establishing larger shared keying material using ML-KEM, formal symbolic proofs to evaluate these operational setups remain sparse. This work addresses this gap by conducting a formal symbolic analysis of ML-KEM using \textsf{ProVerif}. First, we verify the core primitive, establishing symbolic proofs for session key confidentiality, key agreement soundness, and Fujisaki--Okamoto implicit rejection fallback secrecy. Second, we examine the temporal security guarantees of ML-KEM under long-term static key leakage. Using \textsf{ProVerif}'s global phase constructs, we demonstrate that standalone static ML-KEM does not preserve Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS), rendering repeated static encapsulation for additional key share establishment vulnerable to retroactive decapsulation. Lastly, we formally model and verify that deploying ML-KEM with ephemeral key rotation or ratcheting mechanisms mitigates this vulnerability, providing robust forward secrecy and complete session domain separation.
papers.authors: Varsha Jarali, Shashi Kant Pandey

papers.title: Exploiting Matrix-Vector Multiplication in AIMer: Single-Trace Attacks on Key Generation and Signing
papers.abstract: This paper presents two side-channel attacks against AIMer v3.0, one of the two signature schemes selected in the Korean Post-Quantum Cryptography (KpqC) competition. Both are single-trace attacks that recover the full secret key without a profiling phase, one against key generation and one against signing. Both target the same routine: the matrix-vector multiplication invoked by either phase expands each bit of its secret operand into an all-zero or an all-one mask, which then gates the accumulation of the corresponding public matrix row. A single execution therefore leaks one distinguishable segment per secret bit. What makes the attacks non-profiled is that each attacked trace carries its own labelled training set. During key generation, creating the dense invertible public matrices invokes the matrix-vector multiplication routine hundreds of times, on operands that are public. In signing the same derivation takes place, and in addition the signature itself opens all but one of the $N$ parties of every repetition, so the bits of nearly every multiplication in the trace are public. In both attacks we use a supervised classifier to recover the unknown value. In key generation that value is the private key itself, whereas in signing there are three distinct routes to it: the key itself, a party's share of the key, and a party's share of an S-box output. Recovering any one of them is enough to recover the private key. We validate both attacks on an ARM Cortex-M4: one trace recovers the exact secret key from every capture we took, $100$ key generations for each of AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256, and $100$ signatures for each of AES-128f, AES-192f and AES-256f. We also discuss possible countermeasures.
papers.authors: Süleyman Emir Akın, Abdullah Talayhan, Özcan Öztürk

papers.title: Empirical Assessment of Post-Quantum Cryptography Adoption Status in TLS
papers.abstract: Anticipating Q-day security concerns, major CDNs and cloud providers are migrating to post-quantum cryptography (PQC). While existing literature benchmarks PQC performance, empirical research evaluating real-world adoption data remains scarce. We present an empirical assessment of PQC deployment across seven critical protocols (HTTPS, LDAPS, SMTPS, IMAP-SSL, POP3-SSL, TELNETS, and RDP) using 10,000 target IP addresses per protocol. At the origin-server level, PQC algorithm support reaches 9.1% for HTTPS and 7.39% for LDAPS, while falling below 1% for all other evaluated protocols. At the entity level, PQC support is 11% for HTTPS and 5.4% for LDAPS, while the remaining protocols have less than 5% of entities supporting PQC on the hosted servers. We further correlate these adoption trends against organizational digital and financial footprint, and industry sectors, yielding a multi-dimensional empirical assessment of PQC deployment. Finally, at the domain level, we perform a comparative analysis of PQC adoption in Cloudflare-hosted domains against baseline Cloudflare datasets. Collectively, our findings provide critical insights into the current state of PQC readiness over Transport Layer Security (TLS).
papers.authors: Md Ariful Haque, Sander Vinberg, Ben Edwards, João Cruz

papers.title: Empirical Study of Post-Quantum Cryptography Adoption Status in SSH Infrastructure
papers.abstract: With the anticipated arrival of Q-day, quantum computers threaten current cryptographic schemes for encryption and digital signatures. In response, major content delivery networks and cloud service providers are already adopting Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC). The current state-of-the-art focuses on benchmarking the operational performance of implementing PQC, but the real-world adoption status remains under-researched. This work utilizes large-scale SSH fingerprint data from a proprietary scanning tool to analyze PQC adoption across 1.52 million hosts and 27,012 entities. Our study shows that the PQC transition in the SSH protocol is underway but highly polarized: 45.2% of SSH hosts on port 22 support PQC, while 54.8% remain classical-only. At the entity level, 39.9% have enabled PQC on at least one host, whereas 60.1% have no PQC support. By correlating PQC adoption with industry, geography, and organizational size (digital and financial), this study provides a comprehensive empirical assessment of PQC adoption status in SSH infrastructure.
papers.authors: Md Ariful Haque, Sander Vinberg, Ben Edwards, João Cruz

papers.title: Filtered merges make deeper representation trees pay: Subset Sum and Meet-LWE
papers.abstract: Dubiner's bucketing codes, used as type-class filters on representation coordinates, let a merge avoid generating matched pairs with the wrong split pattern. We show that in representation trees their main effect is to make depth pay. For random density-one Subset Sum they improve the exponent of Bonnetain, Bricout, Schrottenloher and Shen from 0.2831 (our recomputation) to 0.2690, at depth 5; no better point was found up to depth 9. For May's Meet-LWE on ternary keys they improve the asymptotic exponent by 0.013–0.023 for key weights ω ≥ 0.375. Filters can pay only at merges where most matched pairs have the wrong split pattern, and do pay where such merges bind; we show both where this holds and where it fails. A survival recursion justifies the accounting, a symmetry lemma shows that the filters cannot bias the planted solution, and simulations support the remaining heuristics.
papers.authors: Nick Howgrave-Graham

papers.title: Performance Bottlenecks in Computing ZK Proofs on a GPU
papers.abstract: Zero-knowledge proofs allow one party to prove the correctness of a statement or execution of a computation while revealing no more than the statement of correctness itself. Recent use cases, such as AI datasets, suggest the need for faster proof generation over increasingly large constraint sets. This paper explores efforts in optimizing zero-knowledge proof generation, specifically PlonK, using GPUs, for applications that are not amenable to solution via incrementally verifiable computing (IVC). Our intention with this work is to improve ZK performance by introducing fundamental changes in the low-level architectural structure of proof generation. These changes affect performance curves for most current proof generation algorithms. In particular, this paper explores the trade-offs between increased parallelization on GPUs and the resultant memory management problems that occur due to this parallelization. We implement a parallelized PlonK in order to analyze these trade-offs and make arguments concerning the nature of data flows within the proving protocol. Our results lead us to consider multi-GPU environments to maximize performance for large circuit sizes. Such environments introduce issues of communication, efficient hardware management, data partition, and data transfers. This paper further discusses the use cases that motivate multi-GPU implementations, their cost models, and the use of remote direct memory access (RDMA) for data transfer among GPUs.
papers.authors: Victor Carolino, Caleb Geren, Michael Kaufman, Maximilian Nussbaum, William Scott, Henry F. Korth

papers.title: Logit Laundering: Evading Data-Use Auditing in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Data-use auditing in Large Language Models (LLMs) aims to determine whether the given data has been used for training, thereby supporting data ownership safeguards. A dominant solution is data watermarking, which embeds traceable signals into training data and detects them in model outputs. Recent studies have proposed many watermarking-based auditing methods in LLMs. However, systematic investigation from an adversarial perspective remains limited: non-compliant LLM providers would use unauthorized copyrighted datasets for training their own models to enhance model capabilities, while attempting to evade detection by auditors, thereby avoiding legal liability. To fill this research gap, we propose a novel evasion framework, termed Logit Laundering, where the non-compliant LLM provider manipulates model outputs at inference time to undermine detectable watermark signals. Specifically, we design a logit reshaping module to suppress watermark-induced statistical signals by integrating a statistical bias estimator as a plug-and-play component. This design keeps the model parameters unchanged and performs manipulation only in the logit space, thereby enabling auditing evasion while minimizing the impact on model's learned knowledge. To further balance evasion effectiveness and model utility, we introduce a confidence-aware scaling module to adaptively calibrate the suppression strength based on next-token prediction confidence. Extensive evaluations show that Logit Laundering can successfully evade existing various state-of-the-art auditing methods, significantly attenuating detectable signals, while preserving model utility on downstream tasks. Our work highlights the need for exploring more robust auditing methods to guard against evasion behaviors.
papers.authors: Ruihan Hu, Wei Luo, Yu-Ming Shang, Jiakai Wang, Chuxuan Zhang, Mei Li, Xi Zhang, Meikang Qiu

papers.title: Tamper-Resilient Quantum Key Encapsulation with Coherent Ciphertexts from qOWFs in the QROM
papers.abstract: Kitagawa et al. (CRYPTO 2024) constructed the first tamper-resilient, chosen-ciphertext-secure public-key encryption from quantum-secure one-way functions (qOWFs). However, their construction assumes authenticated classical channels and measures intermediate signed-phase states to produce classical ciphertexts. Therefore we ask whether coherent quantum ciphertexts can support active security and certified deletion over unauthenticated classical and quantum channels. We construct the first tamper-resilient quantum key-encapsulation mechanism (QKEM) from qOWFs with coherent quantum ciphertexts and genuine validity-feedback confidentiality in the quantum random-oracle model. Our scheme, designated Signed-Fourier QKEM, retains signed coherence through honest encapsulation to form a state-consuming quantum ciphertext. Aside from an authentic root verification key, all transmitted classical metadata and quantum registers are subject to arbitrary adversarial tampering and entanglement. With one quantum public key per independent signing domain and a challenge serial unused in pre-challenge decapsulation queries, we prove session-key confidentiality under genuine different-header decapsulation, including queries sharing the challenge serial, and genuine same-header validity feedback. We also establish fixed-header key robustness against adaptive decapsulation attacks, bounding wrong-key acceptance by a negligible probability. Furthermore, our scheme provides publicly verifiable computational certified deletion, protecting session-key privacy against subsequent, complete exposure of the receiver's secret state. Finally, composing our QKEM with a classical one-time private data encapsulation mechanism yields header-restricted chosen-ciphertext confidentiality for arbitrary polynomial-length messages.
papers.authors: Shiyu He

papers.title: Applying Combinatorial Techniques To Find Minimal Non-Complete Set Coverings
papers.abstract: One of the most prominent hardware countermeasures against side-channel attacks are threshold implementations (TIs). The technique uses masking to split the operations in a cryptographic algorithm into several ones operating on shares. The coverage and non-completeness requirements of TIs are mathematically described by the notion of non-complete set coverings (NCSCs). Importantly, the number of members inside an NCSC determines the number of output shares and therefore directly impacts the complexity of the resulting TI. In this work, we derive new lower bounds on the minimal number of members of NCSCs and obtain new upper bounds by explicit constructions. We present a group-theoretic construction of balanced NCSCs, in which the numbers of input and output shares coincide, together with a search algorithm based on intersections of group translates. Our methods determine the smallest balanced coverings in two previously unresolved cases and yield exact minima and classifications of optimal coverings for an infinite family of parameters. These results resolve all four explicit open problems posed by Farr\`as, Fidalgo and Lara-Nino.
papers.authors: Enrico Piccione, Jan Vorloeper

papers.title: NotaryMark: Multi-Bit Watermarking for Black-Box DatasetUsage Auditing in Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) models increasingly require data, more publicly available yet licensed data is being harvested and used without authorization. Although several previous studies have proposed watermarking methods for dataset copyright auditing, their applicability to the text-to-image (T2I) setting remains notably limited. The core drawback is that watermarks embedded by existing techniques are often treated as noise and are gradually filtered out and attenuated during the latent noising-denoising process of diffusion model training. We propose NotaryMark, to our knowledge the first multi-bit watermarking method specifically designed for black-box auditing of T2I training dataset use. The core idea of NotaryMark is to align the watermark with the latent denoising of diffusion models, thereby overcoming the signal decay that plagues existing multi-bit methods during sampling. We evaluate NotaryMark across three datasets and three diffusion models spanning watermark capacities from 8 to 1024 bits. With a watermark capacity below 32 bits, it achieves a high average bit accuracy of 0.85-0.90. With a watermark capacity exceeding 32 bits, it maintains bit accuracy between 0.67 and 0.80, consistently outperforming existing multi-bit watermark methods whose bit accuracy is around 0.42-0.60. Furthermore, we design a voting-based aggregation scheme to boost the bit accuracy with a modest budget of 30 queries. Building on this, we incorporate error-correcting codes to enable reliable decoding and tracing of the embedded identifier information. Robustness evaluation against fifteen evasion attacks spanning seven categories shows that NotaryMark remains robust under most evaluated settings, while stronger attacks generally suppress watermark evidence only at the cost of substantial utility degradation, demonstrating its practical reliability against malicious tampering.
papers.authors: Xinyi Yu, Linkang Du, Zhou Su, Min Chen, Yuntao Wang, Zhikun Zhang

papers.title: Differentially Private Distance-Sensitive Representations for General Metrics
papers.abstract: A distance-sensitive set representation stores a set $S$ from a metric space $(U,d)$ and answers queries of the form "is some element of $S$ within distance $r$ of $q$?''. Existing differentially private constructions are confined to Hamming space, because they route the query through a signature map built for that metric. We give a framework that removes this restriction. The released object records only the occupancy of a fixed public partition of $U$, so privacy transfers unchanged from an off-the-shelf private membership structure, and the entire metric dependence collapses into one packing quantity, the straddle number $\kappa$: the largest number of cells a ball of radius $r$ can meet. Any metric admitting a partition of width at most $(c-1)r$ and straddlenumber $\kappa$ then has an $\varepsilon$-differentially private $(c,r)$-representation with $\varepsilon =\ln(2\kappa/\alpha)$ in $O(k\log(\kappa/\alpha))$ bits. Instantiating $\kappa$ gives matching upper and lower bounds in $\ell_\infty$ for partition-based constructions ($\varepsilon=O(\log d)$ at $c=\Theta(d)$, against $\varepsilon=\Omega(d)$ at constant $c$), and a randomized, dimension-free construction for every $\ell_p$ (one probe and $\varepsilon=\ln(2/\alpha)$ regardless of $d$) at the cost of a weaker, non-oblivious guarantee whose price is exactly this $\log d$ gap. For metrics available only through a distance oracle, we build the partition from a public net and a public navigable graph, and show that greedy search on that graph both locates and enumerates the cells a query must probe; on a $\lambda$-doubling metric this gives $\varepsilon\le 5\ln\lambda+\ln(2/\alpha)$. We further show that the per-query form of the guarantee is forced rather than chosen: any representation correct on all queries simultaneously requires $\varepsilon\ge\ln M+\ln(1/\alpha)-O(1)$ for $M$ the packing number of the whole space, and on doubling metrics this is achievable up to an additive $O(dim_D\log\frac{c}{c-1})$. Finally, the space bound is optimal in $k$ and $\alpha$.
papers.authors: Paul Cesaretti

papers.title: Quantum Key Exchange from Public Quantum Money
papers.abstract: Two-message quantum key exchange (2QKE) cannot be realized in a statistically secure way, and therefore some computational assumptions are required [Malavolta and Walter 2024]. So far, the known weakest assumption for 2QKE is the existence of one-way functions (OWFs): Malavolta and Walter constructed (even everlasting-secure) 2QKE from OWFs [Malavolta and Walter 2024], and Kitagawa, Morimae, Nishimaki, and Yamakawa constructed quantum public-key encryption (QPKE) with quantum public keys, which implies 2QKE, from OWFs [Kitagawa, Morimae, Nishimaki and Yamakawa 2024]. Can we construct 2QKE from a weaker assumption than OWFs? In this paper, we give the first complete characterization of 2QKE. We show that the following four primitives are (existentially) equivalent: everlasting-secure 2QKE, standard 2QKE, efficiently-verifiable state puzzles (EV-StatePuzzs), and one-time secure digital signatures with quantum signatures and signing keys. Because EV-StatePuzzs are potentially weaker than OWFs [Kretschmer, Qian and Tal 2025], the equivalence implies that 2QKE are potentially weaker than OWFs. Moreover, our result shows the equivalence between standard 2QKE and everlasting-secure 2QKE, which means that everlasting security comes for free. Finally, one-shot signatures, quantum lightning, and public-key quantum money mini-schemes imply EV-StatePuzzs, and therefore, our result also gives a new lowerbound, namely everlasting-secure 2QKE, of these public-key unclonable primitives. We also show that one-shot signatures imply QPKE with quantum public keys [Kitagawa, Morimae, Nishimaki and Yamakawa, 2024] constructed QPKE with quantum public keys from OWFs, and it was open whether QPKE with quantum public keys can be constructed from an assumption weaker than or incomparable to OWFs. Our result gives a potential answer to this question since one-shot signatures seem to be incomparable with OWFs. Moreover, QPKE constructed from one-shot signatures has an additional functionality, which we call certified freeze, that allows the receiver to publish a publicly verifiable classical certificate that computationally binds the receiver to an upper bound on the total number of distinct valid ciphertexts under its verification key.
papers.authors: Eli Goldin, Tomoyuki Morimae

papers.title: Exact $\ell_p$-CVP via Euclidean SVP in Polynomial Space
papers.abstract: We give a randomized, rank-preserving reduction from exact $\ell_p$-CVP to exact Euclidean SVP for every integer $p\ge2$. For rational inputs of bit length $\ell$ on full-rank lattices $L\subset\mathbb R^N$, the reduction uses $(Cp)^N\poly(p,\ell)$ oracle calls and additional bit operations, where $C$ is an absolute constant. It uses $\poly(p,\ell)$ working space outside the oracle, and all oracle queries have rank $N$ and $\poly(p,\ell)$ bit complexity. For $p=2$, the reduction transfers polynomial-space exact SVP algorithms to exact CVP with $2^{O(N)}\poly(\ell)$ time overhead. Instantiating it with the SVP algorithms of Kannan and of Feng, Gao and Liu yields randomized polynomial-space CVP algorithms running in time $N^{N/(2e)+o(N)}$ and $N^{N/(4e)+o(N)}$, respectively. For every fixed integer $p\ge3$, the same reduction yields exact $\ell_p$-CVP algorithms for arbitrary rational targets either in randomized time and space $2^{O(N)}$, or in randomized time $N^{N/(4e)+o(N)}$ and polynomial space. These algorithmic bounds are up to polynomial factors in $\ell$. The reduction performs local search sequentially over the cosets of \(2L\), where \(L\) is the input lattice, while tracking the excess of the current objective value over the optimum. Within a coset containing a closest vector, midpoint inequalities bound the unknown correction in terms of this excess, which in turn allows us to construct many short corrections that reduce the excess bound by a factor of four. A counting argument shows that these improving corrections form a sufficiently large fraction of the lattice points in a known search region, and a sparsification-based sampler assigns sufficiently large probability to every nonzero vector in that region, using at most one SVP call per sample. Repeating this improvement over polynomially many stages yields exact recovery. For \(p\ge3\), the same framework is extended using a diagonal weighted norm computed from the current point.
papers.authors: Jiseung Kim, Minkyu Kim, Hyung Tae Lee

papers.title: On the Order of Privacy and Smoothing in Functional Mean Estimation
papers.abstract: Differential privacy (DP) is a leading framework for privacy protection, yet privacy mechanisms tailored to functional data analysis (FDA) remain relatively underexplored. For functional mean estimation, we investigate a fundamental question regarding the ordering of privatization and estimation by comparing two canonical pipelines: Fit-Then-Protect (FTP), which smooths trajectories before privatization, and Protect-Then-Fit (PTF), which privatizes observations at discrete time points before smoothing. When data are observed without error, we prove that FTP achieves strictly smaller mean squared error than PTF asymptotically (as the sample size increases) under the same $μ$-Gaussian differential privacy ($μ$-GDP) budget in both finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces and infinite-dimensional reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS). Simulation studies support our theory and explore settings with observation error and fitting constraints, demonstrating that FTP outperforms PTF under small observation noise, whereas PTF can become preferable in high-noise settings. In addition to this comparison, we establish a novel GDP guarantee for Gaussian perturbations taking values in a Banach space, extending existing results beyond the RKHS setting.
papers.authors: Haotian Chen, Yu-Wei Chen, Qifan Song, Jordan Awan

papers.title: The GGM PRF Construction is Optimal
papers.abstract: We study the complexity of fully black-box constructions of pseudorandom functions (PRFs) from pseudorandom generators (PRGs). The seminal work of Goldreich, Goldwasser, and Micali (JACM 1986), combined with Levin’s domain-extension technique, yields PRFs that make a superlogarithmic number of adaptive calls to a length-doubling PRG. A long-standing open problem is whether fewer calls suffice for fully black-box constructions. Despite progress for restricted classes of constructions and reductions, previous results have not been able to rule out even a single-call construction in full generality. A related question asks how many calls are needed to amplify a PRG’s stretch from \(r\) bits to \(\rho>r\) bits. Our main result establishes the asymptotic optimality of the GGM construction with domain compression, both in the number of calls and in adaptivity, for length-doubling PRGs. More generally, for a PRG with seed length \(n\) and stretch \(r(n)\), we rule out fully black-box PRF constructions with \(d(n)\) adaptive rounds whenever \(d(n)\log(2+r(n)/n)=O(\log n)\), even allowing polynomially many calls per round. Our bounds hold for one-bit weak PRFs on domains of superpolynomial size. In particular, they exclude all polynomial-query nonadaptive constructions from PRGs of arbitrary polynomial stretch and require superlogarithmically many rounds when the underlying PRG doubles its input length. We further show impossibility results for fully black-box non-adaptive PRG stretch amplification. First, we show that a non-adaptive construction of a $\rho$-bit stretch PRG from an $r$-bit stretch PRG requires $\Omega(\tfrac{\rho}{r+\log n})$ calls. Second, we show that it is impossible to construct a length-doubling PRG from an $o(n)$-bit stretch PRG with non-adaptive calls. Our techniques combine and extend two prior lines of work. First, we develop a sensitivity framework that measures the effect of changing a uniformly chosen oracle entry and transfers this stability through black-box reductions, extending the sensitivity arguments of Bitansky et al. (CRYPTO 2017) and Bitansky and Degwekar (TCC 2019). Second, we extend the scoring mechanism of Alon et al. (CRYPTO 2026) and integrate it with our framework. Finally, we show that the sensitivity framework applies to constructions from one-way permutations. Specifically, we show another proof of Simon's impossibility of basing collision-resistant hash functions on one-way permutations. Our new proof can be viewed as an abstraction of the argument by Bitansky and Degwekar.
papers.authors: Bar Alon, Itai Dinur, Muthuramakrishnan Venkitasubramaniam

papers.title: Testing CCZ-equivalence to permutations via projections of Walsh zero spaces, with applications to APN functions
papers.abstract: Whether almost perfect nonlinear (APN) permutations exist in even dimension $n\ge 8$ is a long-standing open question, the big APN problem. The only example known in even dimension, on six bits, was found from a quadratic APN function that is not itself a permutation, by Carlet--Charpin--Zinoviev (CCZ) equivalence. It is therefore natural to test APN functions for CCZ-equivalence to a permutation. This amounts to finding two complementary $n$-dimensional subspaces among the zeros of the Walsh transform, which lie in $\mathbb{F}_2^{2n}$. A known necessary condition only uses their projections to $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ and cannot decide every case. We give an exact test for functions whose Walsh supports are affine, including all quadratic functions. It reconstructs the subspaces from their projections, through searches for subspaces of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ and for constrained bilinear maps. On the benchmarked functions in dimension twelve, it lists them $39$ to $55$ times faster than the generic search of the commonly used sboxU library. We then study the functions $x^3+a^{-1}\mathrm{Tr}(a^3x^9)$, which Göloğlu and Pavlů proved not to be CCZ-equivalent to permutations when $4$ divides $n$. With their result, our computations show that this holds for every even $n\le 24$. In dimension $18$ the necessary condition is satisfied, and the new test decides the case. We conjecture this for every even dimension. We also compile $25$ classes of quadratic APN functions in dimension ten from published instances, with equivalence certificates. No function in these classes or in their switching closure is CCZ-equivalent to a permutation. All code and data are public.
papers.authors: Emanuele Bellini

papers.title: PhotoFinish: Portable Timerless Probing of Microarchitectural Latencies
papers.abstract: Timing measurements are a fundamental building block of microarchitectural attacks, enabling software to convert otherwise invisible latency differences into architectural observations. Thus, restricting high-resolution timers is a common defense, especially in constrained environments such as web browsers. Timerless probing primitives provide an alternative approach. Instead of reading or constructing a timer, they observe architectural events that correlate with the microarchitectural state. However, such primitives typically rely on platform-specific behavior, and none generalizes across the wider computing landscape. In this paper, we present PhotoFinish, a portable timerless probing primitive that converts latency differences directly into an architectural value. PhotoFinish races an operation under test against a fixed reference in two parallel threads that then write unique values to the same shared location, resulting in a latency-dependent architectural value. PhotoFinish only requires parallel execution and shared memory, without constructing or reading a clock. We evaluate PhotoFinish on 38 CPUs spanning four ISAs and demonstrate reliable cache state classification across widely different microarchitectures, with comparable fidelity when compiled to WebAssembly and executed inside a browser. We further use PhotoFinish in AES T-table and Evict+Reload attacks, show that it applies beyond caches to TLB and execution-engine latencies, and demonstrate sufficient precision to identify the LLC slice of an address. Our results demonstrate shared-memory races as a generic and precise replacement for explicit timing, showing that restricting timers alone does not prevent software from observing fine-grained microarchitectural latency differences.
papers.authors: Tristan Hornetz, Eduard Ebert, Lorenz Hetterich, Lukas Gerlach, Michael Schwarz

papers.title: Safety Is $Π_1$, Provability Is $Σ_1$: One Framework for the Hugging Face Breach and OpenAI's Mathematical Proofs
papers.abstract: OpenAI's agents breached Hugging Face in July 2026, and the same company released more than seven hundred AI-generated manuscripts of mathematical proofs in October 2026. The first event is read as a failure in security, while the second is read as a success in mathematics. We read both through the hybrid framework of our paper (Kim and Kang, 2026, arXiv:2611.01914), in which coding, proving, and learning from data are derivations by one and the same deductive mechanism, distinguished by the kinds of premises from which they are derived. Under this framework, the AI systems behind the two events ran the same loop, in which a statistical proposer produces candidate exploits or proofs and a deductive verifier settles each one by a derivation. What separates the events is the logical form of the statement wanted by each of the two domains, security and mathematics. The safety of a program is a $Π_1$ statement, for it says that no exploit exists, which is not assured by any finite list of tests that have been passed by the program. By contrast, the provability of a sentence is a $Σ_1$ statement, for it says that a proof exists, which is assured by a single instance, namely a proof that has been checked by the deductive verifier. The theorem behind both is Turing's Undecidability Theorem: the halting set is $Σ_1$ but not decidable, so its complement is $Π_1$ and not $Σ_1$, which is to say that membership has a finite witness but non-membership has none. We prove that attaching a statistical proposer to a deductive verifier does not change this undecidability result, however good the proposer is. We then discuss what does assure safety and where the residual risk goes.
papers.authors: Jinho Kang, Jinsook Kim

papers.title: Replication Certification at Publication: Checkable by Anyone, Anywhere, in Seconds, Forever
papers.abstract: Authors increasingly deposit replication datasets---the data and code behind publications---in archives, and journals increasingly require them to, under progressively onerous rules. But a deposit alone proves little, so authors keep paying: months for the journal's reanalyses, years answering readers' questions, and rancor as failed replications become accusations because no record establishes what actually ran. We introduce a replication certificate: a cryptographically signed record of the deposited files and logged output. It replaces the journal's reanalyses with evidence anyone can check in seconds, which no one, including the archive, can backdate, and no one can fake without risking detection. Certification asks little of anyone and benefits everyone: The author deposits, then reruns the analysis once under a random seed the archive computes from the deposit's hash and a blockchain block; the archive signs, timestamps (in that blockchain), and stores the record---confidential data included---without rerunning anything; the journal merely checks a website for the certificate; and anyone can check or replay any step decades later.
papers.authors: Gary King, Yiqing Xu, Leo Yang Yang

papers.title: Jev as an LLM Safety Guardrail: An Empirical Study of Input Filtering, Selective Output Review, and Over-Refusal
papers.abstract: External safety filters can prevent unsafe requests from reaching a large language model (LLM), but may also reject legitimate queries. We present an end-to-end empirical evaluation of Jev, a probabilistic decision model, as a safety guardrail for a Qwen2.5-1.5B-based pipeline. Three configurations are compared on 970 benchmark prompts: an unfiltered LLM, Jev input filtering, and tiered Jev input filtering with selective output review. Across 720 prompts labeled harmful (520 AdvBench and 200 XSTest-unsafe), the fraction recorded as answered decreases from 527/720 (73.2%) without filtering to 17/720 (2.4%) with input filtering. On 250 XSTest-safe prompts, however, non-answer/refusal increases from 3/250 (1.2%) to 27/250 (10.8%). Tiered filtering yields 40/720 (5.6%) harmful-prompt answers and 10/250 (4.0%) benign-prompt refusals, with 79/970 (8.1%) of prompts requiring output review. Joint optimization of the tiered thresholds improves macro-F1 from 0.9351 to 0.9512, while reducing harmful-prompt answers and output-review frequency at the same benign-refusal rate. Matched-budget comparisons reveal modest additional gains over a retuned single gate on the evaluation data, although these gains are not consistently observed on a held-out split.
papers.authors: Olivia Cognetti, Bhaskar Krishnamachari

papers.title: On Differentially Private Mechanisms for Linear Regression
papers.abstract: We study the classic least-squares linear regression problem under differential privacy (DP) in the batch and the continual observation setting.
