In the latter setting, the mechanism receives a stream of $n$ data points $(x_i,y_i)$ ($x_i\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and $y_i\in\mathbb{R}$) and must output an estimate of the optimal parameters at each time step $i$. Although differentially private linear regression has been extensively studied in the batch setting, the problem remains underexplored for the continual setting, with prior work being restricted to constrained linear regression and update time polynomial in $n$. In this work, we introduce ContinualAdaSSP, the first mechanism for unconstrained linear regression under continual differential privacy. Our mechanism's suboptimality gap is proportional to $\sqrt{d}\operatorname{polylog}(n)$. It requires $O(d^2\log{n})$ space and $O(d^2\log{n}+d^ω)$ update time, where $d$ is the dimension of the input space. We also study fundamental limits of differentially private linear regression by showing the first lower bounds for the box-constrained least-squares linear regression problem. Our lower bounds are proportional to $\min(n,\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\log^{1.5}d})$ for $(1,O(\frac{1}{n}))$-DP, and $\min(n,\frac{d}ε)$ for $ε$-DP, and are derived using a reduction from a fingerprinting code problem from [Peter et al., 2024], providing new insights into the inherent hardness of this canonical task. Our experimental evaluation on real-world datasets shows that the accuracy of our continual observation mechanism clearly outperforms any other known differentially private mechanism for this problem such as rerunning the batch algorithm at each time step.
papers.authors: Bardiya Aryanfard, Monika Henzinger, Farhood Rostamkhani

papers.title: Optimal Early-Stopping Broadcast via Exponential Information Gathering
papers.abstract: Early-stopping broadcast protocols guarantee termination based on the actual number of malicious parties, $f \leq t$, encountered during execution, rather than the worst-case scenario of $t 0$ is a constant. In this work, we advance the state of the art in two directions. First, in the $t < n/2$ setting with plain PKI, we present a broadcast protocol in which all parties output within optimal $\min\{f+2,\, t+1\}$ rounds. Second, we complete the picture by introducing the first protocol that is optimally resilient ($t < n$) and asymptotically matches the lower bound for any number of corruptions $t < n$. By leveraging exponential information gathering (EIG) graphs, our constructions establish that these round bounds are achievable, providing the first feasibility result for optimal-round protocols, albeit at the cost of exponential communication complexity.
papers.authors: Giovanni Deligios, Fatima Elsheimy, Simon Holmgaard Kamp, Ivana Klasovita, Chen-Da Liu-Zhang, Julian Loss, Charalampos Papamanthou

papers.title: Bridging Correlation Measures and Unpredictability: Sharp Bounds and Insights for TRNG Validation
papers.abstract: Do small correlations certify high unpredictability? We answer this for the high-order correlation measures (Mauduit and Sárközy) and finite-memory sources. We develop minimax sharp bounds on next-bit prediction from high-order correlations and show that the min-entropy-rate deficit is linear in the largest correlation, with optimal first-order constants. We also bridge population and sample correlations through ergodic limits and finite-sample guarantees. As an application, we show that the validation method for true random number generators recently proposed at WAIFI 2026 over-rejects: shrinking (sub-constant) thresholds strongly reject sources of nearly full entropy.
papers.authors: Maciej Skorski, Onur Günlü

papers.title: Breaking $\mathsf{TraintoDefend}$ via Adaptive Neuron Clustering in Cryptanalytic Model Extraction
papers.abstract: Cryptanalytic model extraction poses a fundamental threat to deep learning model confidentiality by enabling precise parameter recovery with theoretical guarantees of functional equivalence. To counter this growing threat, $\mathsf{Train to Defend}$ (NeurIPS 2025) was proposed as the first dedicated defense against cryptanalytic extraction and remains the only defense believed to be effective to date. It encourages neurons to learn similar weights so that they switch activation states together, making their individual contributions harder to distinguish. However, we notice that neurons with similar weights need not switch activation states together under small perturbations. Instead, weight similarity can cause the original clustering rule to merge signatures from distinct neurons when only a subset of their normalized weight coordinates agree. Motivated by this observation, we introduce $\mathsf{SimBreak}$, an adaptive clustering rule that breaks the weight-similarity defense of $\mathsf{Train to Defend}$. $\mathsf{SimBreak}$ estimates a relative scale from all jointly observed weight coordinates and uses the same scale to test both weight direction and bias consistency. Across six protected fully connected networks trained on MNIST, $\mathsf{SimBreak}$ raises target layer signature recovery from $0\%$ to $100\%$, with a maximum relative recovery error of $2^{-22.27}$. Our work challenges the use of neuron weight similarity as a sufficient basis for protection and establishes adaptive evaluation as essential to assessing cryptanalytic extraction defenses.
papers.authors: Haojie Wu, Haolin Liu, Tianshuo Cong, Guoyan Zhang

papers.title: One-Way Functions and Local Descriptions of Random Data
papers.abstract: Sample compression describes a labeled sample by retained examples and extra information from which a decoder recovers the labels. We show that estimating the length of the shortest such description of random data is hard on average if and only if one-way functions exist. As in Hirahara and Nanashima's (FOCS 2023) consistent pointwise programs, the decoder labels each sample point separately, as a hypothesis does, but in our main result the labels are random rather than given by a concept. To label a point, it sees only that point, the retained examples with one extra bit each, a program, and a public random string revealed before the description is chosen. The length counts the choice of retained examples, their extra bits and the program, not the examples themselves. The task is to output a number between the $1/2$ and $3/4$ quantiles of the shortest length over the public string, up to an additive $a\lceil\log_2m\rceil$ for $m$ points and a fixed integer $a\ge0$. The main result takes polynomially many, at least $8n$, uniform $n$-bit points with independent uniform labels and any large enough polynomial time bound per query. If one-way functions exist, every efficient randomized algorithm fails to output such a number for all large $n$ with probability above an inverse polynomial that is the same for all algorithms and time bounds. Otherwise, for every inverse polynomial, some such algorithm fails with at most that probability for infinitely many $n$. For hardness, labels derived from one-way functions look random yet have short local descriptions, which random labels rarely have. The converse inverts a function that generates descriptions. One-way functions also exist if and only if estimating between the quantiles is hard, at some suitable time bound, for some PAC-style samplable data of the same sizes, labeled by a concept independent of the points.
papers.authors: Dimitrios Myrisiotis

papers.title: An improved algorithm to solve the isogeny problem in dimension 2 with precomputation
papers.abstract: We give a new algorithm for the superspecial isogeny problem in dimension $2$. After a one-time precomputation depending only on $p$ (which succeeds with overwhelming probability), each instance is solved in expected time and memory $p^{3/4+o(1)}$. This result is unconditional, relying on no heuristics. Including the precomputation, a single instance is solved in time $p^{19/23+o(1)}$, improving on the $p^{1+o(1)}$ of the Costello-Smith algorithm. The improvement holds even with the same memory as (the rigorous version of) their algorithm. The key ingredient is an algorithm that computes the equations of the Humbert surfaces $\mathcal{H}_{N^2}$ modulo $p$ for all $N$ up to a bound $D$ growing with $p$. These equations give a membership test for optimally $(N,N)$-split surfaces, which we evaluate in batches using fast multipoint evaluation. This speeds up the bottleneck of the Costello-Smith algorithm: finding an isogeny from a superspecial principally polarised abelian surface to a product of supersingular elliptic curves.
papers.authors: Maria Corte-Real Santos

papers.title: FirstSwap: Pre-Consensus Trade Approvals for Decentralized Market Design
papers.abstract: Decentralized exchanges typically give traders no execution guarantee until a block is finalized. In the meantime, external prices move, traders strategically delay submission, and block producers can influence inclusion and ordering. We introduce FirstSwap, a DEX built on a constant-function market maker pricing curve that gives traders an early pre-approval before consensus, guaranteeing inclusion and execution within their submitted price limit, with final ordering determined by limit prices rather than by a block producer. We demonstrate the benefits of trade pre-approvals in an economic model combining auction theory with CEX-DEX arbitrage. When the CEX price changes gradually, FirstSwap rewards earlier traders with better prices, discouraging strategic delay and yielding higher social welfare and gains to AMM liquidity providers than a batch auction. When the CEX price jumps abruptly, FirstSwap yields higher welfare and smaller AMM losses than fair ordering. The central challenge is delivering fast trade pre-approvals without consensus. We introduce a decentralized, scaled admissibility protocol under which each validator reserves only a fraction of the available liquidity at every price. A trader obtains approval in a single round of messages with a quorum of validators. Somewhat surprisingly, despite Byzantine validators who may approve trades arbitrarily, we show that all quorum-certified trades are jointly admissible and execute within their limits. Our protocol extends naturally to a setting where buy and sell orders can be pre-approved against each other before a block is finalized.
papers.authors: William Diamond, Fatima Elsheimy, Dahlia Malkhi, Geoff Ramseyer, Srivatsan Sridhar

papers.title: On Proximity Gaps for Expander Codes
papers.abstract: Proximity gaps describe a phenomenon concerning random linear combinations of words and their distance from a linear error-correcting code. Informally, they address the following question: if a collection of words is jointly far from the code, is a random linear combination of those words likely to also remain far from the code? Motivated by applications to concretely efficient proof systems, in this note we study this question for expander codes, a class of low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes. Recent works of Goyal and Guruswami (STOC 2026) and Goyal, Guruswami, Sun, and Wootters (RANDOM 2026; arXiv 2026) establish proximity gaps approaching capacity for random LDPC ensembles, but only asymptotically and for very large degrees and field sizes, well beyond what is used in practical proof systems. We focus on general expander codes (not necessarily random) with small degree. Building on the smoothness property of expander codes due to Dinur, Sudan, and Wigderson (RANDOM 2006), we show that such codes have proximity gaps up to nearly half of the distance guaranteed by their expansion.
papers.authors: Kobi Gurkan, Andrija Novakovic, Ron D. Rothblum

papers.title: SciCheck: A Framework for Verifying the Integrity of Deep Learning Training
papers.abstract: Deep learning training is difficult to verify within a scientific workflow: its architecture, hyperparameters, and procedure are rarely fixed until training has been attempted, and two honest runs never produce the same weights, so recomputation cannot serve as a check. We present SciCheck, a framework in which the scientist explores training configurations freely and posts a blueprint to a provenance ledger for each candidate they want verified, and a verifying scientist judges the resulting run in two layers: a statistical judge model that compares per-step gradient statistics against the verifier's own reference run, and a spot-check that re-executes randomly chosen training segments whose checkpoints are committed to the ledger one epoch at a time. On an MLP, a CNN, and an autoencoder at 100k-500k parameters, under gradient sign flipping, label poisoning, and fabricated runs, SciCheck reaches F1 of 0.966, 0.906, and 0.976 while rejecting 0-4.4% of honest runs. For the attacks we test, the spot-check accounts for most of this accuracy, and we characterize what each layer can detect. The effective-signal statistic falls as $(1-2s)^2$ under a sign flip of severity $s$, so gradient statistics alone catch strong enough sign flips, while fabricated runs that replay genuine statistics look no more anomalous than honest runs to any statistical detector we test. The spot-check catches fully fabricated segments with probability at least $1-(1-s)^k$ for $k$ sampled segments when the draws stay hidden until the run is committed, which roughly matches our measurements and lets a verifier choose $k$ for a target soundness. Verification costs 1.5-2.3x one retraining, mostly for the verifier's reference run; each submission's spot-check takes under 1.5 s, and per-epoch commitments reduce checkpoint storage 5-17x compared with keeping every checkpoint.
papers.authors: Alexander Nguyen, Dylan Gresham, Gaby G. Dagher, Min Long

papers.title: A Cross-Domain TARA-to-NAC Rule Mapping Methodology: From Automotive OEM Networks to Energy Storage Systems
papers.abstract: Threat analysis and risk assessment under ISO/SAE 21434 ends with cybersecurity goals, but existing methods give little structured guidance for turning those goals into enforceable network access control rules. Compliance standards such as IEC 62443, ISO/SAE 21434, and ISO/IEC 27001 are usually applied as parallel efforts rather than as one enforcement architecture. This paper presents a six-step methodology that maps cybersecurity goals from a threat analysis and risk assessment to network access control rules, each placed at a named enforcement point and traceable to the threat records behind it. It also presents a unified compliance framework that treats IEC 62443 and ISO/IEC 27001 as a fixed substrate and domain-specific regulation as an interchangeable overlay. The methodology is applied to an automotive original equipment manufacturer plant network, addressing multi-tier supplier authorization and legacy operational technology devices, and then to utility-scale battery energy storage, where North American Electric Reliability Corporation Critical Infrastructure Protection standards and ISO/IEC 27019 replace the automotive-specific standard while the substrate stays constant. In the automotive example, 37 threat entries and 24 cybersecurity goals yield 23 rules covering 11 of the 13 in-scope goals; the energy example yields six rules. Three derived rules have no equivalent in the cited standards. Both examples are desk-based: the methodology is applied to them, not tested on them. The result is a reusable pattern for translating risk assessment into enforcement across critical infrastructure sectors, with empirical validation left as future work.
papers.authors: Krishna Teja Medam, Thiago Quinelato

papers.title: MemoryDojo: Benchmarking Poisoning Through LLM Agent Memory
papers.abstract: LLM agents benefit from using memory systems to improve performance on long-horizon, multi-session tasks. However, memory introduces a critical attack surface. Malicious instructions encountered in one session may be stored and propagated through memory before being retrieved and acted upon in later sessions. Because memory systems differ in how they process and retrieve information, the downstream effects of poisoning can vary significantly across systems. To quantify the effects of poisoning across different memory architectures, we introduce MemoryDojo, a benchmark for tracing the lifecycle of poisoned information through agent memory and measuring its influence on subsequent agent behavior. MemoryDojo is easily extensible, consists of 155 multi-session long-horizon trajectories covering four domains, and supports five different memory systems. Through our evaluation, we find that all memory systems are susceptible to memory poisoning, with substantial variation in downstream effects. We further propose a memory-aware poison optimization process that increases the poisoning efficacy, highlighting differences between memory architectures. We hope that MemoryDojo will support research on understanding and mitigating agentic memory risks.
papers.authors: David H. Yang, Blake Bullwinkel, Amanda Minnich, Mohammad Mohammadi Amiri, Giorgio Severi

papers.title: Differentially Private GraphRAG: Protecting Relation Connectivity and Semantics
papers.abstract: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) connects information across documents through entity relationships to support relational reasoning. However, black-box access to GraphRAG systems can enable adversaries to reconstruct knowledge graphs and recover both structural connectivity between entities and the semantics of their relationships. Existing defenses lack formal privacy guarantees and provide limited protection against such reconstruction attacks. We propose RelGuard, the first differentially private framework for GraphRAG, which provides formal privacy guarantees by mitigating connectivity leakage and protecting relations and their semantic meaning through relation removal. We formalize relation differential privacy (relation-DP), which bounds the distinguishability of mechanism outputs according to the semantic distance between alternative relations while accounting for relation removal. Building on this definition, we develop a four-step defense mechanism that sanitizes source documents before GraphRAG indexing by perturbing relation predicates or removing their associated connectivity using the exponential mechanism. Experiments across three GraphRAG systems and two targeted reconstruction attacks demonstrate that RelGuard provides stronger protection against reconstruction attacks than four existing defense mechanisms while better preserving downstream utility.
papers.authors: Jie Fu, Yuan Hong, Yue Ning, Wendy Hui Wang

papers.title: ReplayAudit: Auditing Outsourced LLM Fine-Tuning via Sealed Records and Selective Replay
papers.abstract: Auditing outsourced LLM fine-tuning requires checking an untrusted provider's training while controlling verification cost. Uniform sampling ignores training-time signals, while checking a suspicious record can require replaying several preceding steps. We present ReplayAudit, a telemetry-guided auditing system that seals training records before challenges and independently replays sampled intervals from sealed checkpoints. Loss changes and parameter-update norms guide stratified random sampling; replay determines whether the selected computation agrees with its records. We relate sampling probabilities to replay work and evaluate the system on real LoRA training. A 7B BF16 prototype rejects a false update-norm report during a random audit; targeted checks also reject false loss reports and skipped updates. We calibrate sampling budgets offline to at least a 90% probability of directly selecting an injected step. For two learning-rate deviation settings, executing these budgets on the same honest 1.5B trajectory reduces median complete-audit wall time by 49% and 67% relative to uniform sampling. When skipped updates evade the high-anomaly stratum, the corresponding audit instead costs 38% more. These results show how deviation capture and actual replay work jointly determine the cost of telemetry-guided auditing.
papers.authors: Yihan Xia, Wenxin Xu, Taotao Wang

papers.title: Parallelizable modes for duplex-based authenticated encryption
papers.abstract: This note enriches the SHAKE and TurboSHAKE-based authenticated encryption schemes defined by Daemen et al. at EuroS&P 2025 with parallelizable ones, while keeping their security properties. The main contribution is a new deck cipher mode, called FlightDeck, that has the ability of processing input strings similarly to KangarooTwelve and producing output strings as in counter mode, so both parallelizable. We then instantiate FlightDeck on top of the overwrite duplex (OD) construction, in turn on top of a Keccak-p permutation. Combined with a deck cipher-based mode like Deck-BO, the security of the resulting authenticated encryption schemes reduces to the PRF security of keyed (Turbo)SHAKE and to the collision resistance of (Turbo)SHAKE. Compared to the schemes defined at EuroS&P 2025, replacing UpperDeck with FlightDeck greatly improves their software efficiency as one can implement them with Keccak-p permutations evaluated in parallel.
papers.authors: Joan Daemen, Silvia Mella, Gilles Van Assche

papers.title: Exploring the Set of APN Functions
papers.abstract: An Almost Perfect Nonlinear (APN) function $F : \mathbb{F}_2^n \to \mathbb{F}_2^n$ provides optimal protection against differential attacks, meaning that the equation $F(x+a)=F(x)+b$ has at most 2 solutions~$x$ when $a \neq 0$. Setting aside some sporadic examples, such functions are hard to find in practice, and whether there exists APN bijections of $ \mathbb{F}_2^n$ when $n > 6$ is even (the Big APN Problem) is still unknown. In this paper, we provide the tools needed to explore the complete set of known APN functions. Indeed, for a given APN function $F$, we in fact know many: all functions CCZ-equivalent to $F$ are also APN, and so are its switching neighbours. These notions have been in the literature for many years, but several unknowns remain that complicate the exploration of the corresponding functions in practice: a given function has too many switching neighbours, and the algorithms that are known to iterate through a CCZ-equivalence class return multiple representatives per extended-affine (EA) equivalence class. We solve both problems. First, we show how to partition precisely the CCZ-equivalence class of a quadratic APN function in practice, and thus obtain exactly one representative per EA-equivalence class. To achieve this, we carefully investigate the set of the automorphisms of the graph of a quadratic APN function, and show how to generate them very efficiently using the ortho-derivative. Second, we provide the first detailed investigation of the set of the switching neighbours of a function, show in particular how an overwhelming majority of them are trivial, and explain how to get rid of those. Incidentally, we build a new extended-affine equivalence class invariant using the resulting set of non-trivial switching neighbours. For both theoretical contributions, we pushed highly-efficient and easy to re-use implementations of the corresponding algorithms to the sboxU library. It allowed us to generate databases containing all known APN functions for $n=6$ and $n=7$. For $n=8$, our algorithms are efficient-enough that we can investigate the properties of the millions of quadratic APN function recently exhibited. In the process, we generate a few thousands of new CCZ-equivalence classes. In the light of our work, the successes of the exploration strategies for $n=6$ (i.e. finding an APN function inequivalent to any monomial and quadratic mapping, and finding an APN bijection in even dimension) seems to be an artifact due to the small dimension that we show not to work for dimension 8 and which we do not expect to work either when the dimension is greater.
papers.authors: Jules Baudrin, Pierre Galissant, Léo Perrin

papers.title: Robust & Scalable Website Fingerprinting via Minimal DRAM Traffic
papers.abstract: Website fingerprinting attacks infer websites visited by users and threaten their privacy. These attacks are classified as on-path, which monitor network traffic, and co-located, which exploit shared system resources. Existing co-located attacks, such as sweep-counting and loop-counting, achieve over 90% accuracy but suffer significant performance degradation on many-core systems. Loop-counting accuracy drops from 93% on 8 cores to 50% on 24 cores, while sweep-counting accuracy decreases from 84% to 45% across multiple Core Complex Dies (CCDs). To address these limitations, we propose memory-chasing, a scalable website fingerprinting attack that exploits DRAM traffic interference through pointer-chasing traversals with minimal interference. By counting DRAM accesses over fixed intervals, the attack generates distinctive traces for website classification. Evaluated on the top 50 websites, memory-chasing achieves 96% accuracy on a 24-core system, 86% across multiple CCDs, 80% across multiple sockets, and 97% in an open-world setting. Extensive evaluation across hardware configurations, browsers, operating systems, isolation mechanisms, system noise, and countermeasures demonstrates its robustness and scalability.
papers.authors: Shubham Roy, Samar Perwez, Biswabandan Panda

papers.title: Cutpurse: Decomposing Explanation-Guided Model Extraction on Tabular Data
papers.abstract: Explanation APIs are often treated as increasing model-extraction risk, but an end-to-end attack comparison cannot show whether an explanation reveals model-specific information or merely supplies a convenient next-query coordinate. We study this distinction for explanation-guided extraction of tabular classifiers. We separate an explanation into an attribution channel, which ranks influential features, and a coordinate channel, which supplies candidate feature values for perturbing those features. We then test whether the useful bin edges are privileged to the service or reproducible from the adversary's own data. Across six datasets and five target families, using attribution rankings to choose which features to perturb provides no systematic extraction advantage. Lime's discretization bin edges can improve fidelity by up to 41 percentage points on continuous features, but those edges are quantiles of the explainer's background data rather than properties of the target model. In controlled comparisons, an attacker-side grid reproduces the useful bin-edge gains without querying an explanation API. We use these findings to derive Cutpurse, which combines a self-computed grid with diverse query generation and boundary search. Against a service that withholds bin edges, Cutpurse improves fidelity by 16.3 percentage points on continuous-feature targets. It also exceeds the undefended published attack by 7.0 percentage points. Thus, withholding default Lime bin edges alone does not prevent effective extraction under the in-domain auxiliary-input, probability-output, and same-family surrogate assumptions studied here. Our results concern default Lime and Shap configurations for tabular classifiers. They do not establish the same conclusion for other explainers, target classes, or data-free attackers.
papers.authors: Seyma Selcan Magara, Hanru Zhang, Fatme El Zahraa Hamad, Nico Pfeifer, Mete Akgün

papers.title: When Feedback Becomes a Backdoor: Tracing Backdoor Skill Formation in Text-Space Skill Optimization
papers.abstract: Reference answers are a supervision channel in text-space Skill optimization, which produces reusable text artifacts called Skills that guide future agent behavior. Poisoning those answers can induce a persistent trigger-conditioned rule without giving the attacker access to the model, optimizer, or Skill file. We study this reference-feedback poisoning in SkillOpt by tracing an attacker-supplied trigger--payload mapping from reflection to held-out activation. In SearchQA, where the payload replaces a short answer, the natural attack retains an exact rule in all three seeds; each final Skill emits the payload on 200/200 triggered questions and 0/200 clean questions. In seed 42, removing the rule eliminates activation, and an in-run comparison shows similar clean accuracy to benign SkillOpt (169/200 versus 171/200). In SpreadsheetBench, where the payload requires an additional workbook edit, no natural run retains an exact rule across three seeds. Diagnostic interventions locate two successive bottlenecks: the Analyst abstracts away required literals, and, once literal preservation is enabled, edit-budget ranking can remove exact edits before candidate construction. Poisoned references can therefore create persistent backdoors, but exposure alone does not ensure that the induced rule is formed, selected, and retained.
papers.authors: Louise Nayeong Koh, Yaechan Lee, Myeongjong Lee, Doyeon Kim, Juyoung Park, Seunggyu Kim, Inseo Kim, Chaerin Jung, Hyogon Ryu

papers.title: The Maximum Possible Nonlinearity for a Balanced Boolean Function in 10 Variables is 492
papers.abstract: Determining the maximum nonlinearity of 10-variable balanced Boolean functions has been a long-standing open problem. In this paper, we resolve it by proving that the maximum nonlinearity is exactly 492, thereby confirming Dobbertin’s conjecture in dimension 10. To exclude nonlinearity 494, we derive a quadratic residue for the Walsh spectrum and refine a local energy table from four-block concatenation by retaining the signs of the Walsh coefficients. The resulting bounds exclude all but the largest polar rank; a product inequality and a parity argument eliminate the remaining case.
papers.authors: Youle Xu, Qichun Wang

papers.title: Authorization Drift in LLM Agents: Evaluating Boundary Compliance in Multi-Step Tool Use
papers.abstract: LLM agents can exceed their authorization boundaries while pursuing user goals without an adversary. We formalize this phenomenon as authorization drift across data, tool, scope, and time, and introduce the Authorization Drift Benchmark (ADB): 648 samples across seven domains, each pairing a sufficient compliant path with an attractive unauthorized shortcut. To ensure executable tasks, tempting shortcuts, and feasible compliant paths, Staged Execution-Reflective Synthesis (SERS) grounds benchmark validation in real agent rollouts rather than LLM self-critique. Across 13 LLMs and three frameworks (25,207 trajectories), greater capability accompanies greater drift, with frontier-capable models exhibiting drift rates of 0.43 to 0.61. Yet 86.18% of tasks admit an observed clean-success trajectory, showing that drift is avoidable. Drift is persistent and dominated by early data over-collection; apparent improvements under agentic scaffolds coincide with collapsing clean-completion performance. To understand potential harms to individuals and society, we map drift points to legal provisions across four jurisdictions, connecting overreach to privacy and information-security concerns. Data minimisation is the most frequently implicated provision, and 93.5% of legally grounded drifting runs map to multiple jurisdictions, making the potential consequences of authorization drift more interpretable.
papers.authors: Chuxue Cao, Jingru Zeng, Boqin Yin, Yujin Zhou, Yidan Huang, Sujin Chen, Jinluan Yang, Haoran Li, Yike Guo, Sirui Han

papers.title: Who's Asking? Audience-Conditioned Privatization
papers.abstract: The abundance of user-generated conversational data makes the question of how to responsibly derive insights from confidential data without putting the individuals in it at risk ever more important. However, the majority of existing differentially private (DP) synthetic text generation (SDG) and anonymization approaches ignore the context of the data's downstream usage, which results in loss of important information. DP-SDG provides the same guarantee regardless of the recipient, and anonymization relies on predefined attribute categories. They both ignore the observation that an attribute that is harmless to one audience can be sensitive to another, and each audience typically needs only some attributes preserved. We propose Ext-Classify-Priv, a framework that (1) extracts the information types present in a corpus, (2) classifies which of them are private for a given audience following contextual integrity, and (3) protects only those attributes, using either anonymization or SDG with Feature-DP approaches. On Reddit data with 3 audiences, our audience-specific releases are more faithful than a single audience-agnostic release for every audience. On bioRxiv data, our SDG method improves MAUVE from 0.097 to 0.420 at epsilon=1 and on the proprietary real estate data, our anonymization method improves MAUVE from 0.698 to 0.959 over the best baselines.
papers.authors: Daniil Filienko, Anusha Bagalkotkar, Xan Vongsathorn, Sikha Pentyala

papers.title: Gain-Dependent Entropy Characterization of a Zener Avalanche Noise TRNG via Dual NIST Standards: Toward Low-Cost Hardware Entropy for ICS Deployments
papers.abstract: True random number generators based on Zener avalanche noise offer a low-cost entropy source for industrial control system and IoT edge devices, yet the relationship between amplifier gain, coupling capacitance, and entropy quality remains uncharacterized under current NIST standards. This paper presents a comprehensive entropy assessment of an op-amp-based Zener avalanche noise generator across five gain configurations and two coupling capacitor values, evaluated against the NIST SP 800-22 statistical test suite and the SP~800-90B entropy source assessment using 1.44 billion raw bits per configuration. We identify a three-phase autocorrelation structure, attributed to comparator saturation-recovery dynamics, consistent across all gain settings. A direct-current substitution experiment, replacing the Zener diode with a stable voltage source at the same bias point, reduces switching activity by approximately 97%, confirming that Zener avalanche noise, rather than amplifier self-excitation, is the necessary entropy source. The coupling capacitor is further shown to govern comparator overdrive and entropy quality independent of this source mechanism, with the smaller capacitance improving entropy, throughput, and bias. The combined results identify an optimal gain configuration achieving a perfect statistical test score, NIST-compliant min-entropy, and peak entropy throughput at a bill-of-materials cost under five dollars, offering practical design guidance for low-cost entropy sources in industrial and embedded deployments.
papers.authors: Rishabh Das

papers.title: Conflux: Preventing Privilege Escalation with Principal Contexts and System-Level Evaluation
papers.abstract: LLM agents combine information from multiple principals while acting externally. We formalise privilege escalation (PE) as the system-level security objective: an action may proceed only if every principal that influenced it would allow it. Model-level defences remain probabilistic, so enforcement must sit outside model judgement. We present Conflux, a principal-context defence. Its kernel, ITES, derives authority from provenance and the organisation's existing access-control system and intersects the permissions of every influencing principal. We prove a conditional authority-confinement theorem: under complete mediation, no-laundering provenance, a known non-empty decision context, fresh permission checks, and action binding, the kernel admits no action that escalates privilege with respect to any recorded influencing principal. The theorem covers the represented value-influence fragment; control influence from tool, branch, recipient, or plan-step selection remains a refinement obligation. Conflux extends the kernel with independent policy ports, argument-aware authorisation, disclosure, consent, delegation, restriction, and exposure planning. We describe two system- level evaluators. SLED is a black-box evaluator: it exhaustively explores a declared finite model of a defence up to a bound. SLED-V is a white-box evaluator: it checks a serialisable intermediate representation against security and provenance properties. The evidence is bounded and partial. The appendix reports retained AgentDojo, SLED, and SLED-V results, including the limits of those runs. No result in this paper is an unbounded deployment guarantee.
papers.authors: Raya Buckley, Christian Schroeder de Witt

papers.title: I Don't Care How You Hide It, I Care What You Do: Runtime Detection of Malicious ML Models
papers.abstract: Pre-trained machine learning (ML) models shared through public platforms can be weaponized to execute malicious payloads during loading or inference. Existing scanners prove inadequate for detecting malicious models as they rely on static analysis and function denylists, support limited serialization formats, and miss attacks that replace denylisted functions with equivalent alternatives, exploit unsupported loading paths, or abuse legitimate framework APIs. To address this problem, we present ModelShield, the first runtime behavioral detection system for malicious ML models that attributes observed system-level behavior to specific model operations. It combines application-level instrumentation of ML framework APIs with eBPF-based syscall tracing, tracking model behavior across spawned threads and processes to separate model-triggered activity from environment noise. Attributed syscall sequences are classified using 195 detection patterns mapped to MITRE ATT&CK techniques. We implemented ModelShield to support 17 ML frameworks and 36 formats. On an independent dataset, it is the only evaluated tool to achieve zero false positives, with false negatives limited to payloads that produce no malicious runtime behavior. It detected all 29 published evasion variants spanning function substitution, loading-path obfuscation, and TensorFlow API abuse, where no existing scanner achieved complete coverage. Across 145,000 models scanned from public platforms, it captured 41 malicious models on Hugging Face, including a reverse-shell payload and a payload that performed host reconnaissance and outbound exfiltration. Among these, ModelScan, PickleScan, Fickling, and ModelAudit detected only 29%, 56%, 80%, and 93%, respectively. Despite runtime overhead, ModelShield has a median analysis time of 12.3 seconds, with 90% of scans completing within 35.5 seconds, making it practical for hub-scale screening.
papers.authors: Hala Ali, Andrew Case

papers.title: Memory-Efficient HQC Implementations on Cortex-M3 and Cortex-M7
papers.abstract: In the Hamming Quasi-Cyclic (HQC) key encapsulation mechanism (KEM), eliminating the polynomial product buffer still leaves serialized inputs, operands, and candidate ciphertexts that may coexist during decapsulation. We organize storage around the last use of each value. Comparing each candidate component before producing the next allows both to share one workspace, while deterministic regeneration shortens the lifetimes of ephemeral supports. Our lifetime analysis relates the measured footprint to the values that coexist during reencryption in our compact design. We read dense operands directly from serialized inputs and reuse output storage as workspace before final serialization during key generation and encapsulation. These choices reduce overlapping storage across the complete KEM and complement established support-form and Zero-Buffer multiplication. We evaluate this organization for all three HQC parameter sets on ARM Cortex-M3 and Cortex-M7 under the August 2025 specification. In a cumulative Cortex-M3 HQC-256 comparison, combined representation and lifetime changes reduced the stack by 38.9% relative to a Zero-Buffer configuration that already uses component-wise ciphertext comparison. Using a separate configuration, we measured decapsulation footprints of 36,858 bytes on Cortex-M3 and 36,850 bytes on Cortex-M7, including peak operation stack and serialized input/output storage. The common object layout accounts for most of these footprints. In the evaluated configurations, the relative increase in decapsulation cycles from the direct to the compact implementation is larger on Cortex-M7 than on Cortex-M3. Retaining supports reduces cycles when memory permits. The kernels retain support-dependent control flow and memory accesses; we did not establish complete-KEM constant-time execution or physical side-channel resistance.
papers.authors: Minjoo Sim, Siwoo Eum, Minwoo Lee, Seungwon Lee, Gyeongju Song, Lee Wai Kong, Anupam Chattopadhyay, Hwajeong Seo

papers.title: Optimizations and First-Order Masking of AIMer on Cortex-M4
papers.abstract: We optimize AIMer-128f on Cortex-M4 and propose first-order masking of its signing. Since squaring is a Frobenius map about $\times 16$ cheaper than multiplication, we restructure AIM2's inverse-Mersenne S-box into a Frobenius-shifted addition chain, cutting multiplications per S-box from 24/23 to 9/10. Since one multiplication-check operand is constant across $N = 16$ parties, we build the partial-product table once and reuse it. Both are orthogonal to single-multiplication acceleration, and with a Radix-16 multiplier on NUCLEO-L4R5ZI, keygen/sign/verify drop 18.55%/3.94%/7.30%. 1-PINI gadgets on every sensitive operation give first-order probing security. TVLA finds no first-order leakage in 100,000 traces. Masking costs $\times 10.5$, itself improved 5.20%.
papers.authors: DongCheon Kim, Jaeseung Han, Dong-Guk Han, Seog Chung Seo

papers.title: Quadratic Extractors
papers.abstract: A quadratic source is a random variable $X\sim\mathbb{F}_2^n$ generated by applying $n$ quadratics to a hidden uniform string. Previously, the best-known explicit extractor for this model required min-entropy roughly $k=n-\sqrt{\log n}$. In this paper, we give an explicit construction for min-entropy $k=\mathrm{polylog}(n)$. Even for the special case of $2$-local sources, where each bit of $X$ depends on two hidden uniform bits, achieving an entropy requirement below $k=\sqrt{n}$ was an important open problem. This is because such sources provably cannot be reduced (in a black-box manner) to our most powerful general-purpose seedless extractor, known as a sumset extractor. Our new extractor bypasses this barrier, providing the first explicit construction to go beyond sumset extraction.
papers.authors: Gautam Chandrasekaran, Jesse Goodman, David Zuckerman

papers.title: Breaking the Privacy Promise: Gradient Inversion Attacks on Federated Low-Rank Adapted Vision Transformers
papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has been increasingly adopted to fine-tune pretrained models with low computational cost and is therefore also preferred in the federated learning paradigm to reduce computational and communication overhead. In this work, we investigate the sparsely explored problem of the risk of private data leakage in LoRA-adapted Vision Transformers (ViTs), where low-rank updates weaken the gradient signal available to a server with access to individual client updates. We show that quality of reconstruction is limited by two coupled ambiguities: reduced information in LoRA gradients and missing spatial cues from frozen positional embeddings. To address this, we propose a spatially anchored generative inversion framework that incorporates server-prescribed trainable positional embeddings into ViT blocks during fine-tuning at clients. The resulting positional gradients act as layer-wise spatial anchors, providing additional positional cues, while the generative prior keeps reconstructions on a realistic image manifold, reducing duplicate-data and patch-permutation artifacts, {which produce similar gradients as those produced when the target client images are used}. Adding our proposed spatial anchoring to GIAS improves PSNR by 10.14 dB, SSIM by 0.45, and LPIPS by 0.098 on CIFAR-10, as well as PSNR gains of 7.83 and 11.74 dB on high-resolution CelebA and CARS datasets, respectively, in the FedSGD setting. Such gains in reconstructed image quality metrics are also maintained at higher batch sizes and in FedAvg settings. These results indicate that LoRA-based PEFT does not, by itself, prevent data leakage in FL, and carefully incorporated positional embeddings can help in exposing private information.
papers.authors: Ritik K. Badiya, Siladittya Manna, Ashmit Sinha, M Yashwanth, Anirban Chakraborty

papers.title: Verification of Security Properties of Cryptographic Protocols
papers.abstract: Developing cryptographic protocols that are free from vulnerabilities is very challenging, as evidenced by numerous design flaws and implementation bugs in widely used protocols. Recent work has leveraged model checking to generate negative test cases, that is test cases that include the behavior of Dolev-Yao attacker. In this paper, we address the problem of analyzing execution traces produced by testing protocol implementations with such negative test cases. We propose a method for detecting violations of security properties by model-checking execution traces. Our approach employs a model checker based on DLTL, a Linear Temporal Logic with freeze operators, and supports automation of the testing process through pre- and post-processing steps. These steps, respectively, bridge the gap between different levels of abstraction and synthesize the results produced by the model checker.We present experimental results as a proof of concept for the feasibility of the proposed method.
papers.authors: Simona Bernardi, Joaquín Ezpeleta

papers.title: RL-ATTACK: A Generalized Black-Box Adversarial Attack on Language Models via Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit vulnerabilities to adversarial perturbations that can induce unintended responses. These vulnerabilities can be identified via intentional attacks and subsequently used to improve model safety. In black-box settings where gradients are inaccessible, existing methods tend to guess adversarial transformations using external knowledge, ignoring the information provided by the target model. To mitigate this, we propose a trainable black-box framework based on reinforcement learning, which learns from the target model to generate tailored adversarial transformations. We demonstrate that our approach achieves lower post-attack accuracy, greater query efficiency and better semantic preservation on both natural language inference and generative Q&A tasks. On natural language inference, it drives post-attack accuracy to 2% within 20 queries. Against generative language models, our trained attacker consistently achieves lower post-attack accuracy than the untrained attacker and wins in 4 out of 6 settings when compared to a strong optimization-based baseline. We further experiment with multiple reward designs and training settings, and we find that no design or setting is consistently dominant. Our code is available at https://github.com/taikunudel/RL-ATTACK.
papers.authors: Taikun Chen, Yue Zhang, Wei Qian, Hui Fang

papers.title: GuardrailAgent: An Agentic Framework for Jailbreak Defense
papers.abstract: Despite undergoing safety training to align with human values, large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that circumvent built-in safeguards and elicit malicious behaviors given by the adversary. Existing defenses are mostly static and fail to adapt to new or unknown attack strategies, providing limited resilience. To address these, we propose a multi-agent defense framework, GuardrailAgent, that offers adaptive, end-to-end protection. The system autonomously gathers and summarizes attack characteristics into a continuously updated knowledge base that supports both input- and output-side detection. A feedback module integrates misclassified cases for iterative improvement at minimal cost. Tested on over ten representative jailbreaks, the framework achieved a 93.1% input-side detection rate, 93.9% overall detection, and a 95.8% F1 score, while rapidly adapting to unseen attacks. These results demonstrate GuardrailAgent's outstanding capability to maintain LLM safety in the face of evolving jailbreak tactics.
papers.authors: Tianze Chang, Junjie Chu, Yixin Wu, Michael Backes, Yang Zhang

papers.title: Beyond a Single Commit: Anchor-Guided Reconstruction of Multi-Commit Patches
papers.abstract: Vulnerability patch identification plays a critical role in software security by linking reported vulnerabilities and the corresponding fixes, enabling reliable vulnerability analysis, mitigation, and automated security tool development. As software systems evolve in complexity, vulnerability remediation has increasingly shifted from single-commit fixes to multi-commit fixing processes. Although many studies have been proposed to identify fixing commits associated with target vulnerabilities automatically, they often suffer from inaccurate semantic analysis or excessive workload for language models. These limitations reduce both the effectiveness and comprehensiveness of fixing commit identification. To improve patch identification, we propose an effective and comprehensive patch identification framework, HARPOON, which not only enhances the accuracy of identifying individual fixing commits, but also investigates dependencies among commits to achieve comprehensive commit recognition for target vulnerabilities. Experimental results show that HARPOON significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches. HARPOON successfully identified 895 vulnerability patches that were not previously maintained in public vulnerability databases. Among them, 663 are previously unrecorded fixes associated with 323 CRITICAL- or HIGH-severity vulnerabilities.
papers.authors: Jialiang Dong, Willy Susilo, Xu Gai, Liuhuo Wan, Chao Zhang, Elisa Bertino, Siqi Ma

papers.title: Consensus-Constrained Dual-Federated Optimization with Client-Side Dynamic Weighting for Distributed Android Device Threat Defense
papers.abstract: Smartphones, smart-home hubs, and wearables are increasingly exposed to sophisticated Android malware, while centralized threat-detection pipelines raise privacy and scalability concerns. Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without collecting raw client data, but partial participation and variation in local model quality can destabilize global optimization. In this article, we propose DW-FedADMM, a federated optimization framework that combines primal-dual coordination with performance-dependent client-side weighting. The dynamic coefficient modulates each participating client's local state before the augmented-Lagrangian update, while the dual variables regulate disagreement between local and global model states. We evaluate DW-FedADMM on three Android malware benchmarks, namely Drebin, Malgenome, and TUANDROMD, with 5, 10, and 15 clients holding IID data shards, partial client participation, and communication budgets of 5 and 10 rounds. Each configuration is repeated with ten random seeds. DW-FedADMM obtains the highest seed-averaged accuracy on Drebin (97.64% +/- 0.20%) and the best mean accuracy in 9 of the 18 dataset-client-round configurations, including 7 of the 9 configurations with a 10-round budget. Pooled over all configurations, it reaches 95.42% accuracy, 94.62% F1-score, 96.06% precision, and 99.45% AUC, compared with 95.32%, 94.51%, 95.56%, and 99.41% for FedADMM, while also giving the lowest mean false-positive rate and the smallest client update norm among the six compared methods. Both primal-dual methods are well ahead of the averaging- and proximal-based baselines on Malgenome and TUANDROMD, where the latter often remain at the majority-class solution when clients are fragmented. The gain of dynamic weighting over FedADMM is most pronounced on Drebin and with the longer communication budget, where it also reduces the variation across seeds.
papers.authors: Mohammad Mashreghi, Mohammad Hossein Badiei, Md. Jalil Piran

papers.title: I Think, Therefore I Attack: Evaluating Thought Injection Attacks on Reasoning Agents
papers.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) are one of the key components of current agentic systems. LRMs augment their output with an explicit chain-of-thought reasoning stage, introducing a new attack surface for thought injection, in which untrusted text resembling the model's own deliberation is fed back to the model. We present a two-part study of this attack, performed against the prevailing large, production class open-weight models (e.g., GLM-5.3, MiniMax-M2.5, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next). We first evaluate the effectiveness of static thought-injection prompts under different styles as well as tagged and untagged conditions and find that the effects of thinking tags and payload styles are all properties of the specific target model. In the second study, we exploit this model-specificity in a containerized agentic cyber range, using indirect injection prompts styled in the form of the target model's own reasoning traces to achieve attack success rates (ASR) up to 50% on operational objectives such as reverse-shell exfiltration and repository backdooring. We also find that the same malicious objective in standard prompt injection user voice never succeeds, and thinking tags suppress the agent's tendency to disclose the injection. Our results show that imitating a reasoning model's own thought style is effective for this style of attack, and that tag stripping is an unreliable defense.
papers.authors: Parth Illendula, Garik Livingston, Zain Shamsi, Ravi Srinivasan, Alex Liu

papers.title: AttentionSwitch: Jailbreak Defense for LLMs via Joint Learning of Sparse Attention-Head Selection and Scaling
papers.abstract: Large language models have achieved remarkable performance across a wide range of tasks, yet they remain susceptible to jailbreak attacks that circumvent safety mechanisms and elicit harmful or unintended outputs. Although safety can be improved through model fine-tuning, such approaches can be computationally expensive and may degrade previously acquired capabilities through catastrophic forgetting. Recent jailbreak defenses have therefore explored targeted interventions on specific model components associated with unsafe behavior. However, existing approaches typically decouple two inherently related decisions: where to intervene and how to modify the selected components. Such sequential optimization may be suboptimal because the optimal intervention location can depend on the intervention applied there, and vice versa. In this work, we introduce AttentionSwitch, the first jailbreak defense to jointly optimize intervention sites and strengths within a frozen LLM. Specifically, AttentionSwitch learns a sparse set of attention heads together with query-conditioned multiplicative scaling factors, allowing the outputs of the selected heads to be either attenuated or amplified without altering the directions of their representations. Across popular language models and jailbreak attacks, AttentionSwitch outperforms existing defenses, with particularly strong results when training data is scarce.
papers.authors: Doniyorkhon Obidov, Honggang Yu, Xiaolong Guo, Kaichen Yang

papers.title: AutoPYara: Next-Gen YARA Rule Generator for Malware Family Clustering
papers.abstract: Millions of malware variants threaten users daily, such that clustering these samples is key for fast incident response. AutoYara is the current state-of-the-art for automatic YARA rule generation, but the task remains challenging on realistic datasets, where intra-family diversity and noisy clustering can degrade rule quality. We present AutoPYara, a solution armored with: (1) precise cluster centroid selection based on similarity hashing, and (2) an improved heuristic for estimating subclusters within a malware family using historical VirusTotal data. We implement AutoPYara as an open-source Python package (pip install autopyara) to support reproducibility and practical use. We show that AutoPYara, (1) increases rule coverage by 14 percentage points; (2) reduces variance by 7.1 percentage points, comparing the average variance AutoPYara exhibits to that of AutoYara; and (3) improves threat-hunting accuracy by 10%. AutoPYara produces robust and effective YARA rules than prior automatic approaches in practical settings.
papers.authors: Mabon Ninan, Nhat Nguyen, Soumyajyoti Dutta, Sidharth Anil, Marcus Botacin

papers.title: Federated Forensics: Jurisdictional constraints as a design driver for multi-agency federated learning
papers.abstract: Digital forensic investigations increasingly cross borders, and law enforcement agencies need to build analytical models together without centralizing their data. Federated Learning (FL) keeps data local, yet neither FL nor its frameworks enforce the jurisdictional, governance, and accountability rules that multi-agency forensic work requires. This paper takes a design-first approach to that gap. First, we derive seven requirements that a federated learning system must meet in a forensic setting. Second, we propose Federated Forensics, a three-layer reference architecture whose middle layer, unlike in existing hierarchical FL designs, sits at a jurisdictional border and can use a model update locally while blocking it from crossing that border. Third, we build a prototype of the architecture and test it on a malware-family classification task. In a prototype evaluation, the policy gate blocked every restricted update at the border with zero violations, and restricted-class accuracy rose from 0% under today's compliant alternative to 93.0%, only 4.4 points below ignoring the restriction.
papers.authors: Aruna Withanage, Jessica Herrmann, Hudan Studiawan, Frank Breitinger

papers.title: Separating Pseudorandom Codes from Quantum Random Oracles
papers.abstract: Pseudorandom codes (PRCs) combine two seemingly conflicting goals: robustness to noise and computational indistinguishability from random strings. Recent work has shown that classical symmetric-key PRCs over binary alphabets cannot be constructed from minimal cryptographic assumptions, such as one-way functions, via black-box reductions. In this work, we revisit this question in the presence of quantum computation and quantum information. We first consider pseudorandom codes with classical codewords but quantum algorithms. We prove that symmetric-key pseudorandom codes robust to Bernoulli noise admit no black-box construction from quantum random oracles, and hence from quantum-secure one-way functions. This establishes that the classical black-box barrier for PRCs persists even in the quantum computational setting. Motivated by this separation, we investigate the notion of quantum pseudorandom codes (QPRCs), in which codewords are quantum states and security is defined via computational indistinguishability from Haar-random states. We then present several positive results. Assuming quantum-secure one-way functions, we construct QPRCs that are secure against a single encoding query, allow multiple copies of the challenge state, and tolerate an error rate matching that of any classical uniquely decodable binary error-correcting code against a dephasing or bit-flip channel. We also show that the PRFS with proof of destruction due to Behera et al. (TCC 2023) can be extended to a 0-bit QPRC that is secure against multiple encoding queries and tolerates unbounded phase errors but only a constant number of bit-flip errors. Finally, assuming the existence of quantum-secure single-query pseudorandom states (1PRS), we construct single-query single-copy QPRC that tolerate arbitrary Pauli noise up to the decoding radius of a quantum error-correcting code with unique decoding.
papers.authors: Nico Döttling, Anne Müller, Mahesh Sreekumar Rajasree

papers.title: Structured Quantum Hardness from Unstructured Assumptions
papers.abstract: Whether useful structured hardness can arise from unstructured assumptions is a fundamental question in complexity and cryptography. The longstanding Bennett-Gill question asks whether $\mathsf{NP}\cap\mathsf{coNP}$ remains hard relative to a random oracle; [GIKKLS, STOC 2023] recently gave a conditional affirmative answer in the classical setting. We establish the quantum analogue: if $\mathsf{UP}\not\subseteq\mathsf{BQP}$, then $\mathsf{NP}^{O}\cap\mathsf{coNP}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathsf{BQP}^{O}$ with probability $1$ over a random oracle $O$. Beyond extending the classical result, this separation has a distinctly quantum significance: Shor's algorithms defeat canonical number-theoretic hardness candidates, while lattice assumptions and other leading post-quantum cryptographic assumptions do not directly supply hard languages with two-sided classical certification on every input. Our conditional oracle separation provides evidence that such structured quantum hardness can nevertheless arise from unstructured sources. Complementing this result, we rule out fully black-box quantum reductions of worst-case quantum hardness in $\mathsf{NP}\cap\mathsf{coNP}$ to post-quantum injective one-way functions and indistinguishability obfuscation. This barrier excludes a broad class of black-box approaches to deriving structured quantum hardness from generic cryptographic primitives, providing partial evidence that the non-black-box techniques in our first result are essential.
papers.authors: Xiao Liang, Takashi Yamakawa, Chak Fai Yung

papers.title: SoK: Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) Integration in Software Development: Approaches, Gaps, and Future Directions
papers.abstract: Standardised post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is critical for protecting software systems against future quantum threats, but standardised algorithms alone do not provide a pathway for their secure integration into software. This paper presents a Systematisation of Knowledge (SoK) of PQC integration in software development, synthesising existing approaches across implementation, migration, and developer education. We analyse these approaches against NIST PQC standards and PQC migration guidance, software development lifecycle coverage, cybersecurity practices, deployment maturity, and testing and evaluation evidence. Our analysis shows that existing work establishes important technical and organisational foundations but provides disconnected support across the software development lifecycle, with limited coordination between preparation, implementation, migration, deployment, maintenance, and developer practices. Evaluation evidence also remains concentrated in controlled or early-stage settings, providing stronger evidence of technical feasibility than operational readiness. We identify cross-cutting gaps and research directions for developing lifecycle-oriented, empirically validated approaches that connect technical, developer, and organisational requirements for secure PQC integration.
papers.authors: Shakya R. D. N., Craig Costello, Nalin A. G. Arachchilage

papers.title: Stealthy Malicious Interference Detection in UAV Formations: A Power-Domain Signaling Game Approach
papers.abstract: Reliable intra-swarm communication is fundamental to cooperative sensing, control, and mission execution in unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms. In open low-altitude shared-spectrum environments, coexisting UAVs may cause benign interference through spectrum reuse and signal leakage, while jamming UAVs may deliberately degrade critical intra-swarm links. Since a jamming UAV can adjust its transmit power to disguise signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) degradation as link fluctuation in benign interference, stealthy jammer UAV detection remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose a novel belief-driven stealthy jammer UAV detection scheme from the perspective of Bayesian security game. To capture stealthy interference in shared-spectrum UAV swarms, the interfering UAV is modeled as a hidden benign or jamming type, whose transmit power strategy induces the SINR observed by the defender. The defender updates its posterior belief from the observed SINR and decides whether to maintain normal operation or trigger defensive power boosting. We characterize pure-strategy perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE) conditions under separating structures with distinguishable type and pooling structures with indistinguishable observations. Numerical results show that the proposed scheme improves the defender's expected utility compared to the conventional schemes.
papers.authors: Jianle Ba, Shaolong Guo, Yuntao Wang, Xin Wu, Zhou Su, Zhendong Li

papers.title: AMORT-V1: Checkpointed Post-Quantum Attestation for Industrial Controllers
papers.abstract: Programmable logic controllers often remain deployed for decades, making post-quantum attestation a long-term requirement. Prior measurements of OpenPLC attestation show that post-quantum signing can consume 88--99% of round-trip latency and that durable state can further limit throughput. We introduce AMORT-V1, a checkpointed attestation protocol that moves public-key signing and durable commitment from individual reports to periodic checkpoints. An ML-KEM epoch establishes per-device evidence keys, devices authenticate reports with MACs, and the controller commits ordered evidence through hash-chained Merkle checkpoints signed with ML-DSA or SLH-DSA. Because shared MACs do not provide transferable proof of device origin, AMORT-V1 adds a device-held disclosure chain whose keys are released after checkpoint commitment. We validate the protocol with a 27-case attack matrix, 149 differential-test vectors, and a seven-node Raspberry Pi 5 testbed with five physical OpenPLC provers. Checkpointing reduces controller cost by 90 times relative to per-report ML-DSA without durable logging and by 878 times when durable logging is required. Transferable device-origin verification costs 2.95micro sec per report, while controller-side scaling to 10,000 identities requires 6.18 micro sec and 155 octets per report. AMORT-V1 also supports rollback-resistant restart through TPM-backed monotonic state without placing durable hardware operations on the per-report path.
papers.authors: Rishabh Das, Gerald Agendia, Jibriel Adjei, Ahmed Oun

papers.title: Dynamic Watermarking and Action-Conditioned Latent Dynamics for Secure Vision-Based Controllers
papers.abstract: Replay attacks are difficult to detect in vision-based control systems because previously recorded observations can remain plausible while the physical system follows a different trajectory. This paper develops an adaptive dynamic-watermarking framework for detecting replay attacks against vision-based controllers. A private Gaussian watermark is added to the nominal control input, and a control input-conditioned latent dynamics network (LDN) predicts the corresponding evolution in a compact latent space learned from image observations. Attack evidence is obtained from the discrepancy between the predicted latent response and the latent representation of the received image observation. A reinforcement learning policy adjusts the watermark covariance using the latent state and detector confidence, thereby balancing attack detectability, watermark energy, and control distortion. A Lagrangian penalty on task-specific safety costs is included during training to limit the adverse effect of the excitation. The framework is evaluated on a vision-guided UR5 manipulation task in which the robot reaches a target while avoiding a moving human arm under nominal and replay-attacked observations.
papers.authors: Aditya Parameshwaran, Navid Aftabi, Abhishek Hanchate, Satish T. S. Bukkapatnam, Dan Li, Yue Wang

papers.title: Sumcheck bit packing
papers.abstract: Circuit-based zero-knowledge proofs over large fields waste most of a field element when they commit to a single bit. We study the problem of committing to packed witnesses, in which $m$ bits are stored in one element of $GF(2^m)$, while still allowing the proof system to verify linear claims about the individual bits. Prior approaches to this problem either (a) scale to packing only 4 bits[Fs24], (b) require tensor-structured claims and additional sumcheck rounds that incur larger soundness error [DP23,DP25], or (c) rely on Frobenius automorphisms [Koc26]. In contrast, we present a simpler reduction that exploits only the $GF(2)$-linearity of the field trace and achieves soundness error $2^{-m}$ for arbitrary bit-linear claims. We then use a characterization of trace-zero field elements to make the reduction zero-knowledge over any hiding linear commitment scheme: whereas previous constructions verify $O(m^2)$ or $O(m)$quadratic constraints in the commitment scheme, our protocol requires only linear constraints.
papers.authors: Matteo Frigo, abhi shelat

papers.title: LABBA: LLM-Assisted Behavioral Biometric Authentication
papers.abstract: Behavioral biometrics have emerged as a promising complement to traditional physiological biometrics by leveraging dynamic human characteristics. These modalities offer advantages including continuous authentication, inherent liveness detection, and greater resistance to credential theft and other spoofing attacks. However, existing systems remain limited in adaptability, contextual awareness, and semantic reasoning as they primarily rely on similarity metrics, static thresholds, or supervised classifiers. As a result, they often struggle with real-world conditions such as behavioral variability, environmental changes, contextual changes, and adversarial manipulations. To address these limitations, we systematically integrate LLM-based contextual reasoning into behavioral biometric authentication. LLMs provide capabilities in contextual inference, sequential reasoning, multimodal understanding, and adaptive decision-making. Building on these strengths, we integrate a lightweight LLM-based reasoning module with a novel phone-blowing behavioral biometric technique to develop a context-aware authentication framework. To this end, we first collect blow-acoustic signals from participants and systematically extract spectral and temporal features. These features are aggregated and converted into comparable similarity representations, using either discrete rule-based categories or continuous normalized scores, which are transformed into structured prompts through prompt engineering. We experimentally evaluate the proposed framework using blow-acoustic data collected from 50 participants under diverse behavioral and contextual conditions. The proposed framework achieves 99.46% and 99.38% authentication accuracy in the rule-based and score-based modes, respectively, outperforming its non-LLM counterpart while maintaining strong robustness under dynamic real-world conditions.
papers.authors: Howard Halim, Eyasu Getahun Chekole, Jianying Zhou

papers.title: Zirah: A Post-Quantum True Random Number Generator Hardware Signer With an Avalanche Noise
papers.abstract: Zirah is a hardware signer built around an STM32F407 microcontroller, and its purpose is to find out, on inexpensive hardware, where a post-quantum signing key is exposed and what actually protects it. The device draws every random bit from a reverse-biased 2N3904 junction in avalanche breakdown, amplified by an LM358 and screened by SP 800-90B health tests, computes ML-DSA-65 (FIPS 204, hedged) on the STM32 with two-share arithmetic masking of the secret-key multiplications, and adds ECDSA P-256 from an ATECC608 secure element over the same digest, once a person has matched an eight-digit digest prefix on its OLED with the PC and pressed a button. A desktop application and a command-line tool drive the board and verify its output, and because only a 32-byte manifest digest reaches the device, it signs files of any type and size, returning signed copies for PDF, Office Open XML, ZIP, PNG and JPEG files and detached records for every other format. NIST's SP 800-90B tool rejected the IID assumption for 1,000,000 raw samples and assessed 6.898 bits of min-entropy per byte on the non-IID track, against the 1 bit the firmware credits, while spectral lines near 116 Hz that hold about 5 % of the variance remain unexplained. At 168 MHz the masked signature took a median of 157 ms over 20 runs and a complete signing operation under 0.8 s, and the signer matched the pq-crystals reference in 1,976 checks natively and on an emulated Cortex-M4. The ATECC608 can neither store the 4,032-byte ML-DSA-65 key nor compute with it, so that key sits in ordinary flash behind readout protection, and on an earlier board, before that protection was enabled, a debugger copied it out and the copy produced a valid ML-DSA-65 signature without the device, although the leakage results come from an instruction-level emulator and nothing here is certified.
papers.authors: Muhammad Shaheer Bin Junaid

papers.title: Exact $\ell_p$-CVP via Euclidean SVP in Polynomial Space
papers.abstract: We give a randomized, rank-preserving reduction from exact $\ell_p$-CVP to exact Euclidean SVP for every integer $p\ge2$. For rational inputs of bit length $\ell$ on full-rank lattices $L\subset\mathbb R^N$, the reduction uses $(Cp)^N\poly(p,\ell)$ oracle calls and additional bit operations, where $C$ is an absolute constant. It uses $\poly(p,\ell)$ working space outside the oracle, and all oracle queries have rank $N$ and $\poly(p,\ell)$ bit complexity. For $p=2$, the reduction transfers polynomial-space exact SVP algorithms to exact CVP with $2^{O(N)}\poly(\ell)$ time overhead. Instantiating it with the SVP algorithms of Kannan and of Feng, Gao and Liu yields randomized polynomial-space CVP algorithms running in time $N^{N/(2e)+o(N)}$ and $N^{N/(4e)+o(N)}$, respectively. For every fixed integer $p\ge3$, the same reduction yields exact $\ell_p$-CVP algorithms for arbitrary rational targets either in randomized time and space $2^{O(N)}$, or in randomized time $N^{N/(4e)+o(N)}$ and polynomial space. These algorithmic bounds are up to polynomial factors in $\ell$. The reduction performs local search sequentially over the cosets of \(2L\), where \(L\) is the input lattice, while tracking the excess of the current objective value over the optimum. Within a coset containing a closest vector, midpoint inequalities bound the unknown correction in terms of this excess, which in turn allows us to construct many short corrections that reduce the excess bound by a factor of four. A counting argument shows that these improving corrections form a sufficiently large fraction of the lattice points in a known search region, and a sparsification-based sampler assigns sufficiently large probability to every nonzero vector in that region, using at most one SVP call per sample. For \(p\ge3\), the same framework is extended using a diagonal weighted norm computed from the current point.
papers.authors: Jiseung Kim, Minkyu Kim, Hyung Tae Lee

papers.title: Global Surveillance Under the Lens: Reconstructing Passive Dolev-Yao Intruders
papers.abstract: Global surveillance systems record large volumes of network traffic for retrospective analysis, but packet captures alone reveal little about protocol-level semantics. This paper presents an automated, specification-guided methodology for reconstructing passive Dolev-Yao intruder executions from captured network traffic and validating the reconstructed executions against a formal protocol specification. The framework takes a PCAP capture, an AnBx specification, and the associated deployment metadata; it extracts Java-serialised objects from TCP streams, reconstructs protocol sessions and channel-to-step assignments, and generates a passive intruder that evaluates the Dolev-Yao derived checks produced by the AnBx compiler. Three reconstruction challenges are addressed: multiple serialised objects and object references within a TCP stream, ambiguity in mapping interleaved connections to concurrent protocol sessions, and semantic validation of candidate reconstructions. We evaluate the methodology on 121 protocols from the AnBx test suite. For single-session captures, the standard JDK cryptographic provider recovers 97.8% of expected objects and achieves 94.2% successful reconstruction, where success requires complete object recovery and a clean passive-intruder execution. For the 112 parallel-capable protocols, the toolchain achieves 89.3% successful reconstruction for both two and three concurrent sessions, while recovering approximately 97.2% of expected objects. Experiments with mismatched protocol-role mappings and deliberately mutated traces show that the generated Dolev-Yao checks respond to semantic inconsistencies. By making the reconstruction step explicit, the solution produces protocol-level observations on which assessments of protocol resilience and the design of defensive countermeasures can be built.
papers.authors: Paolo Modesti

papers.title: Beyond Proof of Possession: A Relational Theory of Authority
papers.abstract: Proof-of-Possession (PoP) establishes that an executor controls an artifact (key, token, credential, or capability), but such control alone determines neither the executor's relational profile nor the causal history of an execution occurrence. We separate PoP from Proof of Relationship (PoR), the semantic property that one execution occurrence validly continues another, and from authorization, which is occurrence-sensitive. The foundational change is in the semantic domain of authorization: from holders and authority-bearing artifacts to execution occurrences situated in causal histories. We give authorization models an observation-based occurrence verdict and a separate transition-admissibility relation; kernel inclusion yields a partial order on observation-kernel classes. Building on Provenance Identity Continuity (PIC) and Proof-of-Continuity (PoC), we classify executors by authorization-relevant equivalence relations whose quotients form relational profile spaces, with positive predicates over profile transitions forming a distributive lattice. This adds relational attenuation to authority attenuation: along a valid causal history, $C_{i+1}\subseteq C_i$ and $ρ_{i+1}\Rightarrowρ_i$. We prove dual monotonicity, combined closure, and origin relational closure. Two occurrences of the same authenticated executor, with the same profile and possession evidence, need not be authorization-equivalent, and within a valid PIC lineage a deputy's independent authority cannot be imported outside the origin context. Finally, we prove that the executor-dependent decision factors through the relational profile and is invariant under sound mechanisms establishing it: successor-side PoP is a possible evidence mechanism, not a necessary premise of authorization. Under explicit Witness Assumptions, a boundary-witnessed checkpoint construction realizes the premises without successor-side PoP.
papers.authors: Nicola Gallo

papers.title: The Promise of Strategic Agentic Scambaiting
papers.abstract: Scammers have increasingly adopted AI-driven capabilities, evolving from automated message generation to fully agentic conversational systems that scale operations and maximize the exploitation of fraudulent resources before detection and takedown. In parallel, agentic scambaiting has emerged as a defensive approach in which autonomous agents impersonate potential victims and engage scammers in sustained interactions to extract actionable threat intelligence, such as mule bank accounts and cryptocurrency wallet addresses, that can be reported to disrupt fraudulent infrastructures.
