Together, these developments transform online fraud into an adversarial socio-technical ecosystem in which autonomous scamming and scambaiting agents engage in deceptive interactions while competing over the discovery, preservation, and exploitation of one another's resources. A fundamental and largely unexplored question is how defensive scambaiting can remain effective in an agent-to-agent environment, and under what conditions either side gains a strategic advantage. In this paper, we present a formal model of agent-to-agent fraud interactions that captures the strategic decision spaces available to both attackers and defenders. Using this framework, we analyze the dynamics of engagement, resource consumption, belief adaptation, and disruption outcomes. We find that scammer profitability turns negative once baiting-agent prevalence exceeds certain thresholds, and that when both sides improve at the same pace, defender investment in mimicry quality outpaces equivalent gains in scammer detection capability, so the arms race favors the defender under our baseline parameters. Our model and findings provide insights into the stability, scalability, and long-term effectiveness of autonomous defensive agents in an evolving AI-mediated fraud landscape.
papers.authors: Abhishek Satyam, Hossein Siadati, Haadi Jafarian, Sima Jafarikhah, Juntao Chen

papers.title: Digital Security Under Compound Threats: Surveillance, Threat Reasoning, and Habituation Among North Korean Defectors in China
papers.abstract: North Korean defectors residing in China face persistent uncertainty regarding digital security and privacy. Through semi-structured interviews with 19 defectors, we examine how individuals understand digital threats and adapt their security behaviors. We identify three interrelated conditions: transnational surveillance pressure from North Korea, identity-linked digital infrastructure and intermediary dependency in China, and threat reasoning shaped by prior surveillance schemas. Participants developed uneven protective practices and followed two trajectories: adaptive habituation driven by knowledge acquisition and erosive habituation driven by the prolonged absence of adverse events. Our findings show how compound threats, attribution uncertainty, and constrained agency shape security reasoning among undocumented users.
papers.authors: Yibo Meng, Bingyi Liu, Lionel Z. Wang, Hongkun Yang

papers.title: SensorGuard-RV: Sensor-to-Register Data Protection for Resource-Constrained RISC-V Devices
papers.abstract: Embedded systems rely on sensor measurements that traverse a complex hardware-firmware stack (e.g. peripheral interfaces, communication buses, memory, and drivers) before reaching the applications that use them. At worst, an attacker with access to this path may successfully intercept, overwrite, fabricate, or replay readings. This may cause systems that act on such data, such as flight controllers and industrial processes, to behave incorrectly or unsafely. Existing defences, such as trusted execution environments and trusted I/O paths, still depend on trusted driver software and correctly configured access control, which remain fragile in practice. In response, we present SensorGuard-RV, a hardware-first approach that delivers sensor samples into processor registers without trusting intermediate software, buses, or memory. After configuration, a write-once ownership switch hands the sensor to a fixed-function controller that performs hardware-level authenticated encryption on sensor samples under a key inaccessible to software. We develop a new RISC-V instruction then instructs the CPU to decrypt the sample and writes it to a register only after verifying its tag and rejecting replays, including across resets. We implement SensorGuard-RV on the NEORV32 core with an ADXL362 SPI accelerometer on an Artix-7 FPGA. At 100 MHz, a protected sample reaches a register in 5,191 cycles (51.9 $μ$s), of which the two Ascon authenticated encryption engines account for 30. Because fixed-function acquisition removes per-byte software polling, the protected loop sustains 19,015 transactions/s, 5.3% above a software-driven SPI baseline. The added logic (3,155 LUTs and 2,215 registers; 5.0% and 1.7% of the device) is dominated by the Ascon engine and preserves the 100 MHz clock, while estimated power rises from 118 to 368 mW.
papers.authors: Hamid Noori, Carlton Shepherd

papers.title: Escalate or Close: How Fast-Tier Models Handle Held-Out Web Attack Families in Two-Tier Triage
papers.abstract: In two-tier triage a fast model decides most web requests and escalates the rest to a slow tier, so an attack the fast tier closes is never examined. We hold each of seven attack families out of training, recalibration and thresholds, splice the payloads into parameters of real browsing traffic, and compare zero-shot decision models, which return a probability for a typed question, with supervised detectors, a local language model, the OWASP Core Rule Set and an anomaly baseline. Detectors trained on the known families can give much of a held-out family a confident benign verdict: over 10 training runs, ModernBERT gives 37% to 60% of held-out path traversal a probability below 0.05 and escalates only 50% to 81% of it within a 5% benign budget, against nearly all of the same requests when traversal is known. Jev and Clef, two hosted decision models whose budget decisions do not depend on the held-out family, escalate at least 97.6% of every family within the same budget, but their undisclosed training data may contain these public families. Tests on recent exploits need controls for request shape: Jev escalates 37% of benign twins (exploit requests with the attack replaced by legitimate values), and detectors trained on older exploits learn what scanner requests look like. A search guided by Jev's probability gets 43% of held-out attacks past Jev within 300 queries, but Jev's answers vary: asked again, it escalates those requests in 60% of its answers.
papers.authors: Maciej Kisielewicz, Michał Kędziora, Ngoc Thanh Nguyen

papers.title: Cloudy Skies: Early Detection of Jamming Against Iridium LEO Satellite-IoT Links
papers.abstract: Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite-IoT systems increasingly provide connectivity to mobile assets in remote areas, which makes their resilience to radio-frequency jamming a growing concern. Timely jamming detection, i.e., before complete link failure, has been studied for terrestrial networks and Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS), but it remains unclear whether these approaches are effective on LEO links, where propagation varies rapidly, the received signal is weak, and jamming should be detected from the messages that are still correctly received. This paper investigates the extent to which jamming of Iridium LEO satellite-IoT links can be detected from the physical layer of correctly decoded messages. To this aim, we collect and publicly release a real-world dataset of Iridium messages under 47 jamming conditions, spanning two propagation environments, static and mobile receivers, and different jammer distances, powers, and signal types. We use this dataset to analyze three one-class autoencoder-based anomaly detectors operating on physical-layer information and compare them against two signal-quality estimators commonly used as jamming indicators in GNSS-based applications. Our results show that detectability is governed by the rise of the receiver noise floor, through which jammer power, distance, and receiver mobility act. With 1000-sample chunks, i.e., 40 ms of received signal at 25,000 samples per second (about four correctly decoded messages), the autoencoders reach an AUC of at least 0.84 whenever a noise jammer raises the noise floor by at least 9 dB, whereas the $C/N_0$ and SNR estimators fail, since received messages, although correctly decoded, retain a high SNR under jamming. Therefore, timely jamming detection for LEO satellite-IoT links like Iridium should rely on physical-layer information beyond the signal-quality metrics adopted in the GNSS domain.
papers.authors: Ingrid Huso, Giulia Fliescher, Savio Sciancalepore, Gabriele Oligeri

papers.title: Breaking $\mathsf{TraintoDefend}$ via Adaptive Neuron Clustering in Cryptanalytic Model Extraction
papers.abstract: Cryptanalytic model extraction poses a fundamental threat to deep learning model confidentiality by enabling precise parameter recovery with theoretical guarantees of functional equivalence. To counter this growing threat, $\mathsf{TraintoDefend}$ (NeurIPS 2025) was proposed as the first dedicated defense against cryptanalytic extraction and remains the only defense believed to be effective to date. It encourages neurons to learn similar weights so that they switch activation states together, making their individual contributions harder to distinguish. However, we notice that neurons with similar weights need not switch activation states together under small perturbations. Instead, weight similarity can cause the original clustering rule to merge signatures from distinct neurons when only a subset of their normalized weight coordinates agree. Motivated by this observation, we introduce $\mathsf{SimBreak}$, an adaptive clustering rule that breaks the weight-similarity defense of $\mathsf{TraintoDefend}$. $\mathsf{SimBreak}$ estimates a relative scale from all jointly observed weight coordinates and uses the same scale to test both weight direction and bias consistency. Across six protected fully connected networks trained on MNIST, $\mathsf{SimBreak}$ raises target layer signature recovery from $0\%$ to $100\%$, with a maximum relative recovery error of $2^{-22.27}$. Our work challenges the use of neuron weight similarity as a sufficient basis for protection and establishes adaptive evaluation as essential to assessing cryptanalytic extraction defenses.
papers.authors: Haojie Wu, Haolin Liu, Tianshuo Cong, Guoyan Zhang

papers.title: Vectorized (2, 2)-Isogenies in the Theta Model Using AVX-512 and Applications to SQIsign
papers.abstract: Higher-dimensional isogenies have emerged as a powerful building block for isogeny-based cryptography, with recent protocols such as SQIsign relying on the efficient evaluation of $(2^n, 2^n)$-isogenies. Despite their attractive security and compactness properties, these schemes remain computationally expensive and improving their performance is an important step for their real-world use. In this work, we present a high-performance AVX-512 implementation of two-dimensional isogenies that effectively exploits their data-level parallelism. We develop a code generator that produces efficient AVX-512 implementations of arithmetic over $\mathbb{F}_p$ and $\mathbb{F}_{p^2}$ for Montgomery-friendly primes of the form $p=c\cdot 2^e-1$ with $e\approx \log_2(p)$, covering the family of primes used by several protocols based on two-dimensional isogenies, including SQIsign. Building on this arithmetic, we vectorize the $(2^n, 2^n)$-isogeny formulas by Dartois et al. (ASIACRYPT 2024), achieving significant speedups over the corresponding, highly-optimized scalar implementation that uses x86-64 assembly. As an application, we accelerate the Round 2 version of SQIsign verification and obtain speedups of $2.5\times$ at NIST security level I and $3.2\times$ and $3.3\times$ at levels III and V, respectively. Our code generator also readily supports the larger primes of Round 3 SQIsign, for which we obtain verification speedups between $3.1\times$ and $3.4\times$.
papers.authors: Marius A. Aardal, Diego F. Aranha, Patrick Longa, Giacomo Pope

papers.title: STIR/SHAKEN: A Cocktail of Cryptographic Clumsiness
papers.abstract: Scams and fraudulent robocalls are rampant in the telephone system. Fraudsters often employ call spoofing to impersonate a known caller to the victim, making it difficult to detect and block the fraudster’s calls. In an effort to combat call spoofing, the U.S. government in 2019 mandated the use of a new suite of protocols called STIR/SHAKEN. In STIR/SHAKEN, providers include a cryptographically-signed assertion about the caller’s identity and other metadata in call headers. This serves both to authentically convey this metadata between providers during call routing and to provide reportable, verifiable evidence of bad behavior by providers that originate fraudulent calls. This paper asks whether STIR/SHAKEN achieves its security goals, and at what cost to the telephone system. On security we find serious structural weaknesses: a year of STIR/SHAKEN certificates observed in production call traffic shows a PKI riddled with noncompliance—nearly half of valid certificates violate the specifications—a provider can prevent later verification of a STIR/SHAKEN assertion by taking its certificate offline, and a header-malleability flaw, which we verified in test calls placed with the help of a real telephone provider, causes a spoofed caller ID to be displayed as verified on some phones. The cost, meanwhile, has been steep: STIR/SHAKEN deployment has created systemic new harms to the privacy of all phone users. These new privacy harms take two forms. First, signing call metadata renders it cryptographically non-repudiable: for the first time in the phone system’s 150-year history, there is publicly verifiable proof that a call took place. Second, STIR/SHAKEN’s complexity pushes providers to outsource signing and verification—roughly half of the 29 providers we surveyed do so, most to a handful of dominant vendors—causing widespread new leakage of sensitive call metadata to off-path third parties. (One such off-path third party, Neustar, was acquired in 2021 by TransUnion, one of the three nationwide U.S. credit bureaus. Neustar authenticates over 30 billion calls per month—and TransUnion sells a “Phone Behavior Intelligence” product advertising “insight into billions of call transactions” obtained through its “deep carrier relationships.”) These structural harms sit atop implementation failures: our tests also found implementations that completely break the federally-mandated *67 caller-privacy mechanism. Finally, we propose solutions to the problems we identify. To fix the PKI, STIR/SHAKEN should adopt certificate transparency; a public certificate log also stops providers from taking certificates offline to defeat later verification. Our remaining solutions are cryptographic, and share a prerequisite STIR/SHAKEN cannot currently meet: the origin provider must learn the destination provider’s public key. We thus design a backwards-compatible key discovery mechanism that uses SIP error messages. We then attack the privacy harms directly: replacing STIR/SHAKEN’s signatures with asymmetric message franking (AMF) makes call metadata deniable again, and issuing AMFs blindly keeps it hidden from outsourced signers. We design the first blind signing protocol for the AMF construction of Tyagi et al., along with new security definitions capturing requirements novel to the setting, such as verifier-hiding blindness. To our knowledge, we thereby initiate the formal study of blind signing for designated-verifier signatures; we believe this is of independent interest.
papers.authors: Josh Brown, Matthew Hardeman, Paul Grubbs

papers.title: Can Fully Homomorphic Encryption on Public Blockchains Protect Sensitive Medical Consultations? A Security and Privacy Assessment
papers.abstract: %===================================================================== \begin{abstract} People seeking care for stigmatised conditions often delay treatment because they fear exposure, yet digital health services routinely expose user data and metadata. Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) now allows smart contracts on public blockchains to hold encrypted data whose decryption is governed by contract rules. This paper assesses whether this approach can protect sensitive medical consultations. We present ConfidentialCare, a prototype built on Zama's fhEVM and the Ethereum Sepolia testnet, in which patients' symptoms are encrypted in the browser and only an authorised doctor may decrypt them. We evaluated three versions of the system through metadata inspection, access-control tests and attack experiments, asking what FHE protects and whether access to patient data can be controlled. Consultation content remained confidential in all tested cases, and the design collects no names, emails or accounts. However, public on-chain metadata revealed which wallet consulted which doctor, the doctor's specialty, when, and the approximate length of each message, and this history would be exposed permanently if the wallet were ever linked to the patient. We also found that a doctor granted access could re-share a patient's encrypted data, both through a confused-deputy flaw in the application contract, which we fixed, and directly through fhEVM's access control list, and that neither withdrawing access nor closing a consultation removed it. A redesign based on time-limited, revocable delegation prevented re-sharing, and Zama's live service enforced its revocation and expiry immediately. On Sepolia, Zama's key-management service refused decryption without a valid delegation, and revocation took effect within the same block in all six trials. We conclude that FHE protects what patients disclose, but not the fact or context of seeking care, and that in fhEVM a permission to decrypt is also a permission to share. \end{abstract}
papers.authors: Nizamuddeen Shahruddeen

papers.title: Projective Jet Geometry and Hold-Out Rank of Binary Goppa Codes
papers.abstract: We develop a projective-geometric and algebraic framework for the higher-order polynomial relations among the public generator-matrix columns of a binary Goppa code, the relations exploited by the recent structural distinguishers and key-recovery methods for Classic McEliece. The alternant representation realizes the public columns as rational points on a hidden curve parametrized over $\F_{2^m}$; higher-order vanishing conditions become fat-point conditions, pulled back along the hidden parametrization. Our first contribution is an exact characterization of a codimension-$t$ ambient space containing all products of $d$ code polynomials: the products satisfy $(\pi^dh)'\equiv0\pmod{g^2}$ for the support polynomial $\pi$ and the Goppa polynomial $g$, and the space of degree-$\le dD$ polynomials with this property has dimension $dD+1-t$ once $dD\ge2t-1$. Equality with the actual product space is proved in a local regime, verified computationally on every instance tested, and stated as a conjecture. Our second contribution is a Frobenius-descent theorem: a binary form vanishes on the hidden curve if and only if it vanishes on the union of its $m$ Frobenius conjugates, with the $\F_2$-dimension of such forms equal to the $K$-dimension of the ideal of the union; from it we derive Hilbert-function bounds, including a multilinear version attained on all but one of the twenty-seven keys with $t\ge5$ tested (and missed by one on that key), and the local structure of the pulled-back forms at the roots of $g$. We then analyze the universal dependencies among Hasse-jet conditions in the multilinear setting of the attacks: a closed formula for the rank at a single column, and an explicit family of $\binom{k}{2s-d-2}$ relations between the conditions at any two columns. At a held-out column we prove an exact codimension formula for the Goppa subcode generated by the gradients of the vanishing forms. Finally, running our experimental pipeline (the jet system of the attacks, without the key-recovery steps) on six independently generated keys of a Classic-McEliece-shaped code shows that the kernel dimension is comparable to that of a random control, while every kernel form exhibits the predicted hidden-curve vanishing, the gradients span the predicted subcode, and the first-order normal data of the kernel is nearly independent of the key. Together these results explain the main components of the nuisance space of the recent attacks and isolate the conjectures that remain for an exact description of the kernel.
papers.authors: Yongge Wang

papers.title: Decision Models as Retrieval Gates Against Injection and Pollution
papers.abstract: Retrieved web text can carry instructions aimed at the language model, or synthetic pages written to mislead. We test whether released open-weight decision models, which answer typed questions about a text without generating tokens, can screen retrieved passages against both threats. On a benchmark of 1,000 questions over forum-style web pages with hidden injected instructions, a Kev-4B gate reads each passage's HTML. Attack success, measured automatically, falls from 27.9% with no defence to 13.6% with the published mitigations (sanitisation, normalisation and citation prompting) and to 5.7% with the gate added. The gate takes 76 ms per passage and wrongly flags 4 of 186 benign pages with instructions for human readers. Responsiveness on clean queries stays within a point (85.6% to 86.2%). On a 200-query pollution testbed where two thirds of the candidate pages are fake, filtering the pool before the top ten are chosen keeps fake pages out of the answer (0.5% exposure) and holds accuracy at 83%, against 28% with no filter. Filtering only the top ten leaves the generator too few pages to answer. Large LLMs used as judges rank attacks better (AUROC 0.99 against 0.94) but cost ten times more. Gates catch more attacks when they read the page's HTML than when they read its plain text. Every model is open-weight.
papers.authors: Mahdi Ghadamyari, Reza Habibi

papers.title: KeHoSu: Keyed Homoglyph Substitution for Authenticated Text Provenance over Copy-Paste Channels
papers.abstract: Nowadays, large language models produce text at scale, and much of it is redistributed across platforms. A moderator who finds a suspicious comment, post or article may want to know which platform generated it and for which account. In this paper we study attribution over the channel through which such text actually travels, copy-paste, which discards document metadata but keeps Unicode code points. We present KeHoSu, which turns the confusable characters of homoglyph attacks into a keyed attribution channel: the variant chosen for each carrier letter encodes one bit of an identifier made of a platform field, a user field and a truncated authentication tag. Moreover, given that reshared text is often quoted in fragments, and the placement therefore keeps no positional state, we show that KeHoSu is invariant to sentence reordering up to a constant boundary layer and depends on a partial quotation only through the retained length. We characterize the code-point channel by its capacity, removability and detectability, and provide an achievable region that relates the three. We evaluate KeHoSu over a wide range of use cases and show that the mark survived copy-paste across 18 common platforms, attributing the majority of all excerpts to the correct account at 178 letters (about two sentences) on LLM-generated stories and 167 letters (about one sentence) on standard English prose.
papers.authors: Andrei Alexandru Drăghici, Sediola Ruko, Briland Hitaj, Dorjan Hitaj

papers.title: Signed but Not Safe: Requirement Integrity in Multi-Agent LLM Handoffs
papers.abstract: Enterprise AI agents increasingly split a user's request across subagents and merge their results, and each handoff can summarize away, alter or ignore a requirement. We report a preregistered study with synthetic, exactly scorable tasks comparing free-text, structured JSON and signed requirement-manifest handoffs: the orchestrator extracts each requirement as a verbatim quote plus a checkable predicate, code signs the manifest with HMAC-SHA256, and deterministic code verifies the merger's decision. With Qwen3-8B (1,440 trajectories, five threats), signed manifests cut unsafe commits under attack from 69.4% to 9.0% (60.4 pp, 95% CI [51.4, 69.4]) with no net loss of conformant commits relative to structured handoffs. Signing is what defeats in-transit tampering: an unsigned manifest committed violations in 79% of mutated runs, the signed one in none. On identical trajectories the deterministic verifier caught 78.7% of violating decisions versus 59.0% for an LLM checker, with 7% versus 50% false alarms. An oracle manifest removed all remaining unsafe commits: the residual risk comes from extraction errors made before signing. A preregistered pre-signing injection attack confirmed this boundary: one adversarial line raised signed-manifest violations from 14.6% to 37.5% (Qwen3-8B), 11.1% to 63.9% (gpt-oss-20b) and 8.3% to 75.0% (GPT-5.6-luna), and the signature then authenticated the corrupted manifest. Signing protects requirements in transit, not at extraction; the extraction step is the trust boundary.
papers.authors: Xiaobo Chen, Genliang Zhu, Ziyuan Wang, Chu Wang

papers.title: Quadratic Extractors
papers.abstract: A quadratic source is a random variable $X\sim\mathbb{F}_2^n$ generated by applying $n$ quadratics to a hidden uniform string. Previously, the best-known explicit extractor for this model required min-entropy roughly $k=n-\sqrt{\log n}$. In this paper, we give an explicit construction for min-entropy $k=\mathrm{polylog}(n)$. Even for the special case of $2$-local sources, where each bit of $X$ depends on two hidden uniform bits, achieving an entropy requirement below $k=\sqrt{n}$ was an important open problem. This is because such sources provably cannot be reduced (in a black-box manner) to our most powerful general-purpose seedless extractor, known as a sumset extractor. Our new extractor bypasses this barrier, providing the first explicit construction to go beyond sumset extraction.
papers.authors: Gautam Chandrasekaran, Jesse Goodman, David Zuckerman

papers.title: Full Provenance on the COSS Causal Axis: An Event-Level Closure of Causal Attribution and Confused-Deputy Exclusion
papers.abstract: Provenance Identity Continuity (PIC) represents an authority-use event as an operation/resource behavior situated in a causal lineage, $(o,r,\ell)\in O\times R\times L$. We make the causal occurrence itself primitive: a represented security-relevant causal graph $(E,\to_c)$ in which each occurrence has a unique causal history, so the consistent event-lineage space is canonically isomorphic to $E$. The modeled execution has one causal partial order; distinct lineages are distinct causal histories inside it and may share a root while diverging into incomparable branches. PIC's $O\times R\times L$ is the authority-behavior projection of this space, and Causally Ordered Security-State (COSS) continuity generalizes it to an arbitrary behavior product over the same causal execution. On this semantics we prove an architecture-independent confused-deputy exclusion theorem. PIC continuation requires $C(e')\subseteq C(e)$ on every ordinary causal edge, so descendants are bounded by their ancestors; at an ordinary join, authority available on only one incoming branch cannot be resurrected, even when branches share a common root. Non-conservative combination must be an explicit authorized composition or relaxation event. With protected-effect mediation, an effect caused by request $q$ through an ordinary authority segment can exercise only authority in $C(q)$, so a confused-deputy state is contradictory. The result holds for any system whose protected request-to-effect causes are faithfully represented and whose ordinary authority transport satisfies PIC. We revisit Rajani, Garg, and Rezk: their value, control-flow, and initial-heap attacks are different witnesses of causal ancestry, so full provenance is an evidence mechanism for recovering edges of the causal graph, not the foundation of the PIC theorem. Finally we lift it to the COSS product of heterogeneous security-state coordinates.
papers.authors: Nicola Gallo

papers.title: Cryptanalysis of Pairing-Based Additive Masking with Prime-Field Secrets
papers.abstract: We analyze the public values generated by a pairing-based multi-secret sharing construction in which each secret is added to a power of a common pairing value. The secrets lie in the prime subfield of the extension field containing the public values. We show that the first two public values determine the common mask whenever an explicit nonzero condition holds. We also show that the exceptional case is resolved for the parameter set considered in the numerical example. Consequently, the complete public transcript determines every secret, without requiring a participant share or an initially compromised secret. We further describe two related forms of leakage: recovery of all secrets after disclosure of one suitable secret, and a reduction in the possible values of a secret from a single public value. Our conclusions concern the field-valued, common-base masking construction analyzed here; they do not imply that pairing-based secret sharing in general is insecure.
papers.authors: Harliv Singh

papers.title: FedReason: Large Language Models as Weight-Space Meta-Aggregators for Heterogeneous Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Federated learning servers combine client models with a fixed aggregation rule, and each rule in common use is designed for one kind of heterogeneity. We study whether a large language model (LLM) that inspects the client models can choose the rule itself, without any training on the server. In FedReason, the LLM is called every ten rounds. It analyses the weights by running code in a restricted server-side sandbox, sees only the printed results, may score a few candidates on a 500-image proxy set, and submits a short Python aggregation program. The server applies the program until the next call and falls back to FedAvg whenever its output is invalid. Full weight tensors never leave the server. We evaluated FedReason with Claude Opus 5.5 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18 under Dirichlet label skew, width-heterogeneous sub-models and Byzantine clients, in 168 runs against 14 baselines. Across 12 paired label-skew runs it beat FedAvg by 1.26 percentage points on average (10 wins), and a control that spends the same per-round proxy budget on choosing among standard rules by 1.08 points. It was the strongest server-side rule on CIFAR-100 but did not beat SCAFFOLD, which changes client training. With three of ten clients malicious, it excluded all sign-flipping clients from the first round and stayed about one point below FLTrust without training a root model. Without proxy feedback, accuracy fell from 73.8% to 38.8% in one seed. A 60-round run cost 0.79 USD in API fees on average.
papers.authors: Ali Mohammadi Ruzbahani, Abbas Yazdinejad, Hadis Karimipour

papers.title: AI-Native Task-Oriented Semantic Communications over a Relay: Benefits and Vulnerabilities
papers.abstract: Semantic communication (SemCom) using a relay node is considered, where the relay assists in conveying task-relevant information from a source to a destination, with meaning defined by classification labels. A joint end-to-end design of the source encoder, relay transformation, and destination decoders is developed to optimize both semantic inference accuracy and perceptual reconstruction quality for image data. Relay-assisted schemes are shown to outperform direct transmission, with gains that become more pronounced in low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) regimes across different relaying strategies. Alongside these performance benefits, however, a key security vulnerability introduced by the relay is identified, and a Byzantine attack is formulated in which the relay injects structured, learned perturbations into its transmitted signal. The attack operates on intermediate communication representations subject to channel effects, with perturbations generated through a learned mapping applied at test time. It is shown to significantly degrade semantic inference accuracy at the destination. These results reveal a clear trade-off between SemCom gains and security risks in relay-assisted systems, motivating the need for secure relay designs that account for insider threats.
papers.authors: Yalin E. Sagduyu, Tugba Erpek, Aylin Yener

papers.title: CANMentor: A Large-Small Model Collaboration Framework for CAN Bus Intrusion Detection
papers.abstract: The Controller Area Network (CAN) bus lacks built-in security mechanisms, making real-time intrusion detection necessary. However, resource and latency constraints limit vehicle-side intrusion detection systems (IDSs) to lightweight models, whose detection performance and generalization can degrade under non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data. Meanwhile, uploading original CAN messages to the cloud for more powerful model inference risks exposing sensitive vehicle information. We propose CANMentor, a large-small model collaboration framework in which a cloud-side large language model (LLM) teacher supervises vehicle-side lightweight IDS models for CAN bus intrusion detection. Each vehicle first performs local inference, and a privacy-aware generator then produces proxies from the original CAN messages for cloud-side teacher inference to protect data privacy. The vehicle uses the teacher prediction only when the response arrives within a prescribed latency bound and otherwise retains the local prediction; all returned teacher logits are converted into soft targets for periodic knowledge distillation. On non-IID partitions of the ROAD dataset and the HCRL Car-Hacking dataset, knowledge distillation yields maximum relative Macro F1 improvements of 25.01% and 20.79%, respectively. Teacher predictions also improve detection accuracy for CAN messages near the local decision boundary by 38.71-42.00 percentage points.
papers.authors: Zhiquan Liu, Haolin Gao, Bo Wu, Jingjing Guo, Heng Sun, Jianfeng Ma

papers.title: A Gingerbread House for LLM Agents: Source-Planned Honeypots That Lure Autonomous Attackers into an Isolated Shadow
papers.abstract: LLM agents can exploit web vulnerabilities fast enough that patching may come too late. Deception against such agents has mostly lured them away from a real target that stays reachable. We study a different arrangement: an LLM defender plans a static honeypot from the application's source, and a router sends every later request of a client it confirms as an attacker, including a working exploit, to an isolated shadow copy. We compare no defence, this static plan, and an augmented configuration with a runtime LLM responder and further router rules, graded by the benchmark's own grader on the real target and, for ARTEX, also on the shadow. On the 40 critical CVE-Bench tasks the static plan cut real compromise from 26/40 to 5/40 for Claude Opus 4.8 and from 20/40 to 0/40 (31 valid runs) for the ARTEX attack framework. On 20 new tasks not used in the design, ARTEX went from 15/20 to 0/20. In about half of the deception-arm runs ARTEX's exploit succeeded on the shadow while the real target stayed intact: the defence moved a working exploit rather than stopping it, and the remaining risk lies in requests that reach the real target before confirmation. ARTEX reported a planted fake secret as genuine on 30 of the 120 deception-arm tasks, five times in a report that labelled another item a decoy. With ARTEX's real compromise at zero in both deception configurations, they did not differ significantly on the remaining outcomes, a comparison that does not isolate the responder.
papers.authors: Seungdeok Roh, Seokjun Ryu, Sohee Park, Daeseon Choi

papers.title: MEvince: Knowledge-Constrained LLM Reasoning for Technique Identification from Malware Reports
papers.abstract: Mapping behavioral intelligence in malware analysis reports to ATT&CK techniques supports threat analysis and defense, but reliable identification remains challenging. Supporting evidence is often scattered across long, heterogeneous reports, while closely related techniques share behavioral cues and differ only in subtle but decisive details. While large language models (LLMs) can use external knowledge to interpret reports, they may assign techniques based on plausible associations rather than sufficient evidence. We present MEvince, a knowledge-constrained LLM reasoning framework for report-level malware technique identification. Its core is a shared behavioral representation connecting report observations to technique definitions. This representation is built through agentic mining of technique documentation and supports two online stages: 1) primitive-guided extraction uses behavioral primitives to structure LLM-extracted observations, link them to source passages, and group dispersed evidence; 2) evidence-aligned retrieval matches this evidence to technique profiles through the same concepts, retaining likely candidates and confusable alternatives for LLM comparison of distinguishing behaviors. Controls at both stages validate evidence references and check technique-specific requirements. The representation also supports adaptation without parameter updates, where offline agentic audits diagnose concept weaknesses and refine extraction or retrieval policies. We evaluate MEvince against 11 baselines spanning four method families using a dataset of 610 public malware reports referenced by MITRE ATT&CK. MEvince improves exact-ID F1 over the strongest baseline by 17.4%, and its concept-guided retrieval increases gold-label candidate coverage from 31.6% to 47.9%. With a small adaptation set, offline refinement yields further gains and outperforms baselines that update model parameters.
papers.authors: Hongyu She, Yiling He, Mengda Xie, Yiping Liu, Xingzhi Qian, Zhan Qin, Lorenzo Cavallaro

papers.title: Beyond Instruction Override: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injection with Task-Tampering Attacks
papers.abstract: Indirect prompt-injection (IPI) benchmarks predominantly test planted instructions that redirect a tool-using agent toward an attacker-chosen task. Yet attacker-controlled content can instead tamper with the outcome of the task already in progress. A buyer's dispute evidence can cite a false refund policy to inflate a refund without changing the task. We define IPI by authority rather than instruction-like wording: planted content constitutes an attack when it attempts to influence a decision that its source is not authorized to determine. We introduce a benchmark that makes this boundary explicit: in each of 90 validated cases across three tool-use environments, the user request specifies the source that resolves the targeted decision. Every attack tampers with a decision required by the benign task rather than replacing that task. Each case has attacks with the same harmful outcome that target up to six parts of the agent's decision making: its objective, decision rules, available actions, expected consequences, reading of observations, or beliefs about the current state. Without a defense, attacks on three of the five other targets (decision rules, available actions, and state) have higher mean success than objective attacks across five LLMs. A detection-and-removal defense reduces objective-targeting attacks to 2.4% success but leaves observation- and state-targeting attacks at 9.5% and 12.1%; this gap persists under detection-optimized rewrites. A tool-policy defense still allows 15.4% attack success, close to 17.0% without a defense, because these attacks generally retain expected tools and manipulate values obtained during execution. Evaluations whose attacks redirect the task or target only the agent's objective can therefore overestimate the coverage of these defenses. Code and data are available at https://github.com/amazon-science/task-tampering-prompt-injection.
papers.authors: Rongting Zhang, Martin Bertran, Sandeep Avula, Chia-Jung Lee, Vanessa Murdock

papers.title: JailBound: FOL-Guided Jailbreak Evaluation for Exploring LLM Behavioral Boundaries
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as general-purpose conversational assistants, they must handle diverse user requests while reliably refusing harmful ones. Jailbreak attacks craft adversarial instructions or conversational contexts to elicit unsafe responses despite these safeguards. However, existing jailbreak benchmarks often rely on manually designed or collected prompts, making it difficult to systematically extend coverage to new threat conditions. Moreover, existing attack search methods typically optimize for attack success rate (ASR), providing limited insight into how model behavior changes locally between safe refusal and unsafe response. To address these limitations, we present JailBound, a unified jailbreak evaluation framework that combines automated benchmark construction with first-order loss (FOL)-guided dual-branch search. JailBound organizes threats by risk category, application domain, and attack type. Conditioned on this taxonomy, a fine-tuned meta-attack generator synthesizes evaluation prompts across diverse threat conditions. FOL serves as a local sensitivity signal for exploring high-value attack states and behavior-sensitive states. We evaluate JailBound across 46 LLMs from 13 model families under a unified experimental protocol. Under matched settings, the High-Value Branch improves average ASR over a ZOL-only baseline by 5.1 and 4.9 percentage points across the two evaluation settings. Under local perturbations, states from the Safety-Sensitivity Branch exhibit higher behavioral flip rates than those from the High-Value Branch across all tested radii for JailBound and S-Eval, indicating greater local sensitivity of judge-assigned safety labels. Warning: this paper includes examples that may be offensive or harmful.
papers.authors: Fazong Wu, Xin Wang, Ming Yang, Zhenyong Zhang, Xiaoming Wu

papers.title: SPILLWAY: Separating Target Admission from Sanitization to Defend Tool-Using Agents against Prompt Injection
papers.abstract: Tool-using agents act on email, files, and payments, so an instruction hidden in a web page or a shared document can make an agent send data or money to an attacker. Many runtime defenses put a language model on the decision that lets an action through, so the decision depends on a model that may read the attacker's text and adds model calls to every step. Provenance defenses keep the model off the final check but need a model to plan or route each task first. Where an action goes can instead be read from the tools' typed returns: an email's sender or a payment's account arrives in a typed field, while injected instructions arrive as free text. SPILLWAY turns this observation into a deterministic floor with no per-task plan. The check admits a call when each target value that appears in tool output but not in the user's task was returned by a read-only tool in a typed field or is covered by a fixed delegation rule. A deterministic sanitizer removes instruction-like regions its fixed rules match before the model reads them and retains the removed spans as evidence, and a local judge may restore a refused call, never one whose target lies in the removed text. Across three backbones, and seven task suites on one of them, no standard templated injection redirects an action to an attacker's target under SPILLWAY, at the highest observed mean utility and composite scores (NRP, ERS) of the defenses we run under that attack. A forged chat template also produces a raw zero, and mean in-scope attack success under a released reinforcement-learning attacker is .007. SPILLWAY reaches this floor with no defense-triggered backbone re-run and almost no added model call. As personal AI agents act on users' email, files, and payments, SPILLWAY gives them an auditable refusal floor on where their actions go that keeps them useful and holds across backbones.
papers.authors: Woosang Lim, Yeseul Chang, Jaewoo Lee

papers.title: An efficient Failure Probability Estimator for LWE-based encryption, and application to IBE
papers.abstract: In recent years, lattice-based cryptography has proven to be a source of post-quantum cryptosystems. In particular, the blueprint of Learning With Errors (LWE) encryption enabled the creation of Kyber, chosen by NIST to be standardized as ML-KEM. Because of the structure of LWE encryption, the decryption of a ciphertext can give an incorrect plaintext. This event (a decryption failure) happens randomly with some probability. Since this is a problem for both functionality and security, we must ensure that this failure probability is cryptographically negligible. Usually, this is assessed with theoretical approximations and upper-bounds. The authors of Kyber used a Python program to compute that probability more precisely, enabling to fine-tune the compression of the ciphertext, hence reducing its size. However, because of its performances, this program has been limited to Kyber, and all the other schemes are still studied theoretically. In this paper, we design a more efficient Failure Probability Estimator, that we implement in low-level languages (C and CUDA C++), to reach higher parameters used in real schemes based on structured LWE. We illustrate some benefits of our tool with two Identity-Based Encryption schemes. For the first scheme, our tool allows to reduce the size of the ciphertext by about 20%. For the second one, we reduce the failure probability (thus improving security) without impacting the scheme (key size, ciphertext size, etc.).
papers.authors: Julien CAM

papers.title: Information Loss Is All You Need: TC⁰ Pseudorandomness from Worst-Case Lattices
papers.abstract: Pseudorandomness plays a central role in algorithms, complexity theory, and cryptography. We ask whether deterministic information loss alone can yield post-quantum pseudorandomness with $\mathrm{TC}^0$ evaluation. Learning with errors (LWE) hides linear measurements with random noise. Learning with rounding (LWR) replaces noise with deterministic rounding, but a standard polynomial-modulus hardness reduction requires parameters tailored to a predetermined sample bound. Decisional Diffie–Hellman offers a noiseless algebraic route to pseudorandomness, but its standard instantiations are vulnerable to quantum algorithms. We show that deterministic rounding achieves this under quantum worst-case lattice hardness, with fixed polynomial parameters and no predetermined sample bound. We introduce the learning with algebraic rounding (LAR) assumption, which applies an explicit integer rounding map to blocks of secret-dependent linear measurements and encodes the result in a lattice quotient. For one fixed family with polynomially bounded modulus and dimensions, its deterministic labels on exactly uniform, secret-independent public matrices are computationally indistinguishable from independent uniform labels for every polynomial number of classical random examples. Our classical reduction from Gaussian LWE, combined with the quantum worst-case reduction to LWE, bases LAR on GapSVP and SIVP over general lattices at approximation factor $\widetilde{O}(q)$, where $q$ is the modulus. To prove this, we develop a source-independent affine transport framework that may be of independent interest. Using public affine maps sampled independently of the hidden errors, it transports the Gaussian error law close to uniform on the rounding map’s zero-label fiber while preserving exactly uniform public matrices. For every fixed inverse-polynomial accuracy, we give a polynomial-time sampler for the same public parameter family. This yields the first post-quantum weak pseudorandom function with joint key-and-input evaluation in $\mathrm{TC}^0$, secure against uniform quantum polynomial-time distinguishers given any polynomial number of classical uniform random examples. We also establish the hardness of learning polynomial-size two-hidden-layer ReLU networks from noiseless uniform random examples, even for quantum polynomial-time improper learners.
papers.authors: Chen Qian

papers.title: Archive Certificates for ML-DSA-87 Authorizations from an Exact Bounded Relation
papers.abstract: A blockchain that signs every transaction with FIPS 204 ML-DSA-87 keeps 4,627 bytes of signature per transaction forever. We describe and measure an archive certificate: one hash-based proof, for a range of already validated blocks, of knowledge of canonical FIPS 204 signatures on exactly the recorded messages under the keys resolved from chain state. Fresh blocks keep native verification. The construction starts from an exact bounded relation for ML-DSA-87 verification once the high bits $u = w'_1$ are fixed. The main certificate keeps $u$ hidden and proves the SHAKE256 challenge hash inside the proof, by a GKR argument for Keccak-f[1600] over the same WHIR commitment as the lattice relation. For 65,536 signatures we measured 104.09 bytes per signature in a Johnson-regime family, which has a classical bound only, and 126.89 in a unique-decoding family, against 4,627 bytes raw. The price is a slow prover and a verifier slower than native verification. At $2^{64}$ queries and $2^{20}$ verification submissions, under the compiler, coding and extractor-efficiency hypotheses specified in the security analysis, the classical random-oracle extraction error is below $2^{-188.07}$ for the Johnson family and below $2^{-201.99}$ for unique decoding. In the quantum random oracle model we state, for the unique-decoding family only, an extraction-failure bound below $2^{-129.67}$ at $2^{64}$ quantum queries and $2^{20}$ verification submissions; it is not a work factor. Lean 4 checks Lemmas 1 to 4 and the WHIR steps at the scopes detailed in the formal-verification section, the registered interactive theorem's conditions K1–K4, exact ledger arithmetic, and conditional compiler compositions. The extractor's efficiency condition K5 is derived in a defined bit-cost model from two implementation premises that remain open. The link between the interactive predicate and the ledger is proved within an abstract compiler interface; concrete compiled security games and correspondence with the Rust verifier remain outside the checked result. The bundles identified in that section are also verified with AXLE. An external review is outstanding, and certificate-only bootstrap remains disabled under the stated deployment conditions.
papers.authors: Yacine Alloul

papers.title: Leakage-Tolerant Computation without Leakage-Free Setup
papers.abstract: Leakage-tolerant multi-party computation (MPC) ensures that leakage from each honest party’s internal state reveals no more than the leakage from honest parties' individual inputs and outputs, beyond the standard security guarantee of MPC. Previous constructions either require a leakage-free preprocessing, or rely on indistinguishability obfuscation in the common reference string (CRS) model and only achieve semi-honest security. In the computational setting, assuming only an augmented non-committing encryption scheme, we show that every adaptively well-formed functionality admits a semi-honest leakage-tolerant MPC protocol, without any leakage-free preprocessing execution or CRS. Under the decisional Diffie–Hellman assumption, we further extend this result to malicious security in the CRS model for all deterministic functionalities. The limitation of deterministic functions is subject to an impossibility result of leakage-based coin-tossing protocols. In the information-theoretic setting, we show that secure erasure enables statistically secure leakage-tolerant MPC of arbitrary functionalities assuming strictly less than half of the participants are maliciously corrupted. We complement this construction with an impossibility result: without secure erasure, general-purpose statistically secure leakage-tolerant MPC with leakage-oblivious simulation, an important property to enable universal composition, is impossible in the plain model, even when all parties are honest. As a further application, we also obtain information-theoretic leakage-tolerant circuits against bounded communication leakage, while all prior works are restricted only to the weaker variant of leakage-resilient circuits.
papers.authors: Yaohua Ma, Yifan Song

papers.title: On the (Quantum) Communication Complexity of Secure MPC from a Random Oracle
papers.abstract: Information-theoretic MPC among $n$ parties with $t$ corruptions can securely evaluate a circuit $C$ with $O(|C| \cdot t/(n-t))$ online communication in the preprocessing model and $O(|C| \cdot t/(n-2t))$ communication in the honest majority setting. Damg{\aa}rd, Larsen and Nielsen (CRYPTO 2019) showed that both communication bounds are tight for inner products. Fully homomorphic encryption and other assumptions known to imply public-key cryptography beat both communication bounds, but the communication complexity with symmetric-key cryptography alone is less understood. For MPC with preprocessing, we prove that the same $\Omega(|C| \cdot t/(n-t))$ lower bound holds in the random oracle model, so a random oracle cannot reduce the online communication. For honest majority MPC relative to a random oracle, we present an $\Omega(|C|)$ communication lower bound that is matched by a new construction for degree-2 polynomials (including inner products) when $n = O(\log \lambda)$, beating the information-theoretic bound. We also study quantum MPC. First, we prove that information-theoretic protocols with quantum communication (and preprocessing) cannot reduce communication compared to their classical counterparts. Furthermore, we extend our lower bound for MPC with preprocessing to protocols with a quantum-accessible random oracle, but use only classical communication. In contrast, with both quantum communication and a post-quantum one-way function, we present a simple two-party protocol that evaluates the two-party instance of these circuits with $\mathsf{poly}(\lambda, \log |C|)$ communication, beating these lower bounds. Finally, such communication savings do not come for free. We prove that there exist circuits $C$ such that every blackbox protocol with $o(|C|)$ quantum communication must perform $\Omega(|C|)$ cryptographic operations.
papers.authors: Alexander Hoover, Giuseppe Persiano, Kevin Yeo

papers.title: From Claws to Conferences: Device-Independent Key Agreement Beyond Non-Signaling
papers.abstract: Device-independent conference key agreement (DI-CKA) allows a group of users to establish a common secret key without trusting the internal operation of their quantum devices. Existing DI-CKA protocols derive their security from multipartite Bell tests and therefore require the device components not to communicate during each round. We present, to the best of our knowledge, the first DI-CKA protocol that removes this non-signaling assumption: all interfaces and their mutual communication are treated as one untrusted device, which only has to be quantum polynomial-time while the protocol runs. Assuming that the Learning With Errors (LWE) problem is hard for quantum algorithms with quantum advice during the execution, we prove finite-size security against coherent attacks, in which the device may keep quantum memory and correlate and adapt its behavior across rounds. For two parties the protocol is a computational DI-QKD protocol with an explicit finite-size proof against coherent attacks. Technically, we lift the claw state underlying the classical-verifier test of Brakerski et al.\ (FOCS 2018) to multipartite entanglement, obtaining a \emph{GHZ-correlated claw state}. %that is prepared with one coherent claw-free function evaluation and $N-1$ CNOT gates. We then introduce the \emph{collective adaptive hardcore bit}, a multiparty generalization of the adaptive hardcore bit of Brakerski et al.\ and show that it follows from the original property by a tight reduction. Combined with Jordan's lemma, an entropic uncertainty relation, and entropy accumulation, this certifies smooth min-entropy of the key against an external quantum adversary. Our protocol achieves \emph{everlasting security}: LWE needs to hold only during the execution, because the final key is statistically secure and its secrecy persists even if LWE is broken after the protocol ends.
papers.authors: Suvradip Chakraborty

papers.title: MODDIV-WC: Unit-Anchored Toeplitz/Hankel Rounding with Exact Binary-LWE Masking and an IND-CCA Security Route
papers.abstract: \begin{abstract} We present MODDIV-WC, a public-key encryption and key-encapsulation candidate based on a widened Hankel linear map followed by deterministic integer division, together with an implicit-rejection Fujisaki--Okamoto wrapper, MODDIV-WC-FO. The construction uses a secret vector whose first coordinate is fixed to one and whose remaining coordinates are sampled from a positive interval. This unit anchor makes the Hankel map surjective for every admissible secret, a property that is central to the proof. The security analysis has four layers. First, we give an exact embedding of binary-secret LWE into the widened Hankel map using a parity mask that reproduces the MODDIV-WC secret distribution without statistical loss. Second, in an ideal public-key hybrid, a strong leftover-hash argument hides the challenge key. Third, adapting the Renyi-divergence boundary method of prior LWR and MP-LWR work, we prove a transfer lemma for the unit-anchored MODDIV-WC secret distribution. This avoids the earlier requirement that the probability of crossing a rounding boundary be negligible and instead preserves one-way success probabilities with a multiplicative Renyi loss. Fourth, we combine one-way chosen-plaintext security with the implicit-rejection modular Fujisaki--Okamoto analysis of Hofheinz, Hovelmanns, and Kiltz to derive IND-CCA security in the classical random-oracle model. For an explicit asymptotic family, the correctness, Renyi, leftover-hash, binary-secret-LWE, and random-oracle losses are simultaneously negligible, while the source LWE noise remains inverse-polynomial. Together with classical worst-case-to-LWE reductions and the binary-secret/modulus transformations of Brakerski, Langlois, Peikert, Regev, and Stehle, this yields an internally audited candidate route from polynomial-factor worst-case lattice hardness to IND-CCA security. No practical 128-bit parameters, QROM proof, or deployment claim is made. \end{abstract}
papers.authors: Samir Bouftass

papers.title: A Post-Quantum Interactive Hashing Theorem
papers.abstract: Interactive hashing, introduced by Ostrovsky, Venkatesan, and Yung [OVY93], is a building block in many cryptographic protocols, including perfectly hiding commitments from one-way permutations [NOVY92]. Its multi-output generalization is a key ingredient in constructions of statistical zero-knowledge arguments for NP and statistically hiding commitments from arbitrary one-way functions [NOV06,HR07]. In this note, we give a post-quantum security proof for this multi-output interactive hashing protocol with arbitrary relations.
papers.authors: Céline Chevalier, Laurent Holin, Quoc-Huy Vu

papers.title: Kaiburr: ML-KEM at (much) higher security
papers.abstract: With deployment of standardized post-quantum cryptography well on the way, discussions continue about concrete choices of schemes and parameter sets. For example, while NIST standardized structured-lattice-based ML-KEM, European agencies like BSI and ANSSI favor unstructured-lattice-based FrodoKEM. Another discussion revolves around different approaches to hybrid deployments – either combining post-quantum schemes with "traditional" elliptic-curve cryptography (or RSA) or combining multiple different post-quantum schemes. The typical question for systems engineers to ask is what the "best" or "most conservative" approach is within a certain performance budget. In this paper we add a data point to this discussion by investigating how to scale ML-KEM to (much) higher security levels of the underlying MLWE problem. We first observe that increasing security simply by increasing the module rank $k$ quickly reaches a limit imposed by decryption failure probability. We then propose a generalization of the noise distribution, which enables scaling to much larger module rank and MLWE hardness, while preserving the essence of ML-KEM, most notably arithmetic in the ring $\mathbb{Z}_{3329}[X]/(X^{256}+1)$ and a simple and constant-time secret / noise generation. We select three concrete parameter sets of this high-security variant of ML-KEM, which we call Kaiburr. We present benchmarking results for optimized implementations of Kaiburr on 64-bit Intel CPUs and on the Asymmetric Cryptography Coprocessor (ACC) of the Pavona open-source silicon framework. Based on these benchmarks, we argue that, for example, a hybrid of FrodoKEM-976 and Kaiburr-1792 not only offers better performance than FrodoKEM-1344, it also offers protection against a broader range of hypothetical future attacks against (M)LWE.
papers.authors: Swechchha Adhikari, Vadim Lyubashevsky, Peter Schwabe

papers.title: HqcLethe: Streaming HQC Encapsulation for Tiny Stateless Servers
papers.abstract: Stateless post-quantum authenticated key exchanges such as post-quantum WireGuard hedge against unexpected cryptanalytic advances by combining a lattice KEM with code-based Classic McEliece. However, recent attacks have led Germany's BSI to advise against McEliece, which leaves these protocols with lattices alone. HQC, the code-based KEM that NIST selected, could restore diversity, but its keys do not fit in a single packet, so a server would have to buffer multi-packet handshakes. This would leave an attack surface for memory exhaustion, which is what WireGuard's stateless handshake was designed to avoid in the first place. McTiny demonstrated that stateless key encapsulation for Classic McEliece is possible by streaming key blocks one-at-a-time. However, HQC's encapsulation does not split as easily into individual packets, as cyclic polynomial multiplication, unlike matrix-vector multiplication, is inherently non-local. We present HqcLethe, a stateless key exchange that streams an HQC encapsulation in packet-sized pieces. It uses the Chinese remainder theorem to split the polynomial multiplication into independent remainders, one per packet, and masks them so that they reveal no more than an ordinary HQC ciphertext, which we prove in Rocq with SSProve; we also verify session secrecy, server authentication and forward secrecy in ProVerif. Client puzzles bound CPU exhaustion, and HqcLethe removes memory exhaustion: on a Raspberry Pi 3B+, each worker runs in a fixed 1.2-1.6 MiB. At category 5 it sends 27x fewer bytes and uses 9.0x less server CPU than McTiny, the earlier stateless code-based design.
papers.authors: Wind Wong, Klaus v. Gleissenthall

papers.title: AirBB: Lightweight Threshold Anonymous Credentials without Random Oracles from BB Signatures
papers.abstract: Anonymous credentials are a well-studied cryptographic primitive enabling users to prove statements about their identity and selectively present personal information in an unlinkable manner. The issuer, however, is often a single point of failure. Threshold issuance addresses this by distributing the issuer across several parties such that a quorum of them must cooperate to issue credentials. Numerous constructions of single-issuer and threshold issuance anonymous credentials have been proposed. However, existing schemes each have at least one of the following weaknesses: (1) their presentations depend on the number of attributes, (2) they are not concretely efficient, or (3) they rely on the random oracle model (ROM) for non-interactive presentations. In this work, we present a new construction of threshold anonymous credentials that has a constant presentation size of 240 bytes, rivals the efficiency of BBS, and does not rely on the random oracle model. We achieve this by combining techniques from set commitments with Boneh-Boyen (BB) signatures (Eurocrypt'04) and prove our scheme's security in the algebraic group model. This is on par with the tight security proofs of existing schemes, which typically rely on the AGM or GGM, or on assumptions justified in those models. Since signing uses linear operations, the scheme is easily thresholdizable, without requiring interaction between the issuers or preprocessing.
papers.authors: Sebastian Faust, Jonas Hofmann, Philipp-Florens Lehwalder, Hussien Othman

papers.title: Syndrome Decoding out of the Head: Structure-Aided Side-Channel Witness Recovery on SDitH
papers.abstract: Regular syndrome decoding (RSD) underlies several code-based signature schemes, including SD-in-the-Head (SDitH). Its secret witness has exactly one nonzero coordinate per block, and the selected positions must satisfy a public syndrome equation. In this work, we show how these structural constraints can be exploited to recover the complete witness from imperfect side-channel information. We present a profiled power analysis of the witness-embedding operation in the SDitH Round-3 reference implementation. We train convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to classify the mux digits encoding each regular block and use their outputs to rank candidate positions. To correct errors in these predictions, we combine the resulting rankings with the public syndrome and the regularity constraints. We formulate this recovery problem as an affine correction system with block-validity constraints and analyze its rank, consistency, and uniqueness for the systematic parity-check matrix used in SDitH. Based on this analysis, we develop a quotient-syndrome decoder that identifies blocks whose true positions fall outside the initial candidate lists, avoiding exhaustive enumeration of block subsets. We evaluate our attack on an ARM Cortex-M4 using measured power traces. With a single target trace per key, our approach recovers all 100 test witnesses under -Os using 4,000 profiling traces, and 91 out of 100 under -O3 using 16,000 profiling traces. Each successful recovery matches all 616 serialized witness bits. These results demonstrate how the regular structure of RSD and the public syndrome can compensate for imperfect side-channel predictions, thereby enabling full-witness recovery.
papers.authors: Jaeyeon Lee, Jaeho Jeon, Young-Sik Kim

papers.title: Trapdoors Beyond Inversion: Recoverable Information in Public-Key Cryptography
papers.abstract: Classical trapdoor functions recover complete preimages, whereas public-key decryption needs only designated information about an encryption input. We study this distinction through trapdoor hardcore functions (TDHFs), whose trapdoor recovers a prescribed value $h(x)$ from a public evaluation $f (x)$, while $h(x)$ remains pseudorandom given the public key and evaluation. For perfectly correct primitives, we show that adaptive TDHFs characterize IND-CCA2-secure public-key encryption. The constructive direction requires only a single recoverable bit and allows noninjective public evaluations. Extending the rejection-sampling approach, we show that adaptive pseudorandomness itself controls queries to unselected candidate evaluations, without requiring full inversion. We also prove that lossy TDHFs characterize lossy public-key encryption, identifying statistical hiding of the designated recovered value as the relevant lossiness requirement. Fiber samplability together with fiber hiding yields a parameter-preserving correspondence with lossy encryption and, through the known long-message transformation, almost-always lossy trapdoor functions when the recovered-value length exceeds the fiber-sampling randomness length. Ordinary TDHFs provide the corresponding characterization of IND-CPA encryption. Together, these results make explicit the roles of adaptive recovery, conditional sampling, and randomness costs in transformations between public-key encryption and full-inversion primitives.
papers.authors: Kanad Chakravarti, Shreyas Gupta, Bhavana Kanukurthi, Girisha Shankar

papers.title: TFNP in the Random Oracle Model
papers.abstract: We determine which major TFNP classes are hard in the random oracle model (ROM). Prior work establishes average-case hardness of highly structured subclasses of TFNP from strong cryptographic assumptions such as LWE and indistinguishability obfuscation. It is not known whether weaker assumptions such as one-way functions imply hardness of any of the standard TFNP subclasses, even in the worst case. The ROM, where all parties have query access to a random function, lies, morally, between these two regimes: a random function is one-way, but public-key cryptography cannot be built from it in a black-box way. We refer to this setting as \emph{Romantica}. Our first result settles a long-standing open problem: PPAD, the class of total search problems reducible to finding a Nash equilibrium, is hard on average in Romantica. Combined with the known hardness of PLS (local search), this gives average-case hardness of EoPL = PPAD \cap PLS. In contrast, we show that UEoPL can be solved in Romantica with polynomially many oracle queries by a computationally unbounded solver, a sharp distinction between EoPL and UEoPL. This resolves the black-box hardness landscape of all major TFNP classes in Romantica. Finally, we initiate the study of separations between TFNP subclasses in Romantica: PWPP and PPA do not reduce to PLS under \emph{public-coin} reductions.
papers.authors: Noah Fleming, Mika Göös, Ziyi Guan, Oliver Korten, Daniel Mitropolsky, Toniann Pitassi, Artur Riazanov, Dmitry Sokolov, Tianqi Yang, Weiqiang Yuan

papers.title: The Price of Agreement in Secure Multiparty Computation
papers.abstract: Secure multi-party computation (MPC) cannot guarantee output delivery, in general, in the dishonest-majority setting. Security of MPC is therefore relaxed to security with abort, where the adversary may prevent honest parties from obtaining their output. The standard notion of \emph{unanimous abort} (UA-MPC) ensures that either all honest parties obtain their output or all of them abort. Goldwasser and Lindell [JCRYPT '05] introduced the relaxed notion of \emph{selective abort}, allowing some honest parties to abort and others to obtain their output. While two-round SA-MPC can be achieved over point-to-point channels, two-round UA-MPC necessitates the second round to be over broadcast. The price of agreement in dishonest-majority MPC is thus tied to the round complexity of broadcast with unanimous abort (UA-broadcast). The round complexity of broadcast has been extensively studied for more than four decades. Garay, Katz, Koo, and Ostrovsky [FOCS '07] (GKKO) proved that the expected round complexity of broadcast protocols tolerating $t$ corruptions is at least $2n/(n-t)-1$. Their argument, however, relies on all honest parties obtaining an honest sender's input, and does not extend to UA-broadcast. Recently, Cohen {\em et al.} [TCC '26] showed that UA-MPC is possible in an expected constant number of rounds when a constant fraction of the parties is honest, and asked whether this extends to $n-o(n)$ corruptions. In this work we answer this question in the negative: Agreement alone already incurs the GKKO barrier. Concretely, we prove that for $t\leq n-2$, UA-broadcast---and hence UA-MPC---requires at least $t/(2(n-t))$ rounds in expectation, matching the asymptotic bound for broadcast without abort. As a corollary, expected-constant-round UA-MPC is possible if and only if a constant fraction of the parties is honest. Next, we consider UA-broadcast protocols that terminate in an {\em a-priori} known round, and show that the bound that the argument of GKKO gives for broadcast holds for them exactly. Combined with the broadcast protocol of Dolev and Strong [SICOMP '83], our bound is tight for arbitrarily many corruptions.
papers.authors: Ran Cohen, Pouyan Forghani, Juan Garay, Vassilis Zikas

papers.title: Superlattice methods for the shortest vector problem and discrete Gaussian sampling
papers.abstract: We give worst-case algorithms for the shortest vector problem (SVP) and discrete Gaussian sampling (DGS) at arbitrary widths. Both algorithms generate lists on a dense superlattice and combine vectors along a chain down to the input lattice. Random shifts let us control the expected number of representations of a vector regardless of the lattice. For SVP we balance these counts with a novel midpoint-shell test to ensure output distributions are sufficiently uniform. For DGS we use Gaussian weights and correct the probabilities of selecting entries from the final list. For SVP, our optimized algorithm runs in time $2^{0.409 n+o(n)}$ and space $2^{0.259 n+o(n)}$, improving the best $2^{n/2 + o(n)}$ worst-case SVP complexities of Hhan [ePrint, 2026]. For Haar-random lattices, or assuming a natural upper bound on the kissing constant, the costs of the algorithm match the $2^{0.292 n+o(n)}$ time and $2^{0.208 n+o(n)}$ space of Becker-Ducas-Gama-Laarhoven [SODA 2016]. For quantum SVP, through a series of refinements and generalizations we obtain worst-case time and space $2^{0.247n+o(n)}$. This improves the best known heuristic quantum SVP time complexity of $2^{0.256n+o(n)}$ due to Bonnetain-Chailloux-Schrottenloher-Shen [Eurocrypt 2023], without requiring any heuristic assumptions. For discrete Gaussian sampling, we provide a sampling algorithm at any width with distribution error $2^{-\kappa}$, running in worst-case time $2^{0.292 n+o(n)} \operatorname{poly}(\kappa)$ and space $2^{0.208 n+o(n)} \operatorname{poly}(\kappa)$, improving upon the previous best $2^{n + o(n)}$ cost for sampling at arbitrary widths of Aggarwal-Dadush-Regev-Stephens-Davidowitz [STOC 2015]. As further applications, we obtain fast algorithms for approximate-SVP/CVP, bounded distance decoding, and estimating the Gaussian mass and smoothing parameter of any lattice.
papers.authors: Minki Hhan, Jiseung Kim, Sunyeop Kim, Thijs Laarhoven

papers.title: Efficient Polynomial Multiplier Architectures for ML-KEM on Resource-Constrained FPGAs
papers.abstract: The Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) is a key component of polynomial multiplication in Kyber, making its efficient hardware implementation essential for post-quantum cryptographic applications. This paper presents two hardware architectures for Kyber polynomial arithmetic, supporting the NTT, inverse NTT (INTT) and point-wise multiplication (PWM) operations. The first architecture employs a single processing element (PE) to reduce hardware area, while the second uses two PEs to achieve higher throughput and efficiency. Both architectures incorporate a low-complexity modular multiplication and reduction method tailored to the Kyber modulus q = 3329, a unified butterfly unit supporting NTT, INTT, and PWM, and constant-geometry data access with dedicated address-generation algorithms. The dual-PE architecture is implemented without dedicated DSP blocks or BRAMs. FPGA implementation results demonstrate that the dual-PE architecture achieves the lowest area-time product and highest frequency among the evaluated state-of-the-art designs, while providing an effective trade-off between hardware area and execution time.
papers.authors: Hossein Naderi Varandi, Raziye Salarifard

papers.title: Trinetra.Q: Statistical and Behavioral Detection of Attacks on the Quantum-Error-Correction Layer and Classical Control Stack of Quantum Computing Systems
papers.abstract: Most quantum-computer security work targets physical-layer attacks on qubits, while two surfaces remain inadequately defended: the quantum-error-correction (QEC) syndrome-and-decoder pipeline, and the classical control and software stack that runs it. Tampering on these surfaces can corrupt a computation while the physical error rate appears normal, and can stay within a single-circuit integrity tolerance. We present Trinetra.Q, a detection layer of cooperating detectors, each monitoring a statistical or behavioral property of quantum-domain data against an envelope calibrated from honest operation, and raising an indication only on a statistically significant deviation. The detectors cover (A) QEC integrity over per-stabilizer firing rates, syndrome defect-count, and repeated-syndrome rate; (B) decoder confidence over the margin between minimum-weight error explanations in distinct logical classes; (C) behavioral output divergence, flagging crosstalk-class and novel attacks by their effect on a victim's output relative to a matched control; (D) control-stack tampering via known-answer canary circuits, built to be indistinguishable to a resident implant, with a cross-job consistency statistic; and (E) compilation/execution integrity. Each gates on significance, so honest operation raises no alarm. We evaluate in faithful simulation and on three production IBM Heron processors, and bound the physical attack surface with a systematic negative map: most physical-layer attacks return statistically null, the exception an implemented, measured within-job feed-forward covert-channel primitive. Every detector is also evaluated against an adaptive attacker with full knowledge of it. To our knowledge this is the first unified statistical-and-behavioral detection layer for the QEC layer and classical control stack of a quantum computing system, demonstrated on production hardware.
papers.authors: Garrv Sipani

papers.title: Finite-Batch q-ary OT Extension for High-Arity Private Lookup: Certified Radix--Code Co-Design
papers.abstract: High-arity oblivious transfer is a natural abstraction for private lookup: a $\delta$-bit table address selects one entry out of $2^\delta$ candidates. This paper characterizes the finite-batch design space of the CCG q-ary OT-extension family and derives certified radix-selection rules. For $q=2^r$, we formulate radix-code selection as a security-constrained discrete optimization problem that accounts for subfield-check padding, code dimension, required distance, base-OT count, and q-ary symbol width. We derive exact communication thresholds showing when reduced base OTs can compensate for larger q-ary encoding cost. Then we convert the Griesmer bound into communication lower bounds, yielding certificates for regions where non-binary radices cannot improve communication, are provably beneficial, or remain dependent on better code constructions. Finally, we instantiate the framework with simplex and BCH constructions and CodeTables entries, and verify the selected $\delta=12$ codes with Magma.
papers.authors: Zhuoran Zhang

papers.title: Clear Human Web: Where a Person Vouches for Every Client
papers.abstract: The web cannot tell whether a request comes from a person or from a program. Sites have checked the network address and puzzles in its place, and both have given way: automated traffic exceeds human traffic, and puzzles are solved for pay and by agents. This paper proposes the Clear Human Web, the part of the public web that sites open only to clients a person vouches for. A person's wallet presents their person identification data (PID) to one issuer, the only party that registers as a relying party, and receives a bounded number of blind-signed tokens, proofs of personhood that carry no attribute. The browser spends one token at each site that runs the gate, and the site learns that a valid token of a trusted issuer was spent, and nothing else. No field is added to the PID, no protocol is introduced, no site registers, and the publisher of a site holds the same proof as its readers. We define the Clear Human Web through five properties and seven adversaries, and state which properties the construction satisfies against each adversary.
