The identities a person can hold on one site in an epoch are bounded to k. The bound holds once the wallet limits a person to one pseudonym at the issuer. In the optimum k = 1, and a zero-knowledge proof of PID possession and a pseudonym per site replace the tokens.
papers.authors: Lorenzo Porcelli

papers.title: Refined Bounds for the Smoothing Parameter of Lattices
papers.abstract: The smoothing parameter $\eta_\varepsilon(\Lambda)$ is a fundamental invariant in lattice-based cryptography. Zheng, Zhao, and Xu (AAECC 2021) proved $\eta_\varepsilon(\mathbb{Z}) \le \sqrt{\ln(\frac{2}{\varepsilon} + \frac{\varepsilon}{44})/\pi}$ and $\eta_\varepsilon(\Lambda) \le \sqrt{\ln(n - 1 + \frac{2n}{\varepsilon})/\pi}\,\mathrm{bl}(\Lambda)$. Guo, Liu, Wang, and Tian (PLOS One 2025) proposed $\eta_\varepsilon(\mathbb{Z}) \le \sqrt{\ln(\frac{2}{\varepsilon} + \frac{\varepsilon}{m})/\pi}$ for $0 \frac{\varepsilon^2}{4}$, our bound is strictly tighter for all admissible $(\varepsilon, m)$, improving the worst-case gap from $O(\varepsilon^2)$ to $O(\varepsilon^6)$. Second, for all $n \ge 2$ and $0 < \varepsilon < \min\{1, (\rho(\mathbb{Z})-1)n\}$, \[ \eta_\varepsilon(\Lambda) \le \sqrt{\frac{\ln\!\left(\frac{2}{\delta_n} + \frac{\delta_n^2}{4}\right)}{\pi}}\,\mathrm{bl}(\Lambda) < \sqrt{\frac{\ln\!\left(\frac{2n}{\varepsilon} + (n - 1) - \frac{(n^2 - 1)\varepsilon}{6n(1 + \varepsilon)}\right)}{\pi}}\,\mathrm{bl}(\Lambda), \] where $\delta_n = (1+\varepsilon)^{1/n} - 1$; the rational bound is strictly tighter than Guo et al.'s across $100\%$ of their validity window, while remaining valid as $\varepsilon \to 0^+$. Third, for any basis $\mathbf{B}$ with Gram--Schmidt vectors $\mathbf{b}_i^*$ and $M = \max_i \|\mathbf{b}_i^*\|$, define $N_\varepsilon(\mathbf{B}) = \sum_{i=1}^n (\varepsilon/2)^{M^2/\|\mathbf{b}_i^*\|^2 - 1} \in [1, n]$; then \[ \eta_\varepsilon(\Lambda) \le \sqrt{\ln\!\left(\frac{2}{\delta_{\mathrm{eff}}} + \frac{\delta_{\mathrm{eff}}^2}{4}\right)/\pi}\,M, \] where $\delta_{\mathrm{eff}} = \frac{n}{N_\varepsilon(\mathbf{B})}((1+\varepsilon)^{1/n}-1)$. For reduced bases with geometrically decaying Gram--Schmidt lengths, $N_\varepsilon(\mathbf{B}) = O(1)$ is independent of $n$, eliminating the $O(n)$ factor inside the logarithm.
papers.authors: Shanxiang Lyu

papers.title: Blockchain-Anchored Proactive Refresh for Dynamic Threshold Services
papers.abstract: A long-lived threshold service must issue shares to participants that join after deployment, refresh them against a mobile adversary, and allow participants offline during a refresh to recover missed updates. We show that charging exposure solely to committed epochs is fundamentally insufficient: an aborted refresh attempt that publishes candidate update tokens can reveal the secret even if no committed epoch exceeds its corruption budget. To eliminate this exposure leakage, we index security by fine-grained states covering both committed epochs and aborted attempts. Each state's budget bounds all participants whose local material or public update records originate from that state, enforced via an append-only, durable release ledger that is never rolled back upon abort. A fixed dealer committee anchors encrypted update records in blockchain blob storage, enabling non-interactive recovery for offline participants without contacting dealers, while an interactive bisection dispute protocol deterministically attributes faulty records on chain. Our core cryptographic result is an explicit distribution-preserving shift of the actual generation transcript, establishing proactive secrecy and past-share unforgeability after dealer-state disclosure without idealizing the underlying subprotocols. An end-to-end Rust implementation benchmarks complete lifecycles across up to 1,280 participants on an EVM chain, demonstrating sub-second group recovery and practical gas costs.
papers.authors: Seunghyun Cho, Jaeyeon Lee, Myeongjun Kim, Hyunseok Jeong, Young-Sik Kim

papers.title: A note on zero-knowledge ring switching
papers.abstract: We make the ring-switching technique of Diamond and Posen zero knowledge, resolving a problem left open in the literature. Over $\mathbb{F}_{2^n}$, our technique uses $n-1$ auxiliary masks and $n-1$ quadratic constraints, checked in zero knowledge by the underlying commitment scheme.
papers.authors: Andrei Kochergin

papers.title: Leakage-Resilient Computation via Matrix Refreshing
papers.abstract: Leakage-resilient cryptography protects secrets against side-channel attacks, in which a physical implementation reveals partial information about its internal state. A fundamental primitive in this area is a leakage-resilient storage, which allows a secret to be stored in a way that remains secure even if an adversary learns some information about the storage's internal state. A popular approach represents a secret as the inner product of two $n$-bit vectors, called shares. The shares are stored and processed separately by two parts of the implementation, called the left and right parties. Because leakage accumulates over time, the shares must be refreshed repeatedly. We prove that a simple refresh, in which the left party multiplies its share by a uniform invertible matrix $M$ and the right party multiplies its share by $M^{-1}$, is secure under continual local leakage. After $T$ refreshes, each allowing at most $\lambda$ bits of leakage per party, the transcripts for two stored secrets are at statistical distance at most $C\cdot T\cdot 2^{6\lambda-n/9}$ for an absolute constant $C$. We also obtain a Boolean-circuit compiler with statistical privacy error at most $C\cdot S\cdot 2^{18\lambda-n/27}$ for $S$ operations and at most $\lambda$ bits of local leakage per party per operation. The guarantee covers repeated stateful evaluations with adaptively chosen public inputs, with $S$ counting all operations across invocations. Thus, for polynomial-size circuits, a constant leakage fraction is tolerated with share length depending only on the security parameter. We formalize the refreshing bound, the composition and compiler guarantees, and the expected-work bounds in Lean 4. Our results also provide efficient simulation: the leakage can be reproduced from the public inputs and the circuit outputs alone, with expected polynomial overhead.
papers.authors: Stefan Dziembowski, Sebastian Faust

papers.title: Perseus: A Full-Stack System for Homomorphic Model Inference
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have made it exceptionally convenient for users to send their private data to model providers, which process them in plaintext. Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) promises to secure remote inference by computing directly on encrypted data, yet it has remained prohibitively slow. The effort to make it practical remains fragmented, with most existing frameworks being closed-source, which keeps progress from compounding. We present Perseus, a free and open Python software library that supports the full stack of encrypted model inference, from the cryptographic backend and data packing, to encrypted nonlinearities and end-to-end model execution. Perseus ships with built-in novel optimizations, one at each level of the stack: in-kernel regeneration of key-switching keys at the (i) backend level, a complex variant of Cachemir packing at the (ii) data level, and a state-of-the-art bootstrap placer that is both packing- and magnitude-aware at the (iii) model level. Perseus achieves state-of-the-art latency across multiple models and modalities, within $3\%$ of the plaintext models' accuracy and perplexity. Remarkably, it is $3.96\times$ faster at single-token decoding than any other implementation on Llama-3-8B. We initiate, for the first time, a public speedrun on encrypted GPT-2, so that progress can compound.
papers.authors: Alessandro Zirilli, Davide Marincione, Evgenios M. Kornaropoulos, Giuseppe Ateniese, Emanuele Rodolà

papers.title: MuCPay: Breaking the Quadratic Bottleneck in Scriptless Multi-Party Oracle-Based Conditional Payments
papers.abstract: Oracle-based conditional payments triggered by real-world events support decentralized finance applications. However, dense independent bilateral deployments require $\Theta(Nn^2)$ outcome authorizations and $\Theta(n^2)$ settlement signatures for $n$ parties and $N$ outcomes. To go beyond two-party settings, we propose MuCPay, a multi-party oracle-based conditional payment protocol combining (i) $\Theta(Nn)$ off-chain signing shares with one on-chain settlement signature and (ii) BIP340-compatible scriptless settlement on Bitcoin. At its core, MuCPay introduces hash-bound adaptor multi-signatures (HB-AMS) that aggregate parties' conditional authorizations into a compact joint pre-signature. Its single-nonce structure and hash-bound adaptor integration enable efficient multi-party pre-signing. Unlike Double-Layer AMS (EuroS&P'26), HB-AMS produces a standard BIP340 signature under an aggregate public key, enabling direct Taproot key-path settlement. Under static corruption with one honest signer, we prove concurrent new-message unforgeability (CUF) and early-settlement resistance (ES) under our stated algebraic random-oracle model. For 128 parties and 16 outcomes, median complete local preparation takes 2.093 s. For protocol preparation (1.862 s for MuCPay), native-profile projections place VweTS (NDSS’23) and ParaSwap (USENIX’25) work at 1.67 × 10⁴ and 5.05 × 10⁵ times MuCPay's, respectively. Settlement uses one 64-byte signature, while the modeled independent-DLC deployment requires 281.5× as many transaction vbytes. These results demonstrate practical, scalable multi-party oracle-based conditional payments.
papers.authors: Yaning Wang, Na Wang, Chuan Li, Yongda Zhang, Junsong Fu

papers.title: Tight Depth Lower Bounds for Stretch Amplification
papers.abstract: We investigate the depth overhead of stretch-amplification for pseudorandom generators in the black-box model. We show that any black box construction of a PRG $H: \{0,1\}^m \to \{0,1\}^M$ which makes $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ queries to a PRG $G: \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}^N$ in $d$ adaptive phases during each evaluation (and with a black-box reduction to the security of $G$) must satisfy: $M \leq (m + O(\log n)) \Bigl( \frac{N}{n - O(\log n)} \Bigr)^d$. This implies that the standard amplification procedure [GM'84, GGM'86] based on repeated composition of $G$ is essentially optimal. In particular, amplifying $n \mapsto n+1$ to $m \mapsto 2m$ requires depth overhead $d = \Omega(\frac{n}{\log n})$, and amplifying $n \mapsto 2n$ to $m \mapsto m^2$ requires depth overhead $d = \Omega(\log n)$; each of these bounds is tight up to a constant factor. As an immediate corollary we obtain tight lower bounds on the depth complexity of black-box constructions of PRFs from PRGs. Both of these problems (pertaining to amplification and PRF construction) have been studied in various prior works [V'05, MV'11, BJP'11, MV'15, BMM'24, ADV'26]. Despite progress on special cases in which the structure of the reductions is constrained, it was previously unknown whether completely parallel constructions ($d=1$) existed in every stretch regime. The kinds of amplification procedures we investigate have more recently found use outside of cryptography in the study of range avoidance ("Avoid") [K'21]. We show an analogous result in this setting: any black-box $\mathrm{FP^{NP}}$ reduction from an Avoid instance $G: \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}^N$ to a second Avoid instance $H: \{0,1\}^m \to \{0,1\}^M$ which has "depth $d$" in the above sense must satisfy the same bound relating $n,N,m,M,d$. Using this impossibility result for Avoid, we construct an oracle relative to which $\mathrm{E} \not\subseteq \mathrm{NC}/\mathrm{poly}$ but $\mathrm{E^{NP}} \subseteq \mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}$. Our oracle separation implies that in the relativized setting, the bounded arithmetic theory $S^1_2$ cannot prove the existence of functions outside $\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}$, even given as an axiom the existence of functions outside $\mathrm{NC}/\mathrm{poly}$.
papers.authors: Oliver Korten

papers.title: Keyber: Recovering the Signal by Amplifying the Noise in ML-KEM
papers.abstract: ML-KEM (FIPS 203) is now being deployed in real-world applications to provide security against adversaries with quantum computers. Therefore, the resistance of ML-KEM’s implementations to physical attacks requires thorough evaluation. So far, fault attacks on ML-KEM have targeted the decapsulation operation. The key generation operation has received little attention from a fault-attack perspective. In this work, we present Keyber, the first statistical ineffective fault attack (SIFA) on the key generation of ML-KEM. Keyber is a key-recovery attack that needs only a single fault in key generation. The fault adds a known value to the error vector. Thus, the public key becomes faulty, while the seed of the public matrix remains intact. Every subsequent decapsulation, therefore, carries a known induced error. The adversary encapsulates locally and keeps only ciphertexts whose induced error peaks at exactly one coefficient. A decapsulation failure can then be attributed to that coefficient. Each query yields one linear inequality on the secret key, with no further faults. We observe that approximately 0.2-27% of encapsulations are usable for different parameter sets of ML-KEM. The full secret key is recovered using up to 30,000 inequalities across all security levels. We also realise the attack for ML-KEM-512 on an ARM Cortex-M4 device using a single over-clock fault. We then recover the entire secret key end-to-end. A single fault in this one-time operation thus compromises the key for its entire lifetime. Protecting ML-KEM, therefore, demands hardening not only decapsulation, but also key generation.
papers.authors: Vipin Kumar, Prathamesh Ram, Suparna Kundu, Dhiman Saha

papers.title: Reconciling Privacy with Provenance for Language Model Watermarks
papers.abstract: Watermarking has great potential for regulating the use of language models (LMs), but its deployment has been marred by controversy, as many users argue that fine-grained tracking of LM usage violates their privacy. This tension reduces the effectiveness of watermarks, as users engage in evasion strategies such as paraphrasing that can remove much of the watermark signal. We show that provenance and privacy can be reconciled if we shift the goal of watermark design from tracking individuals to estimating aggregate usage. We develop locally differentially private watermarks which provably limit the evidence that any individual text can contribute to detection, while still enabling accurate estimation of population frequencies. We introduce the Red-Green Sequence (RGS) watermark, a private and computationally efficient watermark that achieves accurate frequency estimation at high privacy levels across various models, sample sizes and generation entropies in settings that reflect realistic deployment scenarios. On C4 language modeling tasks, we attain $0.0019$ MSE with $0.0038$ mean absolute bias at a low $\varepsilon$ of 1, while in more challenging settings such as an essay writing task with only 100 text samples, we still find errors on the order of $0.0113$ MSE with $0.004$ mean absolute bias at $\varepsilon=2$.
papers.authors: Elise L. Han, Tatsunori Hashimoto

papers.title: Differentially Oblivious Graph Ball Queries
papers.abstract: A graph ball query returns all vertices within distance $r$ of a source vertex. On $N$-vertex graphs with maximum degree at most $\Delta$, ordinary breadth-first search answers such queries with $O_{\Delta,r}(1)$ record accesses. These accesses depend on private edges and can reveal graph structure. Full obliviousness hides this dependence, but incurs substantial overhead. Differential obliviousness (DO) [Chan et al., SODA'2019] trades off between privacy and efficiency by relaxing full obliviousness to $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy on the access traces of neighboring graphs. We study DO graph ball queries under three widely-adopted edge-level neighboring relations: add/delete, replacement, and $2$-switch. Starting from padded adjacency records, we charge all observable accesses, including preprocessing. For fixed $\Delta,r\ge2$, error probability $0<\beta<1/2$, and $0\le\delta\le(1-2\beta)/2$, we prove an $\Omega_{\Delta,r,\beta}(1+Ne^{-\varepsilon})$ expected lower bound at every sufficiently large connected graph and every public source. For every fixed $r\ge2$, we give $(\varepsilon,0)$-DO sampling algorithms with expected cost $O_{\Delta,r,\beta}(1+Ne^{-\varepsilon/C})$ using constant size of hidden workspace, where $C$ depends only on $\Delta,r$ and the neighboring relation. Especially, for $r=2$, we have $C=1$, which indicates that the algorithm achieves the tight bound under all three relations. Finally, we consider repeated queries on the same graph, where the cost of protected preprocessing can be amortized across queries. For fixed $\Delta,r,\beta$, we construct a linear-size reusable index with $(\varepsilon,0)$-DO preprocessing and constant query cost. The expected preprocessing cost is linear in $N$ when $\varepsilon$ exceeds a sufficiently large constant multiple of $\log N$.
papers.authors: Zimai Guo, Cheng Hong, Zhechen Li

papers.title: Quantum Key Exchange from Public Quantum Money
papers.abstract: Two-message quantum key exchange (2QKE) cannot be realized in a statistically secure way, and therefore some computational assumptions are required. So far, the known weakest assumption for 2QKE is the existence of one-way functions (OWFs). Can we construct 2QKE from a weaker assumption than OWFs? In this paper, we give the first complete characterization of 2QKE. We show that the following four primitives are (existentially) equivalent: everlasting-secure 2QKE, standard 2QKE, efficiently-verifiable state puzzles (EV-StatePuzzs), and one-time secure digital signatures with quantum signatures and signing keys. Because EV-StatePuzzs are potentially weaker than OWFs [Kretschmer, Qian and Tal 2025], the equivalence implies that 2QKE are potentially weaker than OWFs. Moreover, our result shows the equivalence between standard 2QKE and everlasting-secure 2QKE, which means that everlasting security comes for free. Finally, one-shot signatures, quantum lightning, and public-key quantum money mini-schemes imply EV-StatePuzzs, and therefore, our result also gives a new lowerbound, namely everlasting-secure 2QKE, of these public-key unclonable primitives. We also show that one-shot signatures imply QPKE with quantum public keys. [Kitagawa, Morimae,Nishimaki and Yamakawa, 2024] constructed QPKE with quantum public keys from OWFs, and it was open whether QPKE with quantum public keys can be constructed from an assumption weaker than or incomparable to OWFs. Our result gives a potential answer to this question since one-shot signatures seem to be incomparable with OWFs. Moreover, QPKE constructed from one-shot signatures has an additional functionality, which we call certified freeze, that allows the receiver to publish a publicly verifiable classical certificate that computationally binds the receiver to an upper bound on the total number of distinct valid ciphertexts under its verification key.
papers.authors: Eli Goldin, Tomoyuki Morimae

papers.title: Demystifying Information Flow Downgrading using the Real--Ideal Paradigm
papers.abstract: The real--ideal paradigm, an approach to security specification developed in the cryptography community, has the benefit that it can express sophisticated confidentiality and integrity requirements, even for decentralized systems. We show that this paradigm is the basis for a powerful and intuitive new semantic framework for language-based security. Our new framework cleanly and extensionally captures existing security definitions, including not only noninterference but also less understood information flow properties that involve downgrading, such as robust declassification and nonmalleable information flow. Past semantics for these properties have relied on intensional downgrading events. Further, we show that all of these properties can be enforced by a practical information-flow type system for a while-language that supports downgrading. Surprisingly, correctness of this type system is also characterized as a real--ideal simulation, with an important implication: the security of heterogeneous, decentralized systems with a strong (real) attacker can be understood by reasoning about a weak (ideal) attacker whose power is restricted to interaction with downgrading. This result explains the usefulness of nonmalleable information flow and related security properties. The results are fully formalized using the Rocq prover and are publicly available.
papers.authors: Suraaj Kanniwadi, Andrew C. Myers

papers.title: Practical Optimal Bucket Sets with Power-of-Two Radices for LFG-Based MSM Algorithms
papers.abstract: Fixed point multi-scalar multiplication (MSM) is a major computational component of pairing-based SNARK proof generation. The Luo--Fu--Gong (LFG) framework is a variant of Pippenger's bucket method that uses a multiplier set $M$ and precomputed point multiples to reduce the number of buckets and online point additions. For radix $q$ and a positive multiplier set $M$, covering all digit residues requires a bucket set of size at least $q/(2|M|)$. Previous constructions approaching this bound based on primitive roots or power-residue classes impose radix restrictions that exclude $q=2^c$, thereby requiring additional binary-to-radix conversion in software implementations. We present two main bucket set constructions for power-of-two radices $q=2^c$, using the multiplier sets $M=\{1,2,3\}$ and $M=\{1,3\}$, respectively. Their cardinalities are $q/6+O(\log q)$ and $q/4+2$, respectively, so both asymptotically attain the counting bound $q/(2|M|)$ while allowing efficient radix-digit extraction through shifts and masks. We further give two generalizations. Using consecutive powers of $3$ as multipliers yields bucket sets of size $q/(2\ell)+O(\log q)$ for every fixed positive integer $\ell$. For $\ell=2^d$ and $c\ge d+2$, consecutive odd multipliers yield bucket sets of size $q/(2\ell)+d+1$. We also present scalar conversion and two strategies for handling the leading digit, allowing the bucket set constructions to be used within the LFG framework.
papers.authors: Guiwen Luo

papers.title: Shielded Bitcoin: Private Transfers on the Bitcoin L1
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Shielded Bitcoin, a protocol for private transfer of Bitcoin directly on the Bitcoin L1, requiring no changes to Bitcoin consensus. Its design borrows from the architecture of Zcash and earlier shielded-note systems: value is held as encrypted notes, spends are marked by public nullifiers, and validity is established by zero-knowledge proofs. Unlike Zcash, Shielded Bitcoin introduces no dedicated consensus chain: all protocol data is published on Bitcoin, transfer validity is enforced through PIPEs v2 [ACG+26], and shielded state is reconstructed by deterministic replay of accepted transfers in Bitcoin order. At the metaprotocol transfer level, Shielded Bitcoin is non-custodial: spending authority remains with user-controlled wallet keys encrypted in a ciphertext, and neither indexers nor the replay layer receive authority to spend user notes. A shielded transfer does not publicly reveal its amount, sender, receiver, and place in the transfer graph, while keeping the validity of every encrypted state transition publicly verifiable. Shielded state, comprising the note tree, nullifier set, and block-level root history, is maintained entirely off-chain: any two correct implementations replaying the same Bitcoin history derive identical protocol state without coordination. The paper defines the transfer model, note structure, ciphertext-derived note leaves, nullifier rules, transaction binding, replay semantics, and publication assumptions. Peg-in and peg-out, the mechanisms by which value enters and exits the shielded transfer system, belong to the broader system and fall outside the scope of this paper.
papers.authors: Clara Shikhelman, Mikhail Komarov, Aleksei Moskvin

papers.title: Dual Coppersmith: Finding Small Roots Without Multivariate Polynomial Systems
papers.abstract: The multivariate Coppersmith algorithm is a central tool in public-key cryptanalysis for finding a small hidden root of modular polynomial equations. It consists of two stages. First, a lattice-reduction (LR) stage constructs auxiliary equations satisfied by the hidden root over $\mathbb Z$. Second, a root-recovery (RR) stage solves these equations. The RR stage can be a bottleneck: auxiliary polynomials may not isolate the root, and solving them can take exponential time in the worst case, even when LR is feasible. We introduce Dual Coppersmith, which replaces algebraic root recovery with geometric recovery from a modular orthogonal lattice. Our construction embeds the hidden root as a short lattice vector, and we prove that LLL recovers its direction whenever a sufficient gap separates it from all independent lattice vectors. The root can then be recovered directly from coordinate ratios. To analyze this gap, we propose a heuristic model for the second successive minimum by examining both the full lattice and a structured sublattice. Under this model, Dual Coppersmith achieves the standard Coppersmith product-size bound without solving an auxiliary polynomial system. Experiments on the approximate common divisor (ACD) and Herrmann-May (HM) problems support the model's predictions and demonstrate root recovery in higher-dimensional instances where the Gröbner-based baseline reaches its timeout.
papers.authors: Taehun Kang, Jebin Kim, Changmin Lee, JeongHwan Lee

papers.title: Cryptanalysis of MinRank 2.0
papers.abstract: MinRank is an NP-complete problem underlying the security of several post-quantum schemes. It is the hardness assumption of the NIST second-round signature candidate Mirath and of the encryption schemes of Chatterjee et al.\ and Debris-Alazard et al.\ at Eurocrypt 2026. Moreover, it is ubiquitous in the cryptanalysis of multivariate schemes, among them the third-round candidates UOV, MAYO, QR-UOV, and SNOVA. In this work, we revisit the attacks on MinRank. On the combinatorial side, we improve the polynomial part of the kernel-search attack by sharing its linear algebra across guesses, which lowers its cost by 3 to 6 bits on the Mirath parameters and the Courtois challenges, and by up to 3 bits in combination with the hybrid approach. With the improved attack, we solved Courtois challenge~D, open since 2001: an instance over $\mathbb{F}_2$ with $19 \times 19$ matrices, $81$ unknowns, and target rank $10$, solved in 11434 CPU days, an estimated $2^{61}$ bit opetations. Our multi-threaded C++ code is publicly available. On the algebraic side, we show that the complexity of the Kipnis--Shamir (KS) attack is less understood than the literature suggests: the existing estimates rely on a generic Hilbert series that does not predict the rank of the Macaulay matrices of the KS equations. We prove a lower bound on the corank that explains the discrepancy, show that the attack requires a reduced instance with $k \leq m - r$, and derive corrected complexity estimates, which are $1$ to $24$ bits above the best other attack on every Mirath parameter set. We also extend the Support-Minors and Minors modelings with the field equations, which lowers their estimates over small fields: for $q = 2$ and $m = n = 22$, by 9 to 205 bits for Support-Minors and by 17 to 278 bits for Minors. The rank predictions behind the algebraic estimates are stated as assumptions and verified experimentally.
papers.authors: Nicolas Aragon, Maxime Bros, Ray Perlner, Daniel Smith-Tone, Javier Verbel

papers.title: FixSampZ: A Fixed-Point Hardware-Efficient Discrete Gaussian Sampler for Falcon Signatures
papers.abstract: Falcon, a NIST-standardized post-quantum signature algorithm, offers compact signatures but relies on hardware-intensive floating-point arithmetic. Building on recent theoretical fixed-point formulations, we present a completely floating-point-free hardware architecture for SamplerZ, Falcon’s primary signing bottleneck. By utilizing zero-cost hardware bit-sliced retagging of fixed-point data, which software avoids due to instruction overheads, we enforce tighter data formats at every stage boundary without area or latency penalties. Furthermore, executing floor functions as trivial two's-complement arithmetic right shifts eliminates the complex floor-prediction and redundant data-paths required by floating-point designs. Implemented on UltraScale+ FPGA, our fixed-point sampler exactly matches all 1,024 official test vectors and requires 38% fewer LUTs, 21% less FFs and 36% less DSPs compared to the floating-point baseline, with 21% fewer cycles at a higher clock frequency. We also demonstrate that substituting the baseline ChaCha20 PRNG with lightweight NIST-standardized Ascon-XOF128 achieves further 2-3 × hardware resource savings with zero sampling latency overhead.
papers.authors: Pushpendra Singh, Akshara K B, Utsav Banerjee, Navin Kashyap

papers.title: Signed but Steerable: Measuring and Closing the Text-Vector Integrity Gap in Offline Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.abstract: Offline retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) on edge devices is updated through signed knowledge packs that carry text and precomputed embedding vectors. A signature proves who published a pack, not that its vectors encode its text. We study this text-vector integrity gap. A verifier that recomputes vectors and accepts them within a cosine tolerance concedes a predictable share of queries to an attacker who controls the vectors: the hijack rate equals the distribution of angular retrieval margins at the tolerance (the margin law). Margins are small in five corpora and two embedding models, so an idealised tolerance at the level of floating-point noise leaves up to 5.5% of queries exposed (at most 1.2% in any corpus once exact duplicate documents are excluded), and a threshold calibrated from our CPU INT8-FP32 comparison of a small embedding model (at the empirical 0.1% quantile of honest cosines) leaves 98-100% exposed; on a Raspberry Pi 5 running a local language model, such an attack lowers correct answers from 0.75 to 0.39. Integrity audits of compressed vector stores fare no better: on a FAISS product-quantisation index over 57,638 documents, tampered vectors that all pass the audit put the attacker's document first for 25% of targets. Verifying quantisation codes instead, with ambiguity decided by the verifier, a calibrated guard band and canonicalisation, accepted every honest vector in our samples on three platforms and left the publisher no choice. We also show that common floating-point and dynamic-INT8 inference pipelines are not bit-reproducible across batch sizes or architectures, and report pre-registered negative results on abstention, context pruning and semantic screening. We release code and data.
papers.authors: Georgios Feretzakis, Alexandros Papaspyridis

papers.title: PIMROP: A Feasibility Study of Return-Oriented Programming on Commercial Processing-in-Memory Architectures
papers.abstract: Processing-in-Memory places small programmable cores on the memory device, where they execute beside the DRAM banks and beyond the control-flow defenses that protect host programs. The security of this in-memory code is an attack surface that remains largely unstudied. We present PIMROP, to our knowledge the first demonstrated code-reuse attack on a commercial Processing in-Memory ISA. We show that return-oriented programming is feasible on a real, commercially shipped PIM instruction set, the UPMEM DPU, whose DRAM Processing Units run C compiled by a dedicated LLVM toolchain. We build Galileo-for-DPU, a gadget scanner adapted to the DPU's fixed-width, 8-byte-aligned RISC encoding, and run it entirely on the UPMEM functional simulator in a reproducible Docker and VM environment. We find the runtime library that every kernel links already yields 517 non-trivial gadgets covering all five canonical ROP primitive classes, and all 13 PrIM benchmarks we scanned carry gadgets as well. We then demonstrate two verified end-to-end attacks, each reproducible on 10 of 10 runs. In the first, a stack buffer overflow in a DPU kernel overwrites the saved return address and diverts control into a routine that copies a secret into host-readable memory. In the second, we leak the same secret using a chain of reused gadgets alone, without diverting control into any such routine. We further show that two standard defenses--stack canaries and _FORTIFY_SOURCE-style bounds-check fortification--fail on the DPU in ways specific to the platform (misplaced canary, silently inactive wrapper), and we verify a bounds-checked DMA that stops the attack on 10 of 10 runs with no effect on benign requests. To enable further research on PIM security, we open-source Galileo-for-DPU and our testing harness at https://github.com/wtegge2/ROP-in-PIM.
papers.authors: William C. Tegge, Shouzhi Fang, Alex K. Jones

papers.title: CoordX Protocol: Peer to Peer Cryptographically Verified Shared Records
papers.abstract: People, companies and software agents often must work on shared records even when they do not trust each other. Today they usually give those records to a central server. The server keeps the canonical copy, authenticates users, and decides who has permissions to act on the record. The CoordX Protocol removes the need for that central server. In the CoordX protocol the author of a record holds full permission over it. Permission for any other party to create, read or update the record is assigned by explicit grants and keys. An invitation only starts contact between two parties. It gives no permission. Each record is a causal tree of signed entries, and each entry is immutable. Each entry names the permission that allowed it. Any party can get the proof of that permission and check it without help from anyone. Two honest parties that check the same bytes, with the same keys and local settings, always get the same answer. The content is encrypted, so the relays that may carry it in transit see only sealed bytes. To exclude a party from future content, the other parties move to new keys. The protocol does not choose a winning version, does not put entries in time order, and does not need global agreement. Applications decide what the entries mean above the level of the protocol.
papers.authors: David Hyland-Wood, Rob Ewin

papers.title: GRIDSHIELD: Verifiable Grid Feasibility and Manipulation Resistance in Privacy-Preserving Peer-to-Peer Energy Trading
papers.abstract: Blockchain-based peer-to-peer (P2P) energy markets let neighbors trade directly, but concentrate unchecked power in the clearing operator. Most prior work addresses only part of this: network-aware clearing respects grid constraints but operates on plaintext allocations, while privacy-preserving designs hide bids yet either drop the network constraint, enforce it only inside an unauditable computation, or recover it at the cost of a per-circuit trusted setup. Neither considers what happens if an adversary captures the operator's clearing privilege to reorder trades for profit or curtail a rival. We present GRIDSHIELD, a P2P energy-trading system that clears sealed bids with an order-independent batch program, removing the welfare a compromised operator can extract by reordering trades, and proves the result grid-feasible via an aggregated congestion-feasibility proof (ACFP). Exploiting the additive homomorphism of Pedersen commitments, ACFP reconstructs each grid constraint directly from per-bus commitments, reducing feeder-wide feasibility verification over any public grid constraints to a single aggregated range proof over the hidden allocation, with a reveal-and-recompute challenge that catches feasible yet unfair clearings. We introduce congestion-responsibility fairness (CRF), a metric scoring curtailment against each party's physical responsibility for congestion rather than consumption. We evaluate GRIDSHIELD against three prior P2P energy-trading designs across four feeders, including a 240-node Midwest feeder with real hourly loads, on a live Hyperledger Fabric network benchmarked with Hyperledger Caliper. GRIDSHIELD proves an entire round feasible with a few-kilobyte proof and no trusted setup, rejects infeasible allocations two of the three compared designs accept, and sustains $\approx$1064 tx/s.
papers.authors: Abdullahil Kafi, Md Zahidul Islam, Alvi Ataur Khalil

papers.title: Private Vulnerability Testing for User Oversharing
papers.abstract: Users can inadvertently increase their vulnerability to privacy attacks by oversharing personal information. In particular, the combination of individually innocuous attributes can place a user in a sufficiently small population to enable linkage or re-identification attacks. We present a privacy-preserving mechanism that allows users to determine whether the information they disclose places them below a predefined population threshold, without revealing their query or the data of other users. Our setting presents several practical challenges: users contributing data may be offline when queries are made, queries may select arbitrary subsets of attributes, and neither server should learn the queried population or its size. We address these challenges using secret-shared data and queries, private equality testing, and secure threshold computation. Our protocol provides computational privacy against a malicious client and semi-honest, non-colluding servers, while supporting arbitrary queries and dynamic database updates. We define reactive $f$-privacy for a dynamically evolving database and prove that our construction satisfies it, with the sequence of permitted threshold outputs defining the information available to the adversary across an execution. We optimise the protocol using oblivious-transfer extensions and pre-computation, achieving sub-second online query times for 96-bit queries on datasets of up to one million records.
papers.authors: Alexander Boyd, Daniel Gardham, Nishanth Sastry, Suparna De

papers.title: Constraint-Aware Evaluation of Reinforcement Learning and Unsupervised Anomaly Detection for Security Operations Alert Triage
papers.abstract: Security Operations Centers (SOCs) must identify real threats from large alert streams, but limited analyst capacity means that unnecessary escalations can delay more serious investigations. Existing studies often frame SOC alert triage as classification or anomaly detection, but both views are incomplete for production SOCs, where the central problem is selecting alerts worth escalating under limited capacity, asymmetric error costs, and workload constraints. This paper addresses that gap by formalizing alert triage as a constrained decision problem and evaluating three approaches: an offline reinforcement learning policy trained on alert embeddings, an Isolation Forest model built on operational features, and an autoencoder trained on historical benign alerts. These methods represent different triage assumptions: learning actions from reward, isolating unusual operational patterns, and detecting deviations from benign behavior. We evaluate all methods on 74,909 analyst-labeled production alerts under a strict temporal split and benign-escalation constraint. Because the test set contains 503 unique feature patterns, we primarily rank clusters of similar alerts. At the main operating point, all three methods satisfy the constraint, with the reinforcement learning policy achieving the lowest benign-escalation fraction at 0.000, compared with 0.007 for the autoencoder and 0.041 for Isolation Forest. The methods also prioritize largely different alert clusters, showing complementary rather than redundant coverage. These results suggest that production SOC triage can benefit from constraint-aware evaluation and combined or adaptive deployment of different model families.
papers.authors: Radityo Ghifiardi, Rifny Rachman

papers.title: BASTION: Lock-Step, Staggered and Sequential Share Schedules for a First-Order Masked ML-KEM NTT on FPGA
papers.abstract: The Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) is the arithmetic core of ML-KEM (FIPS 203) and a prominent side-channel target in hardware. Because the transform is linear, first-order arithmetic masking applies share-wise without fresh randomness, which leaves one design decision open: when each share is processed. Published designs process the shares in sequence on one datapath, or on one datapath per share started a configurable delay apart and in random order; running both datapaths in lock-step is the third option. We implement the three schedules on one first-order masked NTT core for ML-KEM on Artix-7 and measure their cost and pre-silicon leakage under one synthesis flow. An iso-architectural unmasked control separates the cost of masking from that of parallelisation: the delivered lock-step core costs 1.56x the LUTs, 2.33x the slices and twice the DSPs of the control at an unchanged cycle count and 196.1 instead of 227.3 MHz, while the sequential core needs 9 LUTs more than the control at twice the cycles. We state when a set of samples combines both shares of a secret, measure the criterion on the RTL and use it as a cycle-accurate oracle. On a whole-design toggle model that sums both share domains, calibrated with injected flaws detected within 750 traces, no schedule leaks at first order in five pairs of runs of 10^5 traces. At second order the schedules form a scale: the lock-step core leaks in single samples, the sequential core only at the pair of samples that its public offset relates, and the staggered core in both ways at every delay we tested short of one transform. Every detected sample lies in the support view of the oracle, which flags up to 80% of the samples of a window for the univariate test, and some lie outside its form view, so lazy reduction matters. A check on the routed netlist finds no cell shared by the domains of the lock-step and staggered cores, and finds the cells that synthesis shares once the preservation attributes are removed. Silicon validation is left to future work.
papers.authors: Marcos Lázaro Díaz

papers.title: KVGuard: A KV Cache Safety Checker for LLM Serving Systems
papers.abstract: Modern LLM serving systems manage the KV cache through PagedAttention, a custom GPU allocator that partitions a single CUDA-allocated region into fixed-size physical blocks and maps each request to those blocks through a CPU-built block table. This block-based design exposes a previously unstudied class of memory safety bugs in the KV cache, including double-free, use-after-free, out-of-bounds access, uninitialized read, and permission violation, which silently corrupt outputs or break request isolation without ever crashing the system. Existing memory sanitizers cannot detect them, because they reason about CUDA-level addresses rather than KV cache blocks, requests, and block tables, and their redzone- and quarantine-based designs do not fit the scarce GPU memory budget of LLM serving. This paper presents KVGuard, the first systematic memory-safety abstraction for KV cache management in LLM serving systems. KVGuard maintains a compact shadow block for each physical KV block, recording per-request permission and per-entry initialization, and uses this metadata to perform five safety checks across the PagedAttention workflow, spanning CPU allocation, block table construction and translation, and GPU-side block table lookup and KV entry access. Each check fires at the boundary that introduced the violation, enabling early detection during development rather than reporting downstream output corruption many requests later. A prototype of KVGuard on vLLM and SGLang covers all 29 historical real-world KV cache safety bugs collected from the two systems' patch histories. KVGuard further found 8 previously unknown safety violations while reporting no false positives. It adds 3.0% and 7.4% geomean TPOT overhead on Qwen 2.5 14B on vLLM and SGLang and at most 0.11% of the KV cache in memory overhead, two orders of magnitude below NVIDIA Compute Sanitizer on the same workloads.
papers.authors: Jonguk Cheong, Myungbin Hwang, Eulgyu Kim, Byoungyoung Lee

papers.title: Fine-Grained Proof Complexity for Elementary Arithmetic in Extended Frege
papers.abstract: Proof complexity has historically focused on qualitative results, such as whether natural mathematical statements (e.g. the Pigeonhole Principle) admit polynomial-size proofs in certain proof systems (e.g. Resolution or Frege). In contrast to the rich theory of algorithm design, there is little understanding of how to design quantitatively efficient proofs. We initiate the study of fine-grained propositional proof complexity. Our motivation comes from an emerging line of cryptographic constructions such as the elegant work of Jain and Jin (2022), in which the efficiency of the resulting scheme is governed by the size of the underlying Extended Frege proofs. Our main result is that the basic laws of integer arithmetic —commutativity and associativity of addition and of multiplication, together with distributivity — admit Extended Frege proofs of quasi-linear size, when addition is implemented by the schoolbook algorithm and multiplication by an FFT-based algorithm. This seemingly elementary result turns out to be surprisingly non-trivial: the natural paper-and- pencil arguments for distributivity and for associativity of multiplication translate into Extended Frege proofs of quadratic size. To reach quasi-linear size, we develop a technique we call index generalization, which we believe will find wide application in the design of efficient propositional proofs.
papers.authors: Andrew Krapivin, Jiatu Li, Elaine Shi

papers.title: Affine Advantage in Guess-type Attacks on Goldreich’s PRGs: Generalization, Characterization and Countermeasures
papers.abstract: The recent guess-type attack (Eurocrypt'26) on Goldreich's pseudorandom generators exploits the strong bias toward constants that can arise when some inputs of majority-based predicates are fixed. This attack has demonstrated substantial effectiveness against several concrete parameter instances (Eurocrypt'24\&'25, Asiacrypt'24). In this paper, we generalize this attack paradigm to arbitrary affine approximations, characterize its capabilities, and develop a new predicate as a countermeasure. We introduce a guess-and-affine-approximation (GAA) attack framework that generalizes existing guess-type attacks from constant approximations to arbitrary affine approximations of residual nonlinear predicates. To characterize the capacity of GAA attack, we introduce the bit-fixing affine advantage $\operatorname{adv}_{b'}(M_b)$, defined as the maximum affine advantage of a $b$-ary nonlinear predicate $M_b$ over all residuals with $b'$ unfixed inputs. For polynomial stretch $m=n^s$ and logarithmic nonlinear arity $b=\gamma\log_2 n$, we obtain the optimal attack complexities $C^\star$ linking bit-fixing affine advantages: (1) $C^\star>2^{cn}$ for every $c<2^{-(s-1)/\gamma}$ iff $\operatorname{adv}_{\theta b}(M_b)\to 0$ for every constant $\theta\in(0,1]$; (2) $C^\star=2^{o(n)}$ iff fixing only $o(b)$ predicate inputs can yield a residual with affine advantage $\frac{1}{2}-o(1)$, and the sufficient direction also holds for $b=\Omega(\log n)$. In particular, if $\operatorname{adv}_{b-r}(M_b) =\frac12- O\left(\frac{\log n}{n}\right)$ for $r\le s-1$, then $C^\star$ can further decrease to $n^{O(1)}$. These results complement prior analyses for arities $O(1)$, $\omega(1)\cap O(\log n)$, and $\Omega(n^{1/s})$. Guided by the results above, we introduce the $\XOR_a$--$\MODtwelve_b$ family as a predicate candidate. We prove that every $b'$-input residual of its nonlinear component retains algebraic degree and algebraic immunity $\Theta(b')$, matching the asymptotic orders of $\MAJ$ (STOC'16). Moreover, its bit-fixing affine advantage is at most $2^{-\Omega(b')}$, whereas $\operatorname{adv}_{\theta b}(\MAJ_b)\approx \frac12$ for every fixed $\theta\in(0,1)$. Analysis shows that, for $n=1024$, $m=n^2$, and $b=54$, $\XOR$--$\MODtwelve$ can achieve $\log C^\star \approx 737$, while $\XOR$--$\MAJ$ and $\XOR$--$\MODthree$ have cost exponents of only $182$ and $599$, respectively, under the specified attack. Furthermore, our experiments show that $\MODtwelve$ offers stronger resistance to belief-propagation-based attacks.
papers.authors: Ximing Fu, Mo LI, Shihan Lyu

papers.title: Correlation Power Analysis on SHA-2-Based SLH-DSA
papers.abstract: The stateless hash-based digital signature algorithm (SLH-DSA) repeatedly processes a fixed secret seed with varying public addresses. This paper presents non-profiled correlation power analysis of the address-based pseudorandom function for all six SHA-2 parameter sets, using separate recovery paths through SHA-256 compression rounds and message-schedule expansion. The procedures account for the input layout in which a 22-byte compressed address precedes the secret seed. For the 256-bit sets, a two-stage joint procedure recovers two 16-bit secret portions. We evaluate an STM32F303 ARM Cortex-M4 implementation using 30 secret seeds and 5,000 measured power traces per seed for each evaluated condition. Each recovery stage is evaluated with the required preceding secret values supplied correctly; the reported rates are therefore conditional stage-wise results, not end-to-end seed recovery rates. Compression-round stages achieve 100% success under both forest-of-random-subsets and Winternitz one-time-signature-plus address conditions. Under forest-of-random-subsets addresses, all message-schedule stages achieve 100% success for the 128- and 192-bit sets. For both 256-bit variants, joint recovery achieves 100%, whereas recovery of message word $W_{12}$ achieves 66.7%; recovery of $W_7$ achieves 70.0% and 80.0% for the fast and small variants, respectively. An alternative first stage is also provided for 128-bit Winternitz one-time-signature-plus addresses. These results show that side-channel protection must cover both compression rounds and message-schedule expansion.
papers.authors: Jinwook Chang, Minjeong Lee, JIN YONG MIN, Dong-Guk Han

papers.title: Assurance-Conditioned Continuous Authorization for Autonomous AI Agents
papers.abstract: Autonomous software agents can act through tools, delegate work, and change their models or execution environments while earlier authorizations remain in flight. We present Assurance-Conditioned Continuous Authorization (ACCA), an approach designed to be harness-independent, for maintaining operational authority according to currently justified assurance. It distinguishes evidence validity from contextual applicability, derives assurance claims from eligible evidence, and resolves a multidimensional effective-authority envelope within a principal-declared ceiling and applicable policy. A typed dependency graph supports selective re-evaluation of authorization-relevant changes. An authority epoch changes when effective authority changes; a distinct optional authorization-basis version supports revalidation of action-specific authorization conditions. Protected effect-time enforcement can reject stale actions before a consequential resource change, subject to the available commit mechanism. A compositional Domain Governance Profile expresses domain-specific semantics without granting authority. Controlled scenario tests implemented as a regression suite using a trading profile exercise default-deny rules, evidence-conditioned contraction and recovery, policy divergence, selective non-response, and stale-action rejection at a local gateway before the simulated-broker boundary. The study establishes implementation-level evidence in one domain, not a cross-domain guarantee of harmful-behavior prevention.
papers.authors: Mehdi Shajari

papers.title: Optimal Marginal Mixing for Transvection-Based Trapdoored Matrices over Large Fields
papers.abstract: \emph{Trapdoored matrices} are pseudorandom matrices admitting a fast matrix-vector multiplication algorithm given the secret key. We study a candidate family of such matrices: matrices generated by short random \emph{transvection walks} on \(\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{F}_q)\), whose steps are given by adding a random multiple of a random row of the current state to another. We show that the worst-case time for any nonempty set \(\mathcal{S}\subseteq [n]\times[n]\) of matrix entries to come within TV distance \(\varepsilon\leq \frac{1}{4}\) of its stationary marginal under this walk is \(Θ(|\mathcal{S}|+n\log(n/\varepsilon))\), uniformly over all \(\mathcal{S}\) and \(q\geq Q_\mathrm{all}(n)\). This is asymptotically optimal, and resolves open questions about the mixing times of transvection walks. We derive concrete upper and lower bounds for \(n\geq 256\). Surprisingly, our bounds also hold conditioned on the row-pair structure of the walk, except on a fraction at most \(\varepsilon\) of such structures. This implies that these walks may be pseudorandom even after conditioning on the row-pair structure, and therefore that trapdoored matrices built with these walks may be universal. Assuming the conjectured structure-conditioned pseudorandomness of short walks, we exhibit highly efficient, highly parallelizable, and universal trapdoored matrices over \(\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{F}_q)\), \(\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{F}_q)\), and \(\mathbb{F}_q^{n\times n}\). The families over \(\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{F}_q)\) and \(\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{F}_q)\) admit equally efficient trapdoors for their inverses, making them the first to do so for finite-field trapdoored matrices. We discuss attacks, analyzing one in detail, and lay out directions for further investigation.
papers.authors: Mark Braverman, Aayush Jain, Stephen Newman

papers.title: Differential Cryptanalysis of SPEEDY: Revised Security Evaluation and Improved Key Recovery Attack
papers.abstract: The resistance of a block cipher against differential cryptanalysis (DC) is a fundamental criterion for evaluating its security. SPEEDY is a family of low-latency SPS-type block ciphers designed by Leander et al. The designers presented two evaluations of SPEEDY against DC: the first restricted 1-bit-to-1-bit differential propagations through the S-box and used the higher-order branch numbers to estimate the maximum expected differential probability (EDP) of differential trails; the second imposed a structural restriction and assumed that all 1-bit-to-1-bit propagations through an active S-box are possible to estimate the minimum number of active S-boxes. Zhang later exhibited a counterexample to the designers' first evaluation and introduced the notion of partition branch number, relaxing some of the propagation restrictions to allow multi-bit-to-1-bit transitions on some S-box layers and refining the evaluation. However, these evaluations consider only restricted spaces of differential characteristics and therefore inaccurately estimate the security of SPEEDY against DC, which means that the resistance of SPEEDY against DC remains unclear so far. To address this problem, we propose an efficient search method based on search patterns. Unlike previous evaluations, our method imposes no a priori structural restrictions on the allowed differential characteristics; it uses computational pruning to keep the search tractable and performs a conservative security evaluation of the pruned region, thereby providing an accurate evaluation over the global space. At the framework level, we decompose an r-round differential characteristic into an (r-1)-round core trail and an r-round extended trail. By extending a core trail independently at both ends, the two additional S-box layers are handled by two separate models, each containing only one S-box layer and solvable efficiently. At the implementation level, we further introduce a short-round reuse via hash-map concatenation technique, which concatenates short-round core trails to construct longer-round core trails, thereby avoiding expensive long-round MILP models. For 4 rounds, we narrow the minimum number of active S-boxes from the previously reported 35 to [33,34] and find a characteristic with 34 active S-boxes outside the previous search spaces. We also obtain the highest-probability differential characteristics known to date for 2 to 5 rounds. In particular, the 2-, 3-, and 4-round characteristics disprove the designers' branch-number-based security claims. Furthermore, using the quasidifferential framework, we evaluate the found characteristics and obtain several 5-round distinguishers outperforming those used in existing key recovery attacks in terms of EDP. Finally, we optimize the probabilistic extension parameters used in a previous key recovery attack, which yields the best known key recovery attack on SPEEDY-7-192, with data complexity $2^{173.48}$ and time complexity $2^{173.69}$ encryptions.
papers.authors: Xinwei Yu, Wentao Zhang, Zairui Zhang, Chunning Zhou

papers.title: Differentially $2^t$-uniform quadrinomials with high nonlinearity
papers.abstract: In this paper, we discuss some cryptographic properties of a family of quadrinomials constructed as a generalization of a known family of APN quadrinomials. In particular, we show that this family produces differentially $2^t$-uniform quadrinomials with the same Walsh spectrum as the Gold power function $x^{2^t+1}$ over $\mathbb{F}_{2^n}$. We also discuss whether this family provides permutations.
papers.authors: Niki Spithaki, Enrico Piccione, Lilya Budaghyan, Alexander Kholosha

papers.title: The Fairest of Them All: Best-of-Both-Worlds Fair Leader Election
papers.abstract: Fair leader election is the problem of sampling an unbiased random party out of a set of $n$ parties. The seminal impossibility result of Cleve (STOC 1986) applies to this setting, and shows that the result of the election cannot be unbiased against a dishonest majority. Recent work has achieved the weaker property of game-theoretic fairness, where behaving dishonestly cannot improve one’s chances of being elected. However, such protocols allow even a single corrupt party to bias the outcome. In this work, we introduce best-of-both-worlds (BoBW) fairness, where a small number $t_S$ of corrupt parties cannot bias the result, and even a larger number $t_{GT}$ of corrupt parties still cannot improve their collective election chances (CSP-fairness) nor hurt the election chances of any given honest party (MM-fairness). We present a protocol for BoBW fair leader election for $t_S + t_{GT} < n$. We then prove a generalization of Cleve’s impossibility, and show that this protocol is optimal. Next, in the setting of statistical security we find that BoBW fairness is uninteresting, as it is only possible for an honest majority, where we can get also unbiased leader election. Finally, in the setting of perfect security, we present a BoBW protocol achieving CSP-fairness and strong fairness for $t_S + 1 = t_{CSP} = \frac{n}{3}$, and prove that this is also optimal.
papers.authors: Chen-Da Liu-Zhang, Elisaweta Masserova, Kelsey Melissaris, Lawrence Roy, Sophia Yakoubov

papers.title: PS-BKZ: Decoupling Outer Propagation and Local Processing in BKZ by Parameter Separation
papers.abstract: This work provides a systematic study of parameter separation in Block Korkine–Zolotarev (BKZ) reduction. We propose a general framework with separate parameters for outer propagation and the dominant local computation. The framework covers the local parameter settings of standard BKZ and variants using extended preprocessing, dimensions for free, or progressive sieving, with corresponding adaptations to the outer operations. This allows less expensive local processing without narrowing the outer propagation range. Within this framework, we give idealized and executable constructions that use inner BKZ with a smaller blocksize to supply local vectors for larger outer blocks. We derive a worst-case quality bound for the idealized construction and analyze its quality–cost behavior using a practical fixed-point model. Experiments on the executable construction cover random q-ary bases up to dimension 300 and SVP Challenge bases up to dimension 240. The detailed comparisons at n ≥ 200 show lower mean root-Hermite factors (RHFs) and 14.1%–59.3% shorter mean running times than BKZ 2.0. Joint improvements generally become more frequent with dimension. On q-ary inputs against BKZ 2.0 with blocksize 50, their frequency increases from 15.56% at n = 150 to 73.33% at n = 300.
papers.authors: Hutao Song, Hua Guo, Yang Sun, Fengju Gao, Zongyang Zhang, Qianhong Wu

papers.title: Integrated Identity Protection for Semantic Communications in Embodied IoT Systems
papers.abstract: Embodied Internet of Things (IoT) systems are promoting the adoption of task-oriented semantic communication (SemCom), in which the trustworthy task decisions increasingly require both semantic reliability and source legitimacy. However, existing trustworthy SemCom designs mainly focus on semantic content recovery and protection, with limited attention to source identity protection. Motivated by this limitation, this paper establishes a new information exploitation perspective for integrated SemCom-identity protection that leverages task-level error tolerance to coordinate semantic information and source identity information carried by the same waveform. We first examine these two information resources and then analyze their integration feasibility at the observation, processing, and decision levels. To exploit these resources for different identity protection objectives, we further develop a dual-branch identity protection mechanism with two operating modes. In the authentication mode, semantic recovery and physical-layer source verification are performed in parallel using the same received observation. In the concealment mode, identity exposure is suppressed while semantic reconstruction quality is maintained to support anonymous transmission. Finally, two representative case studies on active source impersonation and passive identity inference are presented to evaluate the proposed framework.
papers.authors: Yu Zhang, JingQi Liu, Shuangrui Zhao, Yuanyu Zhang, Yulong Shen, Xiaohong Jiang

papers.title: Signed, Sealed, Leaked: Trust Beyond Signature for MCP Toolchains
papers.abstract: AI agents rely on third-party tools, such as Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, whose publishers can be authenticated and whose execution can be restricted by runtime security policies. Yet authenticity does not guarantee benign behaviour: a legitimately signed tool may perform its advertised function while concealing malicious code that leaks confidential information. We demonstrate this trust failure with a signed MCP tool that embeds sensitive data in requests to a policy-allowed destination. Meta's MCPGuard-Dynamic, a state-of-the-art runtime defence, blocks a direct exfiltration attempt in the same run, yet fails to prevent this attack in every trial. We introduce germline execution, which limits information disclosure without inspecting or trusting tool implementations. Each tool invocation runs in ephemeral copies forked from a data-free germline process, each receiving only information authorised for its destination. Even if malicious code executes, what it can disclose is bounded by the data available to its copy. Under explicit assumptions on copy confinement and a data-free germline, we prove sink noninterference for every signed release and, for releases deterministic within our replay model, show that a verified witness establishes a flow violation. Across 153 attack runs, no unauthorised disclosure was detected under germline execution, compared with 5.9-74.5% of runs under baseline defences and an ablation. Invocations served by a single copy completed in 10-49 ms, 2-28x faster than restarting the tool for every invocation, the conventional way to clear state. These results show that data-isolated execution protects agent toolchains against malicious code concealed within authenticated software.
papers.authors: Yichiet Aun, Mohammed A. Alhartomi, Jing Jie Tan, Waqas Nadeem, Adeb Salh, Shankar Karuppayah, Sin Chee Tan

papers.title: On Key Recovery from Exposed Neural XOR Activations in DES and TDES
papers.abstract: We study the security of natural ReLU realizations of the Data Encryption Standard (DES) and two-key Triple DES (TDES) when an adversary can submit non-binary inputs and observe selected intermediate neural values. The attack exploits the piecewise-linear extension of XOR: paired inputs that differ in one expanded right-half bit reveal the corresponding round-key bit from the change in a natural XOR node. For DES, the resulting 48-bit first-round subkey leaves only the eight key-schedule bits omitted by PC-2; enumerating these bits and checking an intermediate value recovers the 56-bit effective master key. For two-key EDE TDES, the same technique recovers the first encryption subkey of K_1 and the last DES subkey used by the middle decryption under K_2; two independent 2^8 completions then recover the full 112-bit key pair. The exposed round subkey is recovered with a constant number of leakage observations per bit, giving query complexity linear in the targeted subkey length; the remaining searches are fixed-size for DES. Python experiments report exact recovery for 1,000 random DES keys and 1,000 random two-key TDES key pairs. These results concern a synthetic intermediate-oracle model for natural neural implementations and do not claim a physical attack on conventional DES/TDES hardware or software.
papers.authors: Kwangjo Kim

papers.title: A Bag of Tricks for Defending Deep Learning-based Face Recognition Pipelines against Backdoor Attacks
papers.abstract: The protection of mature, multi-stage Face Recognition Systems is crucial to system providers. This technical report targets the threat model most relevant to industry practitioners: although model training is performed in-house, training data is sourced from possibly-compromised third parties. Given this setting, we present three practical defense "tricks" against data poisoning-based backdoor attacks. The first operates at training-time, detecting poisoned identities during training or prior to a pipeline's deployment. The last two operate at inference-time, filtering suspicious inputs before an answer can be sent back to a potential attacker. Each method is presented with their motivation, algorithms and computational impact, and evaluated on realistic face recognition workloads. Our goal is to provide actionable hardening techniques to system providers.
papers.authors: Quentin Le Roux, Marti Jimenez, Yannick Teglia, Philippe Loubet Moundi

papers.title: Shoot on (Core)Sight: Re-enabling Secure Debug on the RP2350 with Photon-Emission Microscopy and Laser Fault Injection
papers.abstract: Fault-resistant policy storage does not guarantee fault-resistant enforcement. We demonstrated this distinction on the RP2350A4 using differential photon-emission microscopy (PEM) and laser fault injection (LFI). PEM narrowed the area for laser scanning, which found two sites where pulses set the DEBUGEN bits enabling core~1 Secure debug. An online attack sequence using only Serial Wire Debug (SWD) feedback restored sustained access. After rescue reset, the sequence recovered a 128-bit test secret. This reset reloads the secret's runtime page lock from a stored policy that permits Secure reads and prevents user firmware from tightening the lock.
papers.authors: Antoine Plin

papers.title: CoRTeC: A Differentially Private Release for Synthetic Tabular Data, Decodable by Any Generator
papers.abstract: The records that could train the most useful models, such as a hospital's patient files, are often the ones an institution cannot share. We propose CoRTeC, a method that releases synthetic versions of such records under differential privacy. Differential privacy places a proven limit on what the synthetic data can reveal about any person, and in particular on membership inference. CoRTeC spends the privacy budget once, on a small file of noisy counts designed for training a classifier. For each group of records, the file gives the group's size, its balance of outcomes, a histogram of every column for each outcome and the outcome rate in each of several non-overlapping cells. A reviewer can check every number before the file leaves the institution. Anyone can then turn the counts into synthetic rows, as often as they like and at no further privacy cost. A maximum-entropy decoder can do this without any language model, and so can each of the five frozen language models we tested. None of them ever sees a real record. A selection step then matches the rows to the released counts. Decoded without a language model, the automatically configured release at $\varepsilon = 2$ trains classifiers to within 0.02 AUC of a real sample of the same size on the Adult dataset, across three data splits. On NHANES and bank marketing, without the selection step, it stays within 0.05 AUC. On Adult, with a fixed cohort rule, the release carries the outcome rates a deployment names more closely than a real sample does, at some cost in accuracy on pairs of columns. Four controls show that most of the utility comes from the release and the selection step, and that a language model adds what it knows from the column names. No private row ever reaches a model, and no row CoRTeC generates copies a real one. The strongest membership attack stays far below the bound the budget allows.
papers.authors: Calister Nnona

papers.title: A.S.E 2.0: Understanding How Repository Context Impacts the Security of LLM-Generated Code
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding assistants and agents construct a repository context before generating code. For security-sensitive code, this context decides whether the model sees the project's safeguards (e.g., authorization checks) or insecure code to imitate. However, context construction is designed almost exclusively for functional correctness, and secure-code benchmarks treat the context as fixed, so how repository context affects the security of generated code remains unclear. We construct CASE-Bench, a benchmark of 145 repository-level tasks from real CVEs in 51 projects. Each task runs in Docker, has functional tests and a proof-of-concept exploit validated in both directions, and is annotated with the repository code that enforces or undermines its security. Using CASE-Bench, we compare 13 context construction methods and six controls with six LLMs, edit single context elements, and analyze coding-agent trajectories. We find that (1) functionality-oriented context raises the functional pass rate by up to 8.2 percentage points (pp) but the secure pass rate by at most 3.7 pp, (2) withholding a safeguard lowers the secure pass rate by up to 8.1 pp, while one inserted insecure exemplar raises correct-but-exploitable code by 6.3 pp, and (3) coding agents observe the relevant safeguard in only 27-36% of trajectories. These findings inform security-aware context construction and secure-code evaluation.
papers.authors: Jiongchi Yu, Keke Lian, Junqing Wang, Zhikang Fan, Zhaoxuan Li, Yongheng Huang, Ziming Zhao, Dong Zhang

papers.title: Beyond Identity Creation: Bilinear Sybil Cost in Identities and Time
papers.abstract: Sybil defenses price the creation of an identity, yet influence goes, again and again, to active identities. We study the cost of maintaining influence. A defense has a bilinear Sybil cost with ratio $A$ if keeping $s$ identities active for $T$ periods costs at least $sT/A$ honest units: the average cost per identity-window is at least $1/A$ times an honest participant's cost. Recurrence alone does not guarantee this cost. The cost can be carried over from earlier periods, shared among many identities, or be negligible when fast hardware does the work of thousands of honest devices. We give four sufficient conditions for a defense that checks every identity each period to achieve bilinear Sybil cost: identity binding, freshness, a shared deadline, and sequential, non-batchable work. They yield two guarantees: a bilinear total cost, with $A$ the speed advantage of the adversary's fastest hardware, and, because the work must be fresh and finished by a common deadline, a bound on the identities active in a period by the processors running at that time. We prove that none of the four follows from the other three. A verifiable delay function on an identity-bound input meets all four without payments, with $A$ of 2 to 8 for CPUs and about 28 for a hypothetical ASIC, against $10^3$ to $10^7$ for hash puzzles. We measure one active identity per core per period against about 80,000 under a signed heartbeat, no gain from batching up to 1,000 identities, and rejection of all tested attacks.
papers.authors: Homayoun Maleki, Nekane Sainz, Jon Legarda, Igor Santos-Grueiro

papers.title: Explainable Anomaly Detection in 5G Networks through Continuous Time Graphs
papers.abstract: 5G networks increasingly resemble distributed systems in their design. It then becomes crucial to move beyond traditional network-based detection methods and to explore alternative approaches. In this work, we propose a formalization of 5G network exchanges as a dynamic graph, on which we apply techniques from the field of graph-based learning to detect anomalies effectively. This representation allows for fine-grained analysis of packet-level semantic content, while simultaneously capturing sequential and topological contexts, both of which are essential for identifying sophisticated and multi-stage attacks. To assess the effectiveness of this formalism, we evaluate it with the most popular dynamic graph models, demonstrating its potential for 5G anomaly detection.
papers.authors: Thomas Hoger, Philippe Owezarski

papers.title: Beyond the Landing Page: Website Blocking, Tracker Visibility, and Human Alignment in Automated Web Crawls
papers.abstract: Web tracking studies largely rely on automated crawlers, yet their measurements can differ from what people encounter while browsing. Conventional crawlers follow predefined navigation rules, whereas LLM-driven agents decide how to navigate and interact with websites, potentially changing the tracking they encounter. We compare agentic and non-agentic crawlers to examine how websites respond to them, what tracking they record, and how closely their observations match human browsing. Across 2,000 popular websites, we evaluate different navigation strategies, automation frameworks, and stealth configurations, alongside browsing data from 26 participants. We find that website denials increase beyond landing pages for standard browser automation, while a detection-resistant automation framework largely prevents this escalation without increasing recorded tracking. On the same URLs, agentic crawlers record tracking activity from 1.5-1.7 times as many third-party organizations, particularly on consent-managed pages. Agentic crawlers recover 82-87% of tracker organizations observed by participants, compared with 58-68% for non-agentic crawlers, yet roughly half of their own observations are absent from human participant visits. These findings show that avoiding website interventions, increasing tracking visibility, and achieving closer agreement with human observations do not necessarily go hand in hand, highlighting the need to select and validate crawlers according to the measurement objective.
papers.authors: A H M Nazmus Sakib, Mahsin Bin Akram, Raveen Wijewickrama, Igor Bilogrevic, Murtuza Jadliwala

papers.title: Catastrophic Overfitting is Weight Drift the Training Loss Cannot See
papers.abstract: Fast adversarial training (FAT) makes robust training affordable by replacing the multi-step attack with a single-step one, but it suffers from catastrophic overfitting (CO): partway through training, robustness to multi-step attacks collapses to near zero while the single-step attack used for training keeps being repelled. We show that CO is a quiet escape of the weights. Across the event the network's clean behavior quietly improves, and moving from the weights just before CO to those just after it changes the training objective only marginally while destroying most of the robustness. The training objective is therefore nearly blind to the displacement it causes, so it exerts no force to undo it. The exponential moving average (EMA) of the weights, which FAT protocols already maintain, does not accumulate this drift and stays robust through the entire event. This observation suggests a nearly free fix: when validation robustness drops, reset the weights to their EMA. We build this guard on top of a coupling-based base method designed so that its average stays inside the robust region. The resulting training removes CO in every one of our runs and attains the strongest AutoAttack accuracy among fast methods on all three benchmark datasets, including a clear margin on CIFAR-100, where it also clears the multi-step reference at roughly half its cost. Code is available at https://github.com/fzjcdt/co-weight-drift.
papers.authors: Chao Pan

papers.title: Enforcing Accountable Disclosure in Confidential AI
papers.abstract: Advances in CPU and GPU confidential computing enable confidential AI, allowing LLMs to process user prompts without exposing them to service providers or infrastructure operators. However, AI agents often need to send prompt-derived information to external services, and providers may also require limited disclosure for safety monitoring and failure diagnosis. We propose CORDE, a system for confidential virtual machines (CVMs) designed to satisfy the principle of Confine or Declare: user-derived data is confined by default, but when necessary, it may leave the CVM only after being "declared." To "declare" data is to record its exact contents, recipient, and stated reason in a user-accessible, tamper-evident declaration log. To put this principle into practice, we present an integrated system design that combines per-user information-flow control in Rust with a TEE-based ledger and remote attestation. Our evaluation on an NVIDIA H100 GPU shows that declaration before disclosure adds little overhead in task latency, about 0.5% on the AppWorld agent benchmark. CORDE provides a basis for accountable disclosure of user data, supporting responsible and transparent data management in AI services.
papers.authors: Shumpei Shiina, Haruka Takahashi, Kento Sasaki, Takuya Hayashi, Tsubasa Takahashi

papers.title: A Hybrid Approach for Automated Security Pattern Recovery
papers.abstract: Security-by-design emphasises integrating security into software design and development. Security pattern catalogues operationalise this principle by prescribing reusable architectural solutions to recurring security problems. However, recovering their implementations from source code remains challenging because security patterns are abstract, span multiple components, and admit many valid implementations. We present SecPatRec, a hybrid approach for automated security pattern recovery from source code repositories.
