We treat a security pattern as a reference architecture and frame its recovery as a deductive task: determining which prescribed roles are present, grounding them in code entities, and recovering their interaction sequences. SecPatRec pairs a ReAct-style LLM agent equipped with semantic and lexical code search for role detection and grounding with static code property graph analysis for interaction recovery. We curate a human-validated ground-truth dataset of 100 pattern instances covering five security patterns across 93 open-source Java and Python repositories, and introduce a three-level evaluation framework measuring recovery correctness against this ground truth. We evaluate SecPatRec using four LLMs, including proprietary and open-source models. Averaged over all models and pattern instances, SecPatRec achieves role-detection accuracy of 0.84, role-grounding similarity of 0.84, and an interaction-recovery score of 0.66. Compared to a one-shot end-to-end LLM baseline, SecPatRec achieves higher aggregate recovery scores and lower estimated LLM API costs per run, while processing repositories that exceed the baseline's configured input limit. The recovered role mappings and statically derived interaction sequences provide structural and behavioural evidence that can support inspection of security-pattern implementations.
papers.authors: Anh Minh Nguyen, Tuan Dat Tran, Alzubair Hassan, Liliana Pasquale

papers.title: When File Ingestion Misleads Language Models: Measuring and Mitigating Divergences in Office Documents
papers.abstract: Office documents are now routinely uploaded to large language models (LLMs) for processing. However, an LLM does not always see what a human sees, because it typically reads the text that an extractor produces from the document's underlying Office Open XML (OOXML) files. Depending on the implementation, extractors differ in which OOXML parts they read and how they interpret them, so their output can differ from what Office applications display. For example, by slightly shifting the positions of text boxes on a slide, an adversary can swap the order in which the model reads them while the slide looks unchanged. We show that this extraction divergence is an attack surface for LLM applications. In this work, we first measure what an adversary can exploit by analyzing the widely used extractors that LLM applications rely on. By combining static source code analysis with dynamic analysis, we identify 19 OOXML channels where extractors read content a human cannot see and 12 where they drop content a human can. We also find that widely used extractors ignore display formatting and reading order, so even visible content reaches the model in a different form. Building on these findings, we construct five attacks that lead the model to interpret a document differently from a human reviewer, without injecting any instruction. We test the attacks on four major chat assistants (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Microsoft 365 Copilot) and four coding agents (Codex, Claude Code, Antigravity, and GitHub Copilot CLI), and every one of them is misled by at least one attack. Finally, we propose Prism, a lightweight defense that reconstructs the human view from the OOXML specification before passing the text to the model. Prism also generalizes to unseen attack payloads.
papers.authors: Penghui Li

papers.title: Timing is Everything: Inferring Temporal Membership in Continually Updated Models
papers.abstract: Continual model updating has become a common practice in the deployment of machine learning systems. However, the dynamic training behaviors give rise to new risks not sufficiently addressed by existing studies. In this paper, we present the first systematic study of temporal privacy risk in continually updated deep learning models. We formalize the notion of temporal membership in continually updated models. We then define the temporal membership inference attack, which seeks to infer whether and when individual samples were involved in model training, at both timestamp-level and interval-level granularities. To this end, we propose TMIA, a novel black-box attack that leverages bidirectional LSTMs to infer temporal membership from model outputs observed across successive updates. Through extensive experiments on three language models and three image classification models, we show that TMIA is highly effective and significantly outperforms existing baselines. Finally, we evaluate three potential defenses, revealing the trade-off between privacy protection and model utility.
papers.authors: Jie Fu, Xiangpeng Deng, Yuan Hong, Wendy Hui Wang

papers.title: AQUA - A Modular Authentication Quality Modeling Framework
papers.abstract: Authentication solutions are the key design, architectural, and implementation decisions that implement authentication security controls. An example is a password-based authentication solution. While researchers often examine authentication quality, existing approaches do not distinguish which effects on quality stem from which aspect of authentication. For example, multi-factor authentication solutions tend to be less usable because they combine multiple authenticators, whereas passkeys are more secure than passwords because of properties inherent to the authenticator itself. This paper presents AQUA, a modular quality modeling framework for authentication solutions. AQUA's core idea is to decompose authentication into four interrelated concepts, enabling modular specification of authentication quality and tracing quality effects back to their source. We demonstrate AQUA with initial definitional quality models that address the levels of authenticators, authentication techniques, and authentication solutions. We further illustrate the interrelations between these concepts through concrete examples and a usability metric, showing how quality propagates across the concepts and ultimately affects the overall quality of an authentication solution. Our results provide a foundation for future work, including designing assessment and prediction models for authentication solutions and automated quality assessments.
papers.authors: Alex R. Mattukat, Michael Zerbe, Krisa Carka

papers.title: Exploring the Privacy--Size Tradeoff for Differentially Private Self-Attentive Variational Autoencoders
papers.abstract: Data tends to be most useful when it is shared, and the data most worth sharing is often the data that privacy obligations restrict. Synthetic data from a generator trained under differential privacy (DP) is one way to reconcile the two, but its utility depends on the privacy budget $\varepsilon$ and on how much data the generator sees - a parameter that most data sharing applications of synthetic data control. We present SAVANT, a self-attentive variational autoencoder for tabular data trained with DP-SGD that, to our knowledge, is the first to combine attention, a VAE, and DP in one tabular model. We evaluate it against two marginal mechanisms, PrivBayes and MST, jointly over the privacy budget and the dataset size on two public datasets, measuring the utility a downstream classifier loses by training on synthetic rather than real data. We find that, under the same DP guarantee, more data generally means more utility. For the marginal mechanisms it absorbs most of what a strict budget costs, and a noise-scaling argument suggests DP-SGD exchanges data fo budget at a worse rate. Two independent membership-inference attacks, judged against a measured null, found no aggregate membership signal.
papers.authors: Rohit Sadavarte, Dhruvi Kothari, Sparsh Gupta, Eric Van Oeveren

papers.title: Phantom Timing Leaks on Cortex-M4: A Pre-registered Evaluation of ML-KEM Decapsulation
papers.abstract: Fixed-versus-random timing tests in the style of dudect are a cheap first check of constant-time behaviour, and on microcontrollers the cycle counter makes them exact to the cycle. We report a pre-registered evaluation of ML-KEM decapsulation on an STM32F411 (Cortex-M4) covering nine implementations of PQM4 (clean, m4fspeed, m4fstack for ML-KEM-512/768/1024) and a positive control in which we restored the pre-KyberSlash division formulas. Each of the 44 campaigns used in the analysis has 100,000 trials and checks every result. With invalid ciphertexts (random bytes, or one modified byte), no difference is detected in 18 of 18 campaigns, and both classes always have exactly the same cycle count, while the control is detected every time (|t| up to 1,877). With fresh valid ciphertexts, however, all nine implementations are flagged, with differences of 4 to 15 cycles and |t| >= 19,000 (or infinite, when both classes have zero variance). A matched control, in which both classes run the same code before the measured call, removes the difference for seven of the nine. An A/A test, in which both classes decapsulate the same bytes, still yields |t| = 12,864 for one implementation. Deterministic few-cycle differences can therefore come from the measurement harness alone: on a part with flash wait states, an instruction cache and prefetching, they can appear when the code around the measured call changes. We also show that per-trial correctness checks matter: they exposed a functional bug in PQM4's ML-KEM-1024 m4fstack (220 wrong shared secrets out of 49,830), which upstream had fixed shortly before. We report every deviation from the pre-registration, including a build error of our own, and publish data, binaries and code (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23921418).
papers.authors: Amadou Tidiane Anne

papers.title: Challenge Binding in FRESCO SPDZ2k: A Message-Level Case Study
papers.abstract: FRESCO's SPDZ2k suite derives its batched MAC-check coefficients from a setup-time public seed, making the stream predictable before opening shares are sent. We examine this implementation path at a pinned revision. A source-level derivation accounts for low-limb carries and high-bit corrections and shows that the value-share shifts $e=(r_j,-r_i)$ preserve the check residual while retaining the original MAC shares. A message-level harness executes this deviation against unmodified honest opening code. The recorded sum/product outputs violate a relation required for every possible input of the corrupt party, and the test framework records normal completion. The retained evidence includes two-, three-, and four-party executions with dummy preprocessing. The predictable-seed attack template appears in Rushing at SPDZ, and FRESCO's issue tracker recorded the per-check randomness requirement in 2018; our contribution is the SPDZ2k public-seed path, its explicit kernel witness, and the implementation evidence. We also give a conditional single-opening analysis and assess a four-file candidate mitigation that rejects seven recorded tampering scenarios while preserving four honest baselines. Audit tools and descriptive corpora provide context. The proof concerns the specified value-share deviation; unrestricted malicious behavior, production preprocessing, and a complete mitigation argument remain outside the established result.
papers.authors: Mingzhao Huang

papers.title: Quotienting Redundant Tables: Practical Master-Key Recovery from WBSLT White-Box AES
papers.abstract: Enlarging lookup-table addresses does not hide smaller selectors when the complete public table factors through a core with distinct rows and distinct columns. We demonstrate this condition in WBSLT, a white-box AES design presented at NDSS 2026 that reports resistance to several structural attacks. In the released general generator, the joint output of each group of four first-round TypeII tables has an exact 16 × 16 quotient of its 64 × 64 address space. Mapping its row and column classes to observed addresses recovers the original nibble partition of each AES input byte. Public tables implementing encoded XOR supply compatible output coordinates. Under the generator’s strictly linear input decoder, two 16-point restrictions of each keyed AES S-box then identify its embedded key byte; independent exhaustive checks confirm this property for all 256 byte keys. Using public tables and traces of chosen encoded inputs, we recover every key in 200 general instances that passed 200,000 reference AES block tests, after a median of 146 and at most 221 inputs. Separate 200-instance cohorts of the released optimized C source and its one-line functional repair also yield every key; only the repair passes the AES tests. An adjacent-round adaptation recovers 20/20 exact keys on a paired cohort without reconstructing the nibble partition. On those instances, our first-round route uses fewer live trace queries and less public table data. The exact quotient provides a concrete test for selector partitions that survive address enlargement.
papers.authors: Jiseok Bang, Seungkwang Lee

papers.title: Complete Addition Law for Twisted Edwards Curves
papers.abstract: We construct complete addition laws in extended coordinates for twisted Edwards curves \(E_{a,d}:ax^2+y^2=1+dx^2y^2\), where \(a,d\in K^\times\), \(a\ne d\), and \(\operatorname{char}K\ne2\). If \(t\in K\) makes \((t^2-a)(t^2-d)\) a nonzero nonsquare, the construction yields a \(K\)-complete formula valid for every pair of \(K\)-rational points. The proof describes the exceptional fibres through the difference morphism. Over finite fields of odd cardinality \(q>16\), such a coefficient exists for every nonsingular parameter pair, including the same-square-class cases with full rational two-torsion. We give full and mixed evaluation schedules. Full addition costs \(8M+D_c\) in split elementary models and \(10M\) or \(12M\), plus fixed-constant costs, in the same-square-class cases. Doubling costs \(4M+4S+\min(D_a,D_d)\), independently of coefficient selection. Here \(M\) denotes a general field multiplication, \(S\) a squaring, and \(D_c\) multiplication by a fixed \(c\in K\).
papers.authors: Reza Rezaeian Farashahi, Ruhallah Mirzaei Aliarabi, Peyman Shahbazi Dastjerdi

papers.title: Complete Addition on Short Weierstrass Curves with Point-Free Lines
papers.abstract: Let $E_{a,b}:Y^2Z=X^3+aXZ^2+bZ^3$ be a nonsingular short-Weierstrass curve over a field $K$ of characteristic different from $2$ and $3$. A nonvertical line $Y=mX+nZ$ has no $K$-rational point on the curve if and only if $x^3-m^2x^2+(a-2mn)x+b-n^2$ is rootless in $K$. We give coordinate changes and formulas for the corresponding $K$-complete Bosma--Lenstra addition law. An incidence count proves that such a line exists over every finite field in the stated characteristic. The classical five-multiplication cross-product identity reduces the output computation by one multiplication. For normalized horizontal, sloped, and depressed families, the full/full costs are $13M+5D+30A$, $13M+5D+33A$, and $13M+(2\text{ to }5)D+60A$, respectively. Horizontal normalization requires a nonzero cube parameter; the depressed family always contains a point-free line over $\mathbb{F}_p$ for $p\ge47$. The zero-line formula costs $11M+3D_a+2D_{3b}+28A$ and is complete over finite $K$ exactly when $\#E(K)$ is odd. We also give complete doubling formulas, account for changes of coordinates, and apply the five-product identity to published Hessian addition formulas.
papers.authors: Ruhallah Mirzaei Aliarabi, Reza Rezaeian Farashahi

papers.title: SenTrojan: Revealing Analog Hardware Trojan Attacks on Sensors
papers.abstract: Sensors bridge the physical and digital worlds, making their integrity critical to cyber-physical system security. Existing sensor attacks largely exploit unintended and sensor-specific physical vulnerabilities, limiting their generalizability and motivating a different threat model, i.e., whether an adversary can implant hidden attack surfaces into sensors before deployment. In this paper, we present SenTrojan, an analog hardware Trojan framework for sensors. SenTrojan embeds malicious functionality into analog signal circuitry commonly shared across diverse sensor architectures, and activates the hidden behavior through crafted external physical signals. Once activated, SenTrojan can induce sensor malfunctions ranging from permanent denial-of-service to static or dynamic spoofing. To achieve these effects under different architectural constraints, we introduce two complementary designs. The Logic-Rule-Driven (LRD) Trojan adds lightweight analog monitoring logic to detect trigger features such as frequency and amplitude, enabling reliable activation across various sensor types. The Physical-Effect-Driven (PED) Trojan targets sensors with exploitable native analog effects, e.g., nonlinearity and rectification, and realizes attacks with minimal component insertion. We evaluate SenTrojan on 14 sensors spanning 6 transduction principles and demonstrate its effectiveness across diverse real-world scenarios. Overall, SenTrojan achieves an average successful trigger rate above 95%, maintains over 97% similarity to benign behavior, incurs zero false-trigger rate for LRD designs, and introduces less than 5% average deviation in drift, noise floor, and response time. To our knowledge, this work is the first systematic study of analog sensor Trojans, broadening sensor security from unintended physical vulnerabilities to intentional supply-chain compromise.
papers.authors: Kun Wang, Ruochen Zhou, Wenjun Zhu, Shilin Xiao, Kai Wang, Chen Yan, Xiaoyu Ji, Wenyuan Xu

papers.title: Securing Web Agents with the Compile-Then-Execute Paradigm
papers.abstract: Web agents commonly follow the ReAct paradigm, selecting each action from runtime observations that inherently mix trusted and untrusted content. This design makes their control flow vulnerable to prompt injections embedded in webpages. We introduce Baya, a compile-then-execute web agent designed to prevent prompt-injection-driven control-flow hijacking by design. Before accessing the live website, Baya compiles the user's request into an executable Python program that calls a Trusted Website API. The planning model does not observe live website content; only the compiled program processes it. Untrusted data may determine program values or select among branches defined during compilation, but it cannot redefine the user task or cause the model to synthesize new website operations at runtime. The Trusted Website API gives the compiler a unified view of the website's action space, enabling ahead-of-time planning without the stepwise action discovery required by reactive agents. Our evaluation across 581 valid WebArena Verified tasks shows that Baya achieves 77.8% aggregate utility, outperforming browser-only ReAct (55.1%) and API-enabled ReAct (66.7%). On WASP, a security benchmark for web agents, Baya achieves 0% attack success rate, compared with 16.2% for API-enabled ReAct and 25.5% for browser-only ReAct.
papers.authors: Annabella Chow, Jinhao Zhu, Sylvie Venuto, Abdulaziz Alharbi, Basel Alomair, Raluca Popa, David Wagner, Julien Piet

papers.title: Towards Early Warning of Real-World Vulnerabilities: An Evidence-Aware Decoupled Method for CVSS Vector Prediction Based on Unstructured Disclosures
papers.abstract: Early assessment of Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) vectors from Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) can reduce the delay between initial public disclosure and official National Vulnerability Database (NVD) scoring. Existing predictors, trained mainly on standardized late-stage descriptions, degrade on noisy and incomplete pre-NVD reports. We introduce PARSE, a vulnerability-disclosure lifecycle model, and VPre, an early assessment framework built on two-level Evidence-Aware Decoupling. Decoupling Level I, Security-Evidence Screening, separates security-relevant evidence from noisy early reports at the report and sentence levels. Decoupling Level II, Evidence-Matched Routing, decouples the prediction task of the eight CVSS metrics into a scattered-evidence class and an explicit-evidence class based on validation-set measurements, matching each with a targeted predictor: large-language-model reasoning for the former, lightweight supervised classification for the latter. On the 851-report held-out test split of the 5,581-report VPre-Bench, VPre achieves a mean absolute error of 0.7239 -- 44.7% below the reproduced BERT-Small-NVD early-transfer baseline; paired timestamps across the full benchmark show an average 38-day lead before official scoring (observed range 21-60 days). Under the 38:1 PARSE-Triage noise setting, STDU's report-level screening reaches 0.98 precision, 1.00 recall, and 0.99 F1. Controlled ablations support the contributions of both decoupling levels.
papers.authors: Jianhong Ma, Wenhao Li, Xixing Li, Chenyu Yan, Haowen Chen

papers.title: Analysis of Local Open-Weight LLM Agents on Vulnerability-Reproduction Tasks
papers.abstract: Open-weight language models that fit on a single consumer GPU are becoming capable on a growing range of tasks, and they matter because they can run locally without sending the code to a hosted service. Vulnerability reproduction, turning a vulnerability description into an input that crashes the vulnerable build, is a natural target for them, since it is an automated analysis task closer to test generation than to code comprehension and it runs against a build that must be executed rather than read. In order to assess whether current models can perform it, we evaluate twelve configurations of local models, spanning three generations, two architectures and three quantization levels, on ten CyberGym vulnerability-reproduction tasks, three runs each under one harness, and release the full artefact. We show that every configuration, down to the 4B model, solves most of the six easier tasks, and configurations separate only on the remaining four. For the harder tasks, the 27B model is required. Quantization did not change what the models solved in any matched pair, but it changed how fast they got there, and the mixture of experts reached the same scores in less wall clock. We also examine the agent trajectories. Almost every run we examined, including those that fail, names the vulnerable function and states the correct hypothesis, and what separates a solved task from an unsolved one is whether that hypothesis becomes a working input.
papers.authors: Jorge García-Carrasco, Javier Sanchis, Álvaro Navarro, Alejandro Maté, Juan Trujillo

papers.title: Addition by Subtraction: Toward Mitigating Fragile Safety Alignment in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) undergo safety alignment to prevent harmful generations, yet they remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. Recent work reveals a deeper structural weakness: safety alignment can be highly sparse, such that pruning a small number of safety-critical neurons or ablating a single refusal direction can substantially undermine aligned behavior. In this work, we take the first steps toward strengthening safety alignment such that it is less dependent on sparse model components. We propose Addition by Subtraction, which gradually removes identified safety-critical neurons during finetuning and uses preference optimization to re-establish safety-aligned behavior through other parts of the model. Our results show that the resulting models are substantially more robust to pruning-based attacks. Remarkably, these benefits generalize beyond the white-box attacks motivating our design: Addition by Subtraction improves robustness against other sparsity-based interventions, including refusal-direction ablation, as well as a broad range of black-box jailbreak attacks. The finetuned models also exhibit improved truthfulness while largely preserving general capabilities. Comprehensive experiments across four models from three vendors demonstrate consistent improvements in safety robustness, reducing attack success rates by up to 90% for some attacks.
papers.authors: Hamid Dashtbani, Alexandra Dmitrienko

papers.title: Network Intrusion Forensic Detection System with Explainable Artificial Intelligence and Digital Chain of Custody
papers.abstract: Deploying an explainable intrusion detection model from a validated laboratory setting into a forensic workflow requires guarantees that benchmarks do not test: that the certified model is the exact artifact applied to a case, that heterogeneous evidence can be classified reliably, and that every step is verifiable. We present MODEXRE, a forensic pipeline that extends a previously validated synthetic-data-trained XGBoost classifier with SHAP explainability (arXiv:2607.00763) into a dual-mode architecture: a Laboratory mode, where models are trained and certified on public and synthetic data, and a Formal mode, where a frozen, hash-verified model performs inference on case evidence under a SHA-256 hash-chained chain of custody. Suricata alerts, CEF firewall logs and packet captures are normalized through OCSF. Four design decisions, each triggered by an observed failure, shaped the architecture: a timestamp leak that inflated Kitsune performance (F1-macro 0.984, 0.662 after correction); a feature-coverage gap that made the 78-feature reference model misclassify a real SSH alert; causal temporal flow aggregation, which raised Kitsune multiclass F1-macro from 0.394 to 0.932; and a certification defect, exposed only by a real packet capture, whereby the pipeline had always trained a binary classifier. After correction, the same capture went from 100% of events flagged as malicious to 87% classified as Normal, with the scanning host identified as Reconnaissance. The default four-class certified model reaches F1-macro = 0.9538 on CICIDS2017-derived evidence; the recertified 18-category model reaches 0.6214, reflecting the real multiclass task. Chain-of-custody verification, model integrity hashing and per-prediction SHAP explanations are reported as measured outcomes.
papers.authors: Jose Luis Vela Alonso, Carmen Pellicer

papers.title: A Constant-Rate Compiler for Continual Memory Leakage
papers.abstract: Leakage-resilient compilers transform any computation so that physical leakage from its implementation reveals nothing beyond its input-output behaviour. In this work, we investigate this question in the well-motivated continual memory leakage (CML) model, that captures a variety of relevant real-world side-channel attacks and subsumes several other well studied models in the leakage domain. In this model with two independently leaking components (at least two are necessary), all known general compilers tolerate only an inverse-polynomial leakage-rate. We give a compiler with constant leakage-rate, in the hybrid model with a simple inputless leak-free sampler as in Dziembowski and Faust (TCC 2012). It protects any deterministic computation on a fixed secret with public inputs and outputs, and comes with a transfer theorem: any security game in which the adversary has an oracle for the computation remains secure when every oracle call is replaced by a compiled evaluation that leaks continuously. Our compiler uses no computational assumption. Our main application is public-key encryption. Applied to the decryption of any IND-CCA2 secure PKE, the compiler gives IND-CCLA2 security, i.e. CCA2 security even when every decryption leaks, including after the challenge ciphertext, with the same public key, ciphertexts and encryption algorithm. Instantiating the base scheme gives such PKE from LWE and from LPN improving upon the previous best post-quantum constructions in this model, which supported only inverse-polynomial leakage-rate. We also obtain signatures, PRFs and MACs with constant leakage-rate via a natural generalization. Our key idea is to pack the entire configuration of a universal machine into one element of a large extension field, so that any computation keeps only a constant number of inner-product encodings in memory at any time, each for only a constant number of rounds. Our techniques are inspired by packing techniques in homomorphic encryption adapted to a completely different context. We are optimistic that our techniques will find other applications.
papers.authors: Shweta Agrawal, Anuja Modi, Rajeev Raghunath

papers.title: On the (Quantum) Communication Complexity of Secure MPC from a Random Oracle
papers.abstract: Information-theoretic MPC among $n$ parties with $t$ corruptions can securely evaluate a circuit $C$ with $O(|C| \cdot t/(n-t))$ online communication in the preprocessing model and $O(|C| \cdot t/(n-2t))$ communication in the honest majority setting. Damgård, Larsen and Nielsen (CRYPTO 2019) showed that both communication bounds are tight for inner products. Fully homomorphic encryption and other assumptions known to imply public-key cryptography beat both communication bounds, but the communication complexity with symmetric-key cryptography alone is less understood. For MPC with preprocessing, we prove that the same $Ω(|C| \cdot t/(n-t))$ lower bound holds in the random oracle model, so a random oracle cannot reduce the online communication. For honest majority MPC relative to a random oracle, we present an $Ω(|C|)$ communication lower bound that is matched by a new construction for degree-2 polynomials (including inner products) when $n = O(\log λ)$, beating the information-theoretic bound. We also study quantum MPC. First, we prove that information-theoretic protocols with quantum communication (and preprocessing) cannot reduce communication compared to their classical counterparts. Furthermore, we extend our lower bound for MPC with preprocessing to protocols with a quantum-accessible random oracle, but use only classical communication. In contrast, with both quantum communication and a post-quantum one-way function, we present a simple two-party protocol that evaluates the two-party instance of these circuits with $\mathrm{poly}(λ, \log |C|)$ communication, beating these lower bounds. Finally, such communication savings do not come for free. We prove that there exist circuits $C$ such that every blackbox protocol with $o(|C|)$ quantum communication must perform $Ω(|C|)$ cryptographic operations.
papers.authors: Alexander Hoover, Giuseppe Persiano, Kevin Yeo

papers.title: Information Loss Is All You Need: $TC^0$ Pseudorandomness from Worst-Case Lattices
papers.abstract: Can deterministic information loss yield post-quantum pseudorandomness with $TC^0$ evaluation? We show that deterministic rounding achieves this under quantum worst-case lattice hardness, with fixed polynomial parameters and no predetermined sample bound. We introduce learning with algebraic rounding (LAR), which applies an explicit integer rounding map to blocks of secret-dependent linear measurements and encodes the result in a lattice quotient. For one fixed family with polynomially bounded modulus and dimensions, deterministic labels on exactly uniform, secret-independent public matrices are computationally indistinguishable from independent uniform labels for every polynomial number of classical random examples. Our classical reduction from Gaussian LWE, combined with the quantum worst-case reduction to LWE, bases LAR on GapSVP and SIVP over general lattices at approximation factor $\widetilde{O}(q)$, where $q$ is the modulus. The proof uses source-independent affine transport: public affine maps sampled independently of the hidden errors transport the Gaussian error law close to uniform on the rounding map's zero-label fiber while preserving exactly uniform public matrices. For every fixed inverse-polynomial accuracy, we give a polynomial-time sampler for the same public parameter family. This yields the first post-quantum weak pseudorandom function with joint key-and-input evaluation in $TC^0$, secure against uniform quantum polynomial-time distinguishers given any polynomial number of classical uniform random examples. We also prove hardness of learning polynomial-size two-hidden-layer ReLU networks from noiseless uniform random examples, even for quantum polynomial-time improper learners.
papers.authors: Chen Qian

papers.title: Unique Signature Schemes with Tight Security in the Random Oracle Model via Hash-and-Subset-Sign
papers.abstract: Unique signatures are digital signature schemes, where each message has exactly one valid signature. The uniqueness property typically comes at a price: Most unique signature schemes are known to have a security loss at least linear in the number of signature queries when aiming for existential unforgeability under chosen message attacks (EUF-CMA) security, which was shown to be inherent in the standard model by Coron (EUROCRYPT 2002) for signature schemes where public keys are verifiable (i.e., where it can be efficiently checked whether a public key has unique signatures). The only known tight unique signature schemes in the literature that support verifiable public keys are variants of chain-based signatures (CRYPTO 2017, FC 2018, EUROCRYPT 2022), which achieve tight security in the random oracle model. To achieve constant security loss, however, these schemes require $\log q$ calls of the random oracle to sign and verify, where $q$ is an upper bound on the number of signatures generated using the scheme. In this work, we provide the first tight unique signature scheme with verifiable public keys which requires only a constant number (namely, six) random oracle queries to sign and verify. Specifically, we provide a general transformation akin to hash-and-sign which transforms a signature scheme with much weaker security (a variant of random unforgeability) into an EUF-CMA secure scheme. Signatures of our resulting scheme consist of at most 3 sub-signatures in parallel. Furthermore, we consider tightness in the multi-user setting, where the adversary may query signatures relative to many public keys, before deciding for which to forge. In this setting, we provide two constructions which achieve (1) a tight signature scheme, secure against semi-adaptive corruptions (i.e., where the adversary has to decide whether to corrupt a public key *before* making any signature queries relative to this key), and (2) a tight few-time signature scheme, secure against adaptive corruptions, where the scheme's setup is allowed to depend on an a-priori polynomial bound on the number of queries that the adversary has access to. These are the first unique signature schemes which are tightly secure in the multi-user model.
papers.authors: Thomas Attema, Lisa Kohl, Joost van der Laan

papers.title: Authenticated Outsourced Incrementally Verifiable MPC
papers.abstract: Many privacy-preserving applications such as iterative machine learning training require executing ongoing computations over a secret state for long periods of time. While MPC enables secure computation, long-lived secret state is vulnerable to adaptive corruptions, requiring periodic share refreshes and committee rotation. In many settings, it is desirable for external parties to be able to verify that these state updates and rotations are performed correctly, but existing approaches for such public verifiability incur high overhead as they require MPC nodes to generate expensive proofs over secret-shared data. We propose Authenticated Outsourced Incrementally Verifiable MPC (IV-MPC), a framework for efficient public verification of long-running MPC computation. Our approach decouples private proof computation (run by MPC nodes) from public tasks within the proof generation that can be delegated to a single external prover $P^*$. To realize this architecture, we introduce three main components: (1) a Private-opening Polynomial Commitment Scheme (PoPCS) that lets an incoming committee prove they received the correct state shares without revealing the underlying data; (2) an efficient distributed proof system based on the sumcheck protocol and compressed $\Sigma$-protocols to verify state updates; and (3) a stateless handover technique that anchors committee transfers to a fixed state commitment, preventing proof sizes from growing over time. Combined with an incrementally verifiable computation (IVC) proof run by the external prover $P^*$, IV-MPC enables external auditors to verify correctness of MPC computation at every round with verification time asymptotically independent of the total number of epochs.
papers.authors: Anders Dalskov, Anders Kallesøe, Hamidreza Khoshakhlagh

papers.title: Quantum Advantage has Few Complexity Implications
papers.abstract: We consider the complexity implications of proofs of quantumness and (quantum verifier) oblivious state preparation. We show that both of these objects can coexist with the easiness of nondeterministic computation. That is, we give evidence that proofs of quantumness can exist when $\mathsf{P} = \mathsf{NP}$ and that (quantum verifier) oblivious state preparation can exist when $\mathsf{BQP} = \mathsf{QCMA}$. In particular, we give a classical oracle relative to which (1) $\mathsf{P}^\mathcal{O} = \mathsf{NP}^\mathcal{O}$ (2) $\mathsf{BQP}^\mathcal{O} = \mathsf{PSPACE}^\mathcal{O}$ (3) Proofs of quantumness exist. In particular, there exists a language in $\mathsf{IP}^\mathcal{O} \subseteq \mathsf{BQP}^\mathcal{O}$ which is hard on average against $\mathsf{P}^\mathcal{O}/poly$. We give a unitary oracle such that (1) $\mathsf{BQP}^\mathcal{O} = \mathsf{QCMA}^\mathcal{O}$ (2) Quantum verifier oblivious state preparation exists. These oracle separations directly imply a number of related consequences. For example, our first result implies that proofs of quantumness cannot be used to construct classical or quantum cryptography with a relativizing proof. Our second result implies that quantum computation/classical communication oblivious transfer cannot be used to construct post-quantum one-way functions with a relativizing proof.
papers.authors: Eli Goldin, Alex Lombardi, Tomoyuki Morimae

papers.title: Beyond Standard Indifferentiability: Simulator Properties for Fiat-Shamir Security
papers.abstract: The Fiat-Shamir transform converts public-coin interactive arguments into non-interactive arguments (NARGs). Its security is typically analyzed in the random-oracle model, while implementations instantiate the random oracle with structured hash constructions. Standard indifferentiability is the natural abstraction for justifying this replacement. Chiesa and Orru (TCC ’25), however, showed that standard indifferentiability does not generally preserve the information and reset behavior needed by common Fiat-Shamir extraction arguments, and proposed stronger notions of indifferentiability to bridge this gap. We show that standard indifferentiability can nevertheless be retained as the oracle-replacement abstraction. For knowledge soundness, we give generic transfer theorems for three extraction interfaces: proof-only straight-line extraction follows from standard indifferentiability alone; transcript-dependent extraction additionally requires transcript reconstruction; and rewinding extraction requires reconstruction for rewinding, preserving simulator behavior across invocations with the same hidden randomness. Our results apply to worst-case polynomial-time extractors. Moreover, we show that the rewinding requirement is inherent: assuming discrete-logarithm hardness, we construct a perfectly indifferentiable construction and fixed prover admitting error-free rewinding extraction in the ideal world, while every polynomial-time construction-world extractor succeeds only with negligible probability. We instantiate our framework for tagged prefix-free Merkle-Damgard and a fixed-output permutation sponge. The former admits exact transcript and rewinding reconstruction, while the latter admits exact transcript reconstruction and rewinding reconstruction with negligible statistical error incurred only once, independently of the number of restarts. For zero knowledge, we give a semantic formulation where one persistent simulator jointly generates the proof and public-oracle interaction. Here, standard indifferentiability alone yields a generic transfer theorem, requiring neither reconstruction property and incurring only the indifferentiability error. Thus standard indifferentiability provides a common oracle-replacement abstraction for knowledge soundness and semantic zero knowledge, with extraction-specific requirements isolated as separate simulator properties.
papers.authors: Ashrujit Ghoshal, Sikhar Patranabis

papers.title: Proving the Wrong Program: Miscompilations as a Threat to zkVM Guarantees
papers.abstract: A zero-knowledge virtual machine (zkVM) lets an untrusted prover convince a verifier that a program, typically Rust compiled to RISC-V, ran correctly. The proof covers the compiled binary, so a miscompilation can make a correct zkVM produce a valid proof of a computation that differs from the developer's source. We present the first empirical study of miscompilation as a threat to zkVM guarantees, on the production zkVMs SP1 and Jolt. We assemble 88 known rustc and LLVM miscompilations with Rust reproducers, using an LLM agent to recover Rust triggers for 60 of 124 LLVM bugs reported only as LLVM IR. Many of the bugs carry over to zkVMs: 48 of the 88 make a guest commit a wrong output on SP1 and 46 on Jolt, including the same 15 rustc bugs on both. Most bugs that do not reproduce never reach the faulty code on the zkVM's target, e.g. because they need an instruction-set extension. Existing guest programs are rarely affected by accident. Across 13 guests of 10 popular SP1 projects, the buggy and the fixed compiler produce byte-identical binaries in 447 of the 552 guest-bug pairs that build, and the other 105 have the same code or agree on every input we ran. An attacker who contributes code to a guest, however, can trigger these bugs on purpose. For about $40 per project, an LLM agent found patches that look like ordinary optimisations, preserve the behaviour of the guest's source, and expose a known bug in 12 of 366 project-bug pairs, across 11 of 20 projects. In four cases the guest commits a wrong output, including an Ethereum client that rejects a valid block, and in the other eight it fails on a valid input. Reviewing or formally verifying the zkVM or the guest's source cannot catch such a patch, because both are correct. zkVM projects should treat their compiler as part of their trusted base and track the known bugs of their toolchain.
papers.authors: Hui Xuan Tan, Stefanos Chaliasos, Alastair F. Donaldson

papers.title: Leakage-Resilient Computation via Matrix Refreshing
papers.abstract: Leakage-resilient cryptography protects secrets against side-channel attacks, in which a physical implementation reveals partial information about its internal state. A fundamental primitive in this area is a leakage-resilient storage, which allows a secret to be stored in a way that remains secure even if an adversary learns some information about the storage's internal state. A popular approach represents a secret as the inner product of two $n$-bit vectors, called shares. The shares are stored and processed separately by two parts of the implementation, called the left and right parties. Because leakage accumulates over time, the shares must be refreshed repeatedly. We prove that a simple refresh, in which the left party multiplies its share by a uniform invertible matrix $M$ and the right party multiplies its share by $M^{-1}$, is secure under continual local leakage. After $T$ refreshes, each allowing at most $λ$ bits of leakage per party, the transcripts for two stored secrets are at statistical distance at most $C\cdot T\cdot 2^{6λ-n/9}$ for an absolute constant $C$. We also obtain a Boolean-circuit compiler with statistical privacy error at most $C\cdot S\cdot 2^{18λ-n/27}$ for $S$ operations and at most $λ$ bits of local leakage per party per operation. The guarantee covers repeated stateful evaluations with adaptively chosen public inputs, with $S$ counting all operations across invocations. Thus, for polynomial-size circuits, a constant leakage fraction is tolerated with share length depending only on the security parameter. We formalize the refreshing bound, the composition and compiler guarantees, and the expected-work bounds in Lean 4. Our results also provide efficient simulation: the leakage can be reproduced from the public inputs and the circuit outputs alone, with expected polynomial overhead.
papers.authors: Stefan Dziembowski, Sebastian Faust

papers.title: Perseus: A Full-Stack System for Homomorphic Model Inference
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have made it exceptionally convenient for users to send their private data to model providers, which process them in plaintext. Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) promises to secure remote inference by computing directly on encrypted data, yet it has remained prohibitively slow. The effort to make it practical remains fragmented, with most existing frameworks being closed-source, which keeps progress from compounding. We present Perseus, a free and open Python software library that supports the full stack of encrypted model inference, from the cryptographic backend and data packing, to encrypted nonlinearities and end-to-end model execution. Perseus ships with built-in novel optimizations, one at each level of the stack: in-kernel regeneration of key-switching keys at the (i) backend level, a complex variant of Cachemir packing at the (ii) data level, and a state-of-the-art bootstrap placer that is both packing- and magnitude-aware at the (iii) model level. Perseus achieves state-of-the-art latency across multiple models and modalities, within $3\%$ of the plaintext models' accuracy and perplexity. Remarkably, it is $3.96\times$ faster at single-token decoding than any other implementation on Llama-3-8B. We initiate, for the first time, a public speedrun on encrypted GPT-2, so that progress can compound.
papers.authors: Alessandro Zirilli, Davide Marincione, Evgenios M. Kornaropoulos, Giuseppe Ateniese, Emanuele Rodolà

papers.title: ScrambleMark: Zero-Query Watermark-Agnostic Black-Box Evasion of Modern Speech Watermarking
papers.abstract: Speech watermarking is becoming a key defense for digital copyright and content authentication. Existing attacks treat evasion as a removal problem: they erase the watermark, relying on detector access or on speech data that is hard to collect, such as paired clean-watermarked or clean target speaker speech. Commercial platforms are moving to close off these assumptions. TrustedAudio, for instance, restricts detection to authenticated users and denies meaningful detection feedback to unauthorized parties. Adversaries thus cannot tell whether a sample is watermarked or which watermark it carries, nor reliably remove it without degrading speech quality. In this work, we show that evading a speech watermark does not require erasing it: detection relies on the structural consistency of the embedded pattern, and disrupting this consistency is enough to defeat it. Building on this observation, we identify harmonic structure as an effective attack surface, as perturbing it breaks watermark consistency while preserving perceptual quality. We therefore propose ScrambleMark, a zero-query, watermark-agnostic, black-box attack that evades detection through harmonic scrambling. ScrambleMark combines a deterministic engine for discovering transferable harmonic perturbations with a generative model that learns randomized scrambling patterns, avoiding reliance on fixed attack rules. Across three commercial platforms (Google SynthID, Resemble AI, and TrustedAudio), ScrambleMark is the only attack to both evade detection and keep speech natural, achieving nearly 97% evasion and a 4.2/5 human rating, far above the 1.1 to 1.7 of prior attacks. Beyond evasion, ScrambleMark withstands adaptive recovery designed to reverse it, evidence that structural evasion is hard to mitigate in practice.
papers.authors: Binhao Ma, Weikang Ding, Hanqing Guo, Wenwei Zhao, Xiaowen Li, Leah Ding, Zhuo Lu, Rui Duan

papers.title: Revisiting Accountability in Accountable Tracing Signatures
papers.abstract: Accountable tracing signatures (ATS), introduced by Kohlweiss and Miers (PoPETs 2015), classify each group member (user) as either traceable or non-traceable. A traceable user corresponds to one in conventional group signature schemes whose identity can be revealed by the opener from a signature, whereas a non-traceable user cannot be identified from any signature they produce. The opener, who issues a witness, can certify a user's status via the Account algorithm. In this paper, we formalize accountability soundness, which ensures that no two witnesses can simultaneously certify a user as both traceable and non-traceable. We show that the Kohlweiss-Miers ATS scheme admits conflicting witnesses that violate this property. Since accountability is a fundamental aspect of ATS, as reflected in its name, such conflicting witnesses undermine the intended guarantees of the primitive. To address this issue, we propose a patched version of the Kohlweiss-Miers ATS scheme that provides accountability soundness. We also discuss the applicability of our attack to the lattice-based ATS scheme (Ling et al., CT-RSA 2019) and the isogeny-based ATS scheme (Shaw-Dutta, Indocrypt 2021), together with preliminary investigations of possible countermeasures. We emphasize that all our attacks fall outside the original security models.
papers.authors: Rei Naito, Kyoichi Asano, Keita Emura

papers.title: Fast Provable Algorithms for Approximate CVP and Exact SVP on Random \(q\)-ary Lattices
papers.abstract: We give provable randomized algorithms for the $\gamma$-approximate Closest Vector Problem ($\gamma$-CVP) with $\gamma=5/3$ and the exact Shortest Vector Problem (SVP) in the Euclidean norm on random $q$-ary lattices. These lattices consist of the integer vectors mapped to zero modulo $q$ by a uniformly random matrix $\mathbf{H}\in(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})^{m\times n}$, for any integer $q\ge2$. For input density $\delta=m\log_2q/n$ with $0\le\delta\le1$, the running times are $2^{0.2668n+o(n)}$ for $5/3$-CVP and $2^{0.2741n+o(n)}$ for exact SVP, with polynomial input-length factors suppressed. For $1<\delta\le3/2$, the respective bounds are $2^{0.56n+o(n)}$ and $2^{0.468n+o(n)}$. For all but a negligible fraction of matrices, both algorithms succeed with overwhelming probability over their internal randomness. Notably, for $0\le\delta\le1$, our provable bounds fall below even the $2^{0.2925n+o(n)}$ heuristic estimate for classical lattice sieving. As a cryptographic application, we prove that signatures in the original construction of Gentry, Peikert, and Vaikuntanathan (GPV) can be forged in time $2^{0.0534n+o(n)}$ for $n\ge5m\log_2q$. For a $128$-bit security target, a leading-term estimate gives $n\approx2400$ and a public key of roughly $144$ kB, indicating a substantial storage burden.
papers.authors: Jiseung Kim, Junhyuk Kwon, Changmin Lee, JeongHwan Lee

papers.title: Averaging Collusion Breaks Traceability in Personalized Neural Audio Watermarking
papers.abstract: Personalized neural audio watermarking systems embed user-specific payloads into audio to trace the user associated with a leaked or misused copy. Existing evaluations mainly assume access to a single personalized copy, but real-world distribution may expose multiple copies of the same recording. We find that simple sample-wise averaging breaks traceability: averaging only two copies produces tracing-failure rates of 87.7-99.7% across the five systems while largely preserving audio quality. Decoder outputs show distinct responses to coalition payload composition across systems, with high majority agreement in TimbreWM but substantially lower agreement in WMCodec. In a more sophisticated payload-aware setting, mixture weighting can further steer the decoder toward a selected nonmember, achieving a target success rate of 92.3% in TimbreWM. Preliminary confidence screening rejects many collusion-induced assignments while retaining most valid single-copy outputs. Code and results are available at https://github.com/Silwan5z/neural-audio-watermark-collusion-attack. This work highlights multi-copy traceability as an additional evaluation dimension for personalized neural audio watermarking alongside conventional single-copy robustness.
papers.authors: Yangming Liu, Haiyun Li, Dongfu Song, Ziang Xu, Jiehui Luo, Yining Zhang, Zhiyong Wu

papers.title: Gaussian Difference Dynamics: Breaking the $2^{n/2}$ Barrier for the Shortest Vector Problem and Discrete Gaussian Sampling
papers.abstract: We give classical randomized algorithms in a word RAM model that break the $2^{n/2}$ barrier for both discrete Gaussian sampling (DGS) and the Shortest Vector Problem (SVP). For every fixed $α>1$, shifted DGS on arbitrary lattices at width $σ\geαη_{1/2}(L)$ takes $$ (3/2)^{n/2+o(n)}\text{ time} \qquad\text{and}\qquad (4/3)^{n/2+o(n)}\text{ space}. $$ These bounds match the Becker--Ducas--Gama--Laarhoven (BDGL) heuristic sieving exponents. At widths at least $3η_{1/2}(L)/2$, the same total cost suffices for an entire batch of $\lfloor(4/3)^{n/2}\rfloor$ samples jointly close to independent target Gaussians. For SVP on arbitrary lattices, our algorithm returns a shortest nonzero vector with high probability in $$ 2^{0.4130n+o(n)}\text{ time} \qquad\text{and}\qquad 2^{0.3138n+o(n)}\text{ space}. $$ As a corollary, we obtain centered DGS at every width with the same exponents, answering a question of Stephens-Davidowitz (SODA 2016). We introduce Gaussian difference dynamics (GDD), a framework for tracking expected counts and pairwise clustering of vectors through repeated differencing. A closed recursion for the first two counting moments controls these quantities relative to a Gaussian reference, without requiring independence within intermediate lists. Accurate moment bounds let us extract a Gaussian sample by weighted selection, while the weaker bounds needed to establish a shortest vector representation allow us to retain more differences. We perform these transitions on thin spherical shells, where the Gaussian rejection weights can be renormalized at subexponential cost. For batch sampling, we combine this geometry with the double rejection technique of Doulgerakis and Laarhoven to control the joint distribution of outputs while reusing vectors.
papers.authors: Yiming Gao, Xuyuan Han, Honggang Hu

papers.title: VerfGraph: Efficient Zero-Knowledge Verifiable Graph Query Evaluation System
papers.abstract: Graph databases are often used to manage relationship-rich data, whose graph structure and attributes may be sensitive. In many applications, a database owner or a service provider evaluates queries over a private graph for a client. Because the graph cannot be fully disclosed and independently re-executing the query may be impractical, the client cannot directly verify the returned result. This creates a need for verifiable graph query evaluation that preserves data confidentiality. We present VerfGraph, a zero-knowledge system for verifiable graph query evaluation, which enables a client to verify that the query result was correctly computed over a committed graph data, without revealing private graph records or intermediate query values beyond the public inputs and what is implied by the query result. Building on the expansion-centric model introduced by the state-of-the-art zero-knowledge verifiable graph query evaluation system ZKGraph (ICDE'26), VerfGraph achieves more efficient and expressive zero-knowledge verifiable graph query evaluation by advancing design in two key ways. First, we propose novel operator-proof methods for core expansion and shortest-path operations that reduce costly sorting and comparison checks and eliminate edge canonicalization for bidirectional expansion. Furthermore, we introduce correctness proofs for count and weighted shortest-path operators, broadening the class of graph queries that can be verified. We evaluate VerfGraph using the LDBC Social Network Benchmark. Compared with ZKGraph on complex IC queries, VerfGraph achieves $33.9\times$-$59.7\times$ speedups in proof generation and reduces peak prover memory by factors of $4.5\times$-$6.6\times$, while maintaining millisecond-level verification and producing sub-MB proofs.
papers.authors: Tianyi Ma, Yuncong Zhang, Yuanzhuo Yu, Boshi Yuan, Shi-Feng Sun

papers.title: Distill and Conquer: Cryptanalytic Extraction of Local Rules in the Hard-Label Setting
papers.abstract: Cryptanalytic extraction can expose proprietary neural network parameters, but unknown architectures and large parameter counts complicate recovery under hard-label access. Local class-pair rules offer a narrower target by making class-switching conditions explicit and predicting nearby labels under a specified sampling law. Distillation methods mainly return substitute models rather than explicit rules whose local agreement has been tested against the victim. We propose Distill–Probe–Extract to produce such rules without first identifying the victim architecture. Verified boundary events guide student training, and student gradients propose directions at boundary anchors refined through victim queries. Fresh hard-label queries then test the proposed rules, retaining validation inputs and victim labels for each accepted rule. On a digits multilayer perceptron and pooling convolutional networks, fixed-candidate comparisons isolate the savings from replacing victim-normal estimation with student gradients. For the multilayer perceptron, median recorded online cost decreases from 246 to 118 queries per attempt after student preparation. With preparation and failures counted, full Fashion-MNIST sessions produce 2.03–2.23 times Direct's accepted-rule count under the original validation gate at 320,000-call caps. At 320,000 calls, a separate student-level test on trained Blended watermarks yields 99.99% trigger agreement and 91.79% clean agreement, with all three seeds passing joint verification.
papers.authors: Chun Li, Di Li, Liping Zhuang, Siqi Zhu, Yufeng Tang, Xingfu Yan, Zheng Gong

papers.title: Construction and Classification of Minimum-Latency 5-Bit APN S-Boxes
papers.abstract: S-boxes serve as essential nonlinear building blocks in symmetric-key cryptography, where their cryptographic properties and hardware implementation costs jointly dictate the security and efficiency of lightweight primitives. This paper studies the construction and classification of minimum-latency 5-bit APN (Almost Perfect Nonlinear) permutations under a prescribed gate-delay model, using exact minimum latencies of Boolean component functions. Under the fixed gate-delay model of the NanGate 45nm standard cell library, we partition the search space into input-variable permutation (IP) equivalence classes to establish a comprehensive minimum-latency database covering all 5-input balanced nonlinear Boolean functions. This database delivers exact minimum latencies and gate-level implementations for all equivalence classes up to a latency of 150ps, while guaranteeing strict lower bounds on latency for classes exceeding that threshold, combining property filtering with circuit synthesis. We search the five affine equivalence classes of 5-bit APN permutations. For each affine transformation of the input, we use exact component-function latencies to select components with linearly independent masks and choose their polarities, obtaining S-box circuits without repeating gate-level synthesis for each candidate. Exhaustive search with latency-preserving input-variable permutation reduction establishes a minimum latency of 126.745ps over all 5-bit APN permutations under the prescribed gate-delay model, with explicit constructions attaining this minimum in every class.The classification results give the optimized latency distributions and numbers of optimal IP classes of input-affine transformations within each affine class. Comparisons with selected 5-bit S-box implementations under the same model show simultaneous reductions in some cases: latency decreases by $10.20\%$--$29.18\%$ and normalized gate area by $5.37\%$--$27.69\%$, while preserving the original S-box mappings.
papers.authors: Yaqi Qu, Xiutao Feng, Ruanyiyang Sun

papers.title: Polynomial Batch Accumulators for Onboarding-Dominant Zero-Knowledge Membership Proofs
papers.abstract: Zero-knowledge membership accumulators are conventionally tailored for slowly growing sets with frequent proof generation, creating severe efficiency bottlenecks for modern compliance architectures. Governance-driven applications like FATF customer due diligence, eIDAS 2.0 wallet issuance, and MiCA VASP authorization invert this structure. In this regime, rosters are ingested at an enterprise scale, while proofs are requested selectively. To resolve this mismatch, we introduce Polynomial Equation Batching (PEB), a membership accumulator for onboarding heavy workloads. PEB represents up to 128 members per batch as a characteristic polynomial and hashes its coefficients via Poseidon, seamlessly scaling to arbitrarily large populations through parallel batching. We present two variants: PEB-A, which maps member secrets directly to polynomial roots for maximum performance, and PEB-B, which hashes secrets in-circuit for hardened security. Implemented in Noir and Barretenberg on BN254, and evaluated for up to 1,048,576 members, PEB provides significant performance improvements. Compared to incremental Merkle trees, PEB-A achieves up to a 149.07x mean speedup in per-user initialization while incurring a modest 33.87% proof-generation overhead. Additionally, against static Merkle trees, PEB-A delivers a 15.71x speedup during setup. By shifting off-circuit overhead from hash evaluations to field multiplications, PEB provides a highly efficient, scalable solution for real-world zero-knowledge compliance systems.
papers.authors: Samanta Karmaker, Sampad Sikder, Md Ariful Islam, Md Sadek Ferdous

papers.title: Extracting System Prompt of LLM Services in Complex (Agentic) Settings: Hierarchical Optimization and Reliable Evaluation Metrics
papers.abstract: System prompt is a critical intellectual property of large language model (LLM) services. To analyze its leakage, prompt extraction attacks have been extensively studied. However, we validate that existing attacks substantially degrade on recent LLM services, whose complexity has evolved in both the prompt itself and system-level constraints. Specifically, (1) system prompts become longer and more structured to contain pre-defined tool schemas, execution logic, safety guardrails, etc., and (2) only the final post-processed outputs (e.g., agent's actions) but not the raw textual response can be observed. In this paper, we address the above increased complexity by proposing Extraction with Hierarchical Optimization (ExtraHerO), which (1) decomposes the prompt extraction into a hierarchical reconstruction process with a pre-defined structural prompt template, and (2) iteratively updates the adversarial query with guidance of feedback-template differences to observe diverse outputs. In particular, we monitor the information gain of attack optimization to early stop or reset it for a good trade-off between effectiveness and efficiency. We also find that existing evaluation metrics for prompt fidelity can be misleading because they do not account for structural information. Therefore, we rely on global textual similarity and prioritize structural keywords. Moreover, we introduce a system-level metric, adversarial utility, to measure the help of prompt extraction for real-world downstream attacks. Experimental results demonstrate the consistent superiority of ExtraHerO, with average improvements of 12.5\% (fidelity), 2.3\% (functionality), and 6.0\% (adversarial utility) on chatbots, and 12.2\%, 34.3\%, and 30.5\% on agents.
papers.authors: Shuaidong Li, Xinshan Yang, Yufei Chen, Chenhao Lin, Chao Shen, Zhengyu Zhao

papers.title: VeriSpoof: Beyond Real or Fake with One Audio LLM
papers.abstract: A speech deepfake detector estimates whether a recording is synthetic, but a forensic analyst also asks which system produced it, whether recordings share a source, and what evidence supports each conclusion. We present VeriSpoof, an audio language model that unifies five tasks with shared weights: deepfake detection, generator attribution (generator, acoustic model and vocoder), recording-condition analysis, synthesized-span localisation, and source verification. Each decision is supported by grounded rationales whose statements can be independently verified. Answers are scored by sentence likelihood, allowing detection and source verification to be thresholded without separate heads. Rationale statements can be checked against waveform measurements, span labels, or generator metadata. Counterfactual examples train decisions to follow the stated evidence. Across the 14 Speech-DF-Arena test sets, VeriSpoof-Plus achieves 2.14% pooled EER, ranking third of 28 systems and first among open-weight systems. VeriSpoof-Base, trained only on official training splits of eight corpora, achieves 4.43% EER, less than half that of the next open-weight detector. With the same weights, VeriSpoof-Plus verifies whether recordings from generators unseen in training share a source at 6.2% EER. Controlled studies show that the audio representation governs detection, the LLM governs recording comparison, and source supervision is necessary for neural-codec fakes. Statement-checkable rationales catch partial fakes missed by one-step answers (99.6% vs. 78.4% on PartialEdit) and determine decisions under edits unseen in training (99.5%). Training updates only 29.7M of 2.85B parameters, fitting a single 24 GB GPU with gradient checkpointing. We release both models, inference code, a demo, and VeriSpoof-Bench, the evaluation suite covering these questions.
papers.authors: Yang Xiao, Ting Dang

papers.title: Voluntary Servitude: Weaponized Safety Warning Mechanisms for Controlling AI Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly act on information retrieved from public sources they treat as credible, which turns a manipulated recommendation into a transaction, a dependency, or a decision with physical consequences. The security literature models this threat as instruction injection, in which an adversary writes a command into retrieved content and deployed defenses learn to recognize command syntax. We show that an attacker can instead steer an agent through the agent's own harm-avoidance. A single fabricated hazard, written as an ordinary review, leads the agent to disqualify the legitimate options and select the attacker's target by its own reasoning, with no command for a detector to recognize. We call this voluntary servitude. These payloads steer agents about as often as instruction injection (60.4% vs. 66.0%), and deployed injection detectors score them as benign, so behind a filter they are 1.7-4.4x more effective. We measure this at the generation stage across six models and ten consumer-service domains, for three attack families, and show that it transfers to production browser agents, outperforming instruction injection, and to a retrieval pipeline (1.0-57.0% end-to-end success, depending on the retriever). We then show that a corroboration requirement added to the agent's instructions removes roughly 95% of the exposure against a non-adaptive attacker without retraining. With the requirement in place, the agent still reads the planted hazard and no longer acts on it.
papers.authors: Ilan Zendel, Matan Levy, Stav Cohen, Avi Mendelson, Amit LeVi

papers.title: CloakFEM: Agentic FEM Code Generation for Red-Teaming Computational Resource Exhaustion
papers.abstract: Finite element method (FEM) solvers are foundational to scientific and engineering simulation, yet their susceptibility to \emph{efficiency attacks} remains largely unexplored. An adversary can craft syntactically valid and runnable FEM programs that complete successfully while forcing excessive computational work, enabling computational denial-of-service (DoS) attacks. Finding such inputs is challenging because FEM programs occupy a vast, structured space constrained by numerical, geometric, and constitutive requirements. We introduce CloakFEM, a domain-guided LLM-agent framework for automatically generating runnable adversarial FEM programs that amplify solver computation. CloakFEM combines LLM-guided search with an FEM-specific intermediate representation and a deterministic validity gate that enforces runnable constraints. Across three FEM stacks, 17 problem classes, and 1,068 seeds, CloakFEM discovers adversarial inputs that substantially amplify solver work while remaining valid and solvable. In the most extreme case, solver iterations increase from 43 to 247,367, a \(5{,}752.72\times\) amplification. CloakFEM outperforms five generic black-box baselines and retains an advantage over evolutionary search under a controlled bounded action space. Cross-solver analysis further reveals both problem-intrinsic and solver-specific sources of vulnerability. Our results uncover an underexplored efficiency-attack surface in FEM solvers and show that runnable FEM programs can serve as adversarial inputs.
papers.authors: Li Zheng, Simin Chen

papers.title: Permitted but Unauthorized: Affordance-Induced Delegated-Scope Violations in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems place several agents on shared infrastructure, where each agent holds permissions far broader than the task it is delegated -- so every agent is routinely permitted to act on a peer's resources it was never assigned. We ask: under competitive pressure, what determines whether an agent crosses from its delegated scope into a peer's resources, and can such crossings be enforced away? We study this across eight LLMs in two simulated environments -- a CI/CD release pipeline and a security-operations incident queue -- using a deterministic, no-model-in-the-loop detector over hash-chained, replay-verified logs. In a controlled 2x2x2 factorial over competitive incentive, candidate visibility, and payoff information (three models, n=52 per cell), we find that action representation, not permission, governs the behavior: no agent crosses when the peer action is unlisted, whereas listing it under competitive pressure with a stated payoff raises crossings sharply -- up to 52 of 52 episodes for Claude Sonnet 4.5. We also observe a model-dependent split: two newer models (Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5) refuse the identical attack in 0 of 100 episodes, where prior-generation models cross in 9 of 10. We then evaluate two defenses -- a deterministic reference monitor and a model-based pre-execution judge -- both block every crossing and, when the task is winnable, cut avoidable peer deadline misses from 15/40 and 14/40 to at most 1/40. But scope enforcement is not harm prevention: an agent can still set a peer back through an authorized action on its own resources -- misreporting its incident's severity -- which neither defense detects. Our results establish action representation, not permission alone, as a controllable driver of inter-agent scope violations, and show that enforcing delegated scope is distinct from preventing harm, motivating effect-aware authorization.
papers.authors: Shravya Kanchi

papers.title: Gather or Act? Belief-Level Counterfactual Labels for Deadline-Aware Incident Response in Cyber-Physical Systems
papers.abstract: When an industrial control system misbehaves, the defender often must choose between acting now on the most likely cause and first gathering evidence that separates two look-alike causes, while the process drifts toward a shutdown. Learning or evaluating such decisions requires the cost of every candidate action from the same situation, which no public cyber-physical security dataset provides. We present TE-GvA, a counterfactual decision dataset for fault-driven incident response on the revised Tennessee Eastman process, with 9,908 decision points from 1,990 simulated incidents, each with 4 to 35 candidate actions labelled by branched rollouts with common random numbers. Labels computed under the true hidden cause (hindsight labels) make gathering the best choice in only 1.1-1.3% of decisions. For the dominant look-alike pair, a failed network link versus a frozen I/O module, we add pair-conditioned belief labels from twin episodes that replay the defender's history under the other cause, weighted by the exact posterior. With them, gathering is best in 15.5% of ambiguous natural decisions and in 33.1% of ambiguous stress decisions without a backup channel. When the posterior is correct and the twin is faithful, belief labels have the same regression target as hindsight labels and lower variance. In a pre-specified, single-look test evaluation, a gradient-boosted rule trained on belief labels has 11% lower regret on the stress set than the same rule trained on hindsight labels, and 27% lower regret on ambiguous stress decisions without a backup channel, which remains significant after Holm correction. With a backup channel and in the natural distribution, the two label sets perform about the same. Soft labels tolerate moderate posterior errors, whereas hard labels that commit to one cause do worse than hindsight labels.
papers.authors: Ali Mohammadi Ruzbahani

papers.title: Verifiable Data on Bitcoin: FlatMerkle Commitments, Refutable Proofs, and FlatChecks
papers.abstract: We give a method to publish data on Bitcoin and to verify properties of that data on Bitcoin itself, against a publisher who may lie. The data is a FlatMerkle file – a structured byte string whose ordinary SHA-256 supports logarithmic inclusion proofs and logarithmic proofs of malformation – placed in a transaction's annex or, at four times the cost but relayable by Bitcoin Core, in an output. We show that the publisher's ordinary Taproot signature, with a suitably chosen signature-hash type, binds the publisher to the published data in a form that a dispute can authenticate with a single SHA-256 compression plus the signature check, or with three compressions when no annex is used. Claims about the data, and claims about such claims, are published as proof messages in two formats: a plain encoding, refuted by revealing it whole, and a traced encoding that stores the verifier's output after each level, so that any false message is refuted by revealing at most five of its elements. The format, chosen by a cost model that weighs challenge bytes against published bytes, is fixed by public context so that no message can be read in two formats; chains of claims about claims settle at four logical elements. A dispute thus reduces to a few dozen SHA-256 compressions and one Schnorr verification per commitment – too large for Bitcoin Script, but small enough to adjudicate with an interactive bisection game, a chunked script in the manner of BitVM2, or a garbled circuit. The same technique verifies any locally refutable verifier, one whose every rejection is witnessed by a single check over a few words of a canonical trace. In a FlatCheck, the prover publishes only the proof; the trace, the verifier's intermediate values, is published only if a challenger asks for it, and the dispute then examines the single check he names. When the verifier splits into groups that each read a few parts of the proof, a challenge forces the trace of one group only. We give two examples: a toy L2 of signed transfers, whose 512-transfer batches cost 12,200 vbytes to claim, and a Bitcoin header-chain light client verified on Bitcoin itself, which claims a retarget period of 2,016 headers in 45,200 vbytes; a dispute over a local check costs about 37,500 and 49,200 vbytes, and one over a malformed trace about 77,100 and 99,800, independently of the number of groups. Verifying STARK proofs is another application. We also remove FlatMerkle's restriction to power-of-two sizes without padding.
papers.authors: Sergio Demian Lerner

papers.title: Hidden Curves and Short Duals: Cubic Jets, Dual Leaks, and the Limits of Masked-Code Encryption
papers.abstract: Masked-code encryption hides a decodable code behind a transformation meant to make it look random. We study the two masks proposed as compact alternatives to Goppa codes---Wang's RLCE and the $(U\,|\,U{+}V)$ construction of UVW-KEM---over the decodable hidden codes they have been or could be applied to, and find that, among the families examined, none yields a compact trapdoor. Over Reed--Solomon and algebraic-geometry codes the mask hides a \emph{curve}, and curves are not hidden from jets. We explain the October 2026 key recovery of UVW-KEM (NGCC) and show it is not specific to UVW: for \emph{hidden-pairing codes} we bound from below the dependencies among order-$r$ jets of degree-$d$ forms at the columns of any shortening---for cubics $2k_1-k_2-k_l+2$ (UVW) and $2(n{-}k)-w-k_l+2$ (RLCE), attained in every regime tested, and we prove that the structured part of the dependency space carries the pairing and the secret ratios in closed form. Every proposed UVW parameter set has the predicted cubic deficiency (key recovery has been demonstrated at UVW-KEM-128). RLCE's long-key regime $w\ge n-k$, out of reach of the square-code attack for eight years, falls at degree three: on a full-size Level-1 parameter set we recover an equivalent key from the public key alone and decrypt fresh ciphertexts. HermitianRLCE is distinguished the same way. A forcing law, a master count and a redundancy law make the \emph{jet degree} an invariant of hidden-pairing codes: within that model, each unit of structural depth costs a unit of redundancy. Without a curve the masks fail differently: both \emph{preserve the dual} of the hidden code, at most doubling the weight of every dual word. polarRLCE at rate $\le2/3$ leaks dual words found in $47$--$94$ bits; at higher rates no certified decoding radius supports $143$-bit security up to length $16384$, and at $32768$ the key is $58$\,MiB, $234\times$ Classic McEliece. LDPC codes leak their sparse checks, MDPC codes are better left unmasked, and UVW carries a matched-pair subspace for every hidden code. Reed--Muller-heavy codes under RLCE resist every attack here at $4$\,MiB keys, but only if a decoder at $3.4\times$ the bounded-distance radius exists.
papers.authors: Yongge Wang

papers.title: Poly Versus Polyval
papers.abstract: We revisit the basic construction of polynomial evaluation based hash function, which we call Poly, over binary extension fields $GF(2^n)$, where $n=64k$ and $k\geq 2$. Unlike GHASH, the NIST standard polynomial evaluation based hash function for $n=128$, Poly does not perform the unnecessary bit reversals of each $n$-bit block, and consequently is faster than GHASH. Further, Poly differs from Polyval, -- a faster alternative to GHASH, -- in that Poly performs usual reduction, while Polyval performs Montgomery reduction. We identify suitable choices of the field representing irreducible polynomials which make usual and Montgomery reductions efficient. We provide detailed algorithms, and associated proofs of correctness for both kinds of reductions. Based on the algorithms, we report carefully optimised assembly implementation of both Poly and Polyval for $n=128,256$ and $512$. Our theoretical analysis and experimental timing results show that for $n=128$, Polyval is faster than Poly, while for $n=256$ and $512$ (as well as for higher values of $n$), Poly is faster than Polyval. The cases $n=128$ and $n=256$ are of current relevance due to the ongoing NIST process for developing cryptographic accordions.
papers.authors: Kaushik Nath, Palash Sarkar
